notes.content:
Design Distributed Cache

With Advanced Key-Value Store Follow-Ups

![Design Distributed Cache — source diagram](/diagrams/t-zc2e3vmnwi65-kix-gysiwqpwbftx.png)

Scope: cache accelerates read access; the database remains the durable owner in our baseline.

> Learning approach: Start with one cache node. Then solve misses, writes, expiration, scaling, replication and failures. Add complex choices only when a requirement makes them necessary.

### Interview roadmap

| Phase | What to explain | Typical follow-up |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 • Basic | Requirements → cache-aside → read/write flows | Why is the cache not the source of truth? |
| 2 • Correctness | TTL, invalidation, evictions, concurrency | What happens when a record changes? |
| 3 • Distributed | Hashing, virtual nodes, replication | What happens when a node joins or dies? |
| 4 • Scale & reliability | Stampede, hot keys, failover, multi-region | How does it handle one viral key? |
| 5 • Interview finish | Trade-offs, SLOs, failures, cross-questions | Defend decisions under new constraints |

## 1. Problem Statement and Interview Framing

Design a shared in-memory cache used by many application servers to reduce response time and database load. The cache stores frequently used key-value data and must continue working as traffic and node count grow.

- Core actions: GET(key), SET(key, value, TTL), DELETE(key).

- Baseline: cache-aside with a durable primary database; one region at first.

- Important behavior: a cache miss retrieves from DB, fills cache and returns the value.

- Do not assume: strict consistency, multi-region writes, or durable cache storage unless asked.

> Interview scope: First show one-node cache-aside correctly. Only then add sharding, replication, failover and hot-key defenses.

## 2. Clarifying Questions and Functional Requirements

### Questions to ask before drawing

- What data? User profiles, product details, sessions, counters or financial balances? Consistency needs change by data type.

- Operations? GET/SET/DELETE only, or MGET, compare-and-set, atomic increment and bulk invalidation?

- Source of truth? Is there a database behind the cache, or must the cache itself survive data loss?

- Staleness allowed? Can users see data that is 1–5 seconds old, or must reads reflect the newest write?

- TTL and memory? How long can entries live, how big are values, and what happens when memory fills?

- Traffic? Average/peak reads and writes; are a few keys extremely hot?

- Availability? What if a node or whole cache cluster fails?

| Function | Initial assumption | Interview extension |
| --- | --- | --- |
| GET / SET / DELETE | String key → bytes/value | MGET, CAS, INCR |
| TTL | Optional per key | Sliding TTL, refresh-ahead |
| Miss handling | Read source DB and cache | Negative cache, coalescing |
| Invalidation | Explicit delete on DB write | Version/CDC events |
| Scale | Hash partition by key | Virtual nodes, autoscaling |
| Availability | Fallback to DB on failure | Replicas/failover, stale read |

## 3. Non-Functional Requirements and Core Invariants

| Property | Example interview target | Consequence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Read latency | Cache hit p95 under ~10 ms regionally | Memory + few network hops |
| Availability | 99.9%+ cache tier as illustrative | Replica / fallbacks |
| Consistency | Eventual for ordinary product data | TTL + invalidation |
| Capacity | Add nodes without rewriting app | Partition and rebalance |
| Fault isolation | One key/node cannot stall all traffic | Hot-key and overload controls |
| Memory cost | Store working set, not whole database | Eviction + selective admission |

> Core invariants  
> 
> Clear Ownership: Every cache key has one clearly defined owner.
> 
> Bounded Staleness: Cached data must not remain outdated beyond an acceptable limit.
> 
> Durable Storage: The authoritative database protects permanent data.
> 
> Failure Safety: Node failures must not cause incorrect or unnoticed writes.
> 
> Database Protection: Cache overload or failure must not overwhelm the database.

## 4. Design Boundary: Distributed Cache vs Distributed Key-Value Store

Before scaling, clarify whether the system is a disposable cache or a durable key-value database. Both expose key-based operations, but they make different promises.

![4. Design Boundary: Distributed Cache vs Distributed Key-Value Store — source diagram](/diagrams/t-zc2e3vmnwi65-kix-5skmuqn13zma.png)

Both systems use keys; their source-of-truth and recovery requirements differ.

| Question | Cache (main interview design) | Durable KV (advanced follow-up) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| What does GET do? | Return a hot in-memory copy; miss may go to DB. | Return the authoritative stored value. |
| What if data is evicted? | Refetch it; cache may safely forget. | Cannot discard an acknowledged write. |
| Storage | Mostly RAM, TTL and LRU/LFU. | Memory plus durable log/files and replicas. |
| Typical trade-off | Speed vs freshness vs DB load. | Durability vs consistency vs availability. |

- Core operations: GET(key), PUT/SET(key,value), and DELETE(key). Keep keys unique and values opaque to the storage layer.

- A persistent store may support very large total data, small individual key-value records (for example under 10 KB), and automatic node scaling.

- Compression and keeping only hot data in RAM may extend a single node, but eventually sharding becomes necessary.

> Interview boundary: Start with cache-aside and a database behind it. Introduce durable storage-engine internals only if the interviewer changes the problem to a key-value database.

## 5. Capacity Estimation —

## Use estimates to size memory, network and peak load. The values below are interview assumptions, not product measurements.

| Assumption | Value | Why it matters |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Peak read traffic | 200,000 GET/s | Cache-node throughput and hot keys |
| Peak writes | 20,000 SET/s | Invalidation and replication load |
| Hot working set | 50 million keys | RAM footprint |
| Average cached value | 1 KB | Memory and network |
| Cache overhead | ~200 bytes/key | Indexes, TTL, allocator overhead |
| Replication factor | 2 copies | Memory and availability |

- Primary memory: 50M × (1,024 + 200) bytes ≈ 61 GB, before replicas.

- With 2 copies: ≈ 122 GB. At 70% usable memory, plan ≈ 175 GB aggregate deployed RAM (illustrative).

- Read payload throughput: 200k × 1 KB ≈ 200 MB/s before headers, TLS and network hops.

- Shard count: Depends on memory per node *and* measured p99 throughput; neither average QPS nor memory alone is sufficient.

- Peak/hotness matters: One key at 50k RPS may be harder than 50k evenly distributed keys.

> Interview key point: Size the cache for the hot working set, peak QPS, and hottest key—not the entire historical database.

### Why do these numbers actually matter?

The cache needs enough aggregate RAM for hot entries, but also network and CPU capacity for the busiest shard. Suppose we use six cache primaries with roughly 12 GB usable cache space each. The working-set estimate fits, yet a single hot node could still exceed its request-processing limit. Always check both dimensions.

- Do not size from hit ratio alone: High key-hit ratio can hide large missed objects. Track byte-hit ratio too.

- Headroom: Leave room for failover, replication buffers, key churn, allocator overhead, and traffic spikes.

- Bandwidth: 200 MB/s across the fleet does not imply one node must transfer 200 MB/s; distribution and hotspots decide per-node needs.

## 6. API Design and Data Model

Keep the logical API simple before discussing Redis commands or network protocols.

| Operation | Example | Important semantics |
| --- | --- | --- |
| GET | GET user:42 | Value or miss; optional version |
| SET | SET user:42 {…} TTL=300s | Overwrite or conditional write as defined |
| DELETE | DELETE user:42 | Idempotent invalidation |
| MGET (optional) | MGET user:1 user:2 | May cross shards |
| CAS (optional) | SET if version==7 | Prevent lost updates for shared state |
| INCR (optional) | INCR views:42 | Must be atomic if accurate |

### Entry representation

- key: stable and namespaced, e.g. `tenantA:user:42`; never mix tenants accidentally.

- value: serialized bytes (JSON/protobuf) and optional version.

- expiresAt / TTL: used to reject old entries even if background deletion has not happened.

- size: helps enforce max-value limits, memory admission and eviction.

- version: optional; useful for invalidation ordering and optimistic updates.

### How should a client understand misses and errors?

- Miss (not found in cache): Normal, not a service error; the app can read the database.

- Unavailable: Cache could not respond; use a deadline and a controlled fallback policy.

- Expired: Treat as miss even if the old bytes still occupy memory.

- CAS conflict: Return a conditional-update failure, not a silent overwrite.

> Simplify the contract: Start with GET/SET/DELETE and a TTL. Only discuss CAS/MGET/INCR when a follow-up demands them.

## 7. Start Simple — One Cache Node

A single app and cache is enough to explain cache-aside and correctness. It is not yet highly available.

![7. Start Simple — One Cache Node — source diagram](/diagrams/t-zc2e3vmnwi65-kix-48jooystli5s.png)

V1: a cache speeds up reads while the database remains durable.

1. The app receives `GET user:42` and checks the cache.

2. If the key exists and has not expired, return immediately.

3. On a miss, read from the database, fill cache using a TTL, and return.

4. On a database write, update the database first; invalidate the cached key.

> Why not store everything?: RAM is expensive, many records are cold, and a cache can be rebuilt from the authoritative database.

### First improvement: avoid duplicated database reads

Concurrent Cache Misses: Multiple app servers may request the same missing key and fetch data from the database simultaneously.

Small Scale: Duplicate database calls are usually acceptable.

Cache Stampede: For hot keys, many simultaneous cache misses can overload the database.

Solution: Use per-key request coalescing so concurrent requests share a single database fetch.

Interview Approach: Mention the problem initially, but introduce request coalescing only when discussing scaling. No need for distributed locking in the initial design.

## 8. Cache-Aside: Complete Read Path

![8. Cache-Aside: Complete Read Path — source diagram](/diagrams/t-zc2e3vmnwi65-kix-ofhempppamds.png)

Common read flow: hit avoids the database; miss repopulates it.

- Generate Key: Application receives a request and creates a unique cache key.

- Check Cache: If valid data exists, return it immediately (Cache Hit).

- Cache Miss: If data is missing or expired, fetch it from the database with a timeout.

- Update Cache: Store the fetched data with a safe TTL. Avoid caching sensitive data under shared keys.

- Return Response: Return the data to the client, even if updating the cache fails.

- Negative Caching: If data doesn't exist in the database, optionally cache the "not found" result for a short time to avoid repeated database queries.

### Example

At 100,000 reads/s with a 95% hit rate, the database sees about 5,000 cache-miss reads/s rather than 100,000 (ignoring refreshes and bypass traffic).

> Follow-up: first request is slow?: Yes. A cold miss takes a DB round trip; warming known hot entries and request coalescing can reduce that cost.

### Read a practical example

A product detail receives 10,000 requests in one minute. After the first DB lookup, most later requests are served from cache. If the item is updated midway, the write path should invalidate it. The next read repopulates the new value. This explains why a cache needs both a read strategy and an update strategy.

### What if the database is unavailable during a miss?

- No Valid Cache: Return a controlled error instead of incorrect data.

- Stale Cache Fallback: Serve slightly outdated data only when the application allows it.

- Sensitive Data: Never generate default or assumed values when data is unavailable.

## 9. Two Levels: L1 Local Cache and L2 Shared Cache

![9. Two Levels: L1 Local Cache and L2 Shared Cache — source diagram](/diagrams/t-zc2e3vmnwi65-kix-we5li5wag8br.png)

L1 removes network hops; L2 shares a larger working set among app servers.

| Layer | Benefit | Main problem |
| --- | --- | --- |
| L1 in app memory | Fastest read, no network | Inconsistent copies across app instances |
| L2 shared cache | Larger pool, central topology | Network hop and shard ownership |
| CDN/edge (if applicable) | Global delivery of safe public responses | HTTP and invalidation semantics differ |

- Baseline: start with L2; add L1 only if measurements show benefit.

- L1 TTL: usually shorter than L2; invalidation broadcasts are more complicated.

- Private values: do not put user-specific responses into publicly reusable CDN caches.

### L1 invalidation example

Suppose 3 application instances store product:42 in their local L1 caches, while Redis acts as the shared L2 cache.

When the product is updated, clearing only Redis is not enough because application instances may still serve outdated data from L1.

#### Solutions

- Publish Invalidation: Notify all application instances to remove the outdated L1 cache entry.

- Short L1 TTL: Automatically expire local cached data after a short period.

- Version Checks: Compare cache versions to detect outdated entries.

> When L1 is not worth it: If one shared-cache network hop already meets latency targets, skip L1. Simpler invalidation often beats a tiny extra latency gain.

## 10. Write Strategies — Pick One on Purpose

![10. Write Strategies — Pick One on Purpose — source diagram](/diagrams/t-zc2e3vmnwi65-kix-oj9e1qyjamzz.png)

Three write policies; cache-aside invalidation is the interview-friendly default.

| Strategy | How it works | Benefit / risk |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cache-aside + invalidate | Write DB → invalidate key | Simple; brief stale window possible |
| Write-through | Write through cache layer to DB synchronously | Keeps layers aligned but adds write path coupling |
| Write-behind | Write cache → asynchronously flush DB | Fast writes; data-loss/reordering risks |
| Write-around | Write DB only; cache on later read | Avoids caching write-only keys; first read misses |

> Recommended answer: For a read-heavy service where DB is source of truth, write to DB and invalidate the cache; use cache-aside reads.

### Write policy example: update a product price

1. Customer service changes price from ₹999 to ₹899.

2. Application commits ₹899 to SQL/primary store.

3. Application deletes `product:123` from cache (or publishes a versioned invalidation).

4. Next product-page request reads ₹899 and fills the cache.

#### Why Not Update Cache First?

If we update the cache before the database, and the database transaction fails, the cache may contain incorrect data.

Example:

- Cache Update: Product price changes from ₹500 to ₹600 in Redis.

- Database Update: Transaction fails, so the database still has ₹500.

- Problem: Users see ₹600 from the cache, even though the actual price is ₹500.

## 11. Cache Invalidation and Consistency — Critical Interview Topic

A cache becomes dangerous if a recent database update is hidden by an old cached value.

### Write-then-invalidate (common baseline)

1. Commit the new data in the authoritative database.

2. Invalidate the matching cache key (L2 and, if necessary, L1).

3. The next reader misses cache, loads the new value and fills it.

4. If invalidation can fail, use TTL plus retries/change events for eventual recovery.

### Race: delete succeeded but stale value returns

![Race: delete succeeded but stale value returns — source diagram](/diagrams/t-zc2e3vmnwi65-kix-l1y0f6eelr2x.png)

Old readers can fill stale data after a newer writer invalidates the cache.

- Problem: Reader fetches version 1 on a miss; writer commits version 2 and removes cache; older reader then stores version 1.

- Solution A: Include record version in cache value; reject cache fill if newer version/tombstone exists.

- Solution B: Use a short TTL and/or delayed second invalidation when the consistency requirement permits it.

- Solution C: Read from authoritative DB for critical read-after-write sessions, or validate versions before returning.

- Important: Invalidating L2 alone does not remove stale copies already in L1.

> Trade-off  Stronger consistency requires additional coordination, version checks, or DB reads; relaxed freshness gives better hit rate and lower latency.

### Three invalidation choices and their boundaries

| Technique | Use when | What it does not guarantee |
| --- | --- | --- |
| TTL only | Small stale windows acceptable | Immediate visibility after edit |
| Explicit delete | Normal mutable records | Race-free global invalidation alone |
| Versioned events/tombstone | Many caches or regional propagation | Zero lag without coordination |

A `DELETED` tombstone is a small marker indicating a key/version should not be served. It prevents late replayed cache-fill or invalidation events from accidentally reviving old data. It is especially helpful when events are processed out of order.

## 12. Read-After-Write and Strong vs Eventual Consistency

| Requirement | Design choice | Cost |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Eventual freshness | TTL and async invalidation | Small stale window |
| Read your own write | Session bypass or version-aware read | Extra routing/version logic |
| Strict latest value | Authoritative read or coordinated invalidation | More latency and reduced availability |
| Immutable versioned data | Version in key, old entries naturally safe | Metadata pointer must be fresh |

- Read-after-write: The user updating a profile should see their own change immediately, even if replicas or L1 caches lag.

- Versioned keys: `profile:42:v8` avoids overwriting old immutable values; a small pointer identifies current version.

- Keep guarantees scoped: product descriptions may tolerate seconds of staleness; financial balances normally should not rely on a cache as sole authority.

### Example: immediate update visibility

A user changes their display name. The application may return success only after the database commit, then use a short session window that bypasses stale cache copies. More generally, the client may carry version 12 in its next request: a cache entry at version 11 is too old and must not be returned.

> Correct interview distinction  Eventual consistency means old values may be seen for a bounded period. Read-after-write means the same user must observe the committed update on subsequent reads. These are separate promises.

## 13. TTL, Expiration, and Negative Caching

![13. TTL, Expiration, and Negative Caching — source diagram](/diagrams/t-zc2e3vmnwi65-kix-i45ulx54x8nq.png)

TTL is about freshness; eviction is about running out of memory.

- TTL (time to live): Entry becomes invalid after a deadline; read path checks expiration.

- Lazy expiration: Reject expired data during GET and remove it then.

- Background cleanup: Periodically remove expired entries to reclaim memory; exact timing does not affect read correctness.

- Negative caching: Cache missing IDs briefly, e.g. 10–30 seconds, to shield DB from repeated nonexistent-key reads.

- Caution: A long negative TTL may hide newly created records; never share user-specific unauthorized responses under a global cache key.

- Jitter: Slightly randomize TTLs so many entries do not expire simultaneously.

> Interview key point: An expired entry should never be returned just because cleanup has not yet physically removed it.

### TTL choice example

A rarely changed country list may use a TTL of hours. A product stock count may need seconds and explicit invalidation. A highly sensitive account balance may bypass the cache for authoritative reads. There is no universally correct TTL; choose it from the business impact of showing old information.

### Cache-aside + negative caching

If an attacker requests 5,000 nonexistent product IDs per second, looking each up in the database is wasteful. Briefly cache the confirmed not-found outcome, with rate limits. But after creating an ID, invalidate any old negative entry so a new record is not hidden.

## 14. Memory Pressure and Eviction Policies

| Policy | What it removes | When useful |
| --- | --- | --- |
| LRU | Least recently accessed entry | Recency predicts reuse |
| LFU | Least frequently accessed entry | Stable popular keys |
| TTL expiry | Entries whose lifetime ended | Freshness enforcement, not pressure alone |
| Random / approximate | Some candidate entry cheaply | Very high speed/simple policy |
| No eviction / reject | Reject new insert under pressure | When dropping existing entries is worse |

- LRU: Easy to explain, but a one-time scan can evict useful hot entries.

- LFU: Better for stable hot sets but may retain historically popular items too long; use aging.

- Real systems: use approximate LRU/LFU to save metadata/CPU.

- Admission: Not every DB result deserves caching; huge rare objects can crowd out many useful small ones.

- Eviction is normal: Cache eviction should hurt performance, not lose durable records.

> Decision: For typical read-heavy product data, begin with approximate LRU or LFU and measure hit ratio, evictions and memory usage.

### Example: memory becomes full

Assume we have space for 100,000 products. A one-time crawler touches 100,000 unpopular products. Pure LRU may push out the usual hot ones because each scanned key is recent. LFU with sensible aging or an admission filter may preserve frequently accessed items better. Choose from actual workload, not a universal slogan.

### How to measure eviction quality

- Evictions/second: Shows memory pressure.

- Hit ratio after eviction: Rising misses can mean your hot set no longer fits.

- Byte-hit ratio: Shows whether the cache actually saves large DB/network reads.

## 15. Why a Single Cache Node Stops Scaling

- Memory ceiling: Hot keys no longer fit one server.

- Throughput ceiling: CPU, network or request processing reaches a limit.

- Availability: One process/host crash removes the cache.

- Operational constraint: Maintenance restarts make every key cold.

The next step is partitioning: different keys are assigned to different cache nodes. This improves overall capacity, but it does not split traffic for one extremely hot key.

### How do we know that scaling is justified?

- Memory-bound: Usable RAM is near its safe operating limit and useful hot keys are being evicted.

- Throughput-bound: CPU/network or p99 latency rises at peak load even though RAM is available.

- Availability-bound: One node is unacceptable as a single point of failure.

- Operational: Maintenance/restarts cause sustained origin overload.

> Do not overbuild: A single cache instance with a warm standby can be enough for a moderate system. Sharding solves a measured limit at the cost of routing, rebalancing and more failure cases.

## 16. Hash Partitioning and Shard Routing

![16. Hash Partitioning and Shard Routing — source diagram](/diagrams/t-zc2e3vmnwi65-kix-6z3d2d1046nl.png)

The router picks the owner using a stable hash of the key.

1. Hash the full cache key into a large, well-distributed number.

2. Use the ownership map/ring to choose the correct shard.

3. Send GET/SET/DELETE for the key to that shard.

4. Keep routing deterministic across clients or use a central proxy for topology awareness.

### Why not hash(key) % number_of_nodes?

With simple modulo, adding a node changes the divisor, moving many keys. That causes widespread misses. Consistent hashing reduces how many keys move when a node joins or leaves.

### Routing responsibility

A router or cache client maintains a view of which nodes own which key ranges. A topology version helps it notice when that view is outdated. If a request goes to an old owner after a rebalance, the client can refresh the map and retry once rather than scatter the request to every node.

### Quick modulo example

With `hash(key) % 3`, a key with hash 11 maps to shard 2. After expanding to four shards, it maps to shard 3. The key must move even if its old server is healthy. Consistent hashing avoids reshuffling such a large fraction of the namespace.

## 17. Consistent Hashing — Step by Step

![17. Consistent Hashing — Step by Step — source diagram](/diagrams/t-zc2e3vmnwi65-kix-29w1arhryuua.png)

A key is assigned clockwise to the next virtual node; each physical node owns several ring positions.

1. Hash both server positions and cache keys into the same circular number space.

2. Place each key clockwise on the first server position it encounters.

3. When a server is added, it takes only nearby portions of the ring rather than reshuffling most keys.

4. When one server fails, its ranges move to the next owners.

5. Use replicas separately for availability, because hashing by itself does not make lost cache data recoverable.

> Follow-up: If a node is added, movement is much smaller than modulo hashing, but not literally zero. Cache-warming and transfer rate limits can protect the database during rebalancing.

### Ring example in simple words

Imagine nodes A, B, C placed around a circle. Hash a key to position 40; the next clockwise node might be B, so B owns it. If a new node D is inserted before B, only the keys in the range now taken by D need a new owner. Existing keys elsewhere keep their owner.

### What still goes wrong?

- Uneven key popularity: Even perfectly balanced key counts can hide one hot key.

- Uneven key size: A shard with large values may fill before another with more keys.

- Joining storm: Moved/cold keys may suddenly hit DB. Replication or controlled warming is still needed.

## 18. Virtual Nodes (VNodes) and Rebalancing

- Problem: With only one ring position per physical server, ownership may be uneven.

- Virtual nodes: Each physical node owns several ring positions (A1, A2, etc.).

- Benefit: Better balance and smoother incremental movement when adding/removing capacity.

- Adding a node: Transfer selected key ranges, update routing topology, and gradually warm the incoming node.

- During movement: Use a clear old/new ownership rule, safe retries, or temporary forwarding to avoid wrong-shard writes.

- Large-node differences: Assign more virtual nodes or capacity weights to stronger machines.

| Without VNodes | With VNodes |
| --- | --- |
| A server may own a very large ring interval | Ownership spread across many small intervals |
| Adding capacity can move one big range | Ranges are smaller and easier to balance |
| Uneven load even with good hashing | Better probabilistic balance; hot keys remain separate |

### Example: adding a new cache server

1. Control plane marks the new server healthy.

2. Assign several virtual-node positions or weighted key ranges.

3. Old owners transfer/warm appropriate ranges while requests continue.

4. Publish new routing version and gradually shift traffic.

5. Watch miss rate, latency and source DB QPS; slow down if the system starts stampeding.

> Common question: Consistent hashing decides which node should own a key. The rebalance protocol decides how to *safely move* it. They are related but not the same thing.

## 19. Replica Placement on a Hash Ring

Once keys are partitioned, replication provides backup copies so one server failure does not remove every cached copy. Let N be the required number of distinct physical replica owners.

![19. Replica Placement on a Hash Ring — source diagram](/diagrams/t-zc2e3vmnwi65-kix-867uehw76ou5.png)

Virtual nodes on one machine do not count as separate physical replicas.

1. Hash the key on the same consistent-hash ring as the nodes.

2. Walk clockwise to the first physical server and mark it as the primary owner.

3. Continue clockwise and select distinct physical machines until N replicas are chosen.

4. When possible, spread replicas across independent availability zones, not just different processes.

- For N = 3, key K could live on cache nodes A, B and C; two virtual nodes belonging to A are still only one physical copy.

- Unequal machine sizes can have unequal numbers of virtual nodes, placing more keys on larger servers.

- For a disposable cache, fewer or even zero replicas may be a deliberate cost decision because the backing DB can rebuild entries.

> Trade-off: More replicas improve read availability and hot-key read capacity, but use more RAM and can return stale values after asynchronous updates.

## 20. Replication and High Availability

![20. Replication and High Availability — source diagram](/diagrams/t-zc2e3vmnwi65-kix-djivu96x68si.png)

One leader handles authoritative writes while followers keep copies.

- Replication factor 2/3: Stores copies on distinct machines/availability zones to improve availability.

- Leader/follower: Leader accepts writes; followers receive updates.

- Async replication: Fast writes but replicas can lag or miss the last updates during failure.

- Synchronous/quorum replication: Stronger durability/consistency but higher latency.

- Failover: Promote a sufficiently fresh replica, update ownership/routing, and fence the old leader to avoid split-brain.

- Cache vs database: If the DB is source of truth, some cache-data loss is tolerable; losing every cached key simultaneously still creates heavy DB load.

> Interview boundary: Replication improves availability and read throughput. It does not automatically guarantee latest reads or zero data loss.

### What happens if the leader crashes during a write?

If the cache is only an acceleration layer over a durable DB, a cache write may be lost and rebuilt later. If the application has treated a cache write as a durable acknowledged business write, losing it is not acceptable; the design must require a durable path before returning success. State this distinction when asked about persistence.

### Replica promotion safety

- Choose a new owner: Promote a suitable replica and update the shard map.

- Fence the old leader: Prevent it from accepting writes after the new leader is authoritative.

- Replication lag: If asynchronous, newest cached entries may be missing. Re-read from authoritative store where necessary.

## 21. Reads From Replicas — Consistency Trade-offs

| Read choice | Benefit | Risk / use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Leader reads | Most up-to-date on current leader | More leader load |
| Follower reads | Read-scale + locality | Replica lag and stale data |
| Quorum reads (where supported) | Stronger freshness under protocol | More hops and latency |
| Version/session checks | Read-your-writes without all leader reads | Requires version tracking |

- Simplest baseline: Route reads to current owner; use replicated nodes as failover copies.

- If scaling reads: followers may serve reads where bounded staleness is acceptable.

- If strict update visibility: read leader or use versions/consistency checks.

- Avoid dual active leaders without an explicit conflict/consensus design.

### Read from leader or follower?

An ecommerce product description may be served by a slightly stale follower to reduce load. A just-updated authorization permission should be checked against an authoritative version. Mixing these policies is normal: one service can have different cache semantics for different key categories.

> Key distinction: Replication makes data available on multiple nodes; strict freshness requires an explicit read/write consistency policy.

## 22. CAP Theorem — What Changes During a Network Partition?

A network partition occurs when healthy servers cannot communicate with each other. During that failure, the system must choose whether to always respond or to protect a single consistent view of mutable state.

![22. CAP Theorem — What Changes During a Network Partition? — source diagram](/diagrams/t-zc2e3vmnwi65-kix-q6fk50lo1ltx.png)

A partition forces a practical consistency-versus-availability decision.

| Design choice | Behavior during the partition | Use when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Consistency-first | Refuse or pause operations that cannot be safely coordinated. | Stale or conflicting answers are unacceptable. |
| Availability-first | Continue serving reachable nodes and reconcile later. | Briefly stale data is acceptable. |
| Cache-aside baseline | Serve safe unexpired entries; miss may fall back to DB. | The DB owns truth and the cache improves speed. |

- CAP consistency means a single linearizable view, not just replicas eventually agreeing.

- Availability means each request to a nonfailed node receives a successful non-error response; returning a failure sacrifices CAP availability for that operation.

- There is no useful blanket rule that every distributed system permanently picks "two out of three"; explain the choice specifically during a partition.

> Interview-ready answer: For product catalog caching I prioritize availability with bounded staleness. For financial balances, I read the authoritative service rather than trusting an eventually consistent cache.

## 23. Tunable Consistency Using N, W and R (Advanced Follow-Up)

Some replicated key-value stores offer quorum-style reads and writes. It is important to know the idea for cross-questions, even though basic Redis-backed caches do not need this protocol.

![23. Tunable Consistency Using N, W and R (Advanced Follow-Up) — source diagram](/diagrams/t-zc2e3vmnwi65-kix-pzh5u2h67y7u.png)

The coordinator contacts replica owners and waits for the requested number of responses.

| Symbol | Meaning | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| N | Number of distinct replica owners | 3 |
| W | Acknowledgments required to confirm a write | 2 |
| R | Replies required to finish a read | 2 |

1. Write the value to the replica set. With W=2, the coordinator returns write success after two acceptable acknowledgments.

2. For a read, request R=2 replica answers, compare their versions and choose or reconcile the newest valid value.

3. With N=3 and W=2,R=2, read and write sets overlap in at least one replica if they use the same replica membership.

- W=1 usually lowers write latency; R=1 usually lowers read latency, but may increase stale-read risk.

- W=N and R=1 prioritizes read latency but may reduce write availability; W=1 and R=N does the reverse.

- W+R>N is an overlap condition, not an automatic guarantee of strict consistency. Concurrent writes, failures, sloppy quorums, ownership changes and version-selection rules still matter.

- Cache replication is often asynchronous: do not claim a cache read becomes strictly consistent just because three copies exist.

> Key point: Quorums trade response time and failure tolerance against freshness. State the exact guarantee rather than saying every majority configuration is strongly consistent.

## 24. Concurrency: Atomic Counters, CAS and Lost Updates

### Example: lost update

Two clients read a counter value of 10, both calculate 11, and both write 11. One increment disappears.

- Atomic increment: perform read-modify-write on the owning shard as one operation.

- CAS (compare-and-set): update only when current version equals the expected version.

- Distributed lock: useful for rare multi-step work, but adds failure/timeouts; do not lock normal GETs.

- Transactions across keys: more complex because keys may live on different shards; avoid promising cross-shard atomicity for free.

- Idempotency: safe retries require a request identifier if an operation can apply twice after response timeout.

> Interview key point: One logical key needs one clear authority for updates. Routing requests to multiple nodes without coordination can lose changes.

### How does CAS work without low-level internals?

Suppose a cached document has version 7. Two users edit it simultaneously. User A writes using expected version 7 and advances it to 8. User B also submits expected version 7 and gets a conflict instead of silently overwriting A. User B can refresh, merge or retry from version 8.

### When a distributed lock makes sense

Locks are sometimes useful when filling one expensive cache entry or coordinating a rare critical workflow. They need expiry and fencing rules because lock owners can crash. For a normal hot read path, prefer lightweight request coalescing and versioned writes over global locks.

## 25. Concurrent Writes: Versions, Siblings and Vector Clocks

Suppose two clients read the same user profile and update it at the same time through different replicas. Both writes can be valid, so replication can temporarily produce two different values.

![25. Concurrent Writes: Versions, Siblings and Vector Clocks — source diagram](/diagrams/t-zc2e3vmnwi65-kix-jut2uxg8s1a.png)

Two edits based on the same parent version are concurrent siblings.

1. Original record is name=John and version V1.

2. Client A writes "John / SF" while Client B writes "John / NYC" using the same old version.

3. The store sees two concurrent values instead of assuming one automatically came after the other.

4. The application resolves them: preserve both, merge safe fields, ask the user or apply a documented policy.

### How vector clocks help, without going into internals

- A vector clock stores small per-writer counters describing which versions a write has seen.

- If all counters in version B are at least those in A, then A can be an ancestor of B.

- If neither version is an ancestor of the other, they represent concurrent writes that need reconciliation.

- The vector can grow with writers; trimming entries saves space but may lose exact causal history.

- Vector clocks detect conflicts; they do not choose how conflicting business values should be merged.

| Conflict policy | Benefit | Main risk |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Last write wins | Simple and compact | Can silently lose valid concurrent updates |
| Keep siblings + merge | No silent overwrite | Client/application resolution is needed |
| Reject stale base version (CAS) | Simple strong-owner update | Caller must retry and decide how to merge |

> Cache boundary: Ordinary cache-aside designs typically solve stale writes with version checks and invalidation, not vector clocks. Vector clocks belong to an eventually consistent multi-writer data store extension.

## 26. Cache Stampede, Penetration and Avalanche

![26. Cache Stampede, Penetration and Avalanche — source diagram](/diagrams/t-zc2e3vmnwi65-kix-e9orug8vcgd8.png)

Coalescing turns many simultaneous misses for one key into one origin fetch.

| Problem | What happens | Protection |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Stampede / breakdown | One hot key expires; many requests hit DB | Single-flight, stale-if-safe, prewarm |
| Penetration | Repeated reads for keys that do not exist | Negative cache, validation, rate limits |
| Avalanche | Many TTLs expire or nodes fail together | TTL jitter, warming, failover, origin limits |

- Request coalescing: One app/shard fetches a missing key while other concurrent requests await the result.

- Stale-while-revalidate: Serve a short-lived stale value during refresh only when product semantics permit.

- Do not stampede your lock: Bound waiters, use deadlines, and have a fallback response if origin is overloaded.

### Example: popular key expires

Imagine 50,000 requests for a popular product arriving just after its five-minute cache TTL ends. Without coordination, thousands may hit the database at once. A single-flight mechanism lets one fetch the latest product while peers briefly wait or use an allowed stale copy. The database sees far fewer simultaneous queries.

### Do not serve stale everywhere

Stale-while-revalidate is a performance choice, not permission to violate product correctness. It may fit a news headline or product description; it may not fit revoked permissions, deleted sensitive data, or an inventory value requiring exactness.

## 27. Handling Hot Keys and Skewed Traffic

![27. Handling Hot Keys and Skewed Traffic — source diagram](/diagrams/t-zc2e3vmnwi65-kix-7ultgeijpxa.png)

Copies across L1 and cache replicas absorb reads for the same viral key.

- Problem: `hash(key)` sends every request for one key to the same shard, even if you add 100 more shards.

- L1 cache: Replicate hottest read-only values in each application instance.

- Read replicas / hot-key replication: Distribute reads across multiple cache nodes where the product supports it.

- Coalescing: Prevent origin stampede after a hot-key miss.

- Hot-key detection: Track top-key QPS and per-shard network/CPU; avoid logging raw sensitive keys.

- Write-hot key: A counter updated 100k/sec is harder: consider sharded counters with async aggregation only if exactness is not required.

> Interview key point: Partitioning distributes *different* keys; replication and caching distribute reads for *one* hot key.

### Read-hot vs write-hot

For reads of a popular celebrity profile, multiple copies of the same immutable or slowly changing value can serve requests in parallel. For a precise global inventory decrement, copies alone do not solve consistency. The application should update one authoritative owner or redesign the workload around reservation/transactions.

> Practical rule: Ask whether the hot key is read-heavy or write-heavy. That single detail changes the answer.

## 28. Cache Node Failure, Recovery and Cold-Start Storms

![28. Cache Node Failure, Recovery and Cold-Start Storms — source diagram](/diagrams/t-zc2e3vmnwi65-kix-93ry8usy8med.png)

Cache miss/failure fallbacks must be limited to protect the database.

1. Detect unhealthy node using health checks/timeouts; stop routing new requests to it.

2. Switch to a healthy replica or updated shard owner if available.

3. If no cached copy exists, fall back to database but cap concurrent origin requests.

4. Refill the recovering/new node gradually; avoid sending all keys for immediate reload.

5. Rebalance only after membership changes are confirmed; prevent routing flaps.

### Why not unlimited DB fallback?

If a cache absorbs 95% of 200k reads/s, database load may jump from ~10k to ~200k reads/s during a complete outage. That can trigger a cascading failure even though the database was healthy before.

### Recovery without causing another outage

A restarted shard is cold. Flooding it with every possible key immediately consumes bandwidth and may also flood the backing database. Recover top keys first, use request coalescing, and gradually increase allowed miss traffic. Make sure application and cache timeouts are shorter than the overall API deadline.

### Circuit-breaker behavior

After repeated cache connection failures, the app briefly stops expensive attempts to the failing node and follows its safe fallback rule. It occasionally probes recovery. Circuit breakers prevent thread/connection exhaustion; they do not make stale or missing data automatically correct.

## 29. Failure Detection: Health Checks and Gossip

A distributed cluster needs to discover when a machine is unhealthy, and everyone needs a reasonably consistent membership view before sending keys to it.

![29. Failure Detection: Health Checks and Gossip — source diagram](/diagrams/t-zc2e3vmnwi65-kix-6pztlusf2ozb.png)

Nodes exchange heartbeat/membership updates with a few peers, not every peer.

1. Each node tracks a membership list with node IDs, heartbeat counters and last-seen times.

2. Periodically it updates its own heartbeat and shares selected health records with random peers.

3. Peers forward newer information so membership changes spread through the cluster.

4. A node with a missing heartbeat becomes suspect; corroborating probes or peer evidence reduce false failure declarations.

5. Once the cluster confirms a failure, routing and replica placement update in a controlled way.

- All-to-all health messaging grows expensive as node count increases. Gossip reduces direct communication while spreading cluster state.

- A slow machine or brief network pause does not necessarily mean a permanent crash. Avoid constant member flapping.

- Centralized health checks can be sufficient for a managed cache; gossip is a useful decentralized design follow-up.

> Interview key point: A membership mistake can route requests to a dead or wrong owner. Use timeouts, suspect status and stable reconfiguration rather than reacting to one missed heartbeat.

## 30. Temporary Failures: Sloppy Quorum and Hinted Handoff

In an availability-first key-value store, a preferred replica may be unreachable. The system can temporarily write to another healthy node and later transfer the data to its intended owner.

![30. Temporary Failures: Sloppy Quorum and Hinted Handoff — source diagram](/diagrams/t-zc2e3vmnwi65-kix-qt99fexsjbok.png)

A substitute node temporarily holds a replica plus a recovery hint.

1. Key K normally belongs on replicas A, B and C. B becomes unreachable.

2. Coordinator sends the new copy to a healthy substitute D under a clearly defined fallback policy.

3. D saves a hint saying that B was the intended destination.

4. When B returns, D hands over the missed updates; replicas synchronize and the hint can be cleared.

- Sloppy quorum favors availability by using reachable substitute nodes rather than always waiting for the originally assigned replica set.

- Hints need expiry, capacity limits and retry handling so temporary substitutes do not fill up indefinitely.

- This technique does not by itself provide strict latest-value reads or durable linearizability.

- A cache-with-DB baseline usually fails over to replicas or refetches from its database instead; do not introduce hinted handoff unless durable-KV-style availability is requested.

> Trade-off: Fast writes during a replica outage are useful, but they can increase reconciliation work and temporarily weaken freshness guarantees.

## 31. Permanent Failures: Anti-Entropy and Merkle Trees

Temporary handoff helps when a replica returns soon. A long outage or permanent replacement requires checking which ranges of data differ across two nodes and repairing only the missing or outdated items.

![31. Permanent Failures: Anti-Entropy and Merkle Trees — source diagram](/diagrams/t-zc2e3vmnwi65-kix-xhvfzewbyqfs.png)

Equal hashes let the repair process skip whole matching ranges.

1. Split a replica keyspace into fixed logical ranges or buckets.

2. Compute hashes for the keys/values in each range and combine those hashes into a tree.

3. Compare root hashes on two replicas. If equal under the same snapshot rules, no deeper scan is needed.

4. If roots differ, compare child hashes to narrow the mismatch.

5. Read and copy only the ranges or keys that actually differ, then recheck.

- A Merkle tree is a compact summary for finding differences; it is not a replacement for version checks or business conflict resolution.

- The comparison needs consistent key ranges, serialization, snapshots and hash definitions on both sides.

- For disposable caches, bulk refilling all missing entries may be cheaper than building anti-entropy infrastructure.

- For a durable replicated key-value database, background anti-entropy is valuable because missed data cannot simply be forgotten.

> Interview key point: Merkle trees reduce repair bandwidth by finding mismatched subtrees instead of sending the full dataset every time.

## 32. Common Failure Matrix

| Failure | Expected behavior | Protection |
| --- | --- | --- |
| One shard down | Replica takes over or limited DB misses | Health check, failover, limits |
| All cache unavailable | Degrade; do not flood database | Breaker, coalescing, load shed |
| Database unavailable | Serve valid cached data where policy permits | Stale policy, retry limits |
| Replica behind | Avoid if fresh data needed | Leader read/version check |
| Topology update missed | Refresh shard map and retry safely | Routing version, bounded retry |
| Hot key overload | Extra read copies/local caches | Hot-key detection, isolation |
| Invalidation event lost | Stale value until TTL or reconciliation | TTL, outbox/CDC, versioning |

> Failure rule: A cache failure should reduce speed, not silently corrupt durable data. On overload, failing some requests is safer than crashing the database.

### Triage a cache outage in an interview

1. Check user-facing latency/errors and determine affected cache shards.

2. Limit requests going to database; coalesce repeated misses.

3. Fail over healthy replica/region if it is safe for the data category.

4. Stabilize traffic before cache warming/rebalancing.

5. After recovery, investigate why protection failed or worked.

## 33. Multi-Region Distributed Cache (Follow-Up Only)

![33. Multi-Region Distributed Cache (Follow-Up Only) — source diagram](/diagrams/t-zc2e3vmnwi65-kix-fgd4wpkqk80t.png)

Regional caching is simple for reads; globally coordinated writes are harder.

- Start: One authoritative database/home write region with independent regional cache clusters.

- Regional read: Serve local cache if valid; miss fetches from source or suitable regional DB replica.

- Invalidation: Publish versioned change/tombstone events to regions; async delivery creates a stale window.

- Read-your-writes: Temporarily route to home region or use a session/version token.

- Region outage: Fail over reads to healthy region; recently written data may be missing under async replication.

- Avoid: claiming globally strict consistency simply because every region has Redis.

| Choice | Benefit | Cost |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Local region caches + async invalidation | Fast reads, high availability | Eventually stale |
| Global coordinated writes | Stronger global ordering | Cross-region latency and partition cost |
| Versioned immutable values | Easy safe caches | Fresh current-version pointer needed |

### Cross-region update example

A user edits a profile in India while a friend reads from the US. India writes to the authoritative DB and publishes a versioned invalidation. The US cache may still hold an older copy until delivery. If the product promises fresh results, US reads must check a minimum version or fall back to the authoritative path; otherwise document eventual consistency.

### What about global locks or consensus?

Do not add cross-region coordination to every cache GET by default. Global synchronization costs WAN latency and reduces availability during network partitions. It is justified only for keys requiring strict correctness; most public read caches accept bounded staleness.

## 34. Availability-Zone and Data-Center Failure

Replicating data three times on the same rack or zone can still fail together. Place replicas in distinct failure domains when availability goals require it.

![34. Availability-Zone and Data-Center Failure — source diagram](/diagrams/t-zc2e3vmnwi65-kix-fvyduj601i96.png)

Zone-aware replicas reduce common-cause failures.

1. Choose a replica count and identify the failure domains that must be survived.

2. Place owners across independent AZs; cross-region replicas if whole-region recovery is required.

3. Detect a failed zone and route requests only to healthy copies or the underlying primary DB.

4. Before acknowledging stronger write durability, wait for the configured number of appropriately placed replicas or a durable store.

5. When the zone returns, rebuild and rebalance gradually to prevent a recovery storm.

- More distant replicas add network latency, money and operational complexity.

- For a performance cache, loss of one region may be acceptable if requests route to DB or another region safely.

- For an authoritative key-value database, RPO and RTO must state how much acknowledged data may be lost and how quickly traffic recovers.

> Failure design: Replicas improve availability only when failure domains and failover rules are chosen deliberately.

## 35. Security, Isolation and Cache-Key Design

- Namespacing: Include tenant, resource and version in key where relevant.

- Authorization: Check permission before returning protected content; never let shared cache bypass ACL checks.

- Sensitive data: Encrypt transport; use access controls and retention rules; avoid logging raw personal values/keys.

- Cache poisoning: Validate data origin, canonicalize keys and do not mix authenticated variants.

- Large values: Enforce max object size; do not let one large item evict thousands of useful small entries.

- User deletion/privacy: Invalidate all copies and ensure TTL/recovery backups obey policy.

- Untrusted keys: Bound lengths and avoid user-controlled unbounded cardinality.

### Security example: two tenants with the same numeric user ID

Tenant A and Tenant B both have `user:42`. If the cache key contains only the numeric ID, one tenant may accidentally receive the other tenant’s value. Use keys such as `tenant:A:user:42`, and recheck access controls on the request path. Cache namespacing is part of correctness, not merely organization.

## 36. Compression, Serialization and Large Values

| Technique | When to use | Trade-off |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Compact serialization | High-volume structured objects | More schema/version work |
| Compression | Medium/large repetitive values | CPU and decode latency |
| Chunk very large objects | If cache product/flow supports it | More keys and fetch complexity |
| Skip huge rare values | Low reuse/poor byte-hit payoff | May leave some misses |

> Low priority: Know why compression and max-value limits matter. Deep compression internals are not central to most SDE 2 distributed-cache interviews.

### Large-object caching example

Caching a 20 MB report used once may be less valuable than caching 20,000 small 1 KB product entries used repeatedly. Size-based admission and max-entry rules keep one expensive object from dominating memory. Compress only when bytes saved are worth CPU and decode cost.

## 37. When the Key-Value Store Must Be Durable: Write Path

A distributed cache can rebuild data after eviction. If the interviewer instead asks for a distributed key-value database that owns data, it needs an acknowledged-write durability path, often built around a log and sorted on-disk files.

![37. When the Key-Value Store Must Be Durable: Write Path — source diagram](/diagrams/t-zc2e3vmnwi65-kix-d587bwc7t4rz.png)

A common durable-write pattern; storage engines differ in their exact ordering.

1. Client calls PUT(key,value), which is routed to the owner/coordinator.

2. Owner appends the write to a durable commit log (WAL) to support crash recovery.

3. Owner updates an in-memory sorted write buffer called the memtable.

4. When the memtable reaches a threshold, flush it into immutable sorted SSTable files on disk.

5. Replicate according to the chosen acknowledgment policy, then return success only when that durability contract is met.

- WAL (write-ahead log): sequential append that allows recovery after a crash. It is not a cache eviction log.

- Memtable: the fast mutable in-memory representation of recent writes.

- SSTable: an immutable, sorted file of stored key/value records; later compaction merges files and discards obsolete versions safely.

- Compression and retaining hot blocks in RAM reduce disk and network cost, but add CPU/memory trade-offs.

- A cache-aside system does not need to write a new WAL for every cached value because its backing database owns durability.

> Interview boundary: Say: "I would not build disk/SSTable machinery into a simple distributed cache. I would add it if the system itself becomes the durable key-value store."

## 38. Durable Key-Value Read Path: Memtable, Bloom Filter and SSTables

For persistent key-value data, not every GET lives in RAM. A read may find recent data in memory or search immutable sorted files on disk.

![38. Durable Key-Value Read Path: Memtable, Bloom Filter and SSTables — source diagram](/diagrams/t-zc2e3vmnwi65-kix-jmlnivydo0wc.png)

A Bloom filter can avoid unnecessary disk checks for files that definitely lack the key.

1. Route GET(key) to the correct storage owner and check the memtable/recent memory cache first.

2. If not found, use each SSTable's index and optional Bloom filter to decide which files might contain the key.

3. Skip a file when its Bloom filter says "definitely absent"; otherwise inspect its index/data blocks.

4. Select the correct surviving version, respecting tombstones and any replication reconciliation rules.

5. Return the value; optionally cache the hot result in memory.

- Bloom filter result NO -> key definitely absent from that file, assuming correct construction.

- Bloom filter result MAYBE -> key might exist, so a real lookup is still required; false positives can occur.

- SSTable sorted order/index reduces scan work; a background compaction process prevents too many old file versions accumulating.

- For the original distributed-cache question, this is optional storage-engine depth, not something to volunteer early.

> Key distinction: A Bloom filter reduces wasted disk lookups. It does not return the stored value, and a "maybe" does not prove the key exists.

## 39. Observability, SLIs and SLOs

| Metric | What it reveals | Example alert signal |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Hit ratio + byte hit ratio | Does cache save DB I/O and bandwidth? | Sudden drop |
| p50 / p95 / p99 GET latency | User tail latency | p99 rising |
| Evictions + memory pressure | Working set does not fit | Eviction spike |
| Shard QPS / hot key share | Uneven ownership | One shard near saturation |
| Replica lag / failovers | Consistency + resilience | Lag beyond policy |
| Origin fallback QPS | Database protection | Fallback overwhelms DB |
| Invalidation delay / stale reads | Correctness | Age over target |

### Illustrative SLOs

- Latency: 99% of valid regional cache hits complete within an agreed target (e.g., 10 ms).

- Availability: Cache read API reaches target availability (e.g., 99.9%) under stated load.

- Correctness: Version/TTL rules are honored; stale reads measured separately.

- Alert on user impact: Rising application p99 and DB overload matter more than a single component CPU spike.

### Why watch both hit ratio and byte hit ratio?

Suppose 99 tiny keys hit and one 20 MB report misses. Key-hit ratio is 99%, but the missed report still consumes most of the bytes transferred from origin. Byte-hit ratio tells a different story and may show that a seemingly excellent hit rate does not save bandwidth.

### Testing the distributed cache

- Correctness tests: expired items, concurrent updates, CAS conflicts, invalidate-then-fill race.

- Load tests: even distribution vs one hot key; p99 latency during eviction.

- Failure tests: kill a cache node, lose a replica, isolate the database, recover a cold shard.

- Rebalance tests: add/remove a node while reading and writing, validate routing and freshness.

- Chaos question: Does a cache outage cause bounded database traffic or a cascade?

## 40. Cost and Practical Scaling Decisions

- RAM: Cache only data with meaningful reuse; track cost per useful byte and byte-hit ratio.

- Replication: More copies improve availability and read scale but increase memory and network cost.

- TTL: Longer TTL raises hit rate but risks staleness; shorter TTL does the reverse.

- Sharding: Adds machines and operational complexity; adopt when memory/throughput/availability requires it.

- Eviction: Keeps memory bounded; pressure suggests either more capacity or smarter admission.

- Cloud egress: Cross-zone/region cache calls can erase latency/cost gains; keep hot paths local.

### Example: what is the actual cost trade-off?

A larger cache costs more RAM but may save database read capacity. Adding one replica doubles data copies but improves cache availability. A 30-minute TTL may give a high hit rate while allowing stale profile details; a 30-second TTL may increase origin cost. State the service requirement before optimizing one number.

## 41. Architecture Evolution — Start Simple, Then Scale

| Stage | Architecture | Trigger |
| --- | --- | --- |
| V1 | One app + DB | Correctness first |
| V2 | One shared cache, cache-aside | Repeated DB reads |
| V3 | Multiple app instances + L2 cache | App horizontal scale |
| V4 | Hash-partitioned cache cluster | RAM/throughput limit |
| V5 | Virtual nodes and topology control | Rebalancing / skew |
| V6 | Replicas + failover | Availability requirements |
| V7 | L1 + hot-key copies + coalescing | Viral traffic / DB stampede |
| V8 | Regional caches + event invalidation | Global latency / DR |

> Interview recommendation  Do not memorize V1–V8 as an order. Explain the bottleneck that justifies each addition.

## 42. Final Production Architecture

![42. Final Production Architecture — source diagram](/diagrams/t-zc2e3vmnwi65-kix-tgr084etu6ct.png)

A scaled design with local hits, distributed shards, replicas, and DB fallback.

### Normal GET

1. Resolve canonical key and check L1 if enabled.

2. Use shard routing/consistent hash to find L2 owner.

3. Serve unexpired value; on miss, coalesce fetch from authoritative store.

4. Populate safe cache entry and return.

### Normal UPDATE

1. Commit to DB; maintain record version where needed.

2. Invalidate or update L2/L1 with ordering/version protection.

3. Readers refill on next miss; async invalidation is allowed only under agreed freshness.

### Failure mode

Replica/promote or controlled origin fallback. Apply a request limit and circuit breaker before missing traffic becomes a database incident.

## 43. Decentralized Coordinator-Based Key-Value Architecture (Follow-Up)

In a decentralized key-value database, each cluster node may handle client traffic, forward requests, replicate values, detect failures and participate in repair. The node that first accepts the request acts as its coordinator.

![43. Decentralized Coordinator-Based Key-Value Architecture (Follow-Up) — source diagram](/diagrams/t-zc2e3vmnwi65-kix-ihx8hveuqs43.png)

A coordinator routes an operation to the correct replicas; it does not need to own the key itself.

| Component | Responsibility | How it fits |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Client API | GET / PUT | Simple operations on one key |
| Coordinator | Route and gather responses | Any healthy entry node may coordinate |
| Hash ring/partition map | Find primary and replica owners | Move few keys during membership changes |
| Replication/versions | Store copies and detect conflicts | Read/write consistency is a design decision |
| Failure detector/repair | Gossip, handoff, anti-entropy | Keeps data available and eventually synchronized |
| Storage engine | WAL, memtable, SSTables, Bloom filters | Only for persistent authoritative values |

- A fully decentralized design reduces dependency on one coordinator instance, but it needs robust membership, routing and repair protocols.

- For a distributed cache, a simpler client library or cache router plus shard primaries and replicas is typically a better initial interview answer.

- A good follow-up asks: Can any node accept writes? If yes, discuss versions/conflicts. If no, define the per-shard leader and failover fence.

> Architecture decision  Do not combine every subsystem by default: start with the cache. Present the decentralized durable-KV extension only when the interviewer asks about data ownership, writes during partitions or disk durability.

## 44. Interview Presentation — 45-Minute Plan

| Time | What to present |
| --- | --- |
| 0–5 min | Clarify data type, read/write mix, durability and allowed staleness |
| 5–10 min | Simple cache-aside and GET/SET/DELETE contracts |
| 10–18 min | Read/write flows, TTL and invalidation consistency |
| 18–27 min | Partitioning, consistent hashing, virtual nodes |
| 27–34 min | Replication, failover, rebalancing |
| 34–40 min | Hot keys, stampede, rate limiting DB fallback |
| 40–45 min | Requested follow-up, trade-offs and concise summary |

> Presentation tip: Spend time explaining the *why* of each component. Let the interviewer choose which advanced branch to explore.

## 45. Cross-Questions — Interview-Ready Answers

Q. Why use a cache if the database already has indexes?

A. Memory lookup and reduced repeated DB work lower latency; indexes still may require disk/network/CPU at peak traffic.

Q. Why is the database still source of truth?

A. Caches can evict/expire/restart; durable business data must survive those events.

Q. What happens on a cache hit?

A. Return the valid cached value without querying the DB.

Q. What happens on a cache miss?

A. Fetch DB, populate cache if safe and return; coalesce when many requests miss the same key.

Q. Why not cache the entire DB?

A. RAM cost and changing cold data make caching the hot working set more efficient.

Q. How do you handle an update?

A. Commit the DB, then invalidate/cache refresh with TTL and version protection for races.

Q. What if invalidation event is lost?

A. TTL bounds staleness; retry/replay versioned events when stronger freshness is required.

Q. What is cache-aside vs write-through?

A. Cache-aside fills on reads and invalidates after writes; write-through updates the backing store through the cache write path.

Q. Why avoid write-behind for critical data?

A. Acknowledged cache writes can be lost before asynchronous DB persistence.

Q. What is TTL vs eviction?

A. TTL determines expiry by time; eviction removes entries under memory pressure.

Q. LRU vs LFU?

A. LRU follows recency; LFU follows access frequency. Choose from traffic measurements.

Q. What happens when one cache server is added?

A. Consistent hashing moves some ranges to the new node and routing updates; warm keys to limit misses.

Q. Why virtual nodes?

A. Spread key ranges across multiple points per physical node to improve balance and scaling.

Q. Does sharding fix one viral key?

A. No. That key still has one owner; use read copies, L1 and coalescing.

Q. What if a cache node dies?

A. Fail over to a replica or route controlled misses to DB; avoid request spikes.

Q. Why replicate if cache is disposable?

A. Improves uptime and reduces miss storms, even when database remains durable.

Q. Can reads from replicas be stale?

A. Yes if replication is asynchronous; use leader/version reads for freshness-sensitive data.

Q. What is a cache stampede?

A. Many requests simultaneously miss a hot key, overwhelming origin; use single-flight and controlled refresh.

Q. Negative caching risk?

A. A missing entry cached too long can hide a newly created value.

Q. How can two writers lose updates?

A. Both read old state and overwrite each other; use atomic operations or version-based CAS.

Q. What if Redis/cache is down completely?

A. Use bounded database fallback and possibly load shedding; do not permit an unbounded origin storm.

Q. How do you guarantee read-after-write?

A. Route the creator to authoritative reads or require a version token; plain async replicas do not guarantee it.

Q. When would you use a CDN instead?

A. For public, cache-safe HTTP content near global users; it is not a replacement for private application key-value caching.

Q. What changes for multiple regions?

A. Keep regional caches local, define authoritative writes, and propagate versioned invalidations with explicit staleness.

Q. What would you monitor first?

A. End-user p99, hit ratio, database fallback QPS, errors, memory/evictions, replica lag and hot shards.

Q. Why not just add more shards for traffic?

A. It improves aggregate capacity, but hot keys and origin failures require separate solutions.

Q. How do you prevent cache poisoning across tenants?

A. Namespace keys, canonicalize identities and enforce authorization before serving protected data.

Q. What is the biggest trade-off?

A. Latency/hit rate versus freshness and complexity; choose according to the application’s correctness needs.

## 46. Additional Cross-Questions: Key-Value Store Extensions

Q. How is a distributed cache different from a key-value database?

A. A cache can evict and rebuild from a durable source. A key-value database is responsible for preserving acknowledged values; it needs durable storage and replica recovery.

Q. When does CAP matter?

A. During a network partition, decide whether to refuse uncoordinated operations or continue with potentially stale/conflicting values. The choice depends on the data contract.

Q. Why do replica owners need to be distinct physical nodes?

A. Two virtual nodes on one physical server fail together. Count separate machines and spread them across AZs for stronger availability.

Q. What are N, W and R?

A. N copies, W write acknowledgments and R read responses. Larger W or R can improve freshness but costs latency/availability; quorum overlap by itself is not strict linearizability.

Q. Why can W+R>N still return stale data?

A. A sloppy quorum, membership change, concurrent writes or incorrectly selected latest version may defeat the simple overlap argument. State the protocol assumptions.

Q. What if two regions update the same key simultaneously?

A. Use optimistic version checks for single-owner writes, or track causal versions/siblings under multi-writer eventual consistency and merge according to product policy.

Q. Does a vector clock automatically solve write conflicts?

A. No. It can identify ancestors versus concurrent writes; application logic still chooses to merge, keep both or reject an edit.

Q. How do distributed nodes detect a failed replica?

A. Use timeouts and heartbeats; decentralized designs gossip membership and verify suspicion before stable rerouting.

Q. What is hinted handoff?

A. A healthy substitute temporarily keeps data intended for an unavailable owner and transfers it back later; it mainly improves availability in durable KV systems.

Q. Why use Merkle trees?

A. Two replicas compare hierarchical hashes to locate mismatched key ranges and repair only differences rather than copying everything.

Q. What changes if an entire availability zone fails?

A. Place replicas in distinct AZs, fail over to healthy copies, limit cold misses to origin, and define RPO/RTO if data is authoritative.

Q. Why use a WAL and SSTables?

A. A durable key-value store writes to a log for recovery and keeps sorted immutable disk files for scalable storage. A disposable cache usually does not need that machinery.

Q. What does a Bloom filter answer?

A. A negative result safely skips that SSTable; a positive result only means the key may be present, so a real lookup is still needed.

Q. What is a coordinator?

A. It is the node that receives a request, locates relevant replicas and collects the configured replies. It does not have to store that key itself.

> Cross-question rule: Explain requirement -> design choice -> what can fail -> trade-off. Bring durable-KV techniques into the conversation only after the interviewer changes the availability or durability requirements.
> 
> Cross-question rule: Explain requirement -> design choice -> what can fail -> trade-off. Bring durable-KV techniques into the conversation only after the interviewer changes the availability or durability requirements.

## 47. Scenario Drills

### Scenario A — Product price changes but users see the old value

1. Check whether DB commit happened and which caches hold the price.

2. Invalidate L2 and any local copies; inspect event lag and stale-fill race.

3. For strict price correctness, read authoritative version until copies are updated.

### Scenario B — One key gets 1 million GET/s

1. Serve at CDN only if HTTP and public-safe; otherwise L1 and replicated hot entries.

2. Use request coalescing and warmup; limit origin concurrency.

3. Monitor per-shard bottlenecks; do not propose ordinary sharding as the sole fix.

### Scenario C — Add 5 new cache nodes

1. Assign ring virtual nodes/capacity weights.

2. Move owned ranges gradually and refresh client routing.

3. Warm frequently accessed data; monitor DB miss rise and rollback if overloaded.

### Scenario D — Primary cache cluster loses an AZ

1. Detect shard/replica loss and promote healthy copies with fencing.

2. Bound database fallback to avoid cascading failures.

3. Rebuild replicas/warm data after service stabilizes.

## 48. Fast Revision Cheat Sheet

| Topic | Interview default |
| --- | --- |
| Baseline | DB source of truth + cache-aside |
| GET path | L1 (optional) → L2 owner → DB miss → fill |
| SET path | Commit DB → invalidate cache |
| Partition key | Stable hash of full key |
| Consistent hashing | Move limited ranges on topology changes |
| Virtual nodes | Balance ownership and make rebalancing smooth |
| Replication | Availability + read copies; watch lag |
| Expiration | TTL read check + background reclaim |
| Eviction | Approx LRU/LFU under memory pressure |
| Hot key | L1 + read replication + coalescing |
| Stampede | Single-flight + TTL jitter + safe stale refresh |
| Consistency | Version-aware invalidation or authoritative reads |
| Failure | Replica → controlled DB fallback → shed if unsafe |
| Multi-region | Regional caches + explicit write/invalidations |

### 10 Quick Quiz Questions

1. Why is cache-aside a good baseline?

2. How is TTL different from eviction?

3. What is a stale cache fill race?

4. What moves when adding a node with consistent hashing?

5. What do virtual nodes improve?

6. Can replication provide strict freshness by itself?

7. How do you stop a cache stampede?

8. Why does sharding not solve one hot key?

9. How do you protect DB during a cache outage?

10. What would you choose for read-your-writes?

## 49. 30-Second Final Interview Answer

> Interview answer: I would start with a cache-aside design: an application reads from a shared in-memory cache and falls back to the database on misses. The database stays the source of truth, and updates invalidate cached keys. I would enforce TTL and use approximate LRU/LFU eviction. When one node is insufficient, I would hash-partition keys with consistent hashing and virtual nodes, add replicas for availability, and handle hot keys and cache stampedes using local caching and request coalescing. During cache failures, I would use controlled DB fallback and load shedding so the cache outage does not bring down the database.
