notes.description: Goal This document is intentionally self-contained. It covers the simple crawler, the scaled distributed design, URL frontier scheduling, politeness, robots.txt
notes.content:
Design a Web Crawler

Complete System Design Interview Guide

Section 3 — Problem 4 | End-to-End Design, Deep Dives, Follow-ups & Interview Q&A

> Goal
> This document is intentionally self-contained. It covers the simple crawler, the scaled distributed design, URL frontier scheduling, politeness, robots.txt, deduplication, recrawling, traps, failure handling, multi-region concerns, and detailed interviewer follow-ups. The aim is to make this the only reference you need for a Web Crawler interview.

## 1. Problem Statement

Design a large-scale web crawler that begins with seed URLs, downloads pages, extracts hyperlinks, discovers new URLs, and continuously schedules useful pages for future crawling. The crawler should operate at internet scale without repeatedly fetching the same content or overwhelming external websites.

> Core interview question
> How do we continuously discover and fetch billions of web pages at high throughput while remaining polite to each host, avoiding duplicate work, surviving failures, and keeping important pages fresh?

## 2. What the Interviewer Is Testing

- Requirement scoping: crawling is not the same as indexing, ranking, or search serving.

- Capacity estimation and throughput-driven architecture.

- Queue/frontier design rather than a naive FIFO queue.

- URL and content deduplication at massive scale.

- Per-host politeness, robots.txt compliance, and DNS efficiency.

- Partitioning work across many crawler workers without duplicate ownership.

- Retry semantics, leases, checkpoints, poison URLs, and crash recovery.

- Recrawl scheduling and freshness prioritization.

- Protection against crawler traps, infinite URL spaces, spam, and oversized content.

- Ability to explain trade-offs instead of simply naming technologies.

## 3. Clarifying Questions to Ask First

- What content types are in scope: HTML only initially, or PDFs/images/video too?

- Are we crawling the public internet or a bounded set of domains?

- Is the goal one-time discovery or continuous recrawling for freshness?

- How quickly should important changed pages be revisited?

- Do we need to respect robots.txt and crawl-delay directives? We should assume yes.

- Do we need JavaScript rendering? Start with static HTML; treat browser rendering as a costly follow-up.

- Do we need exact-once crawling? Usually no; at-least-once processing with deduplication is simpler.

- How much content do we retain: raw page bytes, parsed text, metadata, or all of them?

- Are there legal/product policies restricting domains, geography, login walls, or personal data?

> Interview-ready opening
> I will design a continuous public-web crawler for HTML pages. It will respect robots.txt and per-host politeness, tolerate occasional duplicate fetches, store raw content and metadata, and prioritize important/fresh pages. Indexing and ranking are downstream systems.

## 4. Functional and Non-Functional Requirements

| Category | Requirement | Design impact |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Core | Accept seed URLs and discover links recursively | URL frontier + parser |
| Core | Fetch pages and store content/metadata | Fetcher + object storage + metadata store |
| Core | Avoid repeated URL work | URL normalization + seen-URL dedupe |
| Core | Avoid duplicate content | Content fingerprinting |
| Core | Respect robots.txt and host limits | Robots cache + host scheduler |
| Core | Retry transient failures | Leases, retry queues, backoff |
| Freshness | Recrawl changing/important pages | Recrawl scheduler |
| Safety | Detect traps and bound resources | Budgets, canonicalization, limits |
| NFR | Horizontal scalability | Partitioned frontier and worker fleet |
| NFR | High availability | Durable queues/state, idempotent workers |
| NFR | Politeness over raw throughput | Per-host next-eligible-time |
| NFR | Observability | Host/error/frontier/freshness metrics |

## 5. Back-of-the-Envelope Estimation

Use round numbers. The purpose is to derive architecture, not to guess Google’s exact workload.

| Dimension | Assumption | Calculation | Approx. |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Target pages | 10B pages | Given interview scale | 10 billion |
| Average page size | 500 KB compressed/body+metadata | 10B × 500 KB | ~5 PB raw |
| Fetch rate | 100K pages/s | 100K × 86,400 | 8.64B/day |
| Inbound bandwidth | 100K × 500 KB | ~50 GB/s | ~400 Gbps |
| Links/page | 50 average | 100K × 50 | 5M discovered URLs/s |
| URL record | ~200 B normalized+metadata | 10B × 200 B | ~2 TB minimum, much more with indexes/history |

> Key implication
> The URL discovery rate can be tens of times larger than the page-fetch rate. Therefore deduplication and frontier admission must be extremely cheap, horizontally scalable, and mostly asynchronous.

## 6. APIs and Internal Contracts

A crawler is mostly an internal pipeline, so queue/event contracts matter more than a public REST API.

| Contract | Example fields | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Seed submission | url, priority, source | Inject initial URLs |
| Frontier task | url_id, normalized_url, host_key, priority, eligible_at, attempt | Work scheduling |
| Fetch result | status, headers, bytes_ref, latency, fetched_at | Downloader output |
| Parse result | canonical_url, outlinks[], content_hash, metadata | Discovery + dedupe |
| Recrawl record | url_id, last_fetch, change_score, next_fetch_at | Freshness scheduling |

## 7. URL Canonicalization — Do This Before Deduplication

Different strings may identify the same resource. If normalization is inconsistent, the crawler wastes capacity and the seen-URL set explodes.

- Lowercase scheme and host; normalize default ports.

- Remove URL fragments because #section is normally client-side navigation.

- Resolve relative links against the page’s base URL.

- Normalize dot segments and obvious encoding differences carefully.

- Apply product policy to known tracking parameters where safe.

- Do not blindly sort/remove arbitrary query parameters: parameter order or presence can change semantics.

- Honor canonical-link hints as signals, not as an unquestionable security boundary.

> Important trade-off
> Aggressive normalization improves deduplication but risks merging distinct resources. Conservative normalization wastes crawl budget but preserves correctness. Start conservative and add domain-aware rules.

## 8. Baseline Single-Machine Design

![8. Baseline Single-Machine Design — source diagram](/diagrams/t-2g5ncln1ngy3-kix-wj0o3kvzh4gh.png)

Baseline crawler loop

- Put seed URLs into a queue.

- Pop a URL; if already seen, skip it.

- Fetch the page.

- Store the page.

- Parse HTML and extract links.

- Normalize each link; add unseen URLs back to the queue.

This is correct for a toy crawler, but fails at internet scale: one queue cannot enforce per-host politeness, seen-URL memory becomes enormous, workers duplicate work, and crashes lose in-flight tasks.

## 9. Why a Plain FIFO Queue Is Not Enough

- Ten consecutive URLs may belong to the same host, causing accidental denial-of-service.

- Important pages and low-value pages receive equal treatment.

- Retries can block fresh work.

- Recrawl tasks have time eligibility, not just arrival order.

- One hot domain can dominate the queue.

- Distributed workers need stable host ownership or coordinated scheduling.

> Core design insight
> The URL frontier is a scheduler, not merely a queue. It must combine priority with politeness.

## 10. High-Level Distributed Architecture

![10. High-Level Distributed Architecture — source diagram](/diagrams/t-2g5ncln1ngy3-kix-2kiffahtmrxf.png)

Distributed Web Crawler — high-level design

> Memorize this flow
> Normalize + dedupe → frontier schedules by priority and host eligibility → worker checks robots/DNS and fetches → parser stores content and emits outlinks → outlinks return through normalization/dedupe → recrawl scheduler re-injects due URLs.

## 11. URL Frontier — Two-Level Scheduling

A common design separates importance from politeness.

| Stage | Responsibility | Typical structure |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Front queues | Priority / importance | Multiple priority queues or weighted queues |
| Host routing | Map URL to host/domain shard | Consistent hash(host) |
| Back queues | Per-host or host-group ordering | FIFO/deque per host |
| Heap | Choose next eligible host | Min-heap by next_allowed_fetch_time |

![11. URL Frontier — Two-Level Scheduling — source diagram](/diagrams/t-2g5ncln1ngy3-kix-5dklj84il56v.png)

URL Frontier: priority first, politeness second

After a worker receives one URL for a host, the scheduler advances that host’s next eligible time. This preserves high global throughput while keeping each external site’s request rate bounded.

## 12. Politeness and Host Scheduling

- Maintain next_allowed_fetch_time per host (or registrable domain, depending on policy).

- Limit concurrent requests per host.

- Use adaptive delay based on robots policy, observed latency, HTTP 429/503, and operator rules.

- Use exponential backoff with jitter after transient failures.

- Do not let thousands of workers independently decide host timing; centralize or partition host ownership.

- Pause or heavily slow domains that explicitly signal overload.

> Why host ownership matters
> If 1,000 workers each keep a local '1 request/sec' counter for example.com, the aggregate can become 1,000 requests/sec. Politeness state must have a shared or uniquely owned authority.

## 13. robots.txt Design

- Fetch /robots.txt before crawling a host when no valid cached policy exists.

- Cache parsed rules by host with an expiry; revalidate periodically.

- Apply rules for the crawler’s user-agent.

- Treat robots fetch failure according to explicit product policy; conservative systems may delay crawling.

- Keep robots evaluation off the expensive hot path by caching compiled rules.

- Record policy version/timestamp for auditability.

robots.txt is not authentication. It is a crawling policy signal. Private or sensitive content must still be protected by the origin.

## 14. DNS Resolution and Connection Management

- Cache DNS results with TTL awareness to avoid resolving every URL.

- Use connection pooling and HTTP keep-alive per origin where safe.

- Bound sockets, response size, header size, redirects, and total fetch time.

- Protect against DNS rebinding / SSRF-style access to internal or forbidden address ranges.

- Re-resolve according to DNS TTL and security policy rather than caching forever.

## 15. URL Deduplication

We need to answer: 'Have we already admitted this normalized URL into our crawl universe?'

| Option | Pros | Cons | Use |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Hash set / KV | Exact | Large random I/O/state | Ground truth |
| Bloom filter | Very compact, fast | False positives | Fast admission prefilter |
| Cuckoo filter | Compact; supports deletion | More complexity | When deletions matter |
| Partitioned KV by URL hash | Scales horizontally | Network lookup | Durable exact state |

> Recommended pattern
> Hash the normalized URL. Use a local/partitioned probabilistic filter to reject most repeats cheaply, then durable exact state when false positives are unacceptable. A Bloom false positive means a page may never be crawled, so tune it to the product’s acceptable miss rate.

## 16. Content Deduplication

Different URLs can serve identical or near-identical content. URL dedupe alone cannot detect mirrors, tracking variants, print pages, or copied pages.

- Compute a cryptographic/content hash for exact duplicates.

- Store content_hash → canonical content reference.

- For near-duplicates, use similarity fingerprints such as SimHash/MinHash as an optional downstream optimization.

- Keep URL metadata even when content bytes are deduplicated; different URLs can have different crawl history and link graph meaning.

## 17. Fetcher Worker Lifecycle

- Receive a leased frontier task.

- Re-check task validity and robots policy.

- Resolve DNS / obtain connection.

- Send bounded HTTP request with crawler identity.

- Follow only a bounded number of redirects; normalize redirect targets.

- Stream response with maximum size and timeout limits.

- Persist raw bytes to object storage.

- Emit metadata + parse job.

- Acknowledge the frontier lease only after durable handoff.

> At-least-once, not exactly-once
> Exactly-once network fetching is not realistic: a worker can fetch successfully and crash before recording completion. Design for occasional duplicate fetches and make downstream writes idempotent.

## 18. Parsing and Link Extraction

- Parse only supported MIME types.

- Extract href/src/canonical and other relevant links according to scope.

- Resolve relative URLs using the final page URL/base tag.

- Normalize and validate schemes; reject javascript:, data:, mailto:, unsupported protocols, etc.

- Attach source-page metadata so ranking/prioritization can use link context.

- Batch discovered URLs before sending them to dedupe/frontier to reduce network overhead.

## 19. Storage Design

| Data | Best fit | Key / partition |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Raw page bytes | Object storage | content hash or URL/version id |
| URL metadata | Distributed KV / wide-column | hash(normalized_url) |
| Seen URL state | Partitioned KV + probabilistic filters | URL hash |
| Host state | KV / scheduler state | host hash |
| Robots policy | Cache + durable metadata | host |
| Fetch events | Durable log/stream | time/partition |
| Link graph edges | Batch/graph-oriented storage | source URL id |
| Recrawl schedule | Time buckets / priority scheduler | next_fetch_at + priority |

## 20. Partitioning the Crawler

Partition primarily by host for politeness ownership, while URL metadata can be partitioned by URL hash.

- Consistent-hash host_key to frontier/scheduler shards.

- All URLs for a host should normally be controlled by one logical scheduler owner at a time.

- Replicate scheduler state for failover, but avoid two active owners issuing requests simultaneously.

- URL metadata shards can use hash(normalized_url) for even distribution.

- Object storage naturally scales independently of worker ownership.

> Do not partition only by URL hash for scheduling
> Two different URL hashes from the same host could land on different workers and independently violate the host’s crawl rate. Scheduling partitioning must preserve a host-level authority.

## 21. Task Leases, Crashes, and Retries

- Frontier gives a worker a lease with visibility timeout rather than permanently removing the URL.

- Worker periodically extends lease for long fetches if needed.

- On successful durable handoff, acknowledge task.

- If worker dies, lease expires and task becomes eligible again.

- Retry only transient classes: timeout, selected 5xx, 429, connection failures.

- Use exponential backoff + jitter; cap attempts and move poison tasks to a dead-letter/inspection path.

- 4xx such as 404 usually should not be aggressively retried; schedule a distant recrawl only if product policy requires.

## 22. Recrawling and Freshness

A production crawler is continuous. The question becomes not only 'what have we never seen?' but 'what should we revisit next?'

| Signal | Effect on recrawl |
| --- | --- |
| Page changes frequently | Shorter interval |
| High importance/PageRank-like score | Shorter interval |
| News/homepage/feed | Shorter interval |
| Repeatedly unchanged | Increase interval |
| Last-Modified / ETag | Conditional fetch opportunity |
| 429/slow host | Longer interval / lower concurrency |
| 404/410 repeatedly | Very long interval or retire |

A simple adaptive rule can maintain a change score from recent fetch history and compute next_fetch_at. Use conditional GET with ETag/If-Modified-Since to save bandwidth when origins support it.

## 23. Prioritization

- Seed/source quality.

- Link popularity or graph importance.

- Depth from trusted seed.

- Freshness/change probability.

- Content category/business value.

- Domain quality and spam score.

- Recrawl urgency.

- Fairness so low-priority domains are not starved forever.

> Avoid one magic score
> In practice, use priority classes plus bounded scoring. It is easier to reason about starvation, freshness SLAs, and operational overrides than an unconstrained single floating-point score.

## 24. Crawler Traps and Infinite URL Spaces

Real sites can generate effectively infinite URLs: calendars with 'next month', faceted search combinations, session IDs, random parameters, or cyclic redirect/link structures.

- Per-host URL/page budget.

- Maximum crawl depth for low-trust discovery.

- Maximum unique query-parameter combinations per path template.

- Detect rapidly growing URL patterns and repeated low-value templates.

- Strip known session/tracking parameters where policy allows.

- Bound redirects and reject redirect loops.

- Use content duplicate rates as a signal to reduce exploration.

- Operator/domain rules for known traps.

> Interview signal
> Deduplication does not solve an infinite URL generator because every generated URL may be unique. You need budgets and pattern-based trap detection.

## 25. JavaScript-Rendered Pages

Headless browser rendering is far more expensive than ordinary HTTP fetch + HTML parse.

- Keep static fetch as the default path.

- Detect pages that likely require rendering.

- Send only selected pages to a separate browser-rendering pool.

- Apply stricter CPU/time/network budgets.

- Cache rendered results and isolate untrusted scripts.

- Do not let browser rendering reduce baseline crawler throughput.

## 26. Handling Large and Dangerous Content

- Inspect Content-Type and Content-Length before downloading when available.

- Stream with hard byte limits; abort oversized responses.

- Decompression-bomb protection: cap decompressed bytes and compression ratio.

- Timeout DNS, connect, headers, body idle, and total request duration.

- Sandbox parsers/renderers for untrusted content.

- Block private/link-local/internal address ranges to prevent SSRF-style crawling.

- Rate-limit redirects and cross-scheme transitions.

## 27. Failure Scenarios

| Failure | Expected behavior |
| --- | --- |
| Worker crash | Lease expires; another worker retries |
| Frontier shard crash | Fail over replicated state; temporarily pause owned hosts |
| Dedupe store degraded | Buffer/retry admissions or use bounded local filters; avoid uncontrolled duplicate storm |
| Object storage slow | Backpressure fetchers; do not acknowledge before durable handoff |
| Parser backlog | Scale parsers / reduce fetch intake |
| DNS outage | Use valid cache entries; backoff new resolutions |
| Robots service/cache outage | Use last valid policy or conservative pause according to policy |
| One host returns 429 | Backoff that host only |
| Global traffic spike | Frontier/backpressure protects downstream systems |

## 28. Backpressure

Every stage must be able to slow its producer. Otherwise a parser or storage incident becomes an unbounded memory/queue incident.

- Durable bounded queues between major stages.

- Queue lag and age metrics.

- Fetcher admission tied to parser/storage capacity.

- Priority-aware shedding: preserve important recrawls and critical seeds first.

- Host scheduling remains polite even while the internal system is overloaded.

## 29. Multi-Region Design

- Do not have multiple regions independently crawl the same host without coordinated ownership.

- Assign hosts/domains to a home crawl region or globally coordinated scheduler shard.

- Replicate durable metadata/content asynchronously to other regions.

- Failover host ownership using epochs/fencing tokens so old owners cannot continue issuing work.

- Choose crawl egress regions based on policy, latency, legal requirements, and origin behavior.

> Fencing token
> When ownership changes, attach a monotonically increasing epoch to leases. Workers from an old epoch cannot commit scheduler state after a new owner has taken over.

## 30. Observability and SLOs

| Metric | Why it matters |
| --- | --- |
| Pages fetched/sec | Throughput |
| Frontier size + oldest age | Backlog/starvation |
| Per-host request rate/concurrency | Politeness |
| HTTP status distribution | Origin/system health |
| Fetch latency + timeout rate | Network health |
| Duplicate URL/content rate | Crawl efficiency |
| Bytes/page and bandwidth | Capacity/cost |
| Robots deny rate | Policy behavior |
| Recrawl freshness lag | Product quality |
| Parser/storage queue lag | Backpressure |
| Trap detection / budget exhaustions | Safety/efficiency |

## 31. Evolution: From Simple to Production

| Version | Design addition | Trigger |
| --- | --- | --- |
| V1 | Single queue + fetch + parse | Prototype |
| V2 | URL normalization + seen set | Duplicate work |
| V3 | Distributed workers + durable leases | Throughput/failures |
| V4 | Host-partitioned frontier + politeness heap | Internet-safe crawling |
| V5 | Robots/DNS caches + connection pools | Efficiency/compliance |
| V6 | Content dedupe + object storage | Storage efficiency |
| V7 | Priority + adaptive recrawl | Freshness/quality |
| V8 | Trap detection + budgets + JS render pool | Real web complexity |
| V9 | Regional ownership + fencing | Global resilience |

## 32. Final Production Architecture

The production design separates discovery/admission, scheduling, fetching, parsing, storage, and freshness.

- Admission: normalize URLs, validate scope, deduplicate, attach priority.

- Scheduling: partition by host; maintain per-host queues and next-eligible-time heap.

- Fetching: leased tasks, robots/DNS cache, bounded HTTP client, connection pooling.

- Processing: durable raw content, parser/extractor, content fingerprinting.

- Feedback: discovered URLs re-enter admission; fetch history feeds recrawl scoring.

- Reliability: leases, retries, backoff, checkpoints, replicated scheduler state, fencing.

- Safety: host budgets, trap detection, response limits, SSRF protection, JS isolation.

> Final design in one sentence
> Use a host-partitioned, priority-aware URL frontier that leases eligible URLs to stateless fetchers; persist content durably, parse links asynchronously, deduplicate before re-admission, and continuously reschedule pages using change/importance signals while enforcing robots, politeness, budgets, and retries.

## 33. Consistency and Delivery Semantics

- Seen-URL state should be durable, but temporary eventual consistency is acceptable if duplicates are tolerable.

- Fetcher tasks are at-least-once.

- Raw-content writes should be idempotent by crawl/version identifier or content hash.

- Host scheduler ownership needs stronger coordination than ordinary URL metadata because duplicate active owners can violate politeness.

- Recrawl scheduling is naturally eventually consistent; a slightly late revisit is usually acceptable.

## 34. Technology Choices — Explain the Shape, Not the Brand

| Need | Technology shape | Examples you could mention |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Durable event/queue | Partitioned append log or durable queue | Kafka/Pulsar/SQS-like |
| URL metadata | Distributed KV/wide-column | Cassandra/DynamoDB/Bigtable-like |
| Raw bytes | Object storage | S3/GCS-like |
| Hot robots/DNS | Distributed/local cache | Redis + in-process cache |
| Scheduler | Custom partitioned frontier service | Heap + per-host queues |
| Stream processing | Scalable consumers | Flink/Spark/Kafka Streams-like |

In an interview, first derive the requirement. Mention a product only after explaining why its data model and failure behavior fit.

## 35. Key Trade-offs

| Decision | Option A | Option B | Reasonable choice |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| URL dedupe | Exact only | Probabilistic prefilter | Hybrid |
| Scheduling | Global FIFO | Host-aware frontier | Host-aware |
| Delivery | Exactly once | At least once + idempotency | At least once |
| Rendering | Render every page | Selective browser pool | Selective |
| Recrawl | Fixed interval | Adaptive | Adaptive |
| Multi-region | Every region crawls everything | Host ownership | Host ownership |
| Normalization | Aggressive | Conservative | Conservative + learned rules |

## 36. Common Interview Mistakes

- Calling Kafka/SQS the URL frontier without explaining host politeness.

- Using a global FIFO queue.

- Using only URL-hash partitioning and forgetting host-level request limits.

- Claiming exactly-once crawling.

- Putting all discovered URLs into memory.

- Assuming a Bloom filter has no correctness cost.

- Treating robots.txt as a security mechanism.

- Thinking dedupe alone prevents crawler traps.

- Rendering JavaScript for every page.

- Forgetting backpressure, retries, and poison tasks.

- Storing raw HTML in the scheduler database.

- Designing search indexing/ranking instead of the crawler.

## 37. How to Present Web Crawler in a 45-Minute Interview

| Time | Coverage |
| --- | --- |
| 0–5 min | Clarify scope, content types, continuous recrawl, robots/politeness |
| 5–10 min | Estimate fetch rate, bandwidth, URL discovery amplification |
| 10–17 min | Baseline loop + HLD |
| 17–27 min | URL frontier: priority + per-host queues + eligible-time heap |
| 27–33 min | Normalization + URL/content dedupe |
| 33–38 min | Leases, retries, failures, backpressure |
| 38–42 min | Recrawl, traps, JS rendering, multi-region |
| 42–45 min | Trade-offs + concise summary |

> Do not memorize every paragraph
> Memorize the architecture story: normalize/dedupe → host-aware frontier → leased fetch → durable store → parse/extract → re-admit links → adaptive recrawl. Then keep politeness, traps, retries, and ownership as your deep dives.

## 38. Interviewer Follow-Ups — Complete Discussion

Follow-up: Why not use a normal queue?

Answer: A normal FIFO queue does not understand host-level timing. If many queued URLs belong to one host, many workers can hit it simultaneously. The frontier must schedule by both priority and each host’s next eligible time.

Follow-up: How do you guarantee politeness with thousands of workers?

Answer: Give each host one logical scheduler owner. That owner controls concurrency and next_allowed_fetch_time. Workers receive leases only when the host is eligible. Replication is for failover, not independent active scheduling.

Follow-up: How do you avoid crawling the same URL twice?

Answer: Normalize first, hash the normalized URL, and check durable seen state. A Bloom/Cuckoo filter can cheaply reject most repeats before exact storage. Occasional duplicate network fetches are still possible because of crashes/races, so downstream writes remain idempotent.

Follow-up: What is the difference between URL dedupe and content dedupe?

Answer: URL dedupe prevents scheduling the same normalized address repeatedly. Content dedupe detects different URLs returning identical or similar bytes. We generally preserve URL-level metadata even if the stored content blob is shared.

Follow-up: Can a Bloom filter cause data loss?

Answer: Yes. A false positive can say 'seen' for a never-seen URL, causing the crawler to skip it. Therefore size it for a very low false-positive rate or use it only as a prefilter before exact state when completeness matters.

Follow-up: How do you handle worker crashes?

Answer: Lease tasks with a visibility timeout. Do not permanently dequeue at assignment. A successful worker acknowledges only after durable handoff. If it crashes, the lease expires and another worker can retry.

Follow-up: Why is exactly-once fetching unrealistic?

Answer: The external HTTP request and our internal commit cannot be one atomic transaction. A worker can receive the response and crash before recording completion. At-least-once plus idempotent storage is simpler and robust.

Follow-up: How do you handle a host returning 429?

Answer: Slow only that host: increase next eligible time, reduce concurrency, honor Retry-After when appropriate, and use exponential backoff with jitter. Global crawler capacity can continue serving other hosts.

Follow-up: How do you prevent crawler traps?

Answer: Use per-host budgets, depth limits, query-pattern controls, redirect bounds, content-duplicate signals, and anomaly detection for rapidly expanding URL templates. Unique-URL dedupe alone cannot stop an infinite generator.

Follow-up: How do you decide when to recrawl?

Answer: Estimate change probability and importance from history. Frequently changing or important pages get shorter intervals; repeatedly unchanged pages back off. ETag/Last-Modified enable cheaper conditional requests.

Follow-up: How would you crawl JavaScript-heavy sites?

Answer: Keep a separate, expensive browser-rendering pool. Static fetch remains the default. Detect pages needing rendering and enforce strict CPU/time/network limits so dynamic pages cannot consume the entire crawler.

Follow-up: How do you make the crawler multi-region?

Answer: Assign host ownership to one region/shard at a time. Replicate metadata/content asynchronously. During failover use epochs/fencing tokens so the previous owner cannot continue issuing valid work.

Follow-up: What happens if the dedupe store is down?

Answer: Prefer backpressure/buffering over admitting everything blindly. A bounded local filter can reduce repeats temporarily, but prolonged exact-state loss should slow discovery to avoid a duplicate storm.

Follow-up: How do you prioritize pages?

Answer: Use priority classes informed by seed trust, graph importance, freshness urgency, domain quality, depth, and product value. Add fairness so low-priority work is not permanently starved.

Follow-up: Where do you store raw pages?

Answer: Object storage. Large immutable blobs are cheap and scalable there; the metadata database stores references, status, timestamps, hashes, and scheduling information.

Follow-up: How do you prevent SSRF-like behavior?

Answer: Reject forbidden schemes and internal/private/link-local address ranges, validate redirects, re-check resolved addresses, bound DNS behavior, and sandbox untrusted rendering/parsing.

## 39. Detailed Interview Questions with Answers

1. What is the core design insight in a web crawler?

Answer: The hard component is the frontier scheduler. Fetching HTTP is easy; deciding which URL is eligible now while respecting priority, host politeness, deduplication, retries, and recrawl timing is the distributed-systems problem.

2. What happens to a newly discovered URL?

Answer: Resolve and normalize it, validate scope/scheme, derive host key, perform seen-URL admission, attach priority, and route it to the frontier shard responsible for that host.

3. Why partition scheduler work by host?

Answer: Politeness is a host-level invariant. A single logical owner can enforce one concurrency/rate policy. Random URL partitioning could create many independent owners for the same origin.

4. How does the eligible-host heap work?

Answer: Each host queue has next_allowed_fetch_time. The scheduler keeps hosts ordered by that timestamp. When the minimum host becomes eligible, it leases one or more allowed URLs, then advances that host’s timestamp and reinserts it.

5. What if one host has millions of URLs?

Answer: Its queue can live in durable segmented storage while the scheduler keeps only the active head and timing metadata in memory. Per-host crawl budgets and prioritization prevent it from monopolizing resources.

6. What if a page contains five million links?

Answer: Apply page-level extraction limits and batch processing. Validate/normalize/dedupe incrementally. One pathological page should not create an unbounded memory spike or frontier flood.

7. How do you deal with redirects?

Answer: Follow a bounded number, detect loops, validate every target, and treat the final URL as a discovered/canonicalization signal. Persist redirect metadata because it is useful for future scheduling and indexing.

8. How do you handle duplicate pages served under many URLs?

Answer: Compute exact content hashes after fetch. Reuse the content blob while retaining per-URL crawl records. Optional similarity fingerprints can identify near duplicates.

9. How do you reduce bandwidth?

Answer: Conditional GETs with ETag/If-Modified-Since, adaptive recrawl intervals, content compression, connection reuse, and not fetching unsupported/oversized resources.

10. How do you avoid starving small sites?

Answer: Use weighted/fair scheduling across priority classes and host queues. Priority influences selection but does not permit one domain or class to consume all crawler capacity.

11. What state must be strongly coordinated?

Answer: Host scheduler ownership/epoch and any state whose duplication would violate politeness. Seen-URL and recrawl metadata can often tolerate eventual consistency because duplicate or slightly delayed work is acceptable.

12. How would you recover a lost frontier shard?

Answer: Promote a replica or reconstruct active scheduling state from durable host queues/checkpoints. Ownership changes receive a new epoch. Old leases/owners are rejected using fencing.

13. What are the most important crawler SLOs?

Answer: Fetch throughput alone is insufficient. Track politeness violations, freshness lag for important pages, frontier age, error/timeout rate, duplicate work, parser/storage lag, and crawl coverage.

14. Would you use BFS or DFS?

Answer: Neither directly at scale. BFS is a useful conceptual starting point, but production crawling is priority- and host-time-driven. DFS can over-focus on one site and is especially poor for broad discovery.

15. What database schema would you use for URL metadata?

Answer: Key by URL hash or stable URL id and store normalized URL, host key, status, last/next fetch times, content hash, retry state, priority, robots/canonical signals, and version/history references.

16. What if two workers fetch the same URL concurrently?

Answer: It is inefficient but should remain correct. Use leases/admission state to reduce it, and idempotent version/content writes so duplicate completion does not corrupt metadata.

17. Why not store all frontier URLs in Kafka only?

Answer: A log is useful transport/durability, but frontier scheduling needs mutable per-host state, eligibility times, priority, and controlled leasing. A plain partitioned log does not by itself implement those semantics.

18. How would you crawl 100K pages/sec without overwhelming DNS?

Answer: Use TTL-aware distributed/local DNS caches, asynchronous resolution, bounded resolver concurrency, and connection reuse. DNS is part of the capacity plan, not an afterthought.

19. What should happen when robots.txt changes?

Answer: Expire/revalidate cached rules, version policies, and ensure future leases use the new policy. If newly disallowed URLs are already queued, the worker/scheduler should re-check policy before fetch.

20. What is your final architecture summary?

Answer: A distributed admission layer normalizes and deduplicates URLs, then routes them to a host-partitioned frontier. The frontier combines priority queues with per-host eligibility and leases tasks to fetchers. Fetchers obey robots/DNS/security limits, store bytes durably, and emit parse jobs. Parsers extract links back into admission. Fetch history drives adaptive recrawl, while leases, retries, backpressure, budgets, and fencing provide reliability and safety.

## 40. 30-Second Final Interview Answer

> 30-second summary
> I would normalize and deduplicate every discovered URL before admitting it to a distributed URL frontier. The frontier is partitioned by host and combines priority with per-host next-eligible-time, so thousands of workers can crawl at high throughput without violating politeness. Workers receive leased tasks, check cached robots and DNS state, perform bounded HTTP fetches, persist raw content to object storage, and emit parse jobs. Parsers extract links that re-enter admission. Durable metadata tracks seen URLs, retries, content hashes, and fetch history; an adaptive recrawl scheduler revisits important or frequently changing pages. At scale I add backpressure, trap detection, host budgets, fencing for failover, and a separate browser-rendering pool for selected JavaScript pages.

## 41. Final Checklist

- Clarified scope and separated crawling from indexing/ranking.

- Estimated fetch rate, bandwidth, storage, and link amplification.

- Explained URL normalization before dedupe.

- Designed host-aware frontier rather than FIFO.

- Explained robots.txt, DNS cache, connection reuse, and politeness.

- Covered URL and content deduplication.

- Used leases + at-least-once + idempotency.

- Covered retries, backoff, poison tasks, and backpressure.

- Explained adaptive recrawl and conditional GET.

- Handled traps, infinite spaces, oversized content, redirects, and JS rendering.

- Explained partitioning, failover, multi-region ownership, and fencing.

- Finished with trade-offs and a concise architecture story.

notes.title: Design a Metrics & Monitoring System
notes.description: Goal Design a large-scale metrics and monitoring platform that ingests billions of time-series samples, supports high-cardinality labels, stores data efficientl
notes.content:
Design a Metrics & Monitoring System

Advanced System Design Interview Guide

Problem 32 | Datadog / Prometheus-style Metrics, Time-Series Storage, Querying & Alerting

> Goal
> Design a large-scale metrics and monitoring platform that ingests billions of time-series samples, supports high-cardinality labels, stores data efficiently at multiple retention tiers, serves dashboards and ad-hoc queries, evaluates alert rules, and remains available during traffic spikes or partial failures.

> Core interview idea
> Monitoring workloads are fundamentally time-series workloads: append-heavy ingestion, label-based filtering, range aggregation, retention/downsampling, and alert evaluation. The biggest traps are cardinality explosion, hot shards, expensive wide queries, and allowing the query/alert path to overload ingestion.

## 1. Functional Requirements

| Capability | Requirements |
| --- | --- |
| Ingestion | Push and/or pull numeric metrics with timestamp and labels |
| Dashboards | Graph metrics over time, group/filter by labels |
| Query | Range, aggregation, rate, percentile, top-K, joins where supported |
| Alerting | Threshold, rate, absence, composite rules |
| Retention | Raw recent data + downsampled historical data |
| Metadata | Metric names, labels, units, ownership |
| Multi-tenancy | Tenant isolation, quotas, RBAC |
| Integrations | Agents, exporters, cloud services, application SDKs |

## 2. Non-Functional Requirements

- Very high sustained write throughput.

- Low-latency ingestion even during spikes.

- Dashboard queries should usually complete in sub-second to a few seconds.

- Query load must not block ingestion.

- High availability with partial regional or shard failures.

- Durable enough for operational monitoring while accepting some trade-offs for cost.

- Support many tenants and protect the system from noisy neighbors.

- Retention should be cost-aware: recent data is hot; old data is mostly aggregated.

## 3. Scope and Clarifying Questions

- Focus on numeric metrics and time-series data, not full-text logs.

- Support counters, gauges, histograms/summaries, and derived rates.

- Prometheus-style labels are in scope.

- Tracing is an extension, not the core design.

- Alert evaluation is near-real-time and must tolerate delayed/missing samples.

- Multi-region federation is included architecturally.

- Exact SQL-like analytics across arbitrary dimensions is not the primary workload.

## 4. Core Data Model

| Concept | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Metric name | Example: http_requests_total |
| Label set | service=api, region=delhi, status=500 |
| Series | Unique metric name + exact label set |
| Sample | timestamp + numeric value |
| Exemplar | Optional pointer to trace/event |
| Tenant | Isolation boundary |
| Retention tier | Raw, downsampled, archival |

## 5. Series Identity

> Critical concept
> A time series is uniquely identified by metric name plus the full label set. If one metric has 10 label dimensions and each dimension has many values, the number of distinct series can explode multiplicatively. Cardinality—not just raw sample rate—is a first-class capacity limit.

## 6. Example Metric

| Field | Example |
| --- | --- |
| Metric | http_requests_total |
| Labels | service="checkout", region="in-north", status="500", method="POST" |
| Series key | Hash(metric + sorted labels) |
| Sample | 2026-09-30T20:10:05Z -> 84521 |
| Query | rate(http_requests_total{service="checkout",status="500"}[5m]) |

## 7. Capacity Estimation

| Dimension | Illustrative scale | Implication |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Active series | 100M+ | Cardinality-aware partitioning |
| Samples/sec | 10M+ | Horizontally scalable ingest |
| Sample size | ~16-40 bytes raw plus indexing overhead | Compression essential |
| Retention | 15-30d raw; months/years rolled-up | Tiered storage |
| Dashboards | Millions/day | Query cache + preaggregation |
| Alerts | Millions of active rules | Distributed evaluator |
| Tenants | Thousands+ | Quotas and fairness |

## 8. High-Level Architecture

![8. High-Level Architecture — source diagram](/diagrams/t-ssq2zffcp2f8-kix-hx6s4i5lmwcy.png)

## 9. Push vs Pull Ingestion

| Model | Strengths | Weaknesses |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Pull / scrape | Service discovery, target health, simpler backpressure | Harder across firewalls/mobile/ephemeral jobs |
| Push | Good for short-lived jobs, agents, external integrations | Harder target health semantics; risk of unbounded producers |
| Hybrid | Flexible | More operational complexity |

A Datadog-like platform commonly uses agents pushing to a hosted backend; Prometheus commonly scrapes targets. The backend architecture after ingestion still converges around time-series partitioning, compression, retention, querying and alerting.

## 10. Ingestion Gateway

- Authenticate tenant/API key.

- Validate metric syntax and timestamp bounds.

- Apply quotas and sample/series limits.

- Normalize/sort labels for deterministic series identity.

- Batch samples and compress network payloads.

- Route by tenant + series hash to ingest shard.

- Reject or sample abusive/high-cardinality producers before they destabilize the platform.

## 11. Batch Ingestion

- Never send one network request per sample.

- Agents buffer hundreds/thousands of samples per batch.

- Use compressed protobuf-like or remote-write payloads.

- Batching amortizes TLS, headers, serialization and routing overhead.

- Bound client buffers; if the backend is unavailable, spill to disk or drop according to product policy.

- Expose dropped-sample counters so observability failures are themselves observable.

## 12. Time-Series Partitioning

- Hash each series ID to an ingest/storage shard.

- All samples for one series should preferably land on one logical owner over a time window.

- This improves compression, append locality, ordering and query pruning.

- Partition by tenant first or include tenant in hash to isolate namespaces.

- Time also becomes a physical partition dimension: series + block time range.

- Very large tenants may need dedicated shard groups.

## 13. Write Path

- Ingestion gateway receives compressed batch.

- Resolve each metric+label set to series ID.

- Partition batch by owning ingest shard.

- Shard appends recent samples to WAL and in-memory head chunks.

- Background process encodes chunks using time-series compression.

- Completed immutable blocks are flushed to local/remote durable storage.

- Metadata/index references the new block/time range.

- Compaction later merges and rolls up older blocks.

## 14. Time-Series Compression

- Timestamps are usually regular; delta-of-delta encoding compresses them well.

- Floating values often use XOR-style compression against prior value.

- Counter values may be monotonic and highly compressible.

- Chunks store many consecutive samples for one series.

- Compression ratio improves dramatically when samples of a series are contiguous.

- Do not store each sample as a full row with repeated metric/label strings.

## 15. Storage Layout

| Layer | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| WAL | Recover recent accepted writes |
| Head block | Mutable recent samples |
| Immutable blocks | Compressed time-partitioned TSDB data |
| Index | Label -> series/postings mapping |
| Object store | Cheap durable historical blocks |
| Cache | Hot block/index/query results |

## 16. Block-Based TSDB

![16. Block-Based TSDB — source diagram](/diagrams/t-ssq2zffcp2f8-kix-o467iebptq9p.png)

## 17. Label Index

- Querying by labels requires inverted indexes from label pair -> matching series IDs.

- Example: service=checkout maps to a postings list of series IDs.

- Multiple label filters intersect postings lists.

- Regex/wildcard label queries can be very expensive.

- Store index per time block or segment so old data can be independently compacted/expired.

- High-cardinality labels inflate both series count and index size.

## 18. Cardinality Explosion

| Bad label | Why dangerous |
| --- | --- |
| user_id | Potentially millions of unique values |
| request_id | Nearly one unique value per request |
| timestamp | Creates unique series continuously |
| session_id | Large unbounded cardinality |
| full_url with IDs | Path values explode |

- Prefer bounded dimensions such as service, region, status, endpoint template.

- Keep unique IDs in logs/traces, not metric labels.

- Enforce per-tenant cardinality budgets.

- Detect rapidly growing label values and alert/drop before storage damage.

- Provide cardinality explorer so users can identify expensive labels.

## 19. Counters, Gauges, Histograms

| Type | Semantics | Typical query |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Counter | Monotonically increases except reset | rate(), increase() |
| Gauge | Arbitrary current value | avg/max/current |
| Histogram | Bucket counts + sum/count | percentile approximation |
| Summary | Client-calculated quantiles | Limited aggregatability |

Histograms are generally more aggregatable across instances than client-side quantile summaries because bucket counts can be summed.

## 20. Counter Reset Handling

- Process restarts reset counters to zero.

- rate() must detect decreases and interpret them as reset rather than massive negative traffic.

- Long scrape gaps increase uncertainty.

- Store raw counter samples; calculate rate over a range at query/evaluation time or via safe rollups.

- Use monotonic semantics metadata where possible.

## 21. Query Architecture

![21. Query Architecture — source diagram](/diagrams/t-ssq2zffcp2f8-kix-5bay4ccf9q4d.png)

## 22. Query Planner

- Parse expression and determine time range/resolution.

- Resolve label matchers into candidate series using index.

- Split query by time block and/or shard.

- Push down aggregations where possible.

- Choose raw vs downsampled tier based on requested range/resolution.

- Run shard queries in parallel with bounded concurrency.

- Merge partial aggregates at query frontend.

## 23. Query Cost Controls

- Limit maximum time range and number of matched series per request.

- Estimate cost before execution using index cardinality/time-block count.

- Use tenant query quotas and concurrency limits.

- Kill queries that exceed memory/CPU budgets.

- Prefer step/resolution-aware downsampling for year-long dashboards.

- Cache repeated dashboard queries, especially aligned time windows.

## 24. Dashboard Query Caching

- Dashboards often re-request the same panels every refresh interval.

- Cache historical portions that cannot change.

- Only query the newest tail interval on refresh.

- Use cache keys including tenant, expression, time range and step.

- Align ranges to stable time buckets to improve hit rate.

- Do not serve cached results past freshness requirements for alerts.

## 25. Downsampling

| Tier | Example | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Raw | 10s samples for 15 days | Incident debugging |
| 1m rollup | 1m avg/min/max/count for 90 days | Operational trends |
| 1h rollup | Hourly aggregates for 2 years | Long-term capacity |

- Downsampling cuts storage and query cost for long ranges.

- Keep enough statistics to preserve useful aggregates: count, sum, min, max, histogram buckets where needed.

- Average-of-averages is wrong when bucket counts differ; store sum/count.

- Rollup jobs must be idempotent and versioned.

## 26. Retention and Tiering

- Recent blocks stay on fast local/SSD or hot object-cache tier.

- Older immutable blocks move to cheaper object storage.

- Retention deletes entire time blocks when possible.

- Different tenants/metrics may have different retention policies.

- Legal/compliance retention can differ from operational default.

- Index metadata must expire consistently with underlying blocks.

## 27. Alerting Architecture

![27. Alerting Architecture — source diagram](/diagrams/t-ssq2zffcp2f8-kix-ejptz5cjku5t.png)

## 28. Alert Rule State Machine

| State | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| OK | Condition false |
| PENDING | Condition true but for-duration not yet met |
| FIRING | Condition true for required duration |
| RESOLVED | Previously firing, now healthy |
| NO_DATA | Insufficient/missing samples depending policy |

- Alert state must be durable enough to avoid duplicate pages on every evaluator restart.

- Use dedupe/grouping keys for notifications.

- Evaluation time and data timestamp are different concepts.

- Late data policy should be explicit.

## 29. Alert Scheduling

- Shard rules by tenant/rule ID across evaluator workers.

- Use leases/ownership so only one active evaluator owns a rule at a time.

- Persist last evaluation state/checkpoint.

- Randomize/jitter schedules to avoid every rule firing exactly on the minute.

- Batch rules that query similar series where possible.

- Do not let an expensive alert monopolize query capacity.

## 30. Missing Data Semantics

- Missing samples may mean service down, scrape failed, target removed, or simply sparse metric.

- Alerts can treat missing as OK, firing, or explicit NO_DATA depending rule.

- Generate 'up' / scrape health metrics in pull systems.

- Use staleness markers/TTL to distinguish old values from live values.

- Never silently hold the last value forever for alert evaluation unless metric semantics justify it.

## 31. High Availability for Ingestion

- Ingestion gateways are stateless and horizontally scaled.

- Series partitions are replicated or backed by durable WAL/object storage.

- Client/agent retries use bounded backoff and dedupe/ordering semantics where needed.

- If one ingest shard is unavailable, route to replica/failover owner or buffer temporarily.

- Protect against retry storms with admission control.

- Define whether the system favors accepting duplicate samples or dropping data during uncertainty.

## 32. Duplicate Samples

- Agents can retry the same batch after timeout.

- Series storage can deduplicate exact timestamp/value samples or accept last-write policy.

- Out-of-order samples need a bounded acceptance window.

- Too-old samples may go to a backfill path rather than mutable head blocks.

- Deduplication key can include tenant, series ID, timestamp and source identity where required.

## 33. Out-of-Order and Late Data

- Distributed systems and agents do not guarantee perfect timestamp order.

- Allow a bounded out-of-order window in the head block.

- Beyond the window, route to special backfill compaction or reject.

- Late writes to immutable blocks are expensive because they require block rewrite/overlay.

- Alerting generally evaluates on a watermark/delay window to reduce false NO_DATA.

## 34. Metadata / Series Registry

- Keep metric descriptors, label keys, units, owner/team, type and cardinality estimates.

- Series registry maps normalized label set to internal series ID.

- Cache hot series mappings in ingestion nodes.

- Do not require a centralized RPC for every new sample.

- New-series creation is the expensive path; existing-series append should be cheap.

## 35. Multi-Tenancy

| Resource | Isolation control |
| --- | --- |
| Ingestion | Samples/sec and active-series quotas |
| Storage | Retention and byte quotas |
| Query | Concurrency, scanned series/bytes |
| Alerting | Rule/evaluation quotas |
| Cardinality | New series/sec and max active series |
| Network | Per-tenant rate limits |

> Noisy-neighbor lesson
> One tenant accidentally adding user_id as a label can create millions of series in minutes. Cardinality admission control must exist before data reaches deep storage.

## 36. Hot Shards

- Hashing by series ID distributes series, but a single extremely high-frequency series can still be hot.

- Batch writes per series and compress in memory.

- Rate-limit absurd sample frequency; metrics usually do not need microsecond sampling.

- Shard a logical metric across source instances naturally through labels, then aggregate at query time.

- Very large tenants can use dedicated ingestion/storage shard pools.

## 37. Compaction

- Merge small immutable blocks into larger blocks.

- Rebuild compact indexes/postings.

- Deduplicate overlapping blocks after retries/backfill.

- Generate downsampled blocks.

- Delete expired source blocks only after rollup succeeds.

- Rate-limit compaction to avoid stealing I/O from queries and ingestion.

## 38. Object Storage as Historical Tier

- Immutable TSDB blocks map well to object storage.

- Store index/chunk files under content/versioned block IDs.

- Keep a local cache for hot index/chunks.

- Query frontend can fan out historical reads to stateless store-gateway workers.

- Object storage gives cheap durability but higher latency than local SSD, so caching and range-read efficiency matter.

## 39. Multi-Region Strategy

| Model | Pros | Cons |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Regional independent monitoring | Low latency, blast-radius isolation | Global queries need federation |
| Replicate all raw metrics globally | Simple global read | Very expensive |
| Regional ingest + global rollups | Balanced cost | Global raw drill-down limited |
| Central ingest | Simpler semantics | WAN dependency/latency |

- Operational monitoring should usually remain useful even if WAN between regions is down.

- Keep regional metrics local and federate/replicate selected aggregates globally.

- Global dashboard queries fan out to regions or read global rollups.

- Alert rules tied to a region should not depend on another region's availability.

## 40. Federation

- Regional clusters expose selected aggregated metrics to a higher-level global cluster.

- Federation reduces raw cardinality and WAN bandwidth.

- Use recording/precomputed rules to export service/region-level SLI metrics.

- Global cluster stores fewer long-lived series.

- Keep local raw details for incident investigation.

## 41. SLI / SLO Support

- Metrics platform should efficiently compute request success rate, latency distribution and availability.

- Use counters/histograms rather than one series per request.

- Recording rules precompute expensive rates/ratios.

- Error-budget burn alerts compare short and long windows.

- SLO evaluation is an important workload but should still use bounded, pre-aggregatable metrics.

## 42. Recording Rules / Materialized Metrics

- Evaluate expensive expressions periodically and write results back as new time series.

- Dashboards/alerts then query the precomputed series.

- Useful for repeated aggregations across thousands of instances.

- Adds storage and eventual freshness trade-off.

- Rule evaluation must be idempotent across retries and avoid double-writing buckets.

## 43. Failure Scenarios

| Failure | Expected behavior |
| --- | --- |
| Ingestion gateway dies | Client retries another gateway |
| One ingest shard down | Replica/failover or temporary buffering |
| Object store slow | Recent dashboards continue; historical queries degrade |
| Query fan-out partial | Return partial/error with shard visibility |
| Alert evaluator restarts | Recover durable rule state, avoid duplicate page |
| Cardinality spike | Throttle/drop new series, protect existing workloads |
| Compaction backlog | Storage/query cost rises; ingestion stays prioritized |
| WAN region split | Regional monitoring/alerts continue independently |
| Agent offline | Gap/no-data semantics, local buffer if configured |

## 44. Backpressure

- Bound ingestion queues at every stage.

- Agents receive 429/retry-after or locally buffer/drop according to policy.

- Prefer dropping low-priority telemetry over crashing the monitoring system.

- Compaction/downsampling should yield to foreground ingestion.

- Query concurrency is capped separately from write capacity.

- Alert evaluation has reserved capacity so dashboards cannot starve paging.

## 45. Observability of the Observability System

- Track ingest accepted/dropped samples, batch latency and new-series creation.

- Track active series and cardinality by tenant/metric/label.

- Track WAL/head-block size and flush latency.

- Track compaction backlog and object-store errors.

- Track query scanned series/bytes and p95/p99 latency.

- Track alert evaluation delay and notification backlog.

- Use an independent/minimal health path where possible to avoid total self-dependency.

## 46. Security and Governance

- Authenticate agents and tenants with scoped tokens/certificates.

- Encrypt telemetry in transit and at rest.

- Metric labels can accidentally contain secrets/PII; validate and govern label policy.

- RBAC controls dashboard/query/alert access.

- Audit changes to alert rules and retention policies.

- Per-tenant data deletion/retention needs block-level or logical controls.

## 47. Common Interview Mistakes

- Designing metrics as ordinary rows in a relational database.

- Ignoring label cardinality.

- Storing repeated metric/label strings with every sample.

- No separation between ingest and query workloads.

- No downsampling/retention strategy.

- No index design for label filters.

- No alert rule scheduler/state machine.

- Treating missing data as zero automatically.

- No plan for out-of-order samples.

- Using averages for percentile latency without histograms.

- No noisy-neighbor quotas.

- Letting historical queries overload recent ingestion.

## 48. Final Production Architecture

- Agents/exporters batch and compress metric samples and send/scrape through stateless ingestion gateways.

- Gateways enforce tenant quotas/cardinality limits and route by normalized series ID.

- Ingest shards append to WAL and mutable head chunks, then flush compressed immutable TSDB blocks.

- Label indexes map matchers to series postings; recent and historical storage are separated.

- Older blocks move to object storage and are compacted/downsampled into longer-retention tiers.

- A query frontend plans/splits range queries, selects raw or rollup tiers, fans out to shards/store gateways, and merges aggregates.

- Alert rules are sharded across evaluator workers with durable rule state and isolated capacity.

- Presence of high-cardinality labels, query fan-out, compaction debt and tenant overload are controlled with admission limits.

- Regional clusters remain independently useful and federate selected aggregates globally.

> One-sentence architecture
> Treat metrics as compressed append-only time series: batch them through quota-aware ingestion, partition by series, store recent data in WAL/head blocks and historical data as immutable indexed blocks, downsample older ranges, isolate query/alert workloads from writes, and make label cardinality a first-class controlled resource.

## 49. Detailed Interviewer Follow-Ups

Follow-up: What is the biggest scaling problem in a metrics system?

Detailed answer: Often cardinality rather than raw bytes. An unbounded label such as user_id creates a new series for every value, inflating indexes, memory and query fan-out.

Follow-up: Why not use a relational database?

Detailed answer: The workload is append-heavy time series with huge volume, range scans and repeated dimensions. A TSDB compresses timestamps/values and uses label postings plus immutable blocks far more efficiently.

Follow-up: Push or pull?

Detailed answer: Pull gives service-discovery and target-health semantics; push fits agents, short-lived jobs and hosted products. A hybrid is reasonable. The downstream TSDB architecture is largely similar.

Follow-up: How do you identify a time series?

Detailed answer: Metric name plus the full normalized label set. Hash that identity into an internal series ID.

Follow-up: Why keep all samples for a series together?

Detailed answer: It improves compression, append locality, cache behavior and range reads.

Follow-up: How do you query labels efficiently?

Detailed answer: Use inverted postings lists for label=value pairs and intersect them to find candidate series before reading chunks.

Follow-up: How do regex label queries hurt?

Detailed answer: They can enumerate huge label-value dictionaries/postings and match many series, so enforce cost limits and avoid unbounded regexes.

Follow-up: How do you store old data cheaply?

Detailed answer: Seal immutable blocks, upload to object storage, retain compact indexes/cache, and use store-gateway workers for historical reads.

Follow-up: Why downsample?

Detailed answer: A year-long chart does not need 10-second samples. Rollups reduce bytes and query cost while preserving meaningful aggregates.

Follow-up: Why can't I store only averages in rollups?

Detailed answer: Average-of-averages is wrong when sample counts differ. Keep sum/count, min/max and histogram buckets as needed.

Follow-up: How do histograms support percentiles?

Detailed answer: Aggregate bucket counts across instances/time, build cumulative distribution, and interpolate/estimate the target quantile.

Follow-up: What happens when a counter resets?

Detailed answer: rate/increase detects a downward jump and treats it as a reset rather than negative traffic.

Follow-up: How do alerts avoid duplicate notifications after restart?

Detailed answer: Persist alert state and notification dedupe/grouping keys. Evaluators recover prior state and only emit transitions according to policy.

Follow-up: What is no-data?

Detailed answer: A rule evaluation has insufficient recent samples. It should have explicit semantics rather than silently equaling zero or healthy.

Follow-up: How do you prevent dashboards from starving alerting?

Detailed answer: Separate resource pools/quotas; reserve query capacity for alert evaluators and cap user query concurrency.

Follow-up: How do you handle late samples?

Detailed answer: Accept within a bounded out-of-order window; beyond that use a backfill path or reject. Immutable blocks should not be casually rewritten for every late point.

Follow-up: How do you isolate tenants?

Detailed answer: Separate quotas for active series, samples/sec, storage, query scans/concurrency and alert rules.

Follow-up: How do you survive a region partition?

Detailed answer: Keep regional ingestion/storage/alerting independent. Global views can degrade while local operational monitoring continues.

Follow-up: What happens during a cardinality explosion?

Detailed answer: Detect high new-series rate, throttle or reject new series for that tenant/metric, alert operators, and preserve existing stable series/ingestion.

Follow-up: Give the one-minute architecture.

Detailed answer: Agents batch metrics into stateless gateways that enforce tenant/cardinality limits and route by series ID. Ingest shards append to WAL/head chunks, compress samples and flush immutable blocks with label indexes. Recent data stays hot; older blocks move to object storage and are compacted/downsampled. Query frontends plan by time/shard, resolve labels through postings, read raw or rollup tiers and merge partial aggregates. Alert rules run on dedicated evaluator workers with durable state and isolated query capacity. Multi-tenancy, cardinality controls, backpressure and regional federation protect the system at scale.

## 50. Additional Detailed Q&A

1. What is a postings list?

Detailed answer: A compact list/set of series IDs matching a label pair.

2. What is a head block?

Detailed answer: The mutable recent time window receiving current samples before sealing.

3. Why a WAL?

Detailed answer: To recover accepted recent samples after process/node crash.

4. Why immutable blocks?

Detailed answer: Simpler compression, caching, compaction, replication and object storage.

5. What is query step?

Detailed answer: Requested output resolution, such as one point per 1m or 5m.

6. What is a recording rule?

Detailed answer: A periodically materialized query result stored as another metric.

7. What is scrape interval?

Detailed answer: How often a pull-based collector samples a target.

8. Can gauges be summed?

Detailed answer: Only if semantics make sense; many gauges are instance-local and should be avg/max/current instead.

9. Why are summaries hard to aggregate?

Detailed answer: Quantiles computed independently cannot generally be combined correctly.

10. What is staleness?

Detailed answer: A previously existing series stops producing fresh samples and should no longer be treated as current.

11. What is exemplar data?

Detailed answer: A representative trace/event reference attached to a metric sample/bucket.

12. How do you avoid one panel scanning billions of samples?

Detailed answer: Cost estimation, step-based rollups, max-series/range limits and caches.

13. Why shard alert rules?

Detailed answer: Millions of rules must be distributed; leases prevent duplicate active evaluation.

14. Can query results be partially returned?

Detailed answer: For dashboards, optionally yes with explicit partial-result metadata; alerts usually need stricter semantics.

15. What is compaction debt?

Detailed answer: Accumulated unmerged blocks causing more query/storage overhead.

16. What is active series count?

Detailed answer: Distinct series currently producing recent samples; a major memory/cardinality metric.

17. Why jitter alert schedules?

Detailed answer: Avoid a thundering herd at exact minute boundaries.

18. Why keep regional metrics regional?

Detailed answer: Operational independence and lower WAN cost/latency.

19. How do global dashboards work?

Detailed answer: Federate or query multiple regions, often using selected global rollups.

20. Most important invariant?

Detailed answer: Accepted samples remain queryable according to retention/durability contract, while one tenant/query cannot destabilize ingestion for everyone else.

## 51. Scenario Deep Dives

A deployment accidentally adds request_id as a metric label.

New-series rate spikes dramatically. Gateway/registry cardinality guard detects the explosion, rejects/throttles new series for that tenant/metric, alerts operators, and keeps existing stable series flowing. The bad deployment is fixed before millions more series reach storage.

The object store is unavailable for 20 minutes.

Recent ingestion continues in WAL/head/local block storage within configured buffer headroom. Historical queries degrade or fail clearly. Block uploads retry with backoff. If local durable capacity approaches limits, apply ingestion/backpressure policy rather than silently corrupting data.

A dashboard requests one year of raw 10-second data for 5 million series.

Query frontend estimates cost and rejects or rewrites to a downsampled tier with a coarser step. Without cost controls this query could exhaust memory/network and impact alerts.

Alert evaluator restarts while 50,000 alerts are firing.

Workers reacquire rule leases, restore durable rule state and notification dedupe keys, then continue evaluation. They should not page every rule again merely because the process restarted.

A region loses WAN connectivity to the global monitoring cluster.

Regional ingestion, dashboards and alerts continue from local data. Global views become partial/stale. Federation catches up later, avoiding the failure mode where the monitoring system disappears exactly when the region is unhealthy.

## 52. Advanced Drill: Query Execution Example

- Query: sum(rate(http_requests_total{service="checkout",status=~"5.."}[5m])) by (region).

- Resolve service=checkout postings.

- Resolve status regex to matching label values and postings; intersect with service set.

- Prune to time blocks intersecting requested range.

- Read only candidate series chunks.

- Calculate counter rate with reset handling over 5-minute windows.

- Partially aggregate by region at each shard.

- Merge regional sums at query frontend.

- Cache historical portion and return.

## 53. Advanced Drill: Histogram Percentile

- Each instance exports cumulative bucket counters such as le=100ms, le=250ms, le=500ms, +Inf.

- Query rate/increase of each bucket over the time window.

- Sum bucket counts across instances for the target service/region.

- Convert cumulative counts into distribution.

- Find the bucket where cumulative fraction crosses 0.95/0.99.

- Interpolate/estimate within bucket according to query semantics.

- Remember: percentile accuracy depends on bucket boundaries.

## 54. Advanced Drill: Retention Pipeline

- Raw head block receives samples.

- Seal immutable 2-hour block.

- Upload block to object storage after local validation.

- Compactor merges neighboring small blocks.

- Downsampler writes 1-minute rollup block after raw window ages.

- Retention worker deletes raw block after policy threshold once rollup is durable.

- Later create 1-hour rollup and expire 1-minute tier.

- Metadata catalog updates atomically enough that queries never reference missing blocks indefinitely.
