Immediately tombstone post metadata, make hydration return hidden/deleted, publish delete event to caches/search/CDN cleanup, and lazily remove feed references.

Fanout queue is 10 minutes behind.

Profiles still show newly created posts from primary metadata; home feeds become stale. Scale fanout workers, prioritize recent events, and optionally merge recent author timelines on read to mask lag.

A private user removes a follower.

Follow state update becomes authoritative immediately; stale feed IDs are filtered during read and private media URLs expire quickly.

A Reel suddenly becomes globally viral.

CDN absorbs media reads; ranking/cache tiers carry metadata; watch events stream asynchronously. No single post row is updated for every view.

## 55. Advanced Drill: Post Creation

1. Create resumable upload session.

2. Upload media directly to object store.

3. Validate/process media variants.

4. Persist Post metadata with idempotency key.

5. Emit PostCreated event.

6. Fanout normal-author post IDs.

7. Store high-fanout author post in timeline only.

8. Index search/hashtags.

9. Generate notifications asynchronously.

## 56. Advanced Drill: Feed Read

1. Load viewer feed candidate IDs.

2. Fetch followed celebrity recent timelines.

3. Merge/dedupe candidates.

4. Apply visibility/block/delete filters.

5. Fetch ranking features in batch.

6. Score and rerank.

7. Hydrate top K post/user/media metadata.

8. Return cursor.

9. Emit impressions asynchronously.

## 57. Advanced Drill: Like Write

1. Authenticate user.

2. Insert unique (post_id,user_id) like record idempotently.

3. Emit LikeCreated event.

4. Return success without waiting for exact aggregate counter.

5. Counter worker updates sharded/aggregated count.

6. Notification worker aggregates/delivers event.

## 58. Advanced Drill: Correctness Invariants

| Invariant | Mechanism |
| --- | --- |
| Private/deleted content never leaks | Read-time visibility filter |
| Duplicate post retry does not duplicate post | Idempotency key |
| Fanout retry does not duplicate candidate | viewer_id + post_id upsert |
| Celebrity cannot create unbounded write storm | Hybrid fanout |
| Media upload failure does not create broken visible post | Publish after processed media is valid |
| Viral likes do not hotspot one row | Sharded/async counters |
| Feed cache loss is recoverable | Author timelines + durable events/posts |

## 59. Interview Whiteboard Plan

1. Draw client -> API gateway.

2. Draw post service and follow graph.

3. Draw object store + media processing + CDN separately.

4. Draw PostCreated event bus.

5. Draw fanout workers -> per-user feed store.

6. Add celebrity author timeline bypass.

7. Draw feed service -> merge -> rank -> hydrate.

8. Add likes/comments counters, Stories/Reels, multi-region caches.

## 60. 45-Minute Interview Flow

| Time | Coverage |
| --- | --- |
| 0-5 min | Requirements and scale |
| 5-10 min | Data model/APIs |
| 10-15 min | Media upload/storage/CDN |
| 15-23 min | Feed fanout push vs pull |
| 23-28 min | Ranking/pagination |
| 28-33 min | Likes/comments/counters |
| 33-36 min | Stories/Reels |
| 36-40 min | Privacy/delete/failures |
| 40-43 min | Multi-region/capacity |
| 43-45 min | Trade-offs and summary |

## 61. 30-Second Final Interview Answer

> 30-second answer
> I would store media directly in object storage, asynchronously generate optimized variants, and serve them through a CDN. Post metadata and the follow graph live in sharded databases. On PostCreated, normal creators are fanned out into followers' feed candidate stores, while celebrities stay in author timelines and are merged on read. The feed service combines both sources, applies current privacy/delete/block filters, ranks a bounded candidate set, hydrates metadata and returns cursor pages. Likes/comments use separate records with asynchronous sharded counters. Stories use TTL-based active indexes; Reels use recommendation retrieval and ranking. Durable events drive search, notifications, analytics and cache invalidation.

## 62. Final Interview Checklist

- Requirements and scale estimates.

- Media direct upload.

- Object storage + CDN.

- Media processing/transcoding.

- Follow graph.

- Fanout-on-write.

- Fanout-on-read.

- Hybrid celebrity strategy.

- Feed candidate store.

- Ranking and feature retrieval.

- Cursor pagination.

- Likes/comments and hot counters.

- Stories.

- Reels.

- Search/hashtags.

- Privacy/block/delete correctness.

- Event bus/idempotency.

- Multi-region/failure recovery.

- 20 follow-ups, 20 Q&As, scenarios, algorithms and invariants.

notes.title: Design Facebook “People You May Know”
notes.description: Problem 36 | Social Graph, Candidate Generation, Ranking, Privacy, Freshness & Large-Scale Recommendations
notes.content:
Design Facebook “People You May Know”

Advanced System Design Interview Guide

Problem 36 | Social Graph, Candidate Generation, Ranking, Privacy, Freshness & Large-Scale Recommendations

> Goal
> Design a large-scale friend recommendation system that suggests relevant people a user may know. The system should use social-graph structure, contact/work/school/context signals, rank candidates efficiently, avoid blocked or inappropriate suggestions, refresh recommendations as the graph changes, and scale to billions of users without running deep graph traversals synchronously on every page view.

> Core interview idea
> Separate candidate generation from ranking. Candidate generation finds a manageable set of plausible people using graph and non-graph signals; ranking scores that set. Most heavy graph computation should be precomputed or incrementally maintained. The online path should be cache-friendly and strict about privacy, blocking, already-connected users, and stale suggestions.

## 1. Functional Requirements

- Show a ranked list of people a user may know.

- Use mutual friends and other social/context signals.

- Exclude existing friends/connections.

- Exclude blocked users and policy-ineligible candidates.

- Refresh suggestions as the graph changes.

- Support dismiss/hide suggestion.

- Optionally explain suggestions, e.g. '12 mutual friends'.

- Handle new users with sparse graph history.

- Support pagination/infinite scroll.

## 2. Non-Functional Requirements

- Recommendation page should load in tens to hundreds of milliseconds.

- Candidate generation must scale to billions of graph edges.

- Recommendations should be reasonably fresh, not necessarily transactionally current.

- Privacy and block rules must be enforced before display.

- One viral/high-degree user should not overload graph traversal.

- Offline/streaming computation should absorb expensive work.

- System should degrade safely if ranking/model services are unavailable.

- Feedback should update future recommendations quickly.

## 3. Scope and Assumptions

- Primary relationship is mutual friendship/connection; exact product semantics may differ.

- User profile, workplace, school, city, contact hashes and interaction features may be available subject to consent/policy.

- Deep social discovery beyond a few hops is not performed synchronously.

- Machine learning ranking is included conceptually; proprietary model details are not required.

- Direct messaging, feed ranking and full contact sync products are outside core scope.

## 4. Core API

| API | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| GET /users/{id}/recommendations | Fetch ranked suggestions |
| POST /recommendations/{candidate}/dismiss | Hide candidate |
| POST /connections | Friend/connect action |
| DELETE /connections/{id} | Remove connection |
| POST /blocks/{id} | Block user |
| POST /contacts/sync | Optional contact-signal ingestion |

## 5. Data Model

| Entity | Important fields |
| --- | --- |
| User | user_id, profile features, locale, status |
| Edge | user_a, user_b, edge_type, created_at |
| BlockEdge | blocker, blocked, created_at |
| Candidate | user_id, candidate_id, source, source_score, generated_at |
| FeatureVector | pair/user/context features, version |
| Recommendation | user_id, candidate_id, score, rank, model_version |
| Dismissal | user_id, candidate_id, expiry/permanent flag |

## 6. Social Graph Representation

- Model users as vertices and friendship/connection as edges.

- For undirected friendship, store symmetric adjacency or one canonical edge plus efficient adjacency indexes.

- Partition adjacency lists by user_id.

- High-degree users need sharded adjacency lists or specialized graph storage.

- Keep edge existence checks cheap because ranking/filtering frequently asks 'already connected?'

- Graph snapshots/streams feed candidate-generation jobs.

## 7. High-Level Architecture

![7. High-Level Architecture — source diagram](/diagrams/t-92hrpxm8l5wq-kix-g1tr45fvo82z.png)

## 8. Candidate Generation vs Ranking

| Candidate generation | Ranking |
| --- | --- |
| Find plausible people | Order plausible people |
| High recall | High precision/relevance |
| Graph rules, contacts, school/work, ANN | ML score / weighted features |
| Thousands of candidates | Top tens/hundreds |
| Mostly offline/incremental | Often online or nearline |

> Interview structure
> Always state this split early. Trying to run an expensive ranking model over every user in the platform is impossible; ranking only becomes practical after candidate generation reduces the search space dramatically.

## 9. Primary Candidate Source: Friends-of-Friends

- For user U, retrieve direct friends F(U).

- For each friend f, retrieve F(f).

- Count how many mutual paths reach each candidate c.

- Exclude U and direct friends.

- Mutual friend count is a strong graph-proximity signal.

- Do not synchronously expand thousands of high-degree friends on every request.

## 10. Friends-of-Friends Example

![10. Friends-of-Friends Example — source diagram](/diagrams/t-92hrpxm8l5wq-kix-excslycqhl0.png)

## 11. Why Not Compute Two-Hop Graph Online?

- Average degree may be manageable, but celebrity/high-degree nodes can have millions of neighbors.

- Two-hop expansion can explode to O(d²) candidates.

- Repeated page views would recompute the same work.

- Graph-store fan-out creates tail latency.

- Instead precompute, incrementally maintain, sample, or cap high-degree expansions.

- Online path should usually read a prepared candidate set.

## 12. Offline Batch Candidate Generation

1. Read graph snapshot or partitioned adjacency lists.

2. For each user U, emit friend-of-friend candidate pairs.

3. Aggregate mutual friend counts.

4. Filter existing direct edges.

5. Apply basic safety/block/dismissal constraints where feasible.

6. Keep top K by cheap source score.

7. Write candidate list to distributed candidate store.

8. Repeat periodically, e.g. hourly/daily depending freshness needs.

## 13. MapReduce / Distributed Graph Intuition

- Map each edge U-F into contributions toward neighbors of F.

- Shuffle by target user U and candidate C.

- Reduce counts mutual paths and auxiliary signals.

- High-degree nodes require combiners/sampling/skew handling.

- Use graph snapshots so batch has deterministic input.

- Incremental stream updates reduce the need for full recompute.

## 14. Incremental Candidate Updates

- When a new friendship A-B is created, both sides gain new second-hop opportunities.

- Emit edge-change event.

- Update mutual-count/candidate state for relevant neighbors under bounded fan-out.

- For very high-degree nodes, enqueue a batch recompute rather than synchronous explosion.

- Incremental updates improve freshness while periodic batch corrects drift.

- Candidate generation can therefore be hybrid: streaming + batch.

## 15. Candidate Sources Beyond Mutual Friends

| Source | Example |
| --- | --- |
| Contacts | Phone/email hash match, subject to consent |
| Workplace | Same company/team |
| Education | Same school/university/class year |
| Location | Same city/community |
| Groups/events | Shared communities |
| Interactions | Profile views, mentions, co-engagement subject to policy |
| Embedding similarity | Learned social/context representation |
| Imported network | Other explicitly permitted signals |

## 16. Candidate Source Blending

- Each source emits candidate IDs plus source-specific features/confidence.

- Merge duplicates by candidate_id.

- Record source bitset/list: mutual, contacts, workplace, etc.

- Source itself becomes a ranking feature.

- Use per-source quotas so one source does not crowd out diversity.

- Privacy rules may prohibit displaying the source explanation even if the signal was used internally.

## 17. Contact Matching

- Client hashes/normalizes phone/email before upload where product/privacy design permits.

- Server maps normalized contact identifiers to consenting users.

- Never expose raw uploaded contacts to unrelated users.

- Contact match can be a strong candidate signal.

- Retention/deletion policy must honor contact-sync opt-out.

- False positives from recycled phone numbers require careful identity/account state handling.

## 18. New User Cold Start

- Graph is sparse or empty, so mutual-friend candidates are weak.

- Use contacts, school/work, locale, onboarding-selected interests, imported connections, and popular nearby users where appropriate.

- Ask user to follow/connect with a few known entities during onboarding.

- Cold-start ranking should not over-personalize from weak signals.

- Recommendations improve as accepted/dismissed actions arrive.

## 19. Candidate Store

- Key by user_id; value is top K candidate IDs plus source features/version/timestamp.

- Use a distributed KV/document store for fast lookup.

- Candidates are replaceable/recomputable, so storage durability can be lower than graph source of truth.

- Keep several hundred or thousand candidates to allow online filtering.

- Version candidate lists by generation time/model/input snapshot.

## 20. Feature Engineering

| Feature family | Examples |
| --- | --- |
| Graph | Mutual count, common communities, path strength |
| Profile | Same school, company, city, language |
| Interaction | Recent profile/co-engagement signals |
| Source | Contact match, imported address book |
| Candidate quality | Account age, completeness, safety quality |
| Negative | Dismissals, prior rejected request, low trust |
| Freshness | Recent new mutual friend or job/school change |

## 21. Ranking Model

- Input is user-candidate pair features plus context.

- Output can estimate probability of connection acceptance or expected long-term value.

- Use a lightweight online model or precompute scores nearline.

- Calibrate by geography/network maturity to avoid bias from different graph densities.

- Apply business/policy constraints after/before scoring as appropriate.

- Keep fallback heuristic ranking: mutual count + recency + source priority.

## 22. Ranking Pipeline

![22. Ranking Pipeline — source diagram](/diagrams/t-92hrpxm8l5wq-kix-k2q3v0ov7v9d.png)

## 23. Hard Filters

- Candidate is not the user.

- Not already connected/friends.

- Not blocked in either relevant direction.

- Candidate account active and eligible.

- Respect age/safety/region restrictions.

- Not recently dismissed if dismissal TTL applies.

- Not already pending friend request if product excludes it.

- Privacy settings permit discoverability/recommendation.

## 24. Why Filters Must Run Online Too

- Offline candidate lists become stale.

- A block can happen seconds after candidate generation.

- A friendship may already have been accepted.

- Account may become disabled.

- Privacy settings may change.

- Therefore cache/precompute candidates, but re-check critical hard constraints before display.

## 25. Dismiss / Hide Feedback

- User dismissal is a negative signal and often a hard temporary filter.

- Persist dismissal keyed by user+candidate.

- Use expiry, e.g. do not resurface for 30/90 days, or permanent policy.

- Feed dismissal event into training data carefully—dismissal may mean 'not now', not necessarily negative relationship.

- Repeated dismissals from same source can adjust source blending.

## 26. Friend Request Outcome Feedback

- Accepted recommendation is strong positive label.

- Ignored recommendation is weak/ambiguous.

- Rejected request can be negative.

- Blocked/report outcome is a strong negative/safety label.

- Training must avoid leakage from future events.

- Use delayed labels and appropriate observation windows.

## 27. Freshness

- Friend graph changes continuously.

- Batch-only daily recommendations can feel stale.

- Use stream events to invalidate direct-friend/blocked candidates immediately.

- Incrementally add high-value candidates after new friendships.

- Re-rank cached candidate sets on read using current lightweight features.

- Periodic full recompute repairs accumulated approximation errors.

## 28. Recommendation Cache

- Cache top recommendations per user for fast page load.

- Cache entry includes generation/model version and timestamp.

- On read, remove invalid candidates and backfill from candidate store.

- Short TTL for active users, longer for inactive users.

- Pre-warm cache for highly active users.

- Do not cache across users; recommendations are personalized.

## 29. High-Degree / Celebrity Users

> Graph-skew problem
> A celebrity with 50 million followers/friends should not cause 50 million-neighbor expansions for every connected user. High-degree nodes need caps, sampling, specialized treatment, or exclusion from ordinary friend-of-friend expansion.

- Cap contribution from very high-degree nodes.

- Sample representative neighbors.

- Use logarithmic/normalized mutual features rather than raw degree dominance.

- Route high-degree adjacency to dedicated partitions.

- Treat public figures/pages differently from personal-friend recommendation.

## 30. Graph Partitioning

- Partition adjacency lists by user_id hash.

- Replicate hot/high-degree partitions more aggressively.

- Two-hop batch jobs shuffle intermediate pairs, not synchronous online requests.

- Keep edge-existence cache/Bloom filter for filtering candidate pairs.

- Cross-partition traversals are expected offline; online path avoids arbitrary traversal.

## 31. Edge Storage Options

| Option | Strength | Trade-off |
| --- | --- | --- |
| KV adjacency lists | Simple, scalable | Harder complex graph queries |
| Graph DB | Rich traversal semantics | Operational scale/partition complexity |
| Wide-column rows | Large adjacency lists | Range/shard design needed |
| Offline graph files + online KV | Excellent batch + serving split | Dual data representations |

For an interview, a partitioned adjacency store plus offline graph-processing system and online recommendation KV is a strong, scalable design.

## 32. Mutual Friend Count Maintenance

- Batch recompute exact/approximate counts for all candidate pairs.

- Incremental edge updates adjust counts locally where feasible.

- Counts can be stored in candidate features rather than globally materializing every possible pair.

- High-degree pair explosion makes full pair materialization expensive.

- Keep only top-K mutual candidates per user using bounded heaps/sketches.

## 33. Approximation Techniques

- Cap number of neighbors considered from high-degree users.

- Use MinHash/LSH-like similarity for large sets if suitable.

- Use approximate top-K heavy hitter structures for pair counts.

- Use graph embeddings/ANN to generate candidates without exhaustive two-hop expansion.

- Approximation is acceptable because recommendation ranking is probabilistic, but privacy filters must remain exact.

## 34. Graph Embeddings / ANN

- Train user embeddings from graph structure and interactions.

- Nearest-neighbor search proposes socially similar candidates.

- Useful for weak explicit graph overlap or large networks.

- ANN returns candidates; hard filters still remove friends/blocks/ineligible users.

- Embedding version is part of candidate-generation metadata.

- Combine ANN candidates with mutual-friend candidates rather than relying on one source.

## 35. Diversity

- Top score may return 20 people from the same workplace or one friend cluster.

- Apply source/community diversity in final reranker.

- Limit near-duplicate candidates from same cluster.

- Balance relevance with exploration.

- Diversity improves utility but must not override hard safety rules.

## 36. Explanation Generation

| Signal | Possible explanation |
| --- | --- |
| Mutual friends | 12 mutual friends |
| Work | Works at the same company |
| School | Went to the same university |
| Contacts | In your contacts |
| Group/community | Member of a shared group |

- Explanation must use only signals allowed to be shown.

- Do not reveal sensitive/private information merely because it influenced ranking.

- Select the strongest permitted explanation separately from ranking score.

## 37. Privacy

- Recommendation eligibility respects discoverability settings.

- Do not reveal uploaded contacts or private group membership without product permission.

- Blocked users must not appear even if cached candidate lists contain them.

- Data minimization: only retain signals needed for the feature.

- Honor account deletion and contact-sync deletion.

- Model training datasets need the same privacy governance.

## 38. Safety and Abuse

- Repeated suggestions of reported/blocked users can create harassment risk.

- Use trust/safety account eligibility signals.

- Suppress recommendation after rejected/ignored requests according to policy.

- Rate-limit friend requests sent from recommendation surfaces.

- Detect mass-connect spam behavior.

- Do not let recommendation score override safety restrictions.

## 39. Pending Requests

- If U already sent a request to C, recommendation may be replaced by 'request pending' or suppressed.

- Pending-state check should be low-latency and current.

- Offline generation can be stale; online filter fixes it.

- Accepted request immediately turns candidate into existing friend and removes it.

- Rejected request can write dismissal/suppression state.

## 40. Online Request Flow

1. Recommendation API authenticates user.

2. Read cached top list; on miss read candidate store.

3. Fetch current hard-filter state: existing edges, blocks, pending requests, dismissals.

4. Drop invalid candidates.

5. Hydrate lightweight fresh features.

6. Rank or re-rank candidates.

7. Apply diversity/explanation selection.

8. Return top N and asynchronously log impressions.

## 41. Offline + Online Hybrid

![41. Offline + Online Hybrid — source diagram](/diagrams/t-92hrpxm8l5wq-kix-5a0i46pb76mo.png)

## 42. Recommendation Impression Logging

- Log which candidates were actually shown, not merely generated.

- Include recommendation position, source, model version and request context.

- Accepted/ignored/dismissed outcomes join back to impression ID.

- This enables unbiased evaluation relative to what user saw.

- Sampling may reduce logging cost, but training/evaluation methodology must account for it.

## 43. A/B Testing

- Experiment candidate-source weights, ranking models, diversity rules and explanations.

- Primary metrics: accepted connections, meaningful interaction after connection, hides/reports, request spam.

- Avoid optimizing only click/send-request rate if it harms long-term network quality.

- Experiment assignment should be stable per user.

- Log model/experiment bucket with each impression.

## 44. Recommendation Quality Metrics

| Metric | Interpretation |
| --- | --- |
| Connection acceptance rate | Immediate relevance |
| Meaningful interaction after connect | Long-term quality |
| Hide/dismiss rate | Poor relevance signal |
| Block/report rate | Safety quality |
| Coverage | How many users receive useful candidates |
| Diversity | Variety of source/community |
| Freshness | Time from relevant graph change to suggestion |

## 45. Cold Storage / Recompute Strategy

- Candidate/recommendation lists are derived and can be rebuilt.

- Graph edges, blocks, privacy state are primary durable truth.

- Periodic snapshots support full recomputation.

- Feature/candidate stores can use cheaper durability than source graph.

- Model versions and training data need reproducibility metadata.

## 46. Multi-Region Architecture

- User graph may have a home region or globally replicated adjacency metadata.

- Recommendation serving happens near the user.

- Candidate lists replicate to serving regions asynchronously.

- Critical block/privacy state should propagate quickly or be checked against a strongly consistent/global safety service.

- Model and feature snapshots are versioned and rolled out regionally.

- Recommendation freshness can tolerate some replication lag; safety cannot.

## 47. Failure Scenarios

| Failure | Expected behavior |
| --- | --- |
| Candidate store unavailable | Serve cached list or fallback heuristic |
| Ranker unavailable | Use mutual-count/source heuristic |
| Graph store slow | Avoid deep online traversal; use cached candidates |
| Block update just happened | Online filter removes candidate |
| Batch job delayed | Serve older candidates with freshness checks |
| Feature store partial | Use default/missing features |
| One region isolated | Serve local replicated candidate/model state |
| Stream update lost | Periodic batch recompute repairs drift |

## 48. Backpressure and Cost Control

- Cap candidate count entering online ranker.

- Batch profile/feature fetches.

- Do not hydrate expensive features for candidates already removed by hard filters.

- Limit high-degree graph expansion.

- Use per-user refresh budgets; inactive users do not need hourly recomputation.

- Prioritize active-user candidate refresh.

- Use stale-but-safe recommendations rather than overload graph systems.

## 49. Observability

| Metric | Why |
| --- | --- |
| Recommendation API p95/p99 | Serving SLA |
| Cache hit rate | Online cost |
| Candidate count by source | Generation health |
| Hard-filter drop rate | Staleness/safety |
| High-degree expansion capped | Graph skew |
| Batch/stream freshness lag | Timeliness |
| Ranker latency/error | Model serving health |
| Accept/dismiss/block rates | Quality/safety |
| Candidate coverage | Cold-start/system reach |
| Model/source distribution shift | ML health |

## 50. Common Interview Mistakes

- Doing live two-hop traversal for every request.

- Ranking every user in the platform.

- Ignoring celebrity/high-degree graph skew.

- Only using mutual-friend count and no cold-start plan.

- No block/privacy online filtering.

- Treating cached recommendation lists as always valid.

- No distinction between candidate generation and ranking.

- Storing every possible user pair.

- No feedback/dismissal loop.

- No fallback if ML ranker is down.

- Optimizing request-sent rate without safety/long-term quality.

## 51. Final Production Architecture

- Keep friendship/connection and block/privacy data in durable graph/adjacency stores partitioned by user.

- Generate candidate sets mostly offline/nearline from friends-of-friends plus contacts/work/school/embedding sources.

- Use streaming edge events for incremental freshness and periodic batch recomputation for correctness.

- Store top-K candidate lists per user in a low-latency KV store.

- On request, re-check current hard constraints, hydrate lightweight features, rank, diversify and generate permitted explanations.

- Cache top recommendations for active users.

- Cap/special-case high-degree nodes and use approximation/ANN where helpful.

- Log impressions/outcomes for model training and A/B testing.

- Replicate derived candidate/model state regionally while treating block/privacy state as high-priority current safety data.

> One-sentence architecture
> Precompute and incrementally maintain a bounded set of friend candidates from social-graph and contextual sources, store them per user, then perform fast online privacy/block filtering and lightweight ranking/diversification—avoiding live deep graph traversal while continuously learning from connection, dismissal and safety outcomes.

## 52. Detailed Interviewer Follow-Ups

Follow-up: What is the main candidate source?

Detailed answer: Friends-of-friends with mutual-count/path strength is the classic baseline, blended with contacts, school/work, community and embedding candidates.

Follow-up: Why not compute friends-of-friends online?

Detailed answer: Two-hop fan-out is highly skewed; high-degree nodes make latency and load unpredictable. Precompute or incrementally maintain candidates.

Follow-up: How do you represent the graph?

Detailed answer: Partition adjacency lists by user_id in a scalable KV/wide-column/graph store; keep edge existence checks cheap.

Follow-up: How do you handle celebrity nodes?

Detailed answer: Cap/suppress their expansion, sample neighbors, use normalized features, and store their adjacency on dedicated partitions.

Follow-up: How many candidates do you store?

Detailed answer: Typically hundreds or low thousands per active user, enough for filtering/reranking without excessive storage.

Follow-up: How do you remove existing friends from stale candidate lists?

Detailed answer: Run an online edge-existence filter immediately before ranking/display.

Follow-up: How do you handle blocks?

Detailed answer: Treat them as hard online filters with rapid invalidation; recommendations must never rely solely on stale offline filtering.

Follow-up: What if ranker is down?

Detailed answer: Fallback to a deterministic heuristic such as mutual count, contact match, recency and source priority.

Follow-up: How do new users get recommendations?

Detailed answer: Contacts, onboarding-provided school/work/location, imported connections, community membership and safe popularity priors.

Follow-up: How do you merge candidate sources?

Detailed answer: Union by candidate ID, retain source indicators/features, apply per-source quotas or blending, then rank jointly.

Follow-up: How do you keep candidates fresh?

Detailed answer: Consume graph-change events for incremental updates and run periodic full batch recomputation to repair drift.

Follow-up: How do you update mutual friend counts after one new edge?

Detailed answer: For bounded-degree nodes, update relevant neighbor pairs incrementally; for high-degree cases, enqueue recompute or sample.

Follow-up: Would you use graph embeddings?

Detailed answer: Yes as an additional generator, especially when explicit mutual paths are sparse. ANN candidates still pass exact safety/friend filters.

Follow-up: How do you avoid storing every user pair?

Detailed answer: Generate and retain only top-K plausible candidates per user; pair space is quadratic and impossible to materialize globally.

Follow-up: What does dismissal mean?

Detailed answer: Usually suppress temporarily/permanently and use as a negative feedback feature; semantics are product-specific.

Follow-up: How do you explain a recommendation?

Detailed answer: Choose the strongest permitted signal such as mutual friends or same workplace, independent of the full ranking model.

Follow-up: How do you measure quality?

Detailed answer: Accepted connections plus downstream meaningful interaction, balanced against hide/report/block rate, coverage and diversity.

Follow-up: How do you do multi-region?

Detailed answer: Replicate derived candidate/model state regionally; recommendation freshness tolerates lag, but block/privacy state must propagate quickly or be checked centrally.

Follow-up: What if batch candidate generation is delayed?

Detailed answer: Serve older candidate sets, apply current online filters, and optionally use lightweight online/fallback generation for active users.

Follow-up: Give the one-minute design.

Detailed answer: Store the social graph as partitioned adjacency lists. Generate friends-of-friends and other candidate sources mostly offline or incrementally from graph events, keeping only the top few hundred/thousand candidates per user in a serving KV. At request time, load cached candidates, remove existing friends, blocks, pending requests and dismissed/ineligible accounts using current state, hydrate lightweight pair features, rank with ML or a mutual-count heuristic fallback, apply diversity and safe explanations, and return top N. High-degree nodes are capped/sampled, graph embeddings can add ANN candidates, and periodic batch recomputation repairs stream drift.

## 53. Additional Detailed Q&A

1. What is an adjacency list?

Detailed answer: The set/list of graph neighbors for one user.

2. What is graph degree?

Detailed answer: Number of edges connected to a user.

3. Why is degree skew dangerous?

Detailed answer: A few users can have orders of magnitude more neighbors than average, causing hot partitions and fan-out explosion.

4. What is candidate recall?

Detailed answer: Fraction of truly relevant people present in the generated candidate set.

5. What is ranking precision?

Detailed answer: How relevant the top returned recommendations are.

6. Why top-K storage?

Detailed answer: Bounds space and online ranking cost.

7. What is source blending?

Detailed answer: Combining candidates from multiple generators into one set.

8. What is ANN?

Detailed answer: Approximate nearest-neighbor retrieval in embedding space.

9. Why periodic full recompute?

Detailed answer: Incremental streams can miss events or accumulate approximation error.

10. Why online hard filtering?

Detailed answer: Privacy/block/friend state may have changed since offline generation.

11. What is recommendation freshness?

Detailed answer: Delay between a relevant graph/profile change and reflected suggestion.

12. What is explanation leakage?

Detailed answer: Showing a reason that reveals a private/sensitive signal.

13. What is a candidate impression?

Detailed answer: A record that a suggestion was actually shown to the user.

14. Why log impressions?

Detailed answer: Training/evaluation need to know what users had the opportunity to act on.

15. Why stable experiment assignment?

Detailed answer: Prevents users from bouncing between ranking variants.

16. What is diversity reranking?

Detailed answer: Adjusting final list to avoid redundant candidates from one cluster/source.

17. Can candidate store lose data?

Detailed answer: It is derived and rebuildable, though availability still benefits from replication/cache.

18. What is graph snapshot?

Detailed answer: Consistent-ish frozen representation used by batch candidate jobs.

19. Why not one graph database for everything?

Detailed answer: Online recommendation serving needs predictable KV-style latency; batch graph computation has different access patterns.

20. Most important invariant?

Detailed answer: No recommendation may violate current hard relationship, block, privacy or safety constraints.

## 54. Scenario Deep Dives

A user blocks someone who is already cached as recommendation #1.

Block event updates safety state immediately. On the next request, online hard filter removes the candidate even if candidate cache remains unchanged. Cache may then be invalidated asynchronously.

A celebrity user with 20 million connections joins many users' two-hop paths.

Do not emit all pair combinations. Mark the node high-degree, cap/sample its expansion, or exclude it from ordinary personal FoF generation. Use normalized graph features so its degree does not dominate.

A new user has zero friends.

Use contact matches, school/work/location/community signals and safe popularity priors. As the user accepts connections, incremental graph updates rapidly introduce mutual-friend candidates.

Streaming edge pipeline misses an event.

Nearline candidate state can temporarily be stale. Periodic full graph snapshot recomputation rebuilds top-K candidate lists and corrects drift.

ML ranker times out during peak traffic.

Deadline expires; serving falls back to cached/precomputed score or deterministic heuristic. Hard filters still run, so quality degrades but privacy/safety does not.

## 55. Advanced Drill: Mutual-Friend Candidate Algorithm

1. Load U's direct friend set F(U).

2. Initialize bounded map/heap candidate -> mutual_count.

3. For each f in F(U), read/sample neighbors F(f).

4. For each c in F(f), skip c==U.

5. Skip if c is direct friend, blocked or globally ineligible where known.

6. Increment mutual_count(c).

7. Keep only top K by mutual count/source score to bound memory.

8. Persist candidate ID, count and generation version.

## 56. Advanced Drill: High-Degree Safeguards

- Degree threshold marks heavy users.

- Do not expand all their neighbors in ordinary batch pair emission.

- Sample fixed number of neighbors or use precomputed cluster/embedding representation.

- Store their adjacency in segmented partitions.

- Normalize mutual signal by degree, e.g. common-neighbor similarity instead of raw count.

- Monitor pair-emission skew by source node degree.

## 57. Advanced Drill: Online Filter Order

1. Start with cached candidate IDs.

2. Drop self and malformed/deactivated accounts.

3. Batch-check direct-friend/pending-edge status.

4. Batch-check block/safety/privacy state.

5. Apply dismissal suppression.

6. Only then fetch expensive profile/pair features.

7. Rank remaining candidates.

8. Apply diversity and explanation eligibility.

9. Return top N and log impressions.

## 58. Advanced Drill: Feature Freshness

| Feature | Freshness need |
| --- | --- |
| Block relation | Immediate/strong |
| Existing friendship | Seconds / current |
| Mutual count | Minutes-hours acceptable |
| Work/school profile | Minutes-hours |
| Interaction aggregates | Minutes-hours |
| Embedding | Hours-days |
| Model score | Depends on model rollout |

## 59. Advanced Drill: Recommendation Cache Fill

- Precompute for daily active users before peak traffic.

- Lazy-fill inactive users on first request.

- Cache top 50-200 after online ranking.

- Invalidate on strong events: block, new connection, account disable.

- Allow TTL refresh for softer feature drift.

- Backfill from candidate store if filters remove many cached entries.

## 60. Advanced Drill: Data Pipeline

1. Graph/profile/block events enter durable stream.

2. Stream processors update adjacency indexes and lightweight features.

3. Incremental candidate workers update affected top-K sets.

4. Offline snapshot jobs periodically recompute candidates/features globally.

5. Training pipeline joins impression/outcome labels.

6. Model registry publishes a versioned model.

7. Regional serving clusters load model + candidate/features.

8. Online telemetry feeds monitoring and next training cycle.

## 61. Advanced Drill: Correctness and Safety Invariants

| Invariant | Mechanism |
| --- | --- |
| Blocked user is never displayed | Online exact block filter |
| Existing friend not suggested | Current edge check |
| Dismissed candidate respects policy | Dismissal store/TTL |
| High-degree node cannot explode work | Expansion caps/sampling |
| Stream drift is repaired | Periodic batch recompute |
| Model outage doesn't bypass safety | Filters independent of model |
| Private signal is not exposed in explanation | Explanation allowlist/policy |

## 62. Advanced Drill: Storage Estimate

- Assume 2B users and average 300 social edges -> hundreds of billions of adjacency entries globally.

- If each active user stores 500 candidate IDs + compact features, derived candidate storage is large but manageable when compressed and restricted to active users.

- Serving only the top few hundred recommendations means recommendation KV is far smaller than storing all possible two-hop pairs.

- Graph edge storage dominates durable relational structure; candidate lists are replaceable derived data.

- High-degree adjacency segmentation and compression are essential.

## 63. 45-Minute Interview Flow

| Time | Coverage |
| --- | --- |
| 0-5 min | Requirements and recommendation goals |
| 5-10 min | Graph model + HLD |
| 10-17 min | Candidate generation / FoF |
| 17-22 min | Offline vs incremental updates |
| 22-27 min | Candidate sources + cold start |
| 27-33 min | Features, ranking, diversity |
| 33-37 min | Privacy/block/safety filtering |
| 37-40 min | High-degree nodes and partitioning |
| 40-43 min | Multi-region/failures |
| 43-45 min | Metrics/invariants/summary |

## 64. 30-Second Final Interview Answer

> 30-second answer
> I would keep the friendship graph in partitioned adjacency storage, but avoid live two-hop traversal on every request. Offline and streaming jobs generate a bounded top-K candidate set per user from friends-of-friends, contacts, school/work and optional graph-embedding ANN sources. The serving API reads cached candidates, performs current hard filters for existing friendships, blocks, pending requests, dismissals and privacy, then hydrates lightweight pair features and ranks with an ML model or mutual-friend heuristic fallback. High-degree users are capped or sampled, periodic batch recomputation repairs stream drift, and regional serving caches derived candidate/model state while safety state remains current.

## 65. Final Interview Checklist

- Social graph data model and adjacency storage.

- Candidate generation vs ranking split.

- Friends-of-friends algorithm.

- Batch + incremental hybrid.

- Contact/work/school/community sources.

- Cold-start strategy.

- Candidate store top-K.

- Feature engineering and ranking.

- Online hard filters.

- Dismissals and request outcomes.

- Freshness and invalidation.

- High-degree node handling.

- Graph partitioning and approximation.

- Graph embeddings / ANN.

- Diversity and explanations.

- Privacy and safety.

- Impression logging and A/B tests.

- Multi-region and fallback behavior.

- Observability and quality metrics.

- 20 detailed follow-ups, 20 additional Q&As, scenarios, algorithms, invariants and diagrams.

## 66. Deep Dive: Graph Similarity Scores

- Mutual-friend count is a simple baseline, but raw count can unfairly favor high-degree users and dense communities.

- Jaccard similarity = |N(U) ∩ N(C)| / |N(U) ∪ N(C)| normalizes overlap by neighborhood size.

- Adamic-Adar weights rare mutual neighbors more strongly than extremely well-connected mutuals, because a rare shared connection is often more informative.

- Common-neighbor count, Jaccard, Adamic-Adar, shortest-path indicators, shared-community count, and recency can all become ranking features.

- These graph scores should usually be computed offline/nearline from adjacency snapshots rather than from deep online traversals.

- Do not overfit to one graph metric; candidate generation should maximize recall, while the ranker combines graph similarity with context, safety and freshness.

## 67. Deep Dive: Training Data and Label Leakage

- A recommendation model needs examples of candidates that were actually shown. Training on all generated candidates creates exposure bias because unseen candidates had no chance to receive a response.

- Use impression logs as the base population and join later actions such as request sent, accepted, dismissed, blocked or meaningful post-connect interaction.

- Choose an observation window, for example several days, before assigning the final label.

- Never use features created after the recommendation impression as model inputs; this leaks future information and inflates offline metrics.

- Negative examples are tricky: 'not clicked' may simply mean the user did not scroll far enough. Position and visibility should be logged.

- Use time-based train/validation splits where possible so offline evaluation resembles future production behavior.

## 68. Deep Dive: Privacy and Block Race Conditions

- Candidate list generated at 10:00 may include user C. At 10:01 U blocks C. At 10:02 U opens recommendations. The online block check must remove C regardless of candidate-cache freshness.

- If C changes discoverability settings, the recommendation path should treat the new restriction similarly to a block-style invalidation.

- If U and C have asymmetric privacy rules, eligibility should evaluate both sides according to product policy.

- Cache invalidation is useful for performance, but correctness must come from a current hard-filter source rather than relying only on cache eviction.

- Training pipelines must exclude or appropriately handle interactions that later become privacy-restricted or deleted.

- Deletion workflows should propagate to graph, candidate, feature, cache, logging and training stores according to retention policy.

## 69. Deep Dive: High-Degree Skew Example

- Suppose average degree is 300. A normal two-hop expansion can touch roughly tens of thousands of raw paths before deduplication.

- Now suppose one mutual node has degree 5 million. Expanding it naively for each connected user can dominate the entire batch stage and create enormous shuffle output.

- Mark nodes above a degree threshold as heavy hitters.

- For heavy nodes, sample a bounded neighbor subset, use community/embedding summaries, or entirely exclude them from personal-friend FoF contributions.

- Distributed batch jobs should use skew-aware partitioning so one reducer is not assigned every pair involving a celebrity node.

- Track contribution volume by source-degree bucket; this makes skew visible before the job misses its SLA.

## 70. Deep Dive: Candidate Refresh Scheduling

| User class | Refresh strategy | Reason |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Highly active | Incremental updates + frequent nearline rerank | Changes are likely to be seen quickly |
| Daily active | Hourly/several-hour refresh | Good freshness/cost balance |
| Weekly active | Daily batch | Avoid unnecessary compute |
| Long inactive | Lazy refresh on return | No value precomputing constantly |
| New user | Immediate source generation after onboarding | Cold-start experience |

A large recommendation platform should spend compute proportional to the probability that the result will actually be consumed.

## 71. Deep Dive: Failure Timeline

1. Recommendation API receives request and candidate cache is unavailable.

2. Fallback reads the candidate KV store directly.

3. Online ranker then times out at its deadline.

4. System switches to the stored source score / mutual-count heuristic rather than failing the page.

5. Block/friend/privacy filters still execute from their independent current-state services.

6. Feature enrichment that misses deadline is defaulted rather than retried synchronously many times.

7. Response is returned with a lower-quality but safe ordered list.

8. Telemetry records each degradation path so operators can distinguish quality loss from availability loss.

## 72. More Detailed Interview Follow-Ups

Follow-up: Why is Adamic-Adar sometimes better than mutual count?

Detailed answer: It discounts mutual neighbors with extremely high degree, so a rare shared connection contributes more evidence than a celebrity-like mutual connection.

Follow-up: How do you avoid exposure bias in model training?

Detailed answer: Train primarily from logged recommendation impressions and include position/visibility context, rather than treating every generated candidate as if it was shown.

Follow-up: Can recommendation caches be strongly consistent?

Detailed answer: They do not need to be. Candidate/rank caches are derived and can be stale; hard privacy/block/friend filters must be current before display.

Follow-up: What if a user has millions of direct connections?

Detailed answer: Segment adjacency, avoid full two-hop expansion, rely on sampling, communities, embeddings and bounded candidate generation. Such accounts may require a separate product treatment.

Follow-up: How do you choose K for candidate storage?

Detailed answer: Large enough that online filtering still leaves plenty of results, but small enough to bound storage and ranking cost. Tune using filter-drop distribution and page depth.

Follow-up: How do you prevent one candidate source from dominating?

Detailed answer: Use source quotas, calibrated source features or diversity constraints before final ranking.

Follow-up: What should happen after a user sends a friend request?

Detailed answer: Immediately suppress or replace the recommendation using pending-request state; do not wait for the next offline candidate job.

Follow-up: How do you handle recommendation staleness after someone changes jobs or schools?

Detailed answer: Profile events update feature state and can trigger nearline reranking; full candidate regeneration can happen less frequently.

Follow-up: Would you use Redis for the graph?

Detailed answer: It can cache adjacency or candidate lists, but the durable graph needs storage sized for hundreds of billions of edges and robust partitioning/recovery. Redis alone is not the architecture.

Follow-up: What is the main correctness boundary?

Detailed answer: Recommendation quality may be approximate, but safety/privacy/existing-relationship filters must be exact enough at display time.

## 73. Interview Whiteboard Plan

1. Draw User -> Recommendation API -> Recommendation Cache/Candidate Store.

2. To the side, draw Graph Store and Candidate Generation jobs using two-hop edges plus other sources.

3. Write 'top-K per user' between candidate generation and serving store.

4. On the online path, draw hard filters first: friends, blocks, pending, privacy, dismissals.

5. Then draw feature hydration -> ranker -> diversity/explanation -> top N.

6. Draw edge/block/profile feedback events into incremental updates and periodic batch recompute.

7. Circle high-degree nodes and write 'cap/sample/special handling'.

notes.title: Design Facebook Messenger
notes.description: How to study this design Memorize the messaging invariants: the sender gets a durable server ACK; each conversation has an authoritative order; network delivery
notes.content:
Design Facebook Messenger

Realtime Messaging, Ordering, Delivery, Offline Sync and Groups

How to study this design
Memorize the messaging invariants: the sender gets a durable server ACK; each conversation has an authoritative order; network delivery can duplicate so every send is idempotent; message history is the source of truth for offline/reconnect; persistent connections are an optimization for low latency; delivery/read receipts are separate state; and group fan-out must never make one huge synchronous loop block the send path.

![Design Facebook Messenger — source diagram](/diagrams/t-hkzkiuy3eun9-kix-fnkq072h9yfr.png)

Messenger is a durable ordered-message system with a real-time connection layer on top.

## 1. Problem Statement and Interview Framing

Design a Facebook Messenger-like system that allows users to exchange text messages in real time from mobile and web clients. The system must support online and offline recipients, conversation history, delivery/read receipts, multiple devices, and group chat. The hardest parts are connection management, message ordering, duplicate handling, delivery fan-out, reconnect, and multi-region ownership.

- Baseline: 1:1 text messaging.

- Then add delivery/read receipts and multi-device sync.

- Then discuss groups, attachments, presence, and push notifications.

- End-to-end encryption is an optional follow-up with important product trade-offs.

Scope discipline
Do not turn the first ten minutes into a design for voice/video calling, Stories, social feeds, or collaborative documents. Build reliable text messaging first.

## 2. Functional Requirements

![2. Functional Requirements — source diagram](/diagrams/t-hkzkiuy3eun9-kix-ywejchlmdckz.png)

The delivery semantics must be explicit before implementation.

| Feature | Baseline Behavior | Follow-Up |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Send text message | 1:1 conversation | Group fan-out |
| Receive online | Near-real-time | Slow consumers/backpressure |
| Receive offline | Catch up on reconnect | Push notification wake-up |
| History | Paginated ordered messages | Search / retention |
| Receipts | Sent, delivered, read | Per-device vs user-level |
| Multi-device | Phone/web/tablet | Cursor reconciliation |
| Presence | Optional best-effort | Last seen / typing |
| Attachments | Optional media reference | CDN / object storage |

Recommended baseline
Guarantee durable message acceptance and per-conversation ordering. Do not promise global ordering across every conversation; it has no product value and would destroy scalability.

## 3. Non-Functional Requirements

| Property | Expectation | Architecture Impact |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Latency | Online delivery in tens/hundreds of ms | Persistent connections + regional gateways |
| Durability | No acknowledged message loss | Durable message store before sender ACK |
| Availability | Chat should survive instance failures | Stateless workers + replicated storage |
| Ordering | Consistent order within one conversation | Conversation partition/sequencer |
| Duplicates | Network retries are normal | clientMsgId + idempotent insert |
| Offline support | Users reconnect after hours/days | Durable history + cursors |
| Connection scale | 100M+ concurrent sockets | Dedicated gateway tier |
| Multi-region | Users connect locally | Route to conversation owner |

## 4. Capacity Estimation

![4. Capacity Estimation — source diagram](/diagrams/t-hkzkiuy3eun9-kix-384qhgqfv0y8.png)

The connection count is as important as message QPS.

Illustrative interview assumptions:

- 500 million daily active users.

- 50 messages per active user per day -> 25 billion messages/day.

- Average message event/envelope roughly 500 bytes before indexes/replicas.

- Average ingest ~290K messages/sec; peak ~1.5M/sec using a 5x factor.

- 100 million concurrent online connections.

- Raw message payload/envelope storage ~12.5 TB/day before replication/index overhead.

Why the estimate matters
The average message size is tiny, but connection count and fan-out are huge. This is why connection gateways, partitioned message streams, bounded queues, and asynchronous delivery matter more than large-object storage for the text path.

## 5. WebSockets vs Polling / Long Polling

For interactive chat, a long-lived bidirectional connection is the natural online transport.

| Option | Strength | Weakness | Use Here |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Polling | Very simple | Wasteful + latency | Fallback only |
| Long polling | Works over HTTP | Repeated reconnect/request overhead | Fallback / older environments |
| WebSocket | Bidirectional, low overhead | Stateful connection management | Primary online chat transport |
| SSE | Simple server->client stream | Not bidirectional | Notifications, not full chat transport |

- The socket is not the source of truth; durable message history is.

- Losing the socket should cause reconnect/catch-up, not message loss.

Key distinction
A persistent connection is a latency optimization. Reliability comes from durable message storage, sequence numbers, ACKs, and replay after reconnect.

## 6. Connection Gateway Tier

![6. Connection Gateway Tier — source diagram](/diagrams/t-hkzkiuy3eun9-kix-meeebapc5fsn.png)

Separate millions of stateful sockets from stateless message business logic.

- Terminates WebSocket/TCP connections.

- Authenticates connection/session token.

- Maintains heartbeat and idle timeout.

- Tracks deviceId and userId.

- Maintains bounded per-connection send buffer.

- Routes inbound frames to message ingress.

- Receives delivery events and writes to socket.

Why a separate tier
Application servers handling database/message logic should not also own millions of long-lived sockets. A dedicated gateway fleet can scale on connection count, while message services scale on message throughput.

## 7. Session Registry

Delivery workers need to know where an online user's devices are connected.

- Map userId -> active sessions: deviceId, gatewayId, region, connectionId, lastHeartbeat.

- Store ephemeral entries in a distributed in-memory store or region-local registry.

- TTL/lease entries so dead gateways do not leave permanent stale routes.

- Gateway disconnect removes/lets entry expire.

- One user can have multiple active devices.

Presence is not routing
The session registry is operational routing state. Presence is a user-facing best-effort view derived from connection state and may intentionally lag.

## 8. API / Protocol Design

| Operation | Example Logical Frame / API | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Send | SEND {conversationId, clientMsgId, body} | Idempotent message create |
| Server ACK | ACK {clientMsgId, messageId, seq} | Durable accepted state |
| Deliver | MESSAGE {messageId, seq, body} | Recipient message frame |
| Delivery ACK | DELIVERED {conversationId, seq/device} | Device received |
| Read cursor | READ_UP_TO {conversationId, seq} | User read state |
| History | GET /conversations/{id}/messages?beforeSeq=X | Pagination/backfill |
| Reconnect | SYNC {conversation cursors/device cursor} | Catch-up before live |

- clientMsgId is generated by sender device before network send.

- messageId is authoritative server identity.

- seq is authoritative conversation order.

Protocol rule
Treat all network frames as retryable and potentially duplicated. The receiver and server should be able to process a repeated frame safely.

## 9. Message Data Model

![9. Message Data Model — source diagram](/diagrams/t-hkzkiuy3eun9-kix-jamkx8485de.png)

Conversation ID and sequence number form the natural history access pattern.

| Entity | Key Fields | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Conversation | conversationId, type, latestSeq, metadata | Ordering / chat identity |
| Message | conversationId, seq, messageId, senderId, clientMsgId, payloadRef, timestamp | Durable history |
| MemberState | conversationId, userId, role, joinedSeq, lastDeliveredSeq, lastReadSeq | Membership + receipts |
| DeviceSession | userId, deviceId, gatewayId, region, heartbeat | Ephemeral routing |

- Messages are immutable after accepted except administrative deletion/redaction policy.

- Edits/reactions can be modeled as additional events or message-version state if requested.

- Do not store one enormous mutable conversation JSON blob.

## 10. Send Message - Detailed Write Path

![10. Send Message - Detailed Write Path — source diagram](/diagrams/t-hkzkiuy3eun9-kix-1hgc61hwkhnd.png)

The sender ACK represents durable server acceptance, not recipient delivery.

1. Client creates a globally unique-enough clientMsgId scoped to sender/device.

2. Frame reaches the connection gateway; gateway validates session and rate limits.

3. Message ingress validates membership/permissions and deduplicates clientMsgId.

4. Conversation partition/sequencer assigns the next monotonic seq.

5. Persist the message durably with conversationId + seq + messageId.

6. Publish an event to the delivery/fan-out stream.

7. Return ACK to the sender containing messageId and seq.

8. Delivery workers route to online devices and push/offline mechanisms asynchronously.

ACK semantics
If the server sends 'sent' before durable persistence, a process crash can make a message disappear after the UI showed success. ACK only after the durability threshold is met.

## 11. Retry, Idempotency, and Duplicate Prevention

![11. Retry, Idempotency, and Duplicate Prevention — source diagram](/diagrams/t-hkzkiuy3eun9-kix-pheceknjg80s.png)

Exactly-once network delivery is not required; exactly-once logical insertion is the goal.

- Sender chooses clientMsgId before first attempt.

- Server enforces uniqueness on (senderId/deviceId, clientMsgId) or a similar scope.

- If the client retries after timeout, server returns the previously assigned messageId/seq.

- Delivery frames may duplicate; recipient device deduplicates by messageId/seq.

- ACK frames may duplicate; clients treat them idempotently.

Interview language
I would describe transport as at-least-once with idempotent processing, not claim a magical exactly-once network. Exactly-once user-visible behavior is achieved through stable IDs and deduplication.

## 12. Per-Conversation Ordering

![12. Per-Conversation Ordering — source diagram](/diagrams/t-hkzkiuy3eun9-kix-iug4sovg4g6q.png)

A single conversation needs a stable order; unrelated conversations do not.

### Simple Model

- Hash conversationId to an owning partition/leader.

- Owner maintains nextSeq counter or ordered append log.

- Every accepted message gets seq = previous + 1.

- Persist and publish messages in sequence order.

### Why Timestamps Are Not Enough

- Client clocks differ.

- Two regions can have clock skew.

- Network delay can make an earlier send arrive later.

- Server-assigned sequence gives deterministic order.

Ordering scope
The guarantee should be 'all clients eventually render messages in the same sequence for a conversation', not 'messages everywhere in the system have one global total order'.

## 13. Conversation Partitioning

![13. Conversation Partitioning — source diagram](/diagrams/t-hkzkiuy3eun9-kix-37zvg7y6jpr6.png)

Co-locate ordering and history for one conversation when practical.

- Partition by hash(conversationId).

- All messages for a normal chat route to one logical owner/shard.

- History pagination is efficient by (conversationId, seq).

- Per-conversation sequencing stays local to the partition.

- Very large channels can require sub-partitioned storage while retaining one logical sequence service.

Hot conversation
A celebrity live-chat or giant channel can become a hot partition. Separate the lightweight ordering/metadata owner from horizontally partitioned delivery/storage consumers when one conversation exceeds one shard's capacity.

## 14. Message Store Choice

The storage workload is append-heavy with ordered range reads by conversation.

- Wide-column/log-structured distributed stores fit well at very large scale.

- A relational database can work at smaller scale with sharding by conversation.

- Primary key pattern: (conversationId, timeBucket/partition, seq) if conversations can grow indefinitely.

- Use time buckets only when required so one conversation's history is not one unbounded physical partition.

### Indexes

- Avoid many secondary indexes on the hot write path.

- Conversation list/inbox can be a separate derived store keyed by userId.

Access-pattern design
The message store answers 'give me messages 9000..9050 for conversation C', while the inbox store answers 'which conversations should user U show first?'. These are different access patterns and may deserve separate structures.

## 15. Online Delivery

![15. Online Delivery — source diagram](/diagrams/t-hkzkiuy3eun9-kix-z47qnny06zkp.png)

Delivery is asynchronous fan-out from the durable message event.

1. Delivery worker consumes a persisted-message event.

2. Load conversation membership/recipient(s).

3. Lookup each recipient's active device sessions.

4. Publish delivery frame to the appropriate gateway(s).

5. Gateway enqueues frame in each connection's bounded buffer.

6. Recipient device ACKs the highest contiguous delivered seq or message IDs.

7. Delivery state is persisted/aggregated according to product semantics.

Do not block sender
The sender's durable ACK should not wait for every recipient device, push provider, or read receipt. Those are independent asynchronous outcomes.

## 16. SENT vs DELIVERED vs READ

![16. SENT vs DELIVERED vs READ — source diagram](/diagrams/t-hkzkiuy3eun9-kix-4bepktsdtqrs.png)

Receipts represent different milestones.

### SENT

- Server has durably accepted the message.

### DELIVERED

- At least one recipient device has received/ACKed the message, or product may track per-device delivery.

### READ

- Recipient explicitly advances read cursor after opening/reading conversation.

- Represent read state as lastReadSeq instead of one write per message.

Cursor compression
If a user has read through sequence 50,000, store lastReadSeq=50,000 instead of 50,000 individual read rows. Sequence numbers make receipt state compact.

## 17. Offline Users

![17. Offline Users — source diagram](/diagrams/t-hkzkiuy3eun9-kix-pmc147khozj4.png)

Offline delivery is history catch-up, not a separate fragile queue of full messages.

- Durably store every accepted message.

- If recipient has no active session, optionally send mobile push.

- Track user's lastDeliveredSeq / device cursors.

- On reconnect, query messages after cursor.

- Page old history if many messages accumulated.

Source of truth
Push providers and temporary delivery queues can fail. The durable conversation history is what guarantees an offline user can catch up.

## 18. Reconnect and Catch-Up

![18. Reconnect and Catch-Up — source diagram](/diagrams/t-hkzkiuy3eun9-kix-yeivnnkt1yxx.png)

Backfill missed history before treating the connection as fully live.

- Authenticate and register device session.

- Client provides durable cursors/high-water marks.

- Server returns missing messages/receipt changes, paginated if necessary.

- Client applies in sequence and advances cursor.

- Only then merge into the live delivery stream without gaps.

### Gap Detection

- If client receives seq 105 while expecting 103, buffer 105 and request 103-104.

- Do not display permanently out of order just because network delivery reordered frames.

Reconnect correctness
The client should always be able to rebuild correct state from durable history plus its last cursor, even if every real-time notification during the disconnect was lost.

## 19. Multi-Device Synchronization

![19. Multi-Device Synchronization — source diagram](/diagrams/t-hkzkiuy3eun9-kix-t8t7yjjs7yv.png)

A user can be online on several devices simultaneously.

- Fan out incoming message to all active recipient devices.

- Sender's other devices also need the sent message so conversation history stays consistent.

- Track delivery per device only if product needs it; otherwise aggregate user-level delivered state.

- Read cursor is usually user-level and propagated to all devices, though local unread UX may still have device details.

- Device sessions expire independently.

Important
Do not model a user as one socket. The routing key is userId -> a set of active device sessions.

## 20. Presence and Last Seen

![20. Presence and Last Seen — source diagram](/diagrams/t-hkzkiuy3eun9-kix-ysppv8f5yhqz.png)

Presence should be cheap, ephemeral, and allowed to be slightly stale.

- Gateways update presence leases/heartbeats.

- Presence store uses short TTL.

- Subscribers receive coalesced changes.

- 'Last seen' can be updated less frequently than every heartbeat.

- Privacy settings determine who can observe presence.

- If presence service fails, messaging still works.

Consistency
Presence is a classic eventual-consistency feature. It is acceptable for 'online' to lag by a few seconds; it is not acceptable for durable messages to disappear.

## 21. Typing Indicators

- Ephemeral event: TYPING_START / TYPING_STOP with conversationId.

- Do not persist to the durable message store.

- TTL automatically clears stale typing state.

- Rate-limit/coalesce repeated keystroke events.

- Send only to currently active participants.

Rule of thumb
Typing indicators are best-effort presence-like signals. They should never consume the same durability and storage path as user messages.

## 22. Group Chat - Basic Fan-Out

![22. Group Chat - Basic Fan-Out — source diagram](/diagrams/t-hkzkiuy3eun9-kix-a4fqvmhzwfrm.png)

Persist one group message, then distribute delivery to group members.

- Conversation membership list belongs to group metadata.

- Sender must be an active member at the relevant sequence/version.

- Persist one logical message once.

- Delivery workers fan out to online sessions.

- Offline members catch up from conversation history.

- Membership changes also become ordered events if historical semantics matter.

One copy vs many copies
The canonical message should not be duplicated N times just because a group has N members. Store one message in the group stream and fan out delivery/inbox updates separately.

## 23. Large Groups / Channels

![23. Large Groups / Channels — source diagram](/diagrams/t-hkzkiuy3eun9-kix-zev9nsje45r7.png)

A million-member group cannot run a synchronous per-recipient loop in the send request.

- Persist message and return sender ACK quickly.

- Partition member list/fan-out work into batches.

- Prioritize currently active recipients.

- Offline users can pull from durable group history when they open the group.

- Use bounded queues and backpressure.

- For read-heavy broadcast channels, push-on-read hybrid is often better than eager full fan-out.

Hot group
The group stream may have one ordering owner but multiple fan-out/storage consumers. Separate ordering from delivery throughput so one conversation can scale horizontally.

## 24. Membership Changes and History Semantics

- Store joinedSeq / leftSeq per member.

- A user joining at seq 500 may or may not see earlier history according to product rules.

- Removing a member should block new delivery immediately after the membership change becomes authoritative.

- Group admin role changes require strong conditional metadata updates.

- Membership event can be sequenced into the conversation log to define exact ordering relative to messages.

Why joinedSeq matters
Without membership version/sequence, it is hard to answer whether a user was authorized to receive a message that raced with join/leave events.

## 25. Mobile Push Notifications

![25. Mobile Push Notifications — source diagram](/diagrams/t-hkzkiuy3eun9-kix-nwuau4ebtzfv.png)

Push improves offline UX but is not message transport truth.

- Use APNs/FCM when no active foreground session exists.

- Keep notification payload privacy-safe; consider generic 'new message' for sensitive chats.

- Collapse multiple notifications for busy conversations.

- Push token is per device and can expire/rotate.

- On tap/wake, client connects and pulls missing messages from durable history.

Do not rely on push
Mobile push providers can delay/drop notifications. A lost push may delay user awareness, but it must never lose the underlying message.

## 26. Slow Consumers and Backpressure

![26. Slow Consumers and Backpressure — source diagram](/diagrams/t-hkzkiuy3eun9-kix-fkg14zq9y6ri.png)

Every socket needs a bounded memory budget.

- Each gateway maintains a bounded outbound queue per connection.

- If the device cannot consume fast enough, stop enqueuing indefinitely.

- Options: pause delivery, drop the socket, force reconnect/backfill, or shed low-priority ephemeral events.

- Never drop durable messages permanently; they remain in history.

- Typing/presence updates can be dropped/coalesced first.

Safe degradation
When a connection is too slow, disconnecting it and letting it catch up from history is safer than allowing unbounded gateway memory growth.

## 27. Attachments / Media

![27. Attachments / Media — source diagram](/diagrams/t-hkzkiuy3eun9-kix-mmt2ds4rbjoc.png)

Large media does not belong in the message database.

- Client requests attachment upload session.

- Upload directly to object/media storage using signed URLs.

- Media service scans/transcodes/generates thumbnails as needed.

- After upload is durable, send chat message containing attachmentId/metadata.

- Recipients download through CDN/signed URLs.

- Message history stores the small reference, not the GB-scale bytes.

Ordering
Do not publish a message that references an attachment until the attachment has reached the required durable/ready state, or clearly model a pending attachment state.

## 28. Message Search and Retention Follow-Up

### Search

- Index message text asynchronously by user/conversation if product allows server-side plaintext search.

- Search index can lag; opening result rechecks membership/access.

### Retention

- Policy may keep messages indefinitely, fixed days, or user-managed delete.

- Legal/compliance retention may differ from user-visible deletion.

- Cold history can move to cheaper storage tiers if latency requirements allow.

E2EE impact
True end-to-end encryption changes server-side search/moderation because the server cannot index plaintext. Mention this as a trade-off rather than ignoring it.

## 29. End-to-End Encryption (Optional Follow-Up)

![29. End-to-End Encryption (Optional Follow-Up) — source diagram](/diagrams/t-hkzkiuy3eun9-kix-rgnb21g0ooef.png)

With E2EE, backend stores/routes ciphertext and devices own content keys.

- Device identity keys authenticate devices/users.

- Conversation/session keys encrypt message payloads.

- Multi-device key distribution becomes a major subsystem.

- Server can still sequence ciphertext envelopes and delivery metadata.

- Server-side content search/moderation becomes limited.

- Backups/key recovery become product/security decisions.

Design boundary
You can discuss routing, ordering, delivery, and receipts without designing a full cryptographic protocol. State that production E2EE should use a well-reviewed protocol such as the Signal-style double-ratchet family rather than inventing cryptography in an interview.

## 30. Security and Abuse

- Authenticate every persistent connection.

- Authorize conversation membership before send/history access.

- TLS in transit; encryption at rest.

- Rate-limit messages, conversation creation, invitations, and attachment uploads.

- Spam/abuse detection may operate asynchronously or at send time depending on risk.

- Blocklists should prevent or suppress delivery according to product semantics.

- Audit admin access; minimize logging of message content.

Security ordering
Membership and block-state checks must happen before durable acceptance if the product promises a blocked/removed user cannot send to the conversation.

## 31. Replication and Consistency

- Replicate message partitions across failure domains.

- Sender ACK should wait for the chosen durability threshold (e.g. leader + replica/quorum depending on store).

- Follower reads may lag; live ordering owner should drive new-message sequence.

- History reads can use replicas when cursor/freshness guarantees are satisfied.

- Receipt/presence state can often tolerate weaker consistency than message creation.

Consistency split
Message creation/order and membership authorization need stronger guarantees. Presence, typing, and analytics can be eventually consistent.

## 32. Multi-Region Design

![32. Multi-Region Design — source diagram](/diagrams/t-hkzkiuy3eun9-kix-uozr09qnbl3o.png)

Users connect locally, but one logical owner should serialize each conversation's message order.

- Clients connect to nearby regional gateways.

- ConversationId maps to a home/owner region or globally consistent partition.

- A send from another region routes internally to the owner for sequence + durable append.

- Delivery then fans out to recipient sessions in their local regions.

- Replicate message history to failover/read regions.

### Failover

- Promote a replica/partition with epoch/fencing to prevent two owners.

- After ownership changes, gateways route new sends to the new region.

- Temporary higher latency is preferable to two regions assigning conflicting sequence ranges.

Trade-off
Global active-active writes for the same conversation are much harder than regional connections. Keep connection ingress active-active, but keep conversation ordering single-owner unless a hard requirement justifies consensus across regions.

## 33. Disaster Recovery

- Replicated durable message store across AZs; cross-region replica according to RPO.

- Backups/snapshots for logical corruption recovery, not only live replication.

- Conversation metadata/membership must recover with consistent sequence pointers.

- Session registry/presence is ephemeral and can rebuild after failover.

- Push tokens/device registrations should be replicated/recoverable.

Replication is not backup
A bad delete or corrupted write can replicate everywhere. Keep recoverable historical backups or log-based restore for message/metadata stores according to product policy.

## 34. Failure Modes and Graceful Degradation

![34. Failure Modes and Graceful Degradation — source diagram](/diagrams/t-hkzkiuy3eun9-kix-h6nyok23oc9t.png)

Optional real-time layers can fail without losing durable history.

| Failure | Expected Behavior | Recovery |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Gateway instance dies | Sockets drop | Clients reconnect and catch up from cursor |
| Delivery worker dies | Some frames delayed | Queue/event replay redelivers idempotently |
| Message store unavailable | Cannot safely ACK new sends | Backpressure/fail writes rather than lie |
| Presence service down | Online status stale | Messaging continues |
| Push provider down | Offline notification delayed | History catches up later |
| One region fails | Regional sockets reconnect elsewhere | Promote conversation ownership safely |

Correctness priority
Never show 'sent' for a message that the durable store did not accept. Delayed delivery is tolerable; false durability is not.

## 35. Observability and SLOs

### User-Facing Metrics

- Send acceptance success rate.

- Sender ACK latency p50/p95/p99.

- Online delivery latency: server commit -> recipient socket.

- Reconnect catch-up latency.

- Delivered/read receipt delay.

- Message loss/duplicate correctness incidents.

### Infrastructure Metrics

- Concurrent connections/gateway.

- Outbound buffer high-water / slow consumer rate.

- Message store write latency/replication lag.

- Delivery queue lag.

- Session registry hit/error rate.

- Push failure rate.

- Hot conversation partition load.

Best SLO
A useful messaging SLO measures end-to-end delivery: for an online recipient, what percentage of durably accepted messages reach a healthy connected device within the target time?

## 36. Cost and Capacity Drivers

| Driver | Optimization |
| --- | --- |
| Connection fleet | Efficient event-driven gateways; regional placement |
| Message storage | Compact envelopes, retention tiers, compression |
| Fan-out | Async batch delivery, active-user prioritization |
| Push | Collapse/group notifications |
| Attachments | Object storage + CDN |
| Presence | TTL in-memory data, coalesced updates |
| History reads | Pagination + time-bucketed partitions when needed |

Do not over-cache messages
Recent history can be cached, but the main challenge is usually write throughput, connection routing, and fan-out. Durable storage must remain the source of truth.

## 37. Architecture Evolution

| Stage | Design | Trigger |
| --- | --- | --- |
| V1 | REST/long-poll + SQL | Small product |
| V2 | WebSocket gateway tier | Realtime + connection scale |
| V3 | Partition message store by conversation | Write/history scale |
| V4 | Event stream + async delivery | Fan-out/retry isolation |
| V5 | Session registry + multi-device | Routing complexity |
| V6 | Group fan-out workers + push | Groups/offline UX |
| V7 | Regional gateways + conversation ownership | Global latency |
| V8 | Attachments/CDN/E2EE options | Product expansion |

Interview maturity signal
Show that the service can start simple and evolve. You do not need Kafka, a global session registry, and multi-region sequencing on day one.

## 38. Final Production Architecture

![38. Final Production Architecture — source diagram](/diagrams/t-hkzkiuy3eun9-kix-6e8d3zo1td7f.png)

The final design separates connection state, durable ordered storage, delivery fan-out, and optional media/push layers.

Send path:

- Client -> Connection Gateway -> Message Ingress.

- Ingress validates membership/idempotency.

- Conversation owner assigns sequence and persists durably.

- Sender receives server ACK.

Delivery path:

- Persisted event -> Delivery/Fan-out.
