notes.content:
Design Discord / Real-Time Chat System

Complete System Design Interview Guide

Section 3 — Next Problem | Messaging, Presence, Fan-out & Voice

> Goal
> Design a production-grade Discord-style communication platform with servers/guilds, channels, direct messages, ordered durable chat, real-time delivery, offline sync, presence, typing indicators, unread counts, attachments, search, moderation, and a voice/video extension. The focus is on the trade-off between durable message history and massive real-time fan-out.

## 1. Problem Statement

Users join communities, send messages to text channels or DMs, receive new messages in real time, reconnect and fetch missed history, see online presence, upload attachments, search history, and optionally join voice channels. Large public channels can have millions of members, creating severe fan-out and hotspot challenges.

> Core interview challenge
> A message must be durably stored and ordered within its conversation, yet delivery to connected recipients should be fast and scalable. Do not make every recipient write part of the sender transaction.

## 2. What the Interviewer Is Testing

- WebSocket connection management at millions of concurrent sessions.

- Message ordering, IDs, persistence, pagination, and idempotency.

- Fan-out strategies for small versus huge channels.

- Offline delivery and reconnect synchronization.

- Presence and typing as ephemeral state.

- Unread counts/read cursors without per-message-per-user explosion.

- Partitioning hot channels and preserving conversation ordering.

- Attachments/media, search indexing, moderation, rate limits, abuse controls.

- Failure recovery, backpressure, regional routing, and multi-device semantics.

- Optional voice/video architecture using media servers rather than routing media through chat services.

## 3. Clarifying Questions

- Need guild/server channels and 1:1/group DMs? Yes.

- Message history durable? Yes.

- Ordering scope? Per channel/conversation, not global.

- Delivery guarantee? At-least-once transport with idempotent client/server handling.

- Need edit/delete/reactions? Yes as follow-ups in core model.

- Need presence/typing? Yes, but ephemeral.

- Large channels? Yes; design for very large communities.

- Need attachments? Yes via object storage/CDN.

- Need voice/video? Cover as an extension, not in the core text-message write path.

> Interview-ready opening
> I’ll separate durable conversation state from ephemeral real-time state. Each conversation has an ordering/partition owner that assigns monotonically ordered message IDs, stores messages, then publishes to a fan-out layer. WebSocket gateways deliver to online users; offline users recover from durable history using per-user read cursors.

## 4. Functional Requirements

| Area | Requirement |
| --- | --- |
| Communities | Create/join guilds; roles and channel permissions |
| Messaging | Send/read/edit/delete messages in channels and DMs |
| Realtime | Push messages, reactions, presence, typing |
| History | Cursor-based pagination and reconnect catch-up |
| Unread | Read state, mentions, notification badges |
| Media | Attachments, images, files |
| Search | Search permitted message history |
| Moderation | Delete, mute, ban, rate limit, audit |
| Voice | Join voice channel; audio/video extension |

## 5. Non-Functional Requirements

| Property | Expectation | Implication |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Latency | New messages delivered in hundreds of ms | Persistent connections + local fan-out |
| Durability | Acknowledged messages survive failures | Quorum/durable message store |
| Ordering | Stable order per conversation | Partition owner / ordered key |
| Scale | Millions of concurrent sockets | Gateway sharding |
| Availability | Regional failures should degrade gracefully | Reconnect + durable catch-up |
| Consistency | Strong-ish message append; eventual presence/search | Different stores per semantics |
| Security | Permission checks on every operation | Cached ACLs + authoritative membership |

## 6. Back-of-the-Envelope Estimation

| Dimension | Assumption | Approx. |
| --- | --- | --- |
| DAU | 100M | 100 million |
| Concurrent connections | 10M | 10 million WebSockets |
| Messages/day | 5B | ~58K avg writes/s; much higher peak |
| Average message | 500 B logical | ~2.5 TB/day raw text before replication/indexes |
| Fan-out | 10 recipients avg, extreme channels huge | Delivery events dominate writes |
| Presence heartbeat | 30 sec for 10M sessions | ~333K heartbeats/s if naive |
| Retention | Years | Tiered message storage + archive |

> Capacity insight
> The hard number is not only message writes. A single message may cause many real-time deliveries, notifications, mention updates, moderation checks, and search indexing. Fan-out can dominate the system.

## 7. Core APIs and Realtime Events

| Interface | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| POST /channels/{id}/messages | Send message with client nonce/idempotency key |
| GET /channels/{id}/messages?before= | Cursor pagination |
| PATCH /messages/{id} | Edit message |
| DELETE /messages/{id} | Delete/tombstone |
| PUT /channels/{id}/read-state | Advance read cursor |
| POST /messages/{id}/reactions | Add/remove reaction |
| WebSocket IDENTIFY/RESUME | Open or resume realtime session |
| Gateway MESSAGE_CREATE | Realtime message event |
| Gateway PRESENCE_UPDATE | Ephemeral presence |
| Gateway TYPING_START | Ephemeral typing |

## 8. Data Model

| Entity | Important fields |
| --- | --- |
| Guild | guild_id, name, owner, region/config |
| Channel | channel_id, guild_id/null, type, partition_key, permissions |
| Membership | guild_id, user_id, roles, state |
| Message | channel_id, message_id, author_id, content_ref, created_at, edited_at, flags |
| Reaction | message_id, emoji, user_id or aggregate |
| ReadState | user_id, channel_id, last_read_message_id, mention_count/version |
| Session | session_id, user_id, gateway_id, sequence, resume token |
| Presence | user_id, status, last_seen, device summary, TTL |
| Attachment | attachment_id, owner, object_key, metadata, scan_state |

## 9. Message IDs and Ordering

- Do not require a single global message sequence. Ordering only needs to be meaningful inside a channel/DM.

- Route all appends for a conversation key to one logical partition/leader at a time.

- Assign an ordered message_id using partition sequence, time-sortable ID with tie-breaking, or database sequence scoped by shard.

- The server order is authoritative; client timestamps are not.

- Edits/deletes reference the immutable message identity; deletion usually leaves a tombstone/event for consistency and moderation.

> Important distinction
> Ordering and delivery are different. A message can have a stable position in durable history even if network delivery reaches devices late or twice. Clients reconcile using message_id/sequence.

## 10. High-Level Architecture

![10. High-Level Architecture — source diagram](/diagrams/t-rh6jgzxywb1h-kix-msgwl8edc5cv.png)

Discord-style messaging — high-level architecture

## 11. Message Send Path

- Client sends channel_id, content, attachment references, and client_nonce/idempotency key.

- Edge authenticates user and routes by channel_id.

- Message service checks membership/permission and rate limits.

- Conversation partition validates idempotency and assigns authoritative message_id/order.

- Message is durably appended.

- Only after durable commit, publish MESSAGE_CREATE through outbox/log/pub-sub.

- Fan-out layer determines online subscribers and gateway destinations.

- Gateways push event to connected devices.

- Offline clients later fetch history from durable store.

> Ack rule
> A send acknowledgement should mean the message is durably accepted, not that every recipient has already received it. Recipient delivery is asynchronous.

## 12. Message Write Sequence

![12. Message Write Sequence — source diagram](/diagrams/t-rh6jgzxywb1h-kix-te9tl6vykwxa.png)

Durable append then asynchronous fan-out

## 13. Idempotency and Duplicate Sends

- Mobile clients retry when ACK is lost; retries must not create duplicate messages.

- Use a client-generated nonce/message request ID scoped to user/channel/session.

- Persist nonce → message_id with the append transaction or enforce a unique constraint.

- A retry returns the original message_id and state.

- Realtime delivery can also duplicate; client deduplicates by message_id/event sequence.

## 14. Message Storage and Partitioning

| Choice | Design |
| --- | --- |
| Partition key | channel_id / conversation_id |
| Sort key | message_id descending/ascending |
| Access pattern | Recent history and cursor pagination |
| Store | Wide-column/LSM or sharded relational store |
| Replication | Multiple replicas; durable quorum/leader append |
| Archive | Cold older history to cheaper object/storage tier if needed |
| Hot channel | Dedicated partition/leader; fan-out separated from storage |

> Why channel_id?
> Most reads request contiguous history for one conversation, and ordering is scoped to that conversation. This keeps append and pagination local.

## 15. Cursor Pagination

- Use message_id cursor rather than OFFSET; offset becomes slow and unstable as history grows.

- GET messages before=<message_id> returns the next page in deterministic order.

- Time-sortable IDs help operational debugging and pagination, but server ordering remains authoritative.

- Edits/deletes do not shift message identity; tombstones preserve cursor semantics.

## 16. Fan-Out: Small Channels vs Huge Channels

| Strategy | When | How |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Fan-out on write | DMs/small groups | Publish directly to each online user/session; optional inbox metadata |
| Channel pub-sub | Medium/large channels | Publish once to channel topic; gateway subscriptions deliver to connected members |
| Pull/catch-up | Offline/very large audience | Do not create per-user message copies; clients fetch durable history |
| Hybrid | Production default | Realtime push for online, cursor pull for recovery/offline |

> Avoid the celebrity-channel trap
> Never insert one physical copy of every channel message into millions of user inbox rows. Store the message once and distribute ephemeral delivery events; unread state is represented compactly.

## 17. Fan-Out Architecture

![17. Fan-Out Architecture — source diagram](/diagrams/t-rh6jgzxywb1h-kix-2vj19k4f8epz.png)

Hybrid fan-out for online and offline users

## 18. WebSocket Gateway Design

- Gateways are mostly stateless except live socket/session routing.

- Shard sessions by user/session hash; maintain user_id → active gateway/session mappings in a presence/session directory.

- A user may have multiple devices; publish to each eligible active session.

- Gateway sends monotonically increasing event sequence for resume/recovery.

- Use heartbeats and bounded send buffers. Slow clients trigger backpressure, coalescing, or disconnect/resume rather than unbounded memory.

- On gateway death, clients reconnect elsewhere and RESUME from last sequence when possible; otherwise reload state/history.

## 19. Reconnect and Offline Sync

- Client reconnects with session/resume token and last gateway sequence.

- If gateway/session event buffer still exists, replay missed transient events.

- Regardless, client knows last seen/read message IDs per active conversation.

- Fetch durable messages after last known message_id for channels opened or needing catch-up.

- Presence/typing need not be replayed; they are ephemeral snapshots.

- Recompute unread/mentions from compact read state and message metadata if needed.

> Recovery principle
> The realtime stream is an optimization over durable state. A client must be able to recover correctness after losing the entire socket stream.

## 20. Read Receipts and Unread Counts

- For large channels, do not store one read receipt row for every user-message pair.

- Store per-user per-channel last_read_message_id/read cursor.

- Unread count can be estimated/derived from channel high-watermark versus cursor, or maintained as a projection.

- Mentions may need a compact per-user mention index/counter because not every unread message is equally important.

- DM read receipts can be richer because participant count is small.

## 21. Presence

- Presence is ephemeral and eventually consistent.

- Sessions heartbeat into a TTL-based presence service.

- Aggregate multiple devices into user status according to policy.

- Publish presence only to users who are allowed/likely to care; avoid global broadcast.

- Large guilds may receive coarse/lazy presence rather than exact status for every member.

- After region/gateway failure, presence naturally rebuilds from reconnects/heartbeats.

> Presence is not a database transaction
> If a user appears online for a few seconds after disconnect, that is acceptable. Do not give presence the same consistency machinery as message history.

## 22. Typing Indicators

- Purely ephemeral event with short TTL (for example several seconds).

- Rate-limit client typing events; send start/refresh rather than every keystroke.

- Do not persist to message history.

- Drop under overload before dropping durable message traffic.

## 23. Edits, Deletes, and Reactions

- Edit: update message version/current content and emit MESSAGE_UPDATE; optionally retain revision audit according to policy.

- Delete: tombstone or mark deleted; emit MESSAGE_DELETE; asynchronous cleanup handles indexes/attachments according to retention policy.

- Reaction: idempotent add/remove keyed by message_id + emoji + user_id; maintain aggregates for fast reads.

- Late events include message version so clients do not regress to older content.

## 24. Attachments and Media

- Client requests upload authorization from attachment service.

- Service issues short-lived pre-signed object-storage upload URL.

- Client uploads directly to object storage, not through chat servers.

- Async malware/content scan and metadata extraction run.

- Message references attachment_id/object key.

- CDN serves approved media; private content uses signed access/authorization.

> Why direct upload?
> Large files should not consume message-service bandwidth or memory. The chat write path stores metadata/reference, while object storage handles bytes.

## 25. Search

- Message DB remains source of truth; search index is asynchronous/eventually consistent.

- Outbox/event stream feeds indexer with create/edit/delete events.

- Partition/index by guild/channel/time and enforce authorization filters.

- Deletion must propagate to index; periodic reconciliation repairs missed events.

- Search outage must not block sending messages.

## 26. Permissions and Membership

- Every send/read/search operation enforces guild/channel membership and role/ACL rules.

- Cache role/permission calculations with versioning, but authoritative membership changes must invalidate or carry a newer version.

- For private channels, fan-out service should not blindly trust stale subscription state forever.

- Ban/kick should rapidly revoke gateway subscriptions and future history access.

## 27. Moderation and Abuse

- Per-user/channel/guild rate limits on sends, mentions, joins, reactions, and attachment uploads.

- Spam heuristics and trust/risk signals run synchronously or asynchronously depending severity.

- Moderation actions are durable and audited.

- Content scanning can quarantine attachments/messages while preserving system availability.

- Large raids may trigger guild-level slow mode, verification gates, or stricter admission.

## 28. Hot Channels and Hot Partitions

- A huge live-event channel can create a single write partition and massive fan-out.

- Message append throughput is usually far lower than delivery throughput; isolate fan-out from storage.

- Use dedicated partition ownership/capacity for hot channels.

- Batch/coalesce gateway deliveries where protocol allows.

- Slow mode/rate limits cap sender write rate.

- If one channel exceeds a single ordered writer, advanced designs can partition epochs/lanes and merge by server-assigned ordering, but complexity rises sharply; prefer preserving one logical ordering authority as long as practical.

> Do not casually shard one ordered channel by random message hash
> That destroys straightforward channel ordering. First scale the partition vertically/dedicate it, separate fan-out, and use controlled sequencing if further split is unavoidable.

## 29. Backpressure and Overload

| Layer | Backpressure action |
| --- | --- |
| Gateway socket | Bounded buffer; drop/coalesce ephemeral events; disconnect slow client with resume |
| Fan-out | Partition queues; consumer lag metrics; shed presence/typing first |
| Message write | Rate limit/queue briefly; preserve durable append correctness |
| Search/index | Allow lag; catch up later |
| Notifications | Batch/delay non-critical notifications |
| Attachments | Throttle upload authorization/scanning |

## 30. Failure Scenarios

| Failure | Correct behavior |
| --- | --- |
| Sender retries after lost ACK | Idempotency returns original message |
| Message DB commits; publisher crashes | Outbox/log publishes later |
| Pub/sub duplicates event | Gateway/client dedupe by event/message ID |
| Gateway dies | Reconnect/resume or fetch durable history |
| Recipient offline | No per-user copy required; pull on reconnect |
| Presence store fails | Presence temporarily unknown; rebuild from heartbeat |
| Search index behind | Search stale; messaging unaffected |
| Attachment scan delayed | Keep attachment pending/quarantined |
| Hot channel overload | Slow mode/rate limit/dedicated fan-out capacity |
| Region failure | Reconnect to failover region; durable messages preserved |

## 31. Multi-Region Design

- Terminate WebSockets close to users at edge/regional gateways.

- Assign each conversation/guild to a home message-write region/partition to keep ordering simple.

- Remote send commands route to the conversation owner; recipient delivery can fan out globally.

- Replicate durable message log/history to secondary regions for DR and local reads where safe.

- Use fenced leader/epoch during failover so two regions do not independently assign overlapping sequence/order.

- Presence is regional and mergeable; it can rebuild after failover.

> Ordering versus latency trade-off
> A single home writer per conversation adds cross-region latency for some senders but gives a clear ordering domain. Global active-active writes to one conversation require substantially more coordination.

## 32. Voice / Video Extension

Voice is a different data plane. Do not route raw audio/video through the durable text-message service.

![32. Voice / Video Extension — source diagram](/diagrams/t-rh6jgzxywb1h-kix-3irug3tfzx0e.png)

Voice channel architecture

- Signaling authenticates membership and chooses a nearby media server/SFU.

- Audio/video packets use UDP/WebRTC-like transport where possible; media server forwards streams.

- SFU avoids every participant sending directly to every other participant.

- Text chat and voice presence share identity/channel authorization but have separate scaling/failure characteristics.

- Media quality adapts bitrate/codecs to network conditions.

## 33. Security and Privacy

- TLS for APIs/WebSockets; secure media transport for voice.

- Authorize every channel operation and attachment fetch.

- Rate-limit tokens/sessions and detect credential abuse.

- Encrypt sensitive stored data and protect signing/session secrets.

- Audit moderator/admin actions.

- Retention/deletion workflows propagate to primary history, indexes, caches, and object storage according to policy.

## 34. Observability

| Metric | Why |
| --- | --- |
| Message append latency/error rate | Core durability path |
| Gateway connected sessions | Capacity |
| Fan-out lag by partition | Realtime health |
| Reconnect/resume success | Gateway reliability |
| Duplicate/idempotency rate | Client/network behavior |
| Hot-channel queue depth | Hotspot detection |
| Presence heartbeat lag | Ephemeral health |
| Search indexing lag | Search freshness |
| Attachment scan backlog | Media safety |
| Voice packet loss/jitter/RTT | Media quality |

## 35. Final Production Architecture

- Edge/API authenticates and routes channel commands.

- Conversation owner/partition assigns ordered IDs and durably appends one message copy.

- Transactional outbox/log publishes committed message events.

- Hybrid fan-out pushes to online gateway sessions; offline users recover by cursor from durable history.

- WebSocket gateways use heartbeats, bounded buffers, sequence/resume, and snapshot/history recovery.

- Presence/typing live in TTL-based ephemeral systems and are shed first under overload.

- Read cursors represent unread state compactly; avoid per-user-per-message copies for large channels.

- Attachments use object storage/CDN; search and moderation consume asynchronous events.

- Conversation writes have a home region/leader; global gateways deliver near recipients.

- Voice/video uses a separate signaling + regional SFU media plane.

> Final architecture in one sentence
> Store each message once in an ordered conversation partition, acknowledge after durable append, then fan out asynchronously to online WebSocket sessions while offline clients recover by cursor; keep presence/typing ephemeral, search/media asynchronous, and voice on a separate media plane.

## 36. Key Trade-offs

| Decision | Option A | Option B | Choice |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Delivery | Per-user durable copies | Store once + hybrid fan-out | Hybrid |
| Ordering | Global order | Per-conversation order | Per conversation |
| Presence | Strong durable | TTL/eventual | TTL/eventual |
| Offline | Queue every event | Fetch durable history | History pull |
| Pagination | OFFSET | Message cursor | Cursor |
| Large channel | Fan-out inbox writes | Topic/gateway push + pull | Hybrid |
| Voice | Chat service carries media | Separate SFU plane | Separate |

## 37. Common Interview Mistakes

- Trying to guarantee global ordering for all messages.

- Writing one copy of a large-channel message to every member inbox.

- Acknowledging before durable append.

- No client nonce/idempotency for send retries.

- Treating WebSocket delivery as durable storage.

- Persisting typing indicators like messages.

- No recovery path after gateway reconnect.

- Using OFFSET pagination for huge histories.

- Randomly sharding one hot channel and losing ordering.

- Sending attachment bytes through chat servers.

- Making search synchronous with message send.

- Routing voice media through the text-message backend.

## 38. 45-Minute Interview Flow

| Time | Coverage |
| --- | --- |
| 0–5 min | Requirements, scale, ordering/delivery semantics |
| 5–10 min | APIs + data model + message IDs |
| 10–17 min | HLD + send path |
| 17–24 min | Storage/partitioning + idempotency |
| 24–31 min | Fan-out + WebSocket gateway + offline sync |
| 31–36 min | Presence/read state/hot channels |
| 36–40 min | Attachments/search/moderation |
| 40–43 min | Multi-region + failures |
| 43–45 min | Voice extension + summary |

> Memorize this story
> Send → permission/idempotency → conversation partition → durable append/order → outbox/pub-sub → gateway fan-out → online delivery. Offline recovery comes from message history + read cursor. Presence/typing are ephemeral. Hot channels scale fan-out separately.

## 39. Interviewer Follow-Ups — Detailed Answers

Follow-up: How do you guarantee message order?

Answer: Route one conversation to one logical ordering authority/partition and assign server-side ordered message IDs. Do not attempt a global order.

Follow-up: What if two users send at exactly the same time?

Answer: The conversation partition serializes/assigns a deterministic order. Client timestamps do not decide it.

Follow-up: What if the sender retries because ACK was lost?

Answer: Client nonce/idempotency mapping returns the same message_id instead of appending again.

Follow-up: Do you guarantee exactly-once delivery?

Answer: No. Use at-least-once event delivery plus deduplication by message/event ID. The business state is durable once.

Follow-up: How do offline users receive messages?

Answer: They fetch durable channel history after their last known message_id/read cursor. We do not need to queue every channel message per offline member.

Follow-up: How do you scale a channel with one million members?

Answer: Store the message once, publish a channel event, push only to online subscribed gateway sessions, and let offline members pull history. Avoid million-row fan-out writes.

Follow-up: What if a WebSocket gateway crashes?

Answer: Clients reconnect, resume from event sequence if retained, otherwise reload durable state/history. The gateway is not the source of truth.

Follow-up: How do unread counts work?

Answer: Keep per-user/channel last_read_message_id plus compact mention counters/projections rather than read rows for every message.

Follow-up: How do you implement presence?

Answer: TTL heartbeats per active session, aggregate to user status, and publish selectively. Presence can be stale for seconds.

Follow-up: How do you handle typing?

Answer: Short-lived, rate-limited ephemeral events; never persist; drop first under overload.

Follow-up: How do you partition messages?

Answer: By channel/conversation ID so append ordering and history pagination stay local.

Follow-up: What if one channel becomes a hot partition?

Answer: Dedicate capacity, rate-limit/slow-mode writes, separate fan-out from append, and preserve one ordering authority as long as possible.

Follow-up: How do edits/deletes work with caches and clients?

Answer: Emit versioned update/delete events referencing the same message ID. Clients ignore older versions; durable state/tombstone is authoritative.

Follow-up: How are attachments uploaded?

Answer: Pre-signed direct object-storage upload, asynchronous scan, then message stores an attachment reference. CDN serves authorized content.

Follow-up: How does search stay consistent?

Answer: It is eventually consistent via message events. Create/edit/delete events update the index; reconciliation repairs gaps.

Follow-up: How do permissions affect fan-out?

Answer: Gateway subscriptions are created from authorized membership, but sensitive reads/sends still enforce authoritative/versioned ACL state. Revocations invalidate subscriptions quickly.

Follow-up: How do you handle multiple devices?

Answer: A user has multiple sessions; realtime events can go to all active sessions. Read state can be user-level while local UI state is device-specific.

Follow-up: How do you design multi-region ordering?

Answer: Assign each conversation a home writer/leader region and route sends there. Fan-out occurs near recipients globally. Failover uses fencing/epochs.

Follow-up: Why is voice a separate architecture?

Answer: Audio/video is high-bandwidth, latency-sensitive media traffic using UDP/WebRTC/SFU patterns; it should not pass through durable text-message storage.

Follow-up: What data would you drop first under overload?

Answer: Typing and fine-grained presence, then coalesce non-critical realtime updates. Preserve durable message append and correctness.

## 40. Detailed Interview Q&A

1. What is the core architectural separation?

Answer: Durable ordered message history is one plane; ephemeral realtime delivery/presence is another. The socket layer can fail without losing message truth.

2. Why not use Kafka alone as the message database?

Answer: A log is excellent for streaming/fan-out, but product history needs efficient per-channel pagination, retention, edits/deletes, access control, and long-term querying. A durable message store/read model is still useful.

3. When do you ACK the sender?

Answer: After the message append and idempotency mapping are durably committed. Not after all recipients receive it.

4. What does the outbox solve?

Answer: It prevents a committed message from being missing from downstream fan-out because the service crashed between DB commit and publish.

5. How do clients detect gaps?

Answer: Gateway sequence can detect realtime gaps; message IDs/read cursors allow durable catch-up for conversation history.

6. Can message IDs be Snowflake-like?

Answer: Yes, if they provide uniqueness and useful time ordering, but you still need a clear per-conversation authoritative ordering rule for concurrent appends.

7. Why cursor pagination?

Answer: It is stable and efficient on ordered keys, unlike large OFFSET scans that become expensive and can shift as data changes.

8. Would you store reactions as rows or counters?

Answer: Store idempotent user reaction membership when needed for correctness, plus aggregate counts/projections for fast display.

9. How do you avoid presence fan-out explosion?

Answer: Only publish presence to relevant relationships/visible guild subsets; use lazy/coarse presence in huge communities.

10. What happens if pub/sub is down?

Answer: Committed messages remain durable. Outbox/log backlog catches up; users can still recover history even if realtime delivery is delayed.

11. How do you protect slow clients?

Answer: Bound gateway send queues, coalesce/drop ephemeral events, and disconnect with resumable recovery rather than allowing unbounded memory.

12. How do you handle message deletion from search?

Answer: Delete/tombstone event updates the index asynchronously; periodic reconciliation verifies index state against source-of-truth retention rules.

13. How do DMs differ from guild channels?

Answer: Small participant sets make direct fan-out, richer read receipts, and per-user notification state cheaper. The same durable conversation abstraction can still be used.

14. What consistency does presence need?

Answer: Eventual/TTL consistency. A brief stale online indicator is acceptable; message/permission state is more important.

15. How would you support end-to-end encryption?

Answer: It changes server-side moderation/search and key management substantially. For encrypted conversations, servers store ciphertext and clients manage conversation keys; this is a major product/security trade-off.

16. What should be replicated most strongly?

Answer: Durable message history, membership/permission changes, and moderation records. Presence/typing can rebuild.

17. How do you recover after a region failover?

Answer: Fence old conversation leaders, promote replicas/new owners, reconnect gateways, resume or fetch history, and rebuild ephemeral presence from sessions.

18. What is the biggest scaling trap?

Answer: Confusing durable storage fan-out with realtime delivery fan-out. A large channel should not multiply durable message copies by member count.

19. What are the core SLOs?

Answer: Message append latency/durability, online delivery latency, gateway availability, fan-out lag, reconnect recovery success, and history read latency.

20. Give the final one-minute summary.

Answer: Partition durable history by conversation, assign ordered IDs at the conversation owner, ACK after durable append, publish via outbox, and use hybrid fan-out to online WebSocket sessions while offline clients pull history by cursor. Keep presence/typing ephemeral, attachments in object storage, search asynchronous, and voice on regional SFUs.

## 41. Review Quiz

1. What ordering should the system guarantee?

Answer: Per conversation/channel, not global.

2. When should sender ACK happen?

Answer: After durable message append/idempotency commit.

3. How do you avoid duplicate messages on retry?

Answer: Client nonce/idempotency key mapped to the original message ID.

4. Why not copy a huge-channel message to every member inbox?

Answer: It creates massive write amplification; store once and use hybrid fan-out.

5. How do offline users recover?

Answer: Cursor-based durable history fetch after their last known/read message.

6. What state is ephemeral?

Answer: Presence and typing indicators.

7. What prevents WebSocket loss from losing messages?

Answer: WebSockets are delivery only; durable message store is source of truth.

8. How do attachments scale?

Answer: Direct object-storage upload + CDN; chat stores references.

9. How do you scale voice?

Answer: Separate signaling and regional SFU/media servers.

10. Core flow?

Answer: Send → ordered durable append → outbox/pub-sub → online gateway fan-out; offline history pull.

## 42. 30-Second Final Interview Answer

> 30-second final answer
> I would partition durable message history by conversation and route each conversation to one logical ordering authority. A send carries a client nonce; after permission checks, the partition assigns the authoritative message ID, atomically stores the message and publication intent, then ACKs the sender. An outbox/pub-sub layer asynchronously fans the event to WebSocket gateways for online sessions. Offline users do not need per-user message copies; they recover from durable history using message/read cursors. Presence and typing are TTL-based ephemeral services, attachments go directly to object storage/CDN, search is asynchronous, hot channels scale fan-out separately from ordered append, and voice/video uses a separate regional SFU media plane.

## 43. Final Checklist

- Requirements and ordering scope clarified.

- Message/write QPS and fan-out scale estimated.

- Durable message IDs, idempotency, and ACK semantics covered.

- Conversation partitioning and cursor pagination explained.

- Hybrid fan-out handles both small and huge channels.

- WebSocket gateway, backpressure, resume, and offline recovery covered.

- Read cursors avoid per-message read-receipt explosion.

- Presence/typing separated as ephemeral state.

- Edits/deletes/reactions and versioning covered.

- Attachments, search, permissions, moderation, and rate limits included.

- Hot channels and overload behavior explained.

- Multi-region conversation ownership/failover covered.

- Voice/video extension separated into media plane.

- Detailed follow-ups, Q&A, and review quiz included.

notes.title: Design WhatsApp / Large-Scale Messaging Platform
notes.description: Goal Design a global messaging platform that delivers one-to-one and group messages with low latency, supports offline users and multiple devices, provides sent
notes.content:
Design WhatsApp / Large-Scale Messaging Platform

Advanced System Design Interview Guide

Problem 27 | 1:1 Messaging, Groups, Ordering, Delivery, Presence, Media, Multi-Device & E2EE

> Goal
> Design a global messaging platform that delivers one-to-one and group messages with low latency, supports offline users and multiple devices, provides sent/delivered/read state, handles media efficiently, scales persistent connections, and preserves correct conversation ordering despite retries and failures.

> Central interview idea
> Separate connection delivery from durable message truth. A WebSocket gateway can disappear at any moment; the message log, recipient inbox state, device cursors, idempotency keys and conversation sequence are what make delivery recoverable.

## 1. Functional Requirements

| Area | Requirements |
| --- | --- |
| 1:1 | Send text, emoji, reply, reactions, edit/delete policy |
| Groups | Create group, membership, roles, group messages |
| Delivery state | Sent, server-accepted, delivered, read |
| Offline | Store and deliver after reconnect |
| Presence | Online/last-seen/typing with privacy controls |
| Media | Images, video, audio, documents |
| Multi-device | Phone + web/desktop/tablet synchronization |
| Notifications | Push fallback when app is backgrounded |
| Security | Authentication, abuse controls, E2EE architecture considerations |

## 2. Non-Functional Requirements

- Low end-to-end latency for online users.

- Billions of users and millions of concurrent persistent connections.

- Messages must not silently disappear after server acceptance.

- Duplicate network requests must not create duplicate logical messages.

- Ordering should be well-defined per conversation, not globally.

- Offline backlog and reconnect storms must be handled safely.

- Media should not flow through the same hot path as tiny text messages.

- Regional failures should preserve durable accepted messages and allow recovery.

## 3. Scope and Semantics

- No global ordering across unrelated conversations.

- At-least-once network delivery is acceptable if clients deduplicate; exactly-once transport is not assumed.

- Server acceptance means durable responsibility has been taken.

- Delivered means at least one intended recipient device has acknowledged receipt, depending on product semantics.

- Read receipts are user/device events and can be disabled by policy.

- Group messages use one logical message with fan-out metadata rather than N unrelated messages.

- Voice/video calls are an extension; messaging is the main problem.

## 4. Capacity Estimation

| Dimension | Illustrative scale | Implication |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Users | Billions | Global sharding |
| Concurrent sockets | 100M+ possible | Dedicated connection tier |
| Messages/day | 100B-scale conceivable | High-throughput append path |
| Peak msg QPS | Millions/sec | Partitioned queues/logs |
| Groups | Huge count; skewed sizes | Fan-out strategy matters |
| Media | Dominates bytes | Object storage/CDN |
| Presence events | Very high and ephemeral | TTL/pub-sub, not OLTP |
| Offline backlog | Potentially huge | Inbox cursors + retention |

## 5. APIs and Realtime Protocol

| Operation | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| WS CONNECT | Authenticate device/session |
| SEND_MESSAGE | client_msg_id, conversation_id, payload metadata |
| ACK_RECEIVED | Device received server message |
| READ_UP_TO | Read cursor for conversation |
| SYNC | Fetch messages after cursor/version |
| PRESENCE | Heartbeat/online state |
| TYPING | Ephemeral typing signal |
| POST /media/init | Create upload session |
| POST /groups/... | Membership/admin operations |

## 6. Core Data Model

| Entity | Important fields |
| --- | --- |
| User | user_id, profile, privacy settings |
| Device | device_id, user_id, keys, push token, last_seen |
| Conversation | conversation_id, type, version |
| Membership | conversation_id, user_id, role, joined_seq, left_seq |
| Message | conversation_id, seq, message_id, sender, payload_ref, timestamp |
| InboxCursor | user/device, conversation, delivered_seq, read_seq |
| Outbox/Delivery | message/device target, state, retry metadata |
| MediaObject | media_id, object_ref, metadata, checksum |
| Presence | user/device, state, expiry |

## 7. High-Level Architecture

![7. High-Level Architecture — source diagram](/diagrams/t-pzg8uy5uii6d-kix-dxdk99vzo5gy.png)

## 8. Message Send Lifecycle

- Client creates globally unique client_msg_id and local optimistic UI entry.

- Persistent gateway authenticates device and forwards send request.

- Message service checks idempotency and membership/permission.

- Conversation sequencing assigns the next sequence number or equivalent ordered position.

- Message is durably appended before server acceptance is returned.

- An outbox/event triggers recipient fan-out.

- Online recipient devices receive message through their gateways.

- Offline recipients retain durable inbox/message availability and receive push notification.

- Recipient ACK updates delivered cursor/state; read event later advances read cursor.

> Acceptance rule
> Do not tell the sender 'sent to server' before the message is durably owned. A gateway enqueue in RAM is not enough.

## 9. Message Identity and Idempotency

- Client-generated client_msg_id survives retries after timeout.

- Server maps (sender/device, client_msg_id) to one logical message_id.

- Retry returns the existing result rather than appending a second message.

- Delivery to recipient may still be at least once; recipient deduplicates by message_id.

- Media upload also uses idempotent upload/session IDs.

- Group membership changes and read-cursor updates should be idempotent as well.

## 10. Ordering Model

| Ordering scope | Recommended guarantee |
| --- | --- |
| Global | None |
| Per conversation | Monotonic sequence/order |
| Per sender | Naturally implied by conversation sequence when accepted in order |
| Across devices | Merge through conversation sequence/cursors |
| Presence/typing | Best effort; no durable total order |

The clean interview answer is per-conversation ordering. A conversation_id is routed to one logical sequencing owner/partition at a time. Messages receive monotonically increasing seq values. Clients display by seq, not by arrival time.

## 11. Conversation Sequencing

![11. Conversation Sequencing — source diagram](/diagrams/t-pzg8uy5uii6d-kix-s259yncygka6.png)

- Hash conversation_id to a partition or use directory-based ownership.

- One active sequencer/leader per partition avoids conflicting sequence allocation.

- Batch sequence allocation is possible but can create gaps; gaps are acceptable if semantics permit.

- Failover must fence the old owner so two leaders cannot assign conflicting sequence positions.

- Sequence is about ordering, not wall-clock truth.

## 12. Storage Layout

| Need | Storage pattern |
| --- | --- |
| Conversation metadata | Strongly managed KV/relational |
| Messages | Partitioned append-friendly wide-column/log store |
| Membership | Conversation/user indexed durable store |
| Inbox/read cursors | Small KV records |
| Presence | In-memory TTL store |
| Media bytes | Object storage |
| Media metadata | Durable DB |
| Analytics | Event stream/lake |

A common message key is (conversation_id, sequence). This supports range reads for sync and keeps a conversation ordered. Extremely large/hot conversations may need subpartitioning while preserving a logical order.

## 13. Online Delivery

- Delivery worker resolves recipient's active devices/sessions.

- Connection registry maps device to gateway node.

- Worker publishes message to that gateway or a gateway-scoped queue.

- Gateway writes frame to socket with delivery token/message_id.

- Device persists message locally and returns ACK.

- Server advances delivered cursor/state idempotently.

- If gateway/socket disappears, delivery remains pending/recoverable from durable state.

## 14. Offline Delivery and Sync

- Do not create one unbounded physical queue per user if message store + cursors can represent backlog.

- Store durable messages by conversation and maintain recipient/device delivery cursors.

- On reconnect, client sends last known conversation/global sync cursor.

- Sync service returns missing message ranges and membership changes.

- Use pagination and bounded batches to avoid reconnect storms.

- Push notification is a wake-up hint, not the message source of truth.

## 15. Delivery and Read Receipts

| State | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| LOCAL | Created on sender device |
| SERVER_ACCEPTED | Durably stored by service |
| DELIVERED | Recipient device ACKed receipt |
| READ | Recipient read cursor passed message |
| FAILED | Permanent validation/policy failure |

- Represent read state as highest contiguous read sequence when possible rather than one row per message.

- For groups, receipt aggregation can be expensive; store per-member cursors and compute summaries.

- Receipt events can be batched/coalesced.

- Do not infer read from push delivery.

## 16. Reconnect and Gap Recovery

![16. Reconnect and Gap Recovery — source diagram](/diagrams/t-pzg8uy5uii6d-kix-fcajqytt0x1s.png)

- Client detects sequence gaps or reconnects after offline period.

- Sync reads authoritative ranges rather than trusting missed socket frames.

- Tombstones/edits/reactions need versioned change events too.

- Large backlogs are paginated and can prioritize recent messages first if product allows.

- Device cursor advances only after local persistence.

## 17. Multi-Device Synchronization

- Each user can have multiple independently connected devices.

- A sent message is also synchronized to the sender's other devices.

- Each device has its own delivery cursor because one laptop may be offline for days.

- Read state may be user-level: reading on one device advances user read cursor and syncs to others.

- Device add/remove is a security-sensitive membership event.

- With E2EE, each device may have separate cryptographic identity/session material.

## 18. Group Messaging Basics

| Concern | Design |
| --- | --- |
| Membership | Durable versioned membership |
| Ordering | One logical conversation sequence |
| Fan-out | Recipients derived from membership snapshot/version |
| Roles | Admin/member permissions |
| Join | Usually cannot access messages before allowed join boundary |
| Leave/remove | No delivery after effective membership boundary |
| Large groups | Fan-out and receipt costs dominate |

## 19. Group Fan-Out Strategies

| Strategy | Pros | Cons |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Fan-out on write | Fast reads/delivery | Write amplification for large groups |
| Fan-out on read | Cheap send | Recipient sync more complex/slow |
| Hybrid | Adapt by group size/activity | More system complexity |

For ordinary groups, fan-out on write is straightforward. For very large broadcast-like groups, store one message and fan out references/notifications asynchronously or let clients pull from a shared ordered log. The logical message should not be copied as full payload N times.

## 20. Membership Race Semantics

> Critical question
> If Alice is removed while Bob sends a group message, should Alice receive it? Define membership relative to the message's committed sequence/version.

- Version group membership changes.

- Message append records membership_version or evaluates recipients at an ordered boundary.

- A user removed before the message's effective sequence is excluded.

- A user joining later should not automatically receive earlier history unless product policy says so.

- Fan-out retries use the same recipient snapshot/version, preventing membership drift from changing semantics.

## 21. Presence and Last Seen

- Presence is ephemeral and should not be written on every heartbeat to durable user DB.

- Gateway/session heartbeat refreshes TTL in a presence store.

- Online means at least one active device session within freshness threshold.

- Last-seen can be asynchronously persisted at lower frequency.

- Privacy rules are checked before returning presence.

- Presence fan-out should be subscription-limited; do not broadcast every user's state globally.

## 22. Typing Indicators

- Best-effort ephemeral event; no durable message-store write.

- Rate-limit/coalesce start/stop typing events.

- Expire automatically after a few seconds.

- Send only to currently relevant conversation participants.

- Loss is harmless; stale typing must self-expire.

- Do not let typing traffic compete with durable message delivery.

## 23. Media Upload Architecture

![23. Media Upload Architecture — source diagram](/diagrams/t-pzg8uy5uii6d-kix-td2c00lutwt7.png)

- Client requests upload session/media_id.

- Service returns authorized resumable upload target.

- Client uploads bytes directly to object storage path rather than through message servers.

- Processor validates metadata and creates thumbnails/transcodes if applicable.

- Message payload contains media_id/object metadata, not raw bytes.

- Recipients fetch encrypted/authorized media via CDN/object service.

## 24. Why Media Must Be Separate

- A 20-byte text and 200-MB video have radically different bandwidth/storage behavior.

- Direct-to-object-storage upload prevents gateway/message service saturation.

- CDN absorbs recipient downloads.

- Resumable multipart upload handles mobile failures.

- Message durability can reference media readiness state.

- Retention/deletion policies can manage media independently from message metadata.

## 25. Push Notifications

- Used when no foreground realtime connection is available.

- Push payload should contain minimal metadata, not be the sole durable message.

- Push can be delayed, duplicated or dropped.

- Notification worker is triggered after durable message acceptance/fan-out.

- Suppress duplicate pushes when an online device ACKs quickly.

- Respect privacy settings for notification previews.

## 26. End-to-End Encryption Architecture

> Interview framing
> At HLD level, explain key ownership and routing consequences without inventing cryptographic protocols. With E2EE, servers route/store ciphertext and metadata needed for delivery; message plaintext is encrypted/decrypted on authorized user devices.

- Each device has identity/session key material.

- Sender obtains recipient device key/session information through a key service.

- Client encrypts message for recipient devices or uses a group-key scheme.

- Server stores ciphertext and cannot rely on plaintext for search/moderation features.

- New-device onboarding requires secure key/session establishment.

- Group membership changes may require group key rotation depending on protocol.

## 27. E2EE and Multi-Device Consequences

| Problem | Consequence |
| --- | --- |
| New device | Needs secure device linking/key establishment |
| Offline device | Ciphertext retained until device sync/retention policy |
| Group member removed | Future key material must exclude removed member |
| Server search | Plaintext server-side indexing unavailable |
| Backups | Must define separate encrypted backup/key model |
| Abuse reporting | Usually explicit user-side report can reveal selected content |

## 28. Large Groups and Broadcast Channels

- A 1,000-person group and 10-million-follower broadcast channel should not share identical fan-out mechanics.

- Large broadcast systems favor shared append log + per-user cursor/reference rather than synchronous N-recipient writes.

- Use hierarchical fan-out trees/queues and regional distribution.

- Receipts may be aggregated or omitted at massive scale.

- Hot conversation partitions can require dedicated ownership/sharding.

- Backpressure must prevent one celebrity channel from starving ordinary chats.

## 29. Hot Conversation Mitigation

- Detect conversations whose message QPS or fan-out exceeds normal partition capacity.

- Move them to dedicated partitions/owners.

- Batch fan-out and use regional distribution trees.

- Separate sequencing from downstream fan-out so one slow recipient does not block append.

- Use payload references so large content is not recopied.

- Prioritize durable append and online active recipients; let offline delivery catch up asynchronously.

## 30. Partitioning Strategy

| Domain | Partition key |
| --- | --- |
| Messages | conversation_id |
| Conversation sequence | conversation_id / partition owner |
| Membership | conversation_id with user secondary index |
| Device sessions | device_id/user_id |
| Delivery work | recipient region/user/device |
| Presence | user_id |
| Media metadata | media_id |
| Media bytes | object key/CDN |

## 31. Multi-Region Architecture

- Clients connect to nearest healthy gateway region.

- Conversation has a home sequencing/storage partition or globally coordinated owner.

- Gateway can forward send to conversation home while recipient delivery fans out regionally.

- Message data is replicated according to durability/latency requirements.

- Regional delivery queues let recipients receive locally without moving sequencing authority.

- Failover must fence old conversation owner before a new owner assigns sequence numbers.

- Presence can remain region-local/eventual; durable message ordering cannot split-brain.

## 32. Consistency Matrix

| Data | Consistency | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Message append/order | Strong per conversation/partition | Stable order |
| Idempotency mapping | Strong enough to prevent duplicate logical append | Retry safety |
| Membership boundary | Versioned/ordered | Correct recipients |
| Delivery receipt | Eventual/idempotent | Derived state |
| Read cursor | Monotonic per user/conversation | UI semantics |
| Presence | Eventual TTL | Ephemeral |
| Typing | Best effort | Ephemeral |
| Media processing | Eventual | Async derived artifact |

## 33. Backpressure

- Bound per-connection outbound buffers.

- If a client is slow, persist cursor and disconnect/recover rather than buffer indefinitely.

- Prioritize message frames over typing/presence.

- Batch receipt updates and group fan-out.

- Rate-limit abusive senders and giant attachment attempts.

- Consumer lag drives autoscaling; one hot group gets isolated.

- Reconnect sync uses pagination/jitter to avoid thundering herd.

## 34. Failure Scenarios

| Failure | Recovery |
| --- | --- |
| Gateway dies after send | Client retries client_msg_id; idempotency returns existing append |
| Recipient socket dies | Message remains available; sync after reconnect |
| Delivery worker retries | Recipient deduplicates message_id |
| Sequencer leader dies | Fenced failover continues sequence |
| Group fan-out partial | Retry same membership snapshot/version |
| Push fails | Realtime/sync remains authoritative |
| Media processor delayed | Message shows pending media/metadata |
| Region outage | Reconnect elsewhere; forward to surviving conversation owner |
| Receipt lost | Client/server retry cursor idempotently |
| Presence store lost | Presence temporarily unknown/offline; messages unaffected |

## 35. Message Deletion and Edits

- Represent edit/delete as versioned conversation events rather than rewriting history invisibly.

- Clients apply the newest message version/tombstone.

- Deletion semantics may differ: delete-for-self vs delete-for-everyone.

- A delete-for-everyone request is policy/time-window checked and then propagated as a tombstone event.

- Offline devices receive the tombstone during sync.

- Retention/legal/security policy is separate from UI deletion semantics.

## 36. Reactions and Replies

- Reply references stable message_id, not mutable display position.

- Reaction operations are idempotent by user/message/reaction version.

- High-volume reactions can be aggregated separately from core message payload.

- Clients receive reaction deltas through conversation events.

- Deleting a referenced message should not corrupt the reply event; UI can show unavailable placeholder.

- Ordering of reaction events need not block message sequencing if represented as secondary event stream/version.

## 37. Observability

| Metric | Reason |
| --- | --- |
| Send -> server accepted p95/p99 | Core write latency |
| Accepted -> online delivered p95 | Delivery health |
| Duplicate retry rate | Network/idempotency signal |
| Sequence gap/conflict | Critical ordering invariant |
| Offline backlog age | Sync health |
| Gateway connections/reconnects | Realtime health |
| Fan-out lag | Group scalability |
| Push success latency | Offline wake-up |
| Media upload/process latency | Attachment UX |
| Hot partition QPS | Shard imbalance |

## 38. Security and Abuse

- Authenticate every device/session and support revocation.

- Rate-limit unsolicited messaging, group adds and automated spam.

- Use device reputation and metadata signals without weakening E2EE guarantees.

- Protect key-directory operations against substitution/unauthorized device addition.

- Media scanning architecture depends on encryption/product policy; do not assume server plaintext.

- Audit admin/account recovery flows because account takeover bypasses message-layer correctness.

## 39. End-to-End 1:1 Example

- Alice sends message with client_msg_id C1 to conversation X.

- Gateway forwards to X's message partition.

- Service validates membership and idempotency.

- Sequencer assigns seq 881 and durable store appends ciphertext/payload metadata.

- Alice receives SERVER_ACCEPTED for message_id M1.

- Delivery service resolves Bob's active phone and desktop sessions.

- Phone receives M1 and ACKs; delivered cursor advances to 881.

- Desktop is offline and later syncs from seq 860, receiving 861..latest including M1.

- Bob reads through seq 885; READ_UP_TO 885 is synced to Alice and Bob's other devices.

## 40. End-to-End Group Example

- Bob sends group message at group membership version 42.

- Conversation partition assigns seq 5010 and stores message once.

- Fan-out job uses recipient snapshot consistent with version 42.

- Online members receive through regional gateways.

- Offline members are represented by durable availability/cursors and optional pushes.

- One fan-out shard fails; retry resumes idempotently without creating another logical message.

- A member removed at the next ordered membership boundary does not receive future messages.

- Read receipts are represented by member cursors rather than per-message rows.

## 41. Common Interview Mistakes

- Calling WebSocket delivery 'exactly once'.

- No client_msg_id/idempotency story.

- Global ordering instead of per-conversation ordering.

- Treating gateway memory as durable message storage.

- One physical queue per user with unbounded backlog.

- Sending media bytes through message servers.

- No reconnect/gap-sync design.

- No distinction between delivered and read.

- Ignoring multi-device cursors.

- Fan-out on write for arbitrarily huge broadcast channels without adaptation.

- Persisting every typing/presence event to OLTP.

- Ignoring membership races in groups.

- Saying E2EE while also assuming server plaintext indexing.

## 42. Final Production Architecture

- A global connection tier terminates authenticated persistent device sessions.

- Conversation IDs route sends to ordered sequencing/storage partitions.

- Client-generated idempotency IDs make retries safe.

- Messages are durably appended before server acceptance.

- Asynchronous regional delivery workers fan out to active device gateways and preserve offline recoverability through message logs/cursors.

- Reconnect sync reads authoritative message ranges and change events.

- Presence/typing use ephemeral TTL/pub-sub infrastructure.

- Media uploads directly to object storage and recipients download through CDN.

- Group fan-out adapts to group size; massive broadcast channels use shared logs/reference fan-out.

- Multi-region failover fences old sequence owners to avoid split-brain ordering.

- E2EE keeps plaintext on authorized endpoints while servers route/store ciphertext and delivery metadata.

> One-sentence architecture
> Use durable per-conversation ordered logs with idempotent sends, separate them from ephemeral WebSocket delivery, synchronize devices by cursors, adapt fan-out to group size, keep media in object storage/CDN, and use fenced conversation ownership so retries, disconnects and regional failures never create conflicting message order.

## 43. Interviewer Follow-Ups — Detailed Answers

Follow-up: Can you guarantee exactly-once message delivery?

Detailed answer: Not at the network transport level. Connections can drop after the recipient received a frame but before the ACK reached the server. Use at-least-once retry plus stable message_id/client_msg_id deduplication so the user observes one logical message.

Follow-up: How do you prevent duplicate sends when the sender times out?

Detailed answer: The client retries the same client_msg_id. The server stores an idempotency mapping scoped to sender/device and returns the previously committed message_id/sequence instead of appending again.

Follow-up: How do you preserve ordering?

Detailed answer: Route each conversation to one logical sequencing owner/partition. It assigns monotonically increasing sequence positions before durable append. Failover is fenced so two owners cannot assign conflicting order.

Follow-up: Why not use timestamps for ordering?

Detailed answer: Client clocks drift, network arrival differs, and two regions can observe different order. A server-assigned per-conversation sequence provides deterministic display/sync order.

Follow-up: What happens if a gateway dies after the server accepted the message?

Detailed answer: Nothing is lost. Acceptance happened only after durable append. The sender reconnects and retries/query-syncs; idempotency returns the existing message. Recipient delivery resumes from durable state.

Follow-up: How do offline users receive messages?

Detailed answer: Messages remain in the conversation log and the recipient/device has a delivery/sync cursor. On reconnect the client requests ranges after its cursor. Push only wakes the app; it is not the authoritative payload.

Follow-up: How do read receipts scale?

Detailed answer: Store a highest read sequence per user/conversation rather than one read row per message. In groups, each member cursor implicitly marks all prior messages read, and summaries can be computed/aggregated.

Follow-up: How do you handle multiple devices?

Detailed answer: Track device sessions and delivery cursors separately. Fan out to all authorized devices. User-level read state can merge upward, while an offline device later catches up from its own cursor.

Follow-up: What is the difference between delivered and read?

Detailed answer: Delivered means a recipient device acknowledged local receipt/persistence. Read means the user's read cursor advanced beyond the message. Push notification success means neither.

Follow-up: How do you handle group membership races?

Detailed answer: Order/version membership changes relative to messages. Fan-out uses the membership snapshot/version associated with the committed message boundary, so retries do not accidentally include newly joined or removed users.

Follow-up: Fan-out on write or read?

Detailed answer: Small/ordinary groups favor fan-out on write for low delivery latency. Huge broadcast groups favor a shared message log plus reference/pull/hierarchical distribution. A hybrid based on group size avoids pathological amplification.

Follow-up: How do you handle a celebrity group with millions of members?

Detailed answer: Give the conversation dedicated sequencing capacity, store the payload once, distribute references through regional fan-out trees/queues, avoid per-recipient synchronous writes, aggregate receipts, and isolate its workload from normal chat partitions.

Follow-up: How do you scale WebSockets?

Detailed answer: Use many stateless-ish regional connection gateways, a session registry, bounded outbound buffers and pub-sub/gateway queues. Durable message state lives elsewhere, so a gateway can fail and clients simply reconnect/sync.

Follow-up: What if the client is extremely slow?

Detailed answer: Do not buffer unbounded messages in gateway RAM. Bound the queue, prioritize durable message frames, drop ephemeral typing/presence, disconnect if necessary, and let the client recover from durable cursors.

Follow-up: How should presence be stored?

Detailed answer: As TTL-based ephemeral state refreshed by device heartbeats. Presence can be eventually consistent; last-seen may be persisted asynchronously. It must not share the durable message write path.

Follow-up: How do you send large media?

Detailed answer: Initialize an upload, upload directly/resumably to object storage, process thumbnails/transcodes asynchronously, then send a small message containing media metadata/reference. Recipients fetch through authorized CDN/object paths.

Follow-up: How does E2EE change the architecture?

Detailed answer: Clients encrypt plaintext for authorized recipient devices or group sessions. Servers store/route ciphertext plus metadata needed for delivery. Server-side plaintext search/moderation cannot be assumed, and multi-device/group membership requires key/session management.

Follow-up: What if the sequence leader fails?

Detailed answer: A new owner is elected/acquired with a higher fencing epoch. Storage rejects writes from the stale owner. The new owner resumes from durable sequence state; gaps are acceptable if IDs were reserved but conflicting reuse is not.

Follow-up: How do you recover from a reconnect storm?

Detailed answer: Jitter reconnections, cap sync batch size, paginate backlogs, prioritize recent/active conversations, autoscale gateways/sync workers, and keep CDN/media traffic off the message path.

Follow-up: Give the one-minute architecture summary.

Detailed answer: Clients maintain persistent sessions to regional gateways. Sends carry client_msg_id and route by conversation_id to an ordered partition. The service validates membership, assigns a per-conversation sequence and durably appends before acknowledging. Delivery is asynchronous: online devices receive through gateways; offline devices later sync message ranges by cursor, with push as a wake-up hint. Multi-device uses per-device delivery cursors and user-level read cursors. Groups use versioned membership and adaptive fan-out. Presence/typing are ephemeral, media goes through object storage/CDN, and failover fences the old sequencer. With E2EE, servers route ciphertext rather than plaintext.

## 44. Additional Detailed Q&A

1. Why is message_id different from client_msg_id?

Detailed answer: client_msg_id makes a sender retry idempotent; message_id is the canonical server identity used for delivery, references and deduplication.

2. Can sequence numbers have gaps?

Detailed answer: Yes, if semantics permit. Uniqueness/order matter more than gaplessness.

3. Why partition by conversation?

Detailed answer: It colocates ordered appends and range reads while avoiding global coordination.

4. What if one conversation is too hot?

Detailed answer: Give it dedicated sequencing capacity and decouple fan-out; logical ordering can remain single-owner while downstream work is parallel.

5. Why not store typing events?

Detailed answer: They expire in seconds and loss is harmless.

6. What is a sync cursor?

Detailed answer: A compact marker of the latest durable state/message range a device has applied.

7. When should delivered cursor advance?

Detailed answer: After recipient device has durably accepted the message locally, according to product semantics.

8. Can push be duplicated?

Detailed answer: Yes; push systems are best-effort and clients/server must tolerate duplicates.

9. How are edits synchronized?

Detailed answer: As versioned/tombstone change events applied during realtime delivery or reconnect sync.

10. Why use object storage for media?

Detailed answer: Cheap durable large-object storage, resumable uploads and CDN integration.

11. How do group joins affect history?

Detailed answer: Use joined_seq/history policy to decide earliest visible message.

12. How do removals affect future messages?

Detailed answer: Membership boundary/version excludes the user from subsequent recipient snapshots and, with E2EE, future keys.

13. What is fan-out lag?

Detailed answer: Time between message append and delivery work reaching intended recipients.

14. Why batch receipts?

Detailed answer: Many per-message ACK/read writes would create unnecessary write amplification.

15. How do reactions reference messages?

Detailed answer: By stable message_id.

16. How do you protect against split brain?

Detailed answer: Fencing epochs on conversation ownership/sequencing.

17. What survives gateway loss?

Detailed answer: All durable message/membership/cursor state; only ephemeral connection/presence state is lost.

18. What is the media message payload?

Detailed answer: media_id/reference, content metadata, checksum/encryption metadata—not the raw file.

19. What should never block message append?

Detailed answer: Slow recipient sockets, push providers, thumbnail generation or analytics.

20. Most important invariant?

Detailed answer: Once SERVER_ACCEPTED is returned, the logical message is durably recoverable and has one stable ordered identity.

## 45. Scenario-Based Deep Dives

Sender times out, retries three times, but the first request actually committed.

All retries carry the same client_msg_id. The idempotency store returns the original message_id and sequence. Only one logical append exists. The sender UI replaces its optimistic local entry with that canonical identity.

Recipient receives a message, loses network before ACK, then reconnects.

Server may redeliver because it never saw the ACK. Client recognizes message_id already persisted and does not display a duplicate, then ACKs/advances its cursor. This is user-visible exactly-once behavior built on at-least-once transport.

A group admin removes Alice exactly while Bob sends a message.

Membership change and message have ordered/versioned boundaries. If removal is effective before the message sequence/version, Alice is excluded; if after, she is included according to policy. Fan-out retries reuse that same membership snapshot.

A region holding millions of sockets fails.

Clients reconnect with jitter to healthy gateways. Presence may temporarily be inaccurate, but messages remain durable. Devices send sync cursors and recover missing ranges. Conversation sequencing fails over only after fencing old owners.

A 500-MB video is sent to a group.

The sender uploads directly to object storage using a resumable authorized session. Message service stores a small media reference/ciphertext metadata. Processor creates derived assets. Group fan-out sends only message metadata; recipients download bytes through CDN.

## 46. Advanced Drill: Critical Invariants

| Invariant | Mechanism |
| --- | --- |
| One retry -> one logical message | client_msg_id idempotency |
| Stable per-conversation order | single logical sequencer + fencing |
| Accepted message is recoverable | durable append before ACK |
| Gateway loss cannot erase messages | gateway not source of truth |
| Removed member excluded after boundary | versioned membership |
| Slow device cannot exhaust gateway | bounded buffers + cursor recovery |
| Duplicate delivery not duplicate UI | message_id dedupe |
| Read state never moves backward | monotonic read cursor |

## 47. Advanced Drill: Reconciliation

- Find messages accepted but fan-out event missing and regenerate from outbox/log.

- Find stuck delivery tasks and retry with idempotent message IDs.

- Compare device cursor with acknowledged ranges after reconnect.

- Expire orphan upload sessions and unreferenced media.

- Repair stale session-registry entries using gateway heartbeats.

- Detect membership/fan-out version mismatches.

- Monitor sequencing ownership epochs for stale writers.

## 48. 45-Minute Interview Flow

| Time | Coverage |
| --- | --- |
| 0-5 min | Requirements, delivery semantics, scale |
| 5-10 min | HLD, APIs, data model |
| 10-17 min | Send path, idempotency, ordering/sequencer |
| 17-23 min | Online/offline delivery, ACK/read, sync |
| 23-28 min | Multi-device |
| 28-33 min | Groups, membership races, fan-out |
| 33-36 min | Presence/typing |
| 36-39 min | Media + push |
| 39-42 min | Multi-region, failures, backpressure |
| 42-45 min | E2EE, invariants, summary |

## 49. Review Quiz with Answers

1. Exactly-once transport?

Answer: No. Use at-least-once delivery plus idempotent identities/deduplication.

2. Ordering scope?

Answer: Per conversation.

3. When can sender get server-accepted ACK?

Answer: After durable append.

4. Source of truth after socket loss?

Answer: Durable message log/cursors.

5. How are offline messages recovered?

Answer: Range sync after cursor.

6. Why separate presence?

Answer: It is ephemeral/high-rate and loss-tolerant.

7. Why separate media?

Answer: Large bytes need object storage/CDN, not message hot path.

8. How do group membership races resolve?

Answer: Versioned/ordered membership boundary.

9. How do you avoid split-brain sequence assignment?

Answer: Fenced conversation ownership.

10. Core architecture split?

Answer: Durable ordered message truth vs ephemeral realtime connection delivery.

## 50. 30-Second Final Interview Answer

> 30-second answer
> I would route each conversation to an ordered message partition. Every send carries a client-generated idempotency ID; the service validates membership, assigns a per-conversation sequence, durably appends the message, and only then acknowledges the sender. Delivery is asynchronous through regional WebSocket gateways, while offline and failed deliveries recover from durable message ranges using per-device cursors. Read state is a monotonic cursor, presence and typing are ephemeral TTL/pub-sub data, and media goes directly to object storage/CDN. Groups use versioned membership and adaptive fan-out, and regional failover uses fencing so two sequencers cannot create conflicting order. With E2EE, servers route ciphertext and delivery metadata rather than plaintext.

## 51. Final Interview Checklist

- Requirements and precise sent/delivered/read semantics.

- Persistent connection tier but not as source of truth.

- client_msg_id and idempotent retry.

- Per-conversation sequence/order.

- Durable append before server acceptance.

- Online delivery and ACK.

- Offline cursor-based sync and gap recovery.

- Multi-device delivery/read cursors.

- Group membership versioning and races.

- Fan-out on write/read/hybrid trade-offs.

- Presence and typing as ephemeral systems.

- Media direct upload, processing and CDN.

- Push as wake-up hint.

- E2EE architecture consequences.

- Partitioning, hot conversations and broadcast scale.

- Multi-region ownership/fencing.

- Backpressure, failure recovery and observability.

- 20 detailed follow-ups, 20 additional Q&As, 5 scenarios and colorful diagrams.
