notes.content:
Design Twitter / X - Complete System Design Interview Guide

Section 3 - Design Problem 6 | Tweet Storage, Social Graph, Timeline Fan-Out, Celebrity Users and Search

How to study this design
Learn the core feed decision: tweet writes are cheap, home-timeline reads are frequent, and follower counts are highly skewed. That leads to push fan-out for normal users, pull/merge for celebrities, materialized home timeline IDs for fast reads, and asynchronous event pipelines for search/trends/engagement. Keep tweet storage authoritative and treat timelines as derived data that can be rebuilt.

![Design Twitter / X - Complete System Design Interview Guide — source diagram](/diagrams/t-tmnue3r3trfc-kix-tz26mmmjyzfo.png)

The core Twitter problem is the home timeline: how do we cheaply serve tweets from hundreds of followed users?

## 1. Problem Statement and Interview Framing

Design a Twitter/X-like social network where users publish short posts, follow other users, and read a home timeline containing posts from accounts they follow. The baseline should support tweet creation, user timelines, home timelines, follow/unfollow, and basic engagement. Search, ranking, trends, and media are useful follow-ups.

- The key scaling problem is asymmetric fan-out: most users have modest follower counts, while celebrities may have tens of millions.

- Timeline reads greatly outnumber tweet writes.

- Tweet objects are mostly immutable; home timelines are derived/indexed views.

Recommended baseline
Start with a chronological timeline. It makes feed generation, fan-out, pagination, and consistency clear. Add ranking after the baseline works.

## 2. Functional Requirements

![2. Functional Requirements — source diagram](/diagrams/t-tmnue3r3trfc-kix-svoc4agm9j67.png)

Define timeline semantics before choosing push or pull.

| Feature | Baseline | Follow-Up |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Create tweet | Text + optional media refs | Edit / quote tweet |
| Delete tweet | Author deletes | Retention / moderation |
| Follow/unfollow | Directed relationship | Private accounts |
| Home timeline | Tweets from followees | Ranking / recommendations |
| User timeline | Author's tweets | Pinned tweets |
| Engagement | Like / repost / reply | Counts / notifications |
| Search | Optional | Full-text / hashtags |
| Trends | Optional | Regional top terms |

## 3. Non-Functional Requirements

| Property | Expectation | Consequence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Home timeline latency | Low p95/p99 | Materialized IDs + cache |
| Tweet durability | No acknowledged tweet loss | Durable store before ACK |
| Feed freshness | Seconds for normal follows | Async fan-out acceptable |
| Availability | Reads highly available | Derived timeline can degrade/rebuild |
| Scalability | Skewed follower graph | Hybrid fan-out |
| Pagination | Stable under new inserts | Cursor, not OFFSET |
| Consistency | Tweet object strong enough; feed eventual | Derived data async |
| Abuse | Rate limits / spam controls | WAF/policy pipeline |

## 4. Capacity Estimation

![4. Capacity Estimation — source diagram](/diagrams/t-tmnue3r3trfc-kix-5cescfww3ibk.png)

Illustrative assumptions show reads dominate writes and follower skew dominates fan-out.

- 300M DAU.

- Average 2 tweets per DAU/day -> 600M tweets/day.

- Average ~7K tweet writes/sec; peak ~35K/sec.

- 20 home-timeline reads/DAU/day -> 6B reads/day.

- Average ~70K feed reads/sec; peak ~350K/sec.

- Average user follows ~200 accounts, but distribution is heavy-tailed.

Why the numbers matter
Feed reads are an order of magnitude more frequent than tweet writes, so precomputing/caching home timelines is attractive. But follower counts are extremely skewed, so pure fan-out-on-write becomes dangerous for celebrities.

## 5. High-Level Architecture

![5. High-Level Architecture — source diagram](/diagrams/t-tmnue3r3trfc-kix-sb0vpc4z70hh.png)

Tweet storage is authoritative; timelines, search, and trends are derived systems.

- Tweet Service creates/deletes tweets.

- Tweet Store keeps durable tweet objects.

- Social Graph Store maintains following/follower edges.

- Event Stream carries TweetCreated/TweetDeleted/FollowChanged.

- Fan-Out workers update home timeline materializations.

- Timeline Service serves cached/materialized feed IDs and hydrates tweet objects.

- Search/Trending consume events asynchronously.

- Media bytes live in object storage/CDN.

## 6. API Design

| Operation | Example | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Create tweet | POST /v1/tweets | text, mediaIds, clientRequestId |
| Delete tweet | DELETE /v1/tweets/{tweetId} | author/moderation authorization |
| Home timeline | GET /v1/timeline/home?cursor=...&limit=50 | cursor pagination |
| User timeline | GET /v1/users/{id}/tweets?cursor=... | author index |
| Follow | PUT /v1/users/{id}/following/{targetId} | idempotent |
| Unfollow | DELETE .../following/{targetId} | idempotent |
| Like | PUT /v1/tweets/{id}/likes/me | idempotent set |
| Repost | POST /v1/tweets/{id}/reposts | may create event/tweet ref |

Idempotency
Tweet creation can accept a clientRequestId to prevent duplicate posts if the response is lost and the mobile client retries.

## 7. Tweet ID Generation

- Need unique, sortable-enough IDs for storage and cursor pagination.

- Snowflake-style IDs are a common interview choice: timestamp + worker/region + sequence.

- Benefits: decentralized generation, uniqueness, roughly time-ordered IDs.

- Risks: clock rollback, worker-ID allocation, information leakage if raw IDs expose time/volume.

- Alternative: database sequence or UUIDv7/ULID-like sortable IDs.

Interview choice
Use a distributed time-sortable ID so tweetId can also help chronological pagination. Do not depend on client timestamps for authoritative ordering.

## 8. Tweet Creation Path

![8. Tweet Creation Path — source diagram](/diagrams/t-tmnue3r3trfc-kix-wx3froetkas3.png)

The tweet write path should stay small and durable.

1. Authenticate user and rate limit.

2. Validate text length, media references, mentions/hashtags, policy checks as required.

3. Generate tweetId.

4. Persist tweet durably in Tweet Store.

5. Append tweetId to author's User Timeline index.

6. Publish TweetCreated event.

7. Return success to author.

8. Fan-out/search/trending/notifications continue asynchronously.

Do not block on fan-out
A celebrity tweet may eventually affect millions of timelines. The create request should not wait for that work.

## 9. Tweet Data Model

| Field | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| tweetId | Primary ID; sortable cursor |
| authorId | Author lookup / permissions |
| createdAt | Display / validation |
| text | Tweet content |
| mediaIds | References to media objects |
| replyToTweetId | Reply/thread relationship |
| quoteTweetId | Quoted post reference |
| status | ACTIVE / DELETED / BLOCKED |
| visibility | PUBLIC / FOLLOWERS / PRIVATE-account rules |

- Keep large engagement counters out of the hot tweet row if they update frequently.

- Tweets are mostly immutable; delete/status is a small mutation.

## 10. Tweet Store and Partitioning

- Primary access: tweetId -> tweet object.

- Hash partition by tweetId for even write distribution.

- Replicate across failure domains.

- Cache hot tweets separately.

- Author timeline needs an authorId -> recent tweetIds index.

One store vs indexes
The Tweet Store answers point reads by tweetId. User Timeline and Home Timeline are secondary/derived access paths and should be modeled separately rather than forcing every query into one primary key.

## 11. User Timeline

w

![11. User Timeline — source diagram](/diagrams/t-tmnue3r3trfc-kix-rrmzory1gmpv.png)

An author's own timeline is much simpler than the home feed.

- Maintain index: authorId -> tweetIds ordered by tweetId/creation time.

- Append on tweet creation; remove/filter on delete.

- Cursor pagination by last tweetId.

- Hydrate tweet objects in a batch from Tweet Cache/Store.

- Cache first page for popular authors.

Why separate it
User Timeline is a single-author ordered list. Home Timeline is a multi-author merge/materialization problem; treating them as the same structure hides the central design challenge.

## 12. Social Graph Store

![12. Social Graph Store — source diagram](/diagrams/t-tmnue3r3trfc-kix-8nddg2gbqam.png)

Store both directions because they serve different hot paths.

- Following index: followerId -> followeeIds; used for feed reads/pull model.

- Followers index: followeeId -> followerIds; used for push fan-out.

- Edges should be idempotent and unique.

- Large follower lists must be paginated/partitioned.

- Block/mute/private-account rules add relationship state.

Graph database?
A specialized graph database is not mandatory. Most hot operations are one-hop adjacency-list lookups, which scale well in sharded key-value/wide-column structures.

## 13. Follow / Unfollow Semantics

![13. Follow / Unfollow Semantics — source diagram](/diagrams/t-tmnue3r3trfc-kix-had9aji5jz87.png)

Make the graph edge authoritative; timeline repair can lag.

- Follow is a conditional edge insert.

- Update both 'following' and 'followers' indexes atomically if co-located, or use durable event/reconciliation if split.

- On follow, optionally backfill the followee's recent tweets into follower's timeline.

- On unfollow, future fan-out stops immediately after authoritative graph update; old timeline IDs can be lazily filtered/cleaned.

- Private accounts require approval state.

Consistency
A user may see one stale tweet from a just-unfollowed account for a short period if the product allows eventual timeline cleanup, but the authoritative follow graph must be correct for future fan-out and privacy checks.

## 14. Home Timeline - Option A: Fan-Out on Write

![14. Home Timeline - Option A: Fan-Out on Write — source diagram](/diagrams/t-tmnue3r3trfc-kix-u1gd047a0rzx.png)

Push/precompute gives extremely fast reads.

### How It Works

- TweetCreated event loads follower list.

- Workers batch-insert tweetId into each follower's home timeline.

- Timeline store keeps a bounded recent window, e.g. a few thousand IDs/user.

- Home read becomes simple cache/list lookup.

### Advantages

- Very low read latency.

- Read cost independent of number of followees.

- Good because reads greatly outnumber writes.

### Disadvantages

- Write amplification proportional to follower count.

- Celebrity tweet can create millions of writes.

- Wasted work for inactive followers.

Best fit
Push works very well for normal users with modest follower counts and active followers. It is the default half of the hybrid design.

## 15. Home Timeline - Option B: Fan-Out on Read

![15. Home Timeline - Option B: Fan-Out on Read — source diagram](/diagrams/t-tmnue3r3trfc-kix-4up2wgpiszbo.png)

Pull avoids write amplification but makes every read expensive.

- At feed request, load list of followed users.

- Fetch recent tweet IDs from each user's author timeline/cache.

- Merge sorted lists; optionally rank.

- Return top N.

### Advantages

- Tweet creation is cheap no matter follower count.

- No precompute for inactive users.

### Disadvantages

- Read cost grows with followee count.

- Can require hundreds/thousands of reads and merges.

- Harder to hit low p99 latency.

Best fit
Pull is useful for celebrity/high-fanout authors and as a fallback/repair path, but pure pull is expensive for every home-feed read.

## 16. Hybrid Fan-Out - Recommended

![16. Hybrid Fan-Out - Recommended — source diagram](/diagrams/t-tmnue3r3trfc-kix-gunmuq43rmg7.png)

Push normal authors; pull celebrity authors.

- Classify high-fanout accounts using follower threshold/load policy.

- Normal author's TweetCreated -> push tweetId to followers' timeline stores.

- Celebrity tweet -> store normally, do not mass-push.

- At home-feed read, fetch user's materialized timeline plus recent tweets from followed celebrities.

- Merge/rank/deduplicate the candidate sets.

Why hybrid wins
It preserves fast reads for the majority while preventing catastrophic write amplification for the heavy tail of the follower distribution.

## 17. Celebrity / Hot-Key Problem

![17. Celebrity / Hot-Key Problem — source diagram](/diagrams/t-tmnue3r3trfc-kix-28oxuze7k6aq.png)

Follower skew is the core reason pure push fails.

- A 50M-follower user creates a burst of 50M timeline writes for one tweet.

- Reading/partitioning one enormous follower list can itself become a hotspot.

- A huge queue backlog delays freshness for unrelated users if fan-out resources are shared.

- Hybrid mode stores celebrity tweets once and lets readers merge them.

- Cache celebrity recent tweets aggressively.

Interview follow-up
Sharding the timeline store does not remove the 50M-write amplification. The fix is changing the algorithm from push to pull/hybrid for that class of authors.

## 18. Fan-Out Worker Design and Backpressure

![18. Fan-Out Worker Design and Backpressure — source diagram](/diagrams/t-tmnue3r3trfc-kix-15jw5qkrp9bf.png)

The event pipeline absorbs bursts and protects the timeline store.

- Partition TweetCreated events by authorId or fan-out job ID.

- Follower list is read in pages/batches.

- Each batch updates timeline entries idempotently.

- Use bounded concurrency and rate limits per destination shard.

- Retry transient failures; dead-letter/reconciliation for persistent errors.

- Monitor fan-out lag: tweet creation time -> timeline materialized time.

Freshness SLO
Timeline fan-out is derived data. If workers lag, tweets can appear late but must not be lost permanently; replay/rebuild from TweetCreated events should repair them.

## 19. Home Timeline Store

![19. Home Timeline Store — source diagram](/diagrams/t-tmnue3r3trfc-kix-tnalxo6u205m.png)

Store lightweight tweet IDs/rank metadata, not duplicated tweet bodies.

- Key: userId.

- Values: recent entries (tweetId, timestamp/score/source).

- Keep bounded recent window; older pages can be reconstructed/pulled if necessary.

- Use sorted set/list structures depending on ranking model.

- Hydrate actual tweet objects in batch from Tweet Cache/Store.

Why IDs only
Duplicating full tweet content into every follower timeline would multiply storage and complicate edits/deletes. Store references and hydrate current tweet state at read time.

## 20. Home Timeline Read Path

![20. Home Timeline Read Path — source diagram](/diagrams/t-tmnue3r3trfc-kix-uejyccy4wljr.png)

Feed reads use two distinct caches: timeline IDs and tweet objects.

1. Read recent timeline entries for user from Timeline Cache/Store.

2. Fetch recent tweets from followed celebrity accounts if using hybrid fan-out.

3. Merge/deduplicate by tweetId.

4. Apply visibility, block/mute, deletion, and policy filters.

5. If ranked, score candidate set; otherwise sort chronologically.

6. Batch hydrate tweet objects from Tweet Cache/Store.

7. Attach engagement-count snapshots and media URLs.

8. Return page plus opaque cursor.

Derived-feed rule
Always re-check authoritative tweet status/visibility at hydration/filter time because a timeline can contain stale references to deleted or blocked content.

## 21. Cursor Pagination

![21. Cursor Pagination — source diagram](/diagrams/t-tmnue3r3trfc-kix-lv4p1gsqquj2.png)

OFFSET pagination performs poorly and shifts under concurrent inserts.

- Chronological feed cursor can encode lastTweetId / timestamp plus tie-breaker.

- Ranked feed cursor may encode score + tweetId + session/snapshot context.

- Next page queries 'older/lower than cursor' rather than OFFSET N.

- Opaque cursors allow backend representation changes.

New tweets while paging
Cursor pagination naturally keeps newly inserted tweets above the current cursor instead of shifting page offsets and causing duplicates/skips.

## 22. Chronological vs Ranked Feed

![22. Chronological vs Ranked Feed — source diagram](/diagrams/t-tmnue3r3trfc-kix-xmxyxz4fo9ew.png)

Ranking is an additional candidate/scoring system, not a replacement for storage correctness.

### Chronological Baseline

- Candidate order = creation/tweetId descending.

- Simple and deterministic.

### Ranked Follow-Up

- Retrieve candidates from materialized feed + celebrity pull + recommendations.

- Compute features: freshness, relationship strength, engagement, content quality.

- Score/rank; enforce diversity/policy constraints.

- Cache features/candidates to meet latency.

- Ranking models can update independently from Tweet Store.

Interview boundary
For a general system-design interview, design the candidate/feed infrastructure first. ML ranking can be described at a high level unless the interviewer explicitly asks for recommendation-system depth.

## 23. Likes, Reposts, and Replies

![23. Likes, Reposts, and Replies — source diagram](/diagrams/t-tmnue3r3trfc-kix-7x993pdhx361.png)

Engagement writes have different access patterns from tweet creation.

### Like

- Idempotent membership set: (tweetId,userId).

- Counter may be sharded/aggregated asynchronously.

### Repost

- Can be represented as an event/reference to original tweet.

- May enter followers' timelines like a new activity.

### Reply

- Create normal tweet with replyToTweetId / conversationThreadId.

- Thread index can list children/replies.

Counter accuracy
Exact real-time like counts are usually less important than write scalability. A slightly stale aggregate count is acceptable while whether the current user liked the tweet should be authoritative.

## 24. Tweet Delete and Moderation

![24. Tweet Delete and Moderation — source diagram](/diagrams/t-tmnue3r3trfc-kix-x67uvd6buyyn.png)

Derived timelines can contain stale tweet IDs; read-time filtering preserves correctness.

- Author/moderator marks tweet status DELETED/BLOCKED in authoritative store.

- Invalidate Tweet Cache.

- Emit TweetDeleted event.

- Timeline cleaners asynchronously remove IDs.

- Timeline hydration filters deleted IDs immediately even before cleanup.

- Search index removes/tombstones asynchronously.

Delete semantics
Do not require millions of timeline-row deletions to complete before the tweet is considered deleted. Make the tweet object authoritative, then clean derived references in the background.

## 25. Media Upload and Delivery

![25. Media Upload and Delivery — source diagram](/diagrams/t-tmnue3r3trfc-kix-2en4t8cxg1to.png)

Media bytes follow a separate object-storage path.

- Client obtains media upload session/pre-signed URL.

- Upload directly to object storage/media service.

- Scan/transcode images/video; generate variants/thumbnails.

- Create tweet only after mediaId is valid/ready according to product semantics.

- Timeline carries media references; clients fetch via CDN.

Why separate
Tweet QPS and media-byte throughput are different workloads. Keeping media out of Tweet Store preserves low-latency text/feed operations.

## 26. Search

![26. Search — source diagram](/diagrams/t-tmnue3r3trfc-kix-ru3def6kjwq6.png)

Search is an asynchronous secondary index.

- TweetCreated events feed indexers.

- Tokenize text, hashtags, mentions, language.

- Build inverted index and ranking metadata.

- TweetDeleted event removes/tombstones search doc.

- Search can be eventually consistent.

- Opening a result rechecks current tweet visibility/status.

Do not search the Tweet Store
The primary store is optimized for tweetId/author access, not full-text queries. Use a dedicated search index for a fundamentally different access pattern.

## 27. Trending Topics

![27. Trending Topics — source diagram](/diagrams/t-tmnue3r3trfc-kix-q4b2zri272em.png)

Trends are a streaming analytics problem.

- Extract hashtags/terms from TweetCreated stream.

- Count in short rolling windows by region/language.

- Compare velocity to historical baseline; raw volume alone favors always-popular terms.

- Filter spam/bots and enforce minimum unique-user diversity.

- Maintain Top-K per region in a fast store/cache.

Trend definition
A trend is usually 'rising unusually fast', not simply 'most-mentioned overall'. The exact ranking formula is product-specific.

## 28. Notifications

- Mentions, replies, likes, reposts, follows can emit events.

- Notification service applies user preferences/rate limits.

- Batch/collapse noisy engagement notifications.

- Push mobile notifications asynchronously.

- Notification failures must not affect tweet/feed correctness.

Separation
Notifications are derived UX. Tweet creation should not wait for every mention/like notification to be delivered.

## 29. Privacy, Blocking, and Muting

- Private accounts require follow approval before content is visible.

- Block relationship should prevent visibility/interactions according to policy.

- Mute affects the viewer's feed but may not change graph edges.

- Home timeline read should apply block/mute/visibility filters.

- Fan-out workers may avoid inserting known-blocked content, but read-time filtering remains a safety net.

Correctness boundary
Privacy/authorization state is authoritative. Timeline materializations are caches/derived views and must never be trusted blindly for visibility.

## 30. Consistency Model

- Tweet creation/delete: durable authoritative state.

- Follow graph: stronger for privacy and future fan-out; propagation to feed may be eventual.

- Home timeline: eventual consistency acceptable; seconds of lag may be fine.

- Like counts/trends/search: eventual.

- Current user's like/follow state: should be read-your-write.

Useful interview sentence
I use strong/conditional consistency for user intent and privacy edges, but eventual consistency for derived feeds, counters, search, and trends.

## 31. Multi-Region Design

![31. Multi-Region Design — source diagram](/diagrams/t-tmnue3r3trfc-kix-p75sszu1lwvy.png)

Global reads can be local; tweet write ownership and event replication should be explicit.

- Users hit nearest regional API/cache.

- Assign user/tweet write ownership to a home region or use globally consistent ID/metadata store.

- Replicate Tweet Store for reads/DR.

- Publish TweetCreated events to global/regional fan-out/search consumers.

- Timeline stores/caches can be regional because they are derived.

- Media served from CDN.

Trade-off
Fully active-active tweet writes are possible, but feed derivation is already asynchronous. A home-region write model often provides simpler correctness while global reads remain fast.

## 32. Failure Modes and Recovery

![32. Failure Modes and Recovery — source diagram](/diagrams/t-tmnue3r3trfc-kix-xiuf4hfajxny.png)

Derived systems can lag or rebuild; authoritative tweet/graph data must survive.

| Failure | Behavior | Recovery |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Fan-out workers down | New tweets not immediately in feeds | Replay TweetCreated events |
| Timeline cache/store down | Feed slower/incomplete temporarily | Fallback pull/rebuild from graph + author timelines |
| Tweet Store slow | Tweet create/hydration impacted | Failover/replicas/backpressure |
| Graph Store slow | Follow/fan-out delayed | Retry; preserve authoritative edges |
| Search/trends down | Core product works | Catch up from event stream |
| Region down | Route to healthy region | Promote/repoint ownership; rebuild derived caches |

Derived-data philosophy
Home timelines, search indexes, and trend aggregates should be reproducible from authoritative tweet/graph/event data. This makes failure recovery much safer.

## 33. Rebuilding Home Timelines

- If timeline entries are corrupted/lost, regenerate recent feed from following graph + author timelines.

- For normal authors, replay recent TweetCreated events into timeline.

- For celebrities, no reconstruction push is necessary; they are pulled at read time.

- Use version/checkpoint so rebuild can coexist with new fan-out writes.

- Cache first page after rebuild.

Why this matters
Treating the home timeline as derived means you can optimize aggressively and even lose a cache/shard without losing the user's tweets.

## 34. Observability and SLOs

### Core Metrics

- Tweet-create success and p95/p99 latency.

- Home-timeline p95/p99 latency.

- Fan-out lag: tweet created -> materialized to normal follower timeline.

- Timeline cache hit ratio.

- Tweet hydration miss/error rate.

- Follower graph read/write latency.

- Celebrity pull latency/contribution.

- Search/trend indexing lag.

### Correctness Metrics

- Duplicate/missing fan-out entry rate.

- Privacy filtering incidents.

- Deleted tweet still served incidents.

Best feed freshness metric
Measure how long it takes for a normal author's tweet to become eligible/visible in an online follower's home timeline. That is more meaningful than queue lag alone.

## 35. Cost Drivers and Optimizations

| Cost Driver | Optimization |
| --- | --- |
| Timeline write amplification | Hybrid fan-out / active-user prioritization |
| Timeline storage | Store recent tweet IDs only |
| Tweet reads | Tweet object cache + batch hydration |
| Celebrity reads | Cache recent celebrity tweets |
| Search/trends | Async derived indexes/aggregates |
| Media egress | CDN |
| Inactive users | Avoid deep push fan-out / lazily rebuild |

Active-user optimization
For very inactive followers, you can skip or reduce fan-out and rebuild/pull when they return. Spending constant write work on dormant accounts may be wasteful.

## 36. Architecture Evolution

| Stage | Design | Trigger |
| --- | --- | --- |
| V1 | Tweet service + SQL + simple follow graph | Small product |
| V2 | Tweet cache + author timeline index | Read scale |
| V3 | Fan-out-on-write home timelines | Feed read latency |
