notes.content:
DESIGN YOUTUBE / NETFLIX

Complete Video Streaming System Design Interview Handbook

Upload -> Processing -> HLS/DASH -> CDN -> Playback -> Discovery -> Reliability

Study strategy
In an interview, spend most of your depth on transcoding, adaptive streaming, CDN/origin behavior, hot-video spikes, and playback quality.

![DESIGN YOUTUBE / NETFLIX — source diagram](/diagrams/t-rpbzwlgm2gy2-kix-9grwrsvpw7fx.png)

A modern video platform is a media pipeline plus a global delivery network.

01  Problem Framing

Understand what YouTube and Netflix share and where their product assumptions differ.

Design a large-scale video platform where creators or content providers upload video, the platform processes it into streamable formats, and viewers play it globally with low startup latency and minimal buffering.

- YouTube emphasis: user-generated upload, moderation, enormous catalog, search and recommendations.

- Netflix emphasis: controlled catalog, entitlement, DRM, regional rights, playback quality.

- The shared core is video ingest, transcoding, segmented packaging, origin storage, CDN delivery, playback sessions, and QoE analytics.

![DESIGN YOUTUBE / NETFLIX — source diagram](/diagrams/t-rpbzwlgm2gy2-kix-4tpihpqxcdz9.png)

The streaming core is reusable; ingestion and rights/discovery differ.

02  Requirements

![DESIGN YOUTUBE / NETFLIX — source diagram](/diagrams/t-rpbzwlgm2gy2-kix-l4g46tkg01dr.png)

Separate functional behavior from playback-quality goals.

| Area | Baseline Decision | Likely Follow-Up |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Upload | Resumable creator/source upload | Huge files, mobile upload, quotas |
| Processing | Multiple resolutions/bitrates | Multiple codecs, subtitles, thumbnails |
| Playback | VOD with seek/resume | DRM, regional entitlement, offline download |
| Discovery | Metadata + search | Recommendations, trending |
| Engagement | Optional likes/comments/views | Anti-fraud counts |
| Availability | Playback prioritized over ancillary systems | Multi-CDN, region failover |

Recommended interview scope
Build VOD first. Live streaming is a different latency/ingest problem and should be treated as a follow-up unless explicitly requested.

03  Non-Functional Requirements

- Playback startup should feel fast; time-to-first-frame is a critical user metric.

- Rebuffering should be rare; adaptive bitrate should prefer continuity over maximum resolution.

- Video source and published assets must be highly durable.

- Playback should remain available even if search, comments, or analytics are degraded.

- Media bandwidth is the dominant cost, so CDN hit ratio and codec efficiency matter.

- The system must absorb viral premieres without melting origin storage.

04  Capacity Estimation

![DESIGN YOUTUBE / NETFLIX — source diagram](/diagrams/t-rpbzwlgm2gy2-kix-n4crlo5gqci1.png)

The exact numbers are assumptions; the architectural conclusion is that media bytes dominate.

- Assume 2M uploads/day, average 500 MB source -> ~1 PB/day raw ingest before transcodes.

- Assume 1B playback starts/day -> ~11.6K average play-start requests/sec before peaks.

- A 20-minute video at 3 Mbps transfers roughly 450 MB; higher qualities multiply egress.

- The system therefore needs petabyte-scale storage and multi-terabit global delivery capacity.

Scale takeaway
Metadata QPS is manageable compared with media throughput. Do not route large media through ordinary application servers; use object storage, worker fleets, and CDN.

05  Video Lifecycle and State Machine

![DESIGN YOUTUBE / NETFLIX — source diagram](/diagrams/t-rpbzwlgm2gy2-kix-ciidy7d76t9j.png)

The READY transition is the publication boundary.

| State | Meaning | Viewer Behavior |
| --- | --- | --- |
| UPLOADING | Source bytes not finalized | Not playable |
| PROCESSING | Transcoding/packaging underway | Show processing |
| READY | Required renditions/manifests available | Playable |
| FAILED | Processing failed permanently/needs retry | Creator action/support |
| BLOCKED | Moderation/rights restriction | Not served |
| DELETED | Logically removed | Do not play; clean assets later |

06  High-Level Architecture

![DESIGN YOUTUBE / NETFLIX — source diagram](/diagrams/t-rpbzwlgm2gy2-kix-amwu82iqg7jf.png)

The modern design has a control plane and a media data plane.

- Metadata/API tier owns video records, visibility, publication state, rights, and upload sessions.

- Object storage holds immutable source and generated assets.

- Processing orchestrator places independent jobs onto queues/streams.

- Worker fleets transcode/package thumbnails/subtitles without blocking API requests.

- Playback service issues manifest URLs/tokens; CDN serves the media bytes.

- Search/recommendations/analytics consume metadata and playback events asynchronously.

07  API Surface

| Operation | Example | Important Semantics |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Begin upload | POST /videos/upload-sessions | quota, expected size, idempotency |
| Upload parts | PUT signed object URLs | multipart/resume/checksum |
| Finalize upload | POST /upload-sessions/{id}/complete | source becomes immutable |
| Get video | GET /videos/{videoId} | metadata/status |
| Playback | POST /videos/{id}/playback | authorization + manifest/token |
| Search | GET /search?q=... | eventually consistent index |
| Delete | DELETE /videos/{id} | logical delete first |

08  Metadata Model

![DESIGN YOUTUBE / NETFLIX — source diagram](/diagrams/t-rpbzwlgm2gy2-kix-fk9dyjrllrl.png)

Keep media references and policy state small and queryable.

- Video: videoId, owner/channel, title, description, createdAt, duration, status, visibility.

- Asset/Rendition: codec, resolution, bitrate, manifest/object references, processing state.

- Playback Policy: region rights, age restrictions, subscription tier, DRM requirements.

- Do not store video bytes in the relational/document metadata database.

09  Resumable Upload

![DESIGN YOUTUBE / NETFLIX — source diagram](/diagrams/t-rpbzwlgm2gy2-kix-3tt5v71gxbfw.png)

Application servers coordinate; object storage receives the data.

- BeginUpload authenticates creator and creates uploadSessionId.

- Return short-lived pre-signed URLs or an upload token scoped to the session.

- Client uploads directly to origin/object storage.

- Finalize only after all parts exist and checksums match.

- Source object becomes immutable once the session commits.

Why direct upload
A 20 GB video should not pass through a fleet designed for 10 KB JSON requests. Direct object upload lowers cost and avoids memory/network bottlenecks in the API tier.

10  Multipart Upload and Resume

![DESIGN YOUTUBE / NETFLIX — source diagram](/diagrams/t-rpbzwlgm2gy2-kix-4t4t3m9qm1w7.png)

Failure restarts a part, not the entire video.

- Client stores uploadSessionId and completed part numbers/ETags.

- Parts can upload concurrently with a bounded concurrency limit.

- Retries are idempotent per part number/session.

- On reconnect, ask server/object store which parts already exist.

- Abandoned incomplete sessions expire and their temporary parts are garbage-collected.

11  Processing Pipeline

![DESIGN YOUTUBE / NETFLIX — source diagram](/diagrams/t-rpbzwlgm2gy2-kix-nffd7jd90wrp.png)

Asynchronous staged processing isolates expensive CPU/GPU work.

- Probe source format and validate duration/container/codecs.

- Transcode into required codec/resolution/bitrate variants.

- Package variants into HLS/DASH segments and manifests.

- Generate thumbnails/storyboards, extract captions, and run policy/moderation checks.

- Each job records state so a failed rendition can retry without repeating completed work.

Job orchestration
Treat processing as a DAG/state machine, not one giant worker. It improves retries, parallelism, observability, and the ability to add new renditions later.

12  Transcoding and Encoding Ladder

![DESIGN YOUTUBE / NETFLIX — source diagram](/diagrams/t-rpbzwlgm2gy2-kix-hdal0j5b7l9b.png)

The encoding ladder gives the player choices.

- Generate several resolutions/bitrates rather than one giant file.

- Bitrate should depend on content complexity, not only resolution.

- Avoid producing expensive 4K/AV1 variants for source content/users that do not justify it.

- For long-tail uploads, delayed/on-demand high-end encodes can reduce compute/storage cost.

13  Codec Trade-Off

![DESIGN YOUTUBE / NETFLIX — source diagram](/diagrams/t-rpbzwlgm2gy2-kix-du50yth7gbxc.png)

Codec choice is bandwidth-versus-compute-versus-device compatibility.

- H.264 has broad device support and fast hardware decoding.

- AV1/HEVC-class codecs can reduce egress for the same quality, especially at scale.

- New codecs cost more CPU/GPU time to encode and may require dual catalogs during migration.

- The platform can choose codec per device capability and content popularity.

14  HLS / DASH: Manifests and Segments

![DESIGN YOUTUBE / NETFLIX — source diagram](/diagrams/t-rpbzwlgm2gy2-kix-jxw2buxk04t9.png)

Playback fetches a manifest and then many small immutable media segments.

- Master manifest lists available variants.

- Each variant playlist references time-aligned segments.

- Segment durations are commonly a few seconds; shorter segments improve responsiveness but increase request overhead.

- Segments are immutable and ideal CDN objects.

- Seeking maps playback time to segment ranges rather than random reads inside one monolithic file.

15  Adaptive Bitrate Streaming

![DESIGN YOUTUBE / NETFLIX — source diagram](/diagrams/t-rpbzwlgm2gy2-kix-e7r7oemhskvn.png)

The client chooses quality continuously rather than the server hard-coding it.

- Player estimates recent network throughput.

- Player observes buffer occupancy and recent rebuffer events.

- It chooses the next segment representation conservatively.

- Quality should rise gradually and fall quickly enough to avoid stalls.

- ABR can incorporate device resolution, codec support, data-saver mode, and battery/CPU constraints.

QoE priority
A stable 720p stream is usually a better experience than oscillating 1080p with repeated buffering. ABR optimizes overall quality of experience, not maximum pixels.

16  Playback Path

![DESIGN YOUTUBE / NETFLIX — source diagram](/diagrams/t-rpbzwlgm2gy2-kix-6ui2sqtr3s9n.png)

The API authorizes playback; the CDN carries the heavy traffic.

1. Viewer opens a video page; metadata is served from API/cache.

2. Player requests a playback session/manifest URL.

3. Playback service checks READY status, visibility, entitlement/region/DRM policy.

4. Return master manifest URL plus short-lived playback token if required.

5. Player requests manifest/segments from nearest CDN edge.

6. CDN HIT serves immediately; MISS goes to origin shield/origin.

7. Player emits QoE events asynchronously.

17  CDN and Origin Shield

![DESIGN YOUTUBE / NETFLIX — source diagram](/diagrams/t-rpbzwlgm2gy2-kix-im1g1kfgsviw.png)

The origin should not see one request per viewer.

- CDN caches immutable segments close to users.

- Origin shield/mid-tier cache coalesces simultaneous misses from many edges.

- Use long cache TTLs/versioned object names because segment content never changes.

- Serve manifests with shorter TTL if publication/rights can change; media segments themselves remain immutable.

- Multi-CDN may improve resilience, cost leverage, and geography coverage at very large scale.

18  Hot vs Cold Videos

![DESIGN YOUTUBE / NETFLIX — source diagram](/diagrams/t-rpbzwlgm2gy2-kix-edq2dhfpfs89.png)

One cache policy is inefficient for both a viral premiere and a never-watched upload.

- Hot videos: pre-warm edges, keep early segments resident, possibly replicate across CDN providers.

- Cold videos: leave at origin; cache on demand; use cheaper storage tiers where playback SLO allows.

- Popularity predictors can promote/demote objects between tiers.

- The first few segments are disproportionately valuable because every playback requests them.

19  Viral Premiere / Thundering Herd

![DESIGN YOUTUBE / NETFLIX — source diagram](/diagrams/t-rpbzwlgm2gy2-kix-aws7l4pd75a1.png)

Synchronized viewers create a special burst shape.

- Pre-warm manifests and first segments before a scheduled premiere.

- Origin shield/request coalescing prevents every edge miss from reaching storage.

- Reserve CDN/origin capacity and use multi-CDN failover for massive launches.

- Gracefully reduce top quality variants before allowing widespread rebuffering if capacity is constrained.

20  Storage Strategy

- Source master: highest durability, retained per product policy.

- Published renditions: immutable generated assets; can be recreated from source if necessary, but regeneration may be expensive.

- Long-tail/cold assets can move to colder object tiers.

- Thumbnails/manifests are tiny and widely cached.

- Use lifecycle/retention rules for failed/abandoned uploads and obsolete rendition versions.

Source vs derived assets
The source upload is usually the strongest recovery asset. Transcoded renditions are derived, but deleting them casually may create huge recompute cost; choose retention based on economics.

21  Metadata Database and Partitioning

- Primary video lookup by videoId should be direct and highly cached.

- Partition metadata by videoId or stable ownership shard.

- Creator/channel listing requires a secondary author/channel index.

- Use transactions/conditional writes for status transitions such as PROCESSING -> READY and delete/visibility changes.

- View counters/search/recommendation features should not overload the metadata row.

22  Search

![DESIGN YOUTUBE / NETFLIX — source diagram](/diagrams/t-rpbzwlgm2gy2-kix-rbuu6xnhuy27.png)

Search is a separate indexing workload.

- Index title, description, tags, channel, captions/transcript, language, and policy metadata.

- Use an inverted index for lexical retrieval; vector/semantic retrieval can be added for modern search.

- Metadata events update the index asynchronously.

- Opening a search result rechecks current visibility/rights because the index may lag.

23  Recommendations

- Candidate sources: subscriptions, similar videos, collaborative behavior, trending, channel affinity.

- Retrieve a few hundred/thousand candidates, score/rank, then apply diversity/safety/business rules.

- Use watch-time/completion/skip signals rather than only clicks.

- Cold-start new videos can use metadata/content embeddings and controlled exploration.

Interview boundary
Unless this is specifically an ML system-design interview, keep recommendation details at candidate retrieval -> scoring -> filtering. Spend the HLD depth on streaming infrastructure.

24  Views, Watch Time, and Playback Analytics

![DESIGN YOUTUBE / NETFLIX — source diagram](/diagrams/t-rpbzwlgm2gy2-kix-idxnvxhv77b2.png)

High-volume telemetry should not update the video row synchronously.

- Player emits play-start, segment-download, bitrate-switch, buffer, error, heartbeat/progress, and finish events.

- Event stream buffers traffic and supports replay.

- Streaming analytics produces real-time QoE dashboards and approximate live counts.

- Warehouse/OLAP computes durable views, watch time, creator analytics, experimentation, recommendations.

- Fraud/anti-bot logic validates view counts separately from raw playback events.

25  DRM, Entitlement, and Regional Rights

![DESIGN YOUTUBE / NETFLIX — source diagram](/diagrams/t-rpbzwlgm2gy2-kix-v8nc71prlinm.png)

Licensed streaming adds a control decision before encrypted media playback.

- Entitlement service checks subscription/account tier.

- Rights policy checks user region and content availability window.

- License service issues short-lived decryption/license material to approved devices.

- Segments stay encrypted in CDN/object storage.

- Keys/licenses should not be embedded permanently in manifests.

26  Security and Abuse

- Authenticate upload/finalize/delete operations.

- Use short-lived scoped pre-signed upload/download tokens.

- Validate MIME/container/codec rather than trusting filename extensions.

- Rate-limit upload sessions and metadata mutations.

- Scan uploaded media for malware and policy violations where applicable.

- Protect private/unlisted content with authorization; an opaque videoId alone is not sufficient for private access.

27  Content Moderation and Copyright

- Run asynchronous visual/audio/text classifiers after ingest; high-risk checks may gate publication.

- Maintain moderation state in authoritative metadata.

- Fingerprinting can detect known copyrighted/reuploaded media.

- If a video is blocked, playback service must deny new sessions even if old CDN objects still physically exist.

- Purge/expire manifests/tokens as required for urgent takedown.

28  Consistency Model

| Data | Recommended Consistency |
| --- | --- |
| Video upload/finalize/status | Strong/conditional state transitions |
| Playback authorization/rights | Current enough to enforce policy |
| Search index | Eventual |
| Recommendations | Eventual |
| View counts | Eventual / approximate in real time |
| CDN segments | Immutable; consistency trivial by versioned key |

Key idea
Strong consistency belongs around user intent, publication state, deletion, and entitlement. Search, recommendations, counters, and analytics can lag.

29  Multi-Region Design

![DESIGN YOUTUBE / NETFLIX — source diagram](/diagrams/t-rpbzwlgm2gy2-kix-89d8m1bhm5fx.png)

Global playback is naturally edge-first; metadata writes still need ownership/failover rules.

- Upload/metadata writes can use a home region per creator/video or a globally consistent metadata service.

- Source/transcoded media replicate across origin regions according to durability/locality policy.

- Playback metadata/cache replicas serve viewers locally.

- CDN handles most segment delivery, so origin regions see only misses.

- Failover must preserve video state machine and avoid two orchestrators publishing conflicting asset versions.

30  Failure Modes and Recovery

![DESIGN YOUTUBE / NETFLIX — source diagram](/diagrams/t-rpbzwlgm2gy2-kix-4v14zuxtdol4.png)

Different layers fail independently and should degrade differently.

| Failure | Expected Behavior | Recovery |
| --- | --- | --- |
| One transcode worker | Only that job/rendition retries | Queue retry, idempotent output key |
| Processing backlog | Publishing delayed | Autoscale, priority queues |
| One CDN POP | Route to another POP/CDN | DNS/anycast/provider failover |
| Origin shield | Edges miss to alternate shield/origin | Capacity guardrails |
| Metadata writer | Uploads/changes pause or fail over | Leader/DB failover |
| Search/recommendation | Playback remains available | Catch up asynchronously |

Failure priority
Playback of already-published videos should survive failures in upload processing, search, recommendations, comments, and analytics.

31  Idempotency and Retry Safety

- BeginUpload uses client idempotency key to avoid duplicate video records.

- Part upload is idempotent by session + part number/object key.

- Processing job output path includes videoId + assetVersion + rendition so retries overwrite/confirm the same logical result safely.

- State transitions use expected previous state/version.

- Analytics events may be at-least-once; downstream aggregates deduplicate where exactness matters.

32  Observability and QoE SLOs

For a streaming platform, backend availability is not enough; measure what the player experiences.

- Time to first frame / startup latency.

- Rebuffer ratio and rebuffer events per hour.

- Average delivered bitrate / quality switches.

- Playback fatal error rate.

- CDN edge hit ratio and origin egress.

- Transcoding queue wait + processing duration per rendition.

- Upload completion/retry rate.

- Manifest/segment p95/p99 latency by ISP/region/device.

Best product metric
A request can return HTTP 200 and still be a terrible stream. Playback QoE metrics such as startup time and rebuffer ratio should be first-class SLOs.

33  Cost Drivers and Optimization

| Cost Driver | Optimization |
| --- | --- |
| CDN egress | Better codecs, CDN price routing, regional peering |
| Transcoding compute | Popularity-aware/on-demand renditions, hardware encoders |
| Origin storage | Cold tiers, lifecycle, deduplicate identical assets where safe |
| Multi-region replication | Replicate based on durability + locality |
| Search/ML | Async batching and tiered inference |
| Viral launch | Pre-warm CDN; origin shield |

Streaming economics
At scale, a 10-20% bitrate reduction can save more money than many backend optimizations because every watched minute crosses the delivery network.

34  YouTube-Specific Product Follow-Ups

- Subscriptions: maintain channel->subscribers and user->subscriptions; notify/feed asynchronously.

- Comments: separate comment service, paginated/threaded store, moderation/ranking.

- Likes: idempotent user-video relation + asynchronous aggregate counters.

- Creator analytics: warehouse from playback/engagement events, not synchronous metadata updates.

- Unlisted/private videos: playback API authorizes every session; CDN uses signed tokens/URLs as needed.

35  Netflix-Specific Product Follow-Ups

- Regional licensing windows and subscription entitlement are part of playback authorization.

- Multiple audio tracks, subtitles, accessibility tracks, and device certification matter.

- Offline download uses encrypted device-bound assets and expiring licenses.

- Catalog may be much smaller than YouTube but each title receives extremely high watch volume and sophisticated encoding.

- Playback quality and DRM are typically deeper interview areas than creator upload moderation.

36  Architecture Evolution

| Stage | Design | Trigger |
| --- | --- | --- |
| V1 | Metadata API + one object store + one encoded file | Small launch |
| V2 | Async transcode workers + several renditions | Device/network diversity |
| V3 | HLS/DASH + CDN | Playback scale |
| V4 | Origin shield + multi-region origin | Viral/global traffic |
| V5 | Search + analytics streams | Discovery/operations |
| V6 | Popularity-aware encoding/storage | Cost scale |
| V7 | DRM/multi-CDN/recommendations | Mature global product |

37  Final Production Architecture

![DESIGN YOUTUBE / NETFLIX — source diagram](/diagrams/t-rpbzwlgm2gy2-kix-hcq8mfxw757f.png)

The final system isolates media transport from control-plane correctness.

Upload/processing path:

- Creator -> Upload API -> direct multipart source upload -> finalize.

- Event/job stream -> transcode/package workers -> immutable segments/manifests -> origin storage.

- Metadata transitions to READY only after required assets are valid.

Playback path:

- Viewer -> Playback API authorization -> master manifest.

- Player -> CDN edge -> origin shield -> origin only on misses.

- ABR chooses each next segment quality.

Derived path:

- Metadata/playback events -> search, recommendations, analytics, creator dashboards, moderation.

38  How to Present This in a 45-60 Minute Interview

| Time | Coverage |
| --- | --- |
| 0-5 min | Clarify YouTube vs Netflix, upload + VOD + playback requirements |
| 5-10 min | Scale: ingest bytes, watch time, egress |
| 10-18 min | HLD + metadata/data-plane separation |
| 18-28 min | Resumable upload + processing/transcoding pipeline |
| 28-38 min | HLS/DASH + ABR + CDN/origin shield |
| 38-46 min | Metadata/storage/search/analytics |
| 46-53 min | DRM/security/multi-region/failures |
| 53-60 min | Interviewer-selected deep dive + final summary |

Do not memorize every paragraph
Memorize this flow: resumable source upload -> durable source -> async transcode ladder -> HLS/DASH segments/manifests -> origin storage -> CDN -> player ABR -> QoE analytics. Then remember the two big interview truths: media bytes bypass normal APIs, and already-published playback should survive failures in noncritical subsystems.

39  Interviewer Follow-Ups

Follow-up: Why not stream the original uploaded file directly?

Answer: The original may use unsupported codecs/resolution/bitrate and is usually one large object. Transcoding creates device-compatible representations; segment packaging enables CDN caching, seeking and adaptive bitrate.

Follow-up: Why split video into segments?

Answer: Segments let the player switch quality between boundaries, retry a small piece, seek efficiently, and cache immutable objects independently at CDN edges.

Follow-up: How do you avoid reuploading a 20 GB file after Wi-Fi fails?

Answer: Use multipart resumable upload with a durable session and per-part checksums/acknowledgements. On reconnect, query completed parts and send only missing ones.

Follow-up: What happens if one transcode job fails?

Answer: Retry that rendition idempotently. Keep processing stages/jobs independent so one failed 4K encode does not repeat thumbnails or block all other videos.

Follow-up: How does adaptive bitrate choose quality?

Answer: Use recent throughput, buffer level, screen/device capabilities and previous rebuffer history. The goal is high stable quality with minimal stalls, not simply the highest resolution.

Follow-up: How do you handle a viral premiere?

Answer: Pre-warm CDN, cache first segments widely, use an origin shield/request coalescing, reserve capacity and optionally route across multiple CDNs.

Follow-up: What if CDN misses increase suddenly?

Answer: Protect origin with mid-tier shield and concurrency/rate limits; investigate cache-key/TTL changes. Prefer graceful quality reduction over origin collapse.

Follow-up: How do deletes/takedowns work if segments are cached?

Answer: Make playback authorization/metadata immediately deny new sessions, purge manifests/tokens/edge objects for urgent cases, and clean immutable segment objects asynchronously.

Follow-up: How do you support multiple codecs?

Answer: Maintain separate rendition sets/manifests and let playback select based on device support. Encode expensive next-gen codecs only where bandwidth savings justify compute/storage.

Follow-up: Why not update view count on every segment/play request?

Answer: It would create hot synchronous writes. Emit playback events to a stream and aggregate validated views/watch time asynchronously.

Follow-up: How does Netflix differ most from YouTube?

Answer: Netflix has controlled ingest and heavier entitlement/DRM/rights logic, while YouTube has user-generated upload, moderation and huge long-tail discovery. Streaming/CDN mechanics are largely shared.

Follow-up: How does multi-region change the design?

Answer: Serve playback locally via CDN/replicated origin and keep explicit ownership/failover for metadata/upload state. Replicate media asynchronously according to durability/locality policy.

40  Detailed Interview Questions with Answers

1. What is the hardest part of a YouTube/Netflix system design?

Answer: The hardest engineering cost is moving and serving enormous media bytes reliably and cheaply while maintaining good playback quality. Metadata CRUD is comparatively small. The design must therefore separate a control plane for video records, rights and sessions from a data plane built around object storage, processing workers, immutable segments and CDN. The key interview deep dives are resumable ingest, transcoding/packaging, adaptive bitrate, CDN/origin behavior, viral spikes and QoE.

2. Why should video upload bypass ordinary application servers?

Answer: Large uploads may be many gigabytes. If every byte travels through stateless API servers, those servers become expensive network proxies and need huge connection/memory budgets. Instead, the API authenticates the creator and creates an upload session, then issues short-lived scoped URLs/tokens so the client sends parts directly to object storage. The API later finalizes the session and starts processing. This cleanly separates control traffic from bulk data transfer.

3. How do you make a huge upload resumable?

Answer: Split the source into independently uploadable parts and persist an uploadSessionId plus expected file metadata. Each part has a stable part number and checksum. The client records completed parts locally; the object store/server also records them. After a disconnect, the client lists completed parts and uploads only the missing ones. Completing the multipart upload atomically creates the source object. Incomplete sessions expire and temporary parts are garbage-collected.

4. When should the platform acknowledge an upload as complete?

Answer: There are two milestones. First, source upload completion means the original source object is durably stored and verified. Second, publication/READY means required processed assets and manifests exist. The creator can receive an upload-success response after the source commit while the UI shows PROCESSING. Normal viewers should only be routed to published/READY assets unless the product deliberately supports progressive/partial publication.

5. Why is video processing asynchronous?

Answer: Transcoding can take seconds to hours and consumes expensive CPU/GPU resources. Running it inside the upload HTTP request would time out, waste server resources and make retries dangerous. An asynchronous job/state-machine pipeline lets workers scale independently, retry failed stages, prioritize jobs, run several renditions in parallel and preserve a durable processing state. It also isolates a bad video or slow encoder from unrelated uploads.

6. What stages would you put in the processing pipeline?

Answer: A practical pipeline probes/validates the source, extracts technical metadata, runs security/moderation checks, transcodes required codec/resolution/bitrate variants, packages them into HLS/DASH segments, creates manifests, generates thumbnails/storyboards, handles subtitles/captions, and updates metadata to READY. Each stage should be idempotent with versioned output keys so retries do not create conflicting assets.

7. Why generate multiple resolutions and bitrates?

Answer: Viewers have different bandwidth, screens, devices and network changes during playback. One 4K file would waste bandwidth for mobile users and fail on slow connections. Multiple representations let the player select a suitable bitrate and switch between them as conditions change. This improves startup speed and reduces buffering. It also lets the platform choose codecs/quality based on device capability and data-saver policy.

8. How do you choose an encoding ladder?

Answer: Start with a small ladder such as 240p/480p/720p/1080p at progressively higher bitrates, then tune based on codec, content complexity and observed devices. Sports/action may need more bitrate than a static lecture at the same resolution. I would not encode every upload into every possible format: popularity-aware encoding can delay or skip expensive 4K/AV1 variants for long-tail videos until demand justifies them.

9. H.264 vs AV1/HEVC - how do you decide?

Answer: H.264 has excellent compatibility and hardware support but needs more bits for comparable quality. Newer codecs can reduce CDN bandwidth substantially but cost more to encode and may not play on all clients or have licensing constraints. A mature platform often stores multiple codec families and chooses per device. For popular content, bandwidth savings may easily justify extra encoding compute; for cold content, simpler encoding may be cheaper overall.

10. What do HLS and DASH solve?

Answer: They package a video as short time-aligned segments plus manifests describing available representations. The player fetches the master manifest, chooses a representation and downloads segments over ordinary HTTP/CDN. This enables seeking, retries, CDN caching and adaptive bitrate switching between segment boundaries. The platform no longer needs a custom continuous video socket for VOD; standard HTTP delivery becomes highly scalable.

11. How does adaptive bitrate streaming work?

Answer: The player continuously estimates sustainable throughput and tracks its playback buffer. Before requesting the next segment, it selects a representation whose bitrate should arrive before the buffer runs out, also considering device resolution, codec support and recent rebuffer history. Good ABR algorithms avoid rapid quality oscillation and prioritize uninterrupted playback. When bandwidth drops, the player quickly chooses a lower bitrate rather than waiting for a high-quality segment that causes a stall.

12. Why is the CDN so important?

Answer: Video egress dwarfs API traffic. Without a CDN, every segment request would traverse to central object storage, causing huge latency, bandwidth cost and origin overload. CDN edges cache immutable segments close to users and absorb repeated demand. Since popular videos account for a large portion of traffic, hit ratio can be extremely valuable. The origin should serve only misses, protected by an origin shield/mid-tier cache.

13. What is an origin shield and why use it?

Answer: When many edge POPs miss the same new segment, they can all request it from origin simultaneously. An origin shield is a regional mid-tier cache that collapses those requests: only one/few requests reach object storage, then the shield serves the edges. This is especially valuable during premieres or sudden viral spikes and reduces origin bandwidth/connection pressure.

14. How do you handle a viral premiere with millions of simultaneous viewers?

Answer: Pre-warm the master manifest and first segments at major edges before launch, use an origin shield/request coalescing, reserve CDN capacity, monitor per-region startup/rebuffer metrics and optionally use multiple CDN providers. First segments deserve special attention because every viewer requests them together. If capacity is constrained, reducing maximum quality is safer than letting widespread buffering occur.

15. What should be cached and for how long?

Answer: Versioned media segments are immutable, so they can use very long CDN TTLs. Manifests may use shorter TTLs if rights/publication state or available renditions can change, although versioned manifests can also be immutable. Metadata pages/API responses use normal application caching. Playback authorization/entitlement should not be hidden behind an unsafe public cache. Cache keys should include asset/version/codec/rendition so objects never mutate in place.

16. How do hot and cold videos differ operationally?

Answer: Hot videos should be present at many CDN edges, may be pre-warmed and can justify expensive efficient codecs because egress dominates cost. Cold long-tail videos may remain only in origin/cold storage and populate edge caches on demand. The platform can use popularity predictions and recent access to tier assets. Applying the same replication/cache/encoding policy to every video wastes enormous storage and compute.

17. How would you model video metadata?

Answer: Use a compact Video record with videoId, owner/channel, title/description, visibility, duration, status and publication fields. Separate Asset/Rendition records describe codec, resolution, bitrate and manifest/object references. A PlaybackPolicy or related records can capture region rights, age restrictions and DRM/entitlement. This keeps the database queryable while all large media bytes remain in object storage.

18. What database would you choose for metadata?

Answer: The metadata workload is relatively small compared with media, and it benefits from conditional state transitions and secondary queries by owner/channel. SQL is a strong starting choice; a sharded/distributed relational or document/KV system can be used at huge scale. The important design is direct videoId lookup, an owner/channel index and safe transitions such as PROCESSING to READY or ACTIVE to DELETED. I would not choose a database based on video file size because files are not stored there.

19. How does video search work?

Answer: Search consumes metadata/READY events asynchronously and builds an inverted index over title, description, tags, captions/transcript, channel and language; modern systems may add vector/semantic retrieval. The search index can lag the metadata store. When a user opens a result, the playback/metadata API rechecks visibility and rights so a stale search document cannot bypass deletion or privacy.

20. How would recommendations fit without turning this into an ML interview?

Answer: Keep it layered: candidate retrieval from subscriptions, similar videos, user history, trending and collaborative signals; then rank a few hundred/thousand candidates using freshness, predicted watch time/engagement and diversity/safety/business constraints. The streaming architecture is independent: recommendations produce video IDs, while playback still uses the same metadata/CDN pipeline. Unless asked, do not dive into model architecture.

21. How do you count views correctly at massive scale?

Answer: Do not increment a single video row for every playback. Players emit start/progress/finish events into a durable stream. Streaming/batch jobs validate sessions, remove obvious duplicates/bots, apply business rules such as minimum watch time and aggregate views/watch time. A real-time counter can be approximate; durable creator analytics can reconcile later from the event log/warehouse.

22. Which playback analytics matter most?

Answer: Time to first frame, rebuffer ratio, rebuffer events per hour, fatal playback error rate, delivered bitrate/resolution, quality-switch frequency and CDN/segment latency by region/ISP/device are core QoE metrics. Watch time and completion matter for product/recommendation, but a streaming team first needs to know whether playback actually starts quickly and continues smoothly.

23. How do DRM and entitlement fit?

Answer: Before issuing a playback session, the service checks that the account is entitled, the title is allowed in the user's region/time window and the device is acceptable. Media segments remain encrypted at rest/in CDN. A license service issues short-lived decryption/license material to the approved client. This protects keys from being permanently embedded in manifests and lets rights changes stop new playback even though encrypted segments are widely cached.

24. How do you delete or block a video that is already cached worldwide?

Answer: First change authoritative metadata/status so playback API denies new sessions immediately. Invalidate API/metadata caches. For urgent takedowns, purge the manifest/segments at CDN or use short-lived signed playback tokens/manifests so stale edge objects cannot be requested by unauthorized clients. Physical deletion from origin/CDN can happen asynchronously after the logical policy is enforced.

25. What happens if a transcoding worker crashes mid-job?

Answer: Jobs are idempotent and persisted in a queue/state machine, so another worker retries the failed rendition. Output object names include videoId, assetVersion, codec and rendition, letting a retry safely detect/replace the same logical output. Completed independent renditions do not need to rerun. The video stays PROCESSING until the required asset set passes validation.

26. What happens if the CDN fails?

Answer: A single POP failure should route users to another POP. A provider-wide regional issue can use multi-CDN or alternate routing for a mature platform. CDN misses can fall back through origin shield/origin, but origin must have capacity guardrails so a CDN outage does not create an uncontrolled thundering herd. Playback may temporarily reduce maximum quality to preserve continuity.

27. What if origin storage becomes slow?

Answer: Edge hits continue normally. Misses will suffer, so the shield should coalesce requests and apply bounded concurrency/backpressure. Popular assets should already have high edge residency. For critical titles, multiple origin replicas/regions reduce risk. The goal is to prevent one origin incident from evicting or bypassing the cached data plane that still works.

28. How would multi-region deployment work?

Answer: Upload/metadata writes have explicit ownership or a globally consistent metadata layer. Source and published assets replicate to durable origin regions. Playback APIs and metadata caches run regionally, while CDN serves most bytes locally. Processing jobs can run where the source/compute is available and publish versioned assets globally. Failover must ensure only one logical publication state/version is authoritative.

29. Why are media segments easy to make eventually consistent?

Answer: They are immutable and versioned. Once a segment object exists, it never changes; a new processing version gets a new key/manifest. Therefore replication can be asynchronous without worrying that two replicas will serve conflicting mutable contents for the same key. The harder consistency problem is the small metadata pointer that decides which asset version is published/authorized.

30. How do you handle subtitles and multiple audio tracks?

Answer: Treat them as timed media assets associated with the same video/version. Processing extracts/generates/transcodes tracks, and the manifest advertises available subtitle/audio alternatives. They are small compared with video and cache well. The playback client selects based on user language/accessibility preferences. Rights/moderation may apply independently to tracks.

31. How would offline downloads work for Netflix-like content?

Answer: The client downloads encrypted segments/manifests to device storage using a controlled workflow. A device-bound DRM license with expiry/offline policy authorizes decryption for a limited period. The app tracks download state and refreshes/invalidates licenses when online. Raw unencrypted files should not be exposed as normal downloadable objects. This is a product/security extension to the same segmented asset model.

32. How do you optimize cost at very large scale?

Answer: Focus on the big multipliers: egress bitrate, transcoding compute, replication and storage. Use more efficient codecs for popular titles, popularity-aware encoding ladders, object lifecycle/cold tiers for long-tail assets, hardware encoders, CDN price/performance routing and regional origin placement. Even a modest bitrate reduction across billions of watched minutes can dwarf savings from optimizing metadata servers.

33. What should be strongly consistent and what can be eventual?

Answer: Strong/conditional consistency is useful for upload-finalization state, publication/deletion, visibility and entitlement/rights because these are user intent/security boundaries. Search, recommendations, view counts, creator analytics and most discovery indexes can be eventually consistent. Media segment objects are immutable/versioned, so their replication can be asynchronous once durability requirements are met.

34. What would you monitor first in production?

Answer: I would monitor playback QoE first: startup time, rebuffer ratio, fatal error rate and delivered bitrate segmented by ISP/region/device. Then CDN hit ratio/origin egress, manifest/segment latency, processing queue wait and job failure rates, upload completion, metadata/playback API errors and multi-region replication health. For a streaming service, HTTP success alone does not prove users had a successful watch experience.

35. Give the complete design in 30 seconds.

Answer: Creators upload source videos directly to durable object storage using resumable multipart sessions. Finalization publishes an asynchronous processing DAG that transcodes multiple codec/bitrate variants, packages HLS/DASH segments, generates manifests/thumbnails and marks the video READY. Playback API checks status, privacy/entitlement/DRM and returns a manifest; the player fetches immutable segments from CDN and uses adaptive bitrate based on bandwidth/buffer. Origin shield protects storage from misses and viral launches. Search, recommendations, moderation and analytics consume metadata/playback events asynchronously, while metadata and publication state remain authoritative.

41  Final Interview Cheat Sheet

| Topic | Recommended Baseline |
| --- | --- |
| Core split | Control plane metadata vs media data plane |
| Upload | Direct resumable multipart to object storage |
| Publication | Source durable first; READY after required assets |
| Processing | Async DAG/state machine |
| Encoding | Multiple bitrate/resolution representations |
| Packaging | HLS/DASH manifest + immutable segments |
| Playback | Playback API auth -> CDN manifest/segments |
| ABR | Client chooses next segment quality |
| CDN | Edge -> origin shield -> origin |
| Hot video | Pre-warm/cache/multi-CDN as needed |
| Cold video | Origin/cold tier; on-demand edge fill |
| Metadata | Small DB records, not video bytes |
| Search | Async inverted/semantic index |
| Analytics | Playback events -> stream -> QoE/warehouse |
| DRM | Entitlement/license + encrypted segments |
| Delete | Authoritative deny first; purge/cleanup later |
| Multi-region | Local playback; explicit metadata write ownership |
| Best SLOs | Startup time + rebuffer ratio + fatal error rate |

30-second final answer
Creators upload source videos directly to durable object storage using resumable multipart sessions. After finalize, an asynchronous processing pipeline validates, transcodes multiple codec/bitrate variants, packages HLS/DASH segments and manifests, and marks the video READY. Playback API checks visibility/entitlement and returns a manifest; viewers fetch immutable segments from CDN, with an origin shield protecting storage and ABR choosing quality based on bandwidth and buffer. Search, recommendations, moderation and analytics are asynchronous derived systems; metadata/publication/rights remain authoritative.

42  Review Quiz - Actual Design Problem

| Question | Answer |
| --- | --- |
| 1. Why not stream the original upload? | It may be too large/unsupported and cannot adapt bitrate; transcode + segment it. |
| 2. What is the publication boundary? | Metadata becomes READY only after required durable processed assets/manifests exist. |
| 3. Why use multipart upload? | Resume/retry only missing parts instead of restarting multi-GB uploads. |
| 4. Why are HLS/DASH segments CDN-friendly? | They are small immutable HTTP objects with stable versioned keys. |
| 5. What does ABR optimize? | Smooth playback and quality under changing bandwidth/buffer constraints. |
| 6. Why use an origin shield? | Collapse many edge misses so origin does not receive a thundering herd. |
| 7. What should happen during a viral premiere? | Pre-warm edges/first segments, reserve capacity, shield/coalesce misses, possibly multi-CDN. |
| 8. Why not update view counts synchronously? | It creates a hot write path; aggregate validated playback events asynchronously. |
| 9. What data needs stronger consistency? | Publication/delete/visibility/entitlement state, not search or view counters. |
| 10. What are the best streaming SLOs? | Startup latency, rebuffer ratio, fatal error rate and delivered quality. |

notes.content:
Design YouTube / User-Generated Video Platform

Advanced System Design Interview Guide

Problem 23 | Uploads, Transcoding, Streaming, Viral Scale, Counters, Search & Recommendations

Goal
Design a global user-generated video platform where creators upload videos and viewers discover, stream, like, comment, subscribe, and receive recommendations. The system must handle huge media objects, asynchronous processing, CDN delivery, viral traffic, very high event volume, mutable social metadata, abuse/moderation, and global availability.

## 1. Why YouTube Is Different from Netflix

Dimension

Netflix-like VOD

YouTube-like UGC

Content producers

Controlled studio/catalog pipeline

Millions of independent creators

Uploads

Curated ingestion

Continuous unpredictable uploads

Catalog

Large but controlled

Enormous long-tail corpus

Quality

Known masters

Arbitrary codecs/resolutions/quality

Social state

Limited

Likes, comments, subscriptions, views

Virality

Planned releases

Unexpected viral spikes

Moderation

Catalog review

Continuous automated + human moderation

Discovery

Recommendations important

Search/recommendations are core

Interview framing
Do not design YouTube as only a video CDN. The hard parts are creator upload reliability, asynchronous media processing, global playback, viral fan-out, counters/social interactions, discovery, moderation, and separating strong metadata correctness from eventually consistent analytics.

## 2. Functional Requirements

Area

Requirements

Upload

Resumable large-video upload, status, thumbnail

Processing

Validate, transcode, segment, generate manifests

Playback

Adaptive streaming, seek, captions

Metadata

Title, description, tags, visibility

Social

Views, likes, comments, subscriptions

Discovery

Search, trending, home/recommendations

Creator

Publish/unpublish/delete, analytics

Safety

Moderation, copyright/abuse workflow

Notifications

Notify subscribers selectively

## 3. Non-Functional Requirements

- Very high playback availability and low startup latency.

- Uploads must survive flaky mobile networks and multi-GB files.

- Processing is asynchronous; publish readiness may take seconds/minutes.

- Playback bytes should come from CDN, not application servers.

- Viral videos must scale without hot-origin collapse.

- View/like counters may be eventually consistent; ownership/visibility changes need stronger semantics.

- Global system with regional failures and graceful degradation.

- Media durability is critical; raw originals must not be lost.

## 4. Scope and Clarifying Questions

- Focus on on-demand uploaded video; live streaming is a detailed extension.

- Support public/unlisted/private visibility.

- Assume adaptive bitrate streaming with HLS/DASH-like manifests.

- Search by title/description/tags/transcript; recommendations are architectural, not model-training deep dive.

- Comments and subscriptions are included.

- Monetization/ads are optional extensions.

- Copyright and moderation are system-design flows, not legal-policy analysis.

## 5. Capacity Estimation

Dimension

Illustrative scale

Implication

Daily viewers

500M+

Global edge delivery

Peak playback QPS

Millions of segment requests/s

CDN-centric architecture

Uploads/day

Millions

Massive async pipeline

Average upload

Hundreds of MB

Resumable multipart upload

Stored renditions

Several per video

Storage amplification

View events

Billions/day

Streaming counters/analytics

Comments/likes

Very high write volume

Partitioned social stores

Catalog

Billions of videos

Search/index partitioning

Capacity lesson
Application QPS is not the dominant bandwidth problem. Video segment delivery is orders of magnitude larger, so the architecture must push bytes to CDN/object storage and keep metadata services off the media data path.

## 6. Core APIs

API

Purpose

POST /videos/uploads

Create upload session

PUT /uploads/{id}/parts/{n}

Upload chunk/part

POST /uploads/{id}/complete

Finalize upload

PATCH /videos/{id}

Edit metadata/visibility

GET /videos/{id}

Video metadata/playback info

POST /videos/{id}/views

Record view event

PUT /videos/{id}/like

Like/unlike

POST /videos/{id}/comments

Create comment

GET /search?q=...

Search

GET /feed/home

Recommendations/home feed

POST /channels/{id}/subscribe

Subscribe

## 7. Data Model

Entity

Key fields

Video

video_id, owner_id, title, description, visibility, state, duration, created_at

UploadSession

upload_id, owner, parts, checksum, status

MediaAsset

video_id, original_uri, rendition, codec, bitrate, dimensions, manifest

Channel

channel_id, owner, profile, counters

Subscription

subscriber_id, channel_id, created_at

Like

video_id, user_id, state

Comment

comment_id, video_id, author, parent_id, text, state, created_at

ViewEvent

video_id, viewer/session, timestamp, watch_ms, context

Counter

entity_id, metric, approximate_value

ModerationState

video_id, checks, restrictions, review state

## 8. High-Level Architecture

YouTube-style high-level architecture

## 9. Upload Architecture

The API server should authorize uploads but should not proxy multi-GB media through itself.

- Client requests an upload session with filename, expected size/type, and metadata.

- Upload service creates video_id/upload_id and returns signed multipart/object-storage upload URLs.

- Client uploads chunks directly to nearby object storage.

- Each part has checksum and idempotent part number.

- Client can resume after network failure by querying completed parts.

- Complete call validates all parts/checksum and atomically marks raw asset available.

- An event starts validation/transcoding/moderation pipelines.

- Video remains PROCESSING until minimum playable renditions and required checks are ready.

## 10. Resumable Multipart Uploads

Resumable direct-to-storage upload

- Chunk size balances retry cost and request overhead.

- Upload session has expiry and ownership checks.

- Part completion is idempotent.

- Storage validates checksums; final object can have whole-file checksum.

- Client retries individual failed parts, not the entire video.

- Regional upload endpoints reduce creator latency.

## 11. Upload State Machine

State

Meaning

CREATED

Metadata/session exists

UPLOADING

Parts arriving

UPLOADED

Original durably finalized

VALIDATING

Container/codec/security checks

PROCESSING

Transcoding, thumbnails, captions, checks

READY_PRIVATE

Playable but not necessarily public

PUBLISHED

Eligible for discovery/playback

RESTRICTED

Moderation/copyright restriction

DELETED

Tombstoned and removal workflow started

Correctness invariant
Never expose a manifest that references renditions which are not durably available. Publish playback metadata only after the minimum playable asset set is committed.

## 12. Media Validation

- Verify declared MIME/container against actual bytes.

- Reject malformed/decompression-bomb-like media and unsafe payloads.

- Extract duration, streams, codec, dimensions, frame rate, audio properties.

- Check corruption and decodeability.

- Normalize rotation/color metadata.

- Enforce size/duration/account limits.

- Create a canonical media-processing job from validated metadata.

## 13. Transcoding Pipeline

Distributed transcoding and packaging

- Job planner chooses codec/resolution/bitrate ladder based on source.

- Independent renditions can run in parallel.

- Long videos can be split into GOP-aligned chunks for distributed encoding, then packaged.

- Workers are stateless; job state lives durably.

- Outputs go to immutable object keys.

- Retries must be idempotent: same job/version writes deterministic or versioned outputs.

- Manifest is generated only after required segments exist.

## 15. Segmentation and Manifests

- Encode each rendition into small time-aligned segments.

- Manifest lists available renditions and segment locations.

- Segment boundaries align across renditions so the player can switch quality cleanly.

- Shorter segments improve adaptation/seek responsiveness but increase request overhead.

- Media segments are immutable and ideal for CDN caching.

- Manifest can be short-lived/versioned if access policy or newly completed renditions change.

## 16. Playback Request Flow

- Viewer opens video page; metadata service checks visibility/restrictions.

- Playback service returns authorized manifest URL/token and video metadata.

- Player fetches manifest from CDN/origin.

- Player estimates bandwidth and selects initial rendition conservatively.

- Segments are fetched from nearby CDN edge.

- Player continuously adapts bitrate based on throughput and buffer.

- Seek jumps to segment near requested timestamp.

- QoE events such as startup time, stalls, bitrate changes, and errors are emitted asynchronously.

## 17. CDN and Origin Architecture

Playback through CDN hierarchy

- CDN edges serve most segment bytes.

- Regional origin shields reduce simultaneous origin misses.

- Request coalescing prevents a viral segment from causing thousands of identical origin fetches.

- Immutable segment URLs permit long TTLs.

- Pre-warming may be used for scheduled high-interest content, but UGC virality is often unpredictable.

- Multi-CDN can improve reach and resilience at extreme scale.

## 18. Viral Video Problem

A previously cold video can become globally viral in minutes. The design must avoid hot metadata keys, origin stampedes, counter contention, and recommendation/feed overload.

- CDN caches absorb media bytes; request coalescing protects origin on first misses.

- Replicate/cache video metadata aggressively.

- Shard view events by random/time bucket rather than incrementing one row synchronously.

- Serve approximate counters from aggregated shards.

- Use queue-based fan-out for notifications; never synchronously notify millions of subscribers.

- Autoscale comment reads/writes and cache top comments separately.

- Trending/recommendation pipelines consume event streams asynchronously.

Key insight
Virality is not just a bandwidth problem. It simultaneously stresses CDN cold misses, metadata, counters, comments, notifications, search freshness, and ranking pipelines.

## 19. View Counting

- Playback emits view/watch events to an ingestion stream.

- Validation filters obvious retries/bots/duplicate noise according to product semantics.

- Partition events by video/time/hash.

- Stream processors maintain near-real-time partial counts.

- Persist aggregates in a scalable counter store and periodically compact.

- Displayed count may lag slightly and be approximate.

- Raw events feed creator analytics and recommendation features separately.

Do not do this
Do not execute UPDATE videos SET views=views+1 for every playback on a single primary row. A viral video turns that row into a global serialization point.

## 20. Likes and Dislikes

- User-video reaction is keyed by (user_id, video_id) for idempotency.

- Changing reaction updates state, not blindly adding another count.

- Write durable user reaction first; emit delta event for aggregate counter.

- Counter is eventually consistent and repairable from source-of-truth reactions/events.

- Read path can return viewer's exact reaction plus approximate aggregate count.

- Partition aggregate updates for hot videos.

## 22. Subscription Model

- Store subscriber→channels for home/subscription feed reads.

- Also store channel→subscriber partitions for notifications/fan-out where needed.

- Celebrity channels create huge fan-out sets; partition heavily.

- Subscription write is idempotent.

- Do not materialize every upload into every subscriber inbox synchronously at upload time for massive channels unless using a hybrid strategy.

- Home feed can use fan-out-on-read/hybrid recommendation generation.

## 23. Notifications for New Uploads

- Video becomes eligible for notification after publish checks.

- Notification event enters durable queue.

- Audience service reads channel subscribers in partitions.

- Apply notification preferences, rate limits, relevance, and dedupe.

- Workers enqueue/send notifications asynchronously.

- Checkpoint progress so retries do not resend uncontrollably.

- For channels with enormous audiences, spread delivery over partitions/time and protect downstream push providers.

## 24. Search Indexing

- Index title, description, tags, channel, language, transcript/captions, and selected engagement/quality features.

- Publishing emits an index event; deletion/restriction emits a tombstone/update.

- Search index is eventually consistent but moderation removals need fast suppression.

- Shard index by document/video and replicate.

- Ranking can combine text relevance, freshness, engagement, channel authority, personalization, and safety.

- Autocomplete/trending queries are separate precomputed structures.

## 25. Recommendation Architecture

Two-stage recommendation system

- Candidate generation retrieves hundreds/thousands from subscriptions, similar-content, collaborative signals, trending, and exploration.

- Ranking scores a much smaller set with user/context/video features.

- Post-ranking applies safety, dedupe, diversity, freshness, and creator/content constraints.

- Feature pipelines consume watch, search, like, skip, and subscription events.

- Fallback recommendations should work when ML services fail.

## 26. Trending

- Consume view/engagement streams in time windows.

- Use velocity and acceleration, not only lifetime views.

- Normalize by geography/category and suppress abuse.

- Compare recent activity to baseline so old mega-videos do not dominate forever.

- Maintain top-K per region/category with streaming heaps/sketches.

- Trending is eventually consistent and can tolerate seconds/minutes of lag.

## 29. Deletion Workflow

- Authoritative metadata marks video DELETED/UNAVAILABLE.

- Playback authorization immediately refuses new manifest access.

- Search/recommendation indexes receive high-priority tombstones.

- CDN URLs/tokens are invalidated or become inaccessible; immutable cached bytes must not be newly authorized.

- Comments/likes become hidden according to policy.

- Async garbage collection removes renditions, thumbnails, originals after retention rules.

- Analytics may retain allowed aggregates separately.

- Deletion workflow is idempotent and auditable.

## 30. Moderation Pipeline

- Run automated checks on upload metadata, frames/audio/transcript, spam, malware, and policy classifiers.

- Some checks block publication; others can run after private processing.

- Store moderation decision/version separately from media.

- Human-review queue handles uncertain/high-impact cases.

- Restrictions must propagate to playback, search, recommendations, comments, and notifications.

- Reprocessing is possible when classifiers/policies change because originals/derived metadata are retained appropriately.

## 31. Copyright / Content Fingerprinting

- Generate robust audio/video fingerprints during processing.

- Compare against reference fingerprint index.

- A match emits a claim/review workflow rather than modifying media pipeline directly.

- Fingerprint lookup must tolerate transformations such as re-encoding/cropping within system capability.

- Keep claim state separate from video asset state.

- Playback/monetization/region restrictions consume resolved claim policy.

- Fingerprint computation is asynchronous and horizontally scalable.

## 32. Captions and Transcripts

- Accept creator-provided caption tracks.

- Speech-to-text jobs can generate automatic captions asynchronously.

- Store timed text separately from video segments.

- Transcript feeds search indexing and accessibility.

- Caption corrections create new track versions without retranscoding video.

- Player fetches selected language track independently.

## 33. Thumbnail Generation

- Generate several sizes/aspect ratios.

- Allow creator-selected/uploaded thumbnail subject to checks.

- Store immutable thumbnail assets behind CDN.

- Recommendation/search cards should never fetch frames from video at request time.

## 42. End-to-End Upload Example

- Creator requests upload session and receives video_id plus signed multipart URLs.

- Client uploads 200 chunks directly to object storage, retrying only failed chunks.

- Finalize verifies all part checksums and creates immutable original asset.

- Upload-complete event starts validation, moderation, thumbnail, caption, and transcode jobs.

- Planner creates 360p/720p/1080p jobs based on source.

- Workers encode and package aligned segments into immutable rendition keys.

- Manifest builder verifies required segments and publishes playback asset version.

- Metadata moves video to READY_PRIVATE.

- Creator changes visibility to PUBLIC after required checks.

- Search/recommendation index events fire; subscriber notification workflow begins.

- CDN fills segments on viewer demand; viral growth does not touch transcoders.

## 43. End-to-End Playback Example

- Viewer opens video page.

- Metadata service returns title/channel/social state and verifies availability.

- Playback authorization returns signed manifest access.

- Player fetches manifest and initial low/medium bitrate segments from CDN.

- ABR increases quality as bandwidth/buffer confidence grows.

- View event is emitted after product-defined qualification threshold.

- Watch events stream to counters, recommendations, creator analytics, and trending.

- Likes/comments write to their own services; playback is isolated from their failures.

- If one CDN edge is unhealthy, traffic moves to another edge/provider.

- Displayed view count may update seconds later without affecting playback.

## 44. Final Production Architecture

- Direct resumable multipart uploads to object storage; application servers only control sessions/auth.

- Durable event-driven processing validates originals and fans out independent transcode, thumbnail, caption, fingerprint, and moderation jobs.

- Immutable segmented renditions and manifests are stored in object storage and served primarily from CDN with origin shielding/request coalescing.

- Authoritative video metadata controls ownership, visibility, publish state, and deletion.

- Views/likes/comments/subscriptions use separate partitioned services and asynchronous aggregate counters.

- Search consumes publish/update/tombstone events into a distributed index.

- Recommendations use candidate generation plus ranking over asynchronously produced features.

- Viral scale is handled with CDN, caches, sharded counters, partitioned comments/subscribers, and asynchronous fan-out.

- Global restrictions/deletions use high-priority propagation paths.

- Playback remains available when analytics, comments, recommendations, or counters are degraded.

One-sentence architecture
Upload originals directly and durably, asynchronously turn them into immutable adaptive-streaming assets, deliver those bytes through CDN, keep mutable metadata/social state in independently scalable services, and drive counters/search/recommendations from durable event streams so viral traffic never creates a single synchronous bottleneck.

## 48. Interviewer Follow-Ups — Detailed Answers

Follow-up: Why should the client upload directly to object storage instead of through the API service?

Detailed answer: Video files can be gigabytes. Proxying them through API servers doubles network transfer, consumes connections and memory, complicates retries, and makes autoscaling the control plane dependent on media bandwidth. The upload service should authenticate the creator, create an upload session, enforce quotas, and issue scoped signed multipart URLs. The client then sends bytes directly to durable storage. The API remains a lightweight control plane, while object storage is the data plane.

Follow-up: How do you make a 10 GB upload reliable on a bad mobile network?

Detailed answer: Use resumable multipart upload. Split the object into independently retryable parts, number them deterministically, and store part completion/checksum state in the upload session or object-store multipart protocol. The client can ask which parts already exist after reconnecting and resume only the missing ones. Finalization is idempotent and verifies all parts plus the expected object checksum before emitting the upload-complete event.

Follow-up: What happens if the client calls complete twice?

Detailed answer: Completion must be idempotent. The upload_id is the idempotency key. The service reads the durable state: if already finalized with the same part set/checksum, return the existing video result rather than creating another asset or duplicate jobs. Downstream processing events also carry a video/version identifier so consumers can deduplicate. Exactly-once delivery is not required if effects are idempotent.

Follow-up: How do you parallelize transcoding a long video?

Detailed answer: Parallelize by rendition and, for very long media, by time chunks aligned to codec GOP/keyframe boundaries. A planner probes the source and creates jobs such as 1080p chunks 0..N, 720p chunks 0..N, and so on. Workers encode independently to versioned temporary outputs. A packaging step verifies continuity, joins/references chunks, creates aligned segments, and publishes only when the rendition is complete. This reduces wall-clock processing time while keeping retries localized.

Follow-up: What if the 1080p transcode fails but 720p is ready?

Detailed answer: That is a product/policy decision encoded in the state machine. A useful design allows publication once a minimum required ladder is ready, while higher renditions continue processing. The manifest version initially exposes only complete renditions and is updated/versioned later when 1080p becomes available. Never expose references to incomplete segments. For premium/quality-sensitive workflows, publication can wait for all mandatory renditions.

Follow-up: How does adaptive bitrate streaming work?

Detailed answer: The manifest advertises multiple time-aligned renditions. The player measures recent throughput, buffer occupancy, device/network constraints, and playback stability. It requests the next segment from an appropriate bitrate. Because segment boundaries align, it can switch quality at a boundary without restarting playback. A conservative startup bitrate reduces time to first frame; quality rises as confidence grows. If throughput falls, the player lowers bitrate before the buffer empties.

Follow-up: How do you handle a video going viral before the CDN has it cached?

Detailed answer: Use regional origin shields and request coalescing. The first edge miss goes to a shield; concurrent requests for the same segment collapse behind one origin fetch rather than all reaching object storage. Once fetched, the immutable segment receives a long cache lifetime. Metadata is independently cached/replicated. View counts are sharded/event-based, and comments/subscriber fan-out are partitioned so the viral event does not simply move the hotspot from media to databases.

Follow-up: How would you count views accurately at massive scale?

Detailed answer: First define product semantics: a segment request is not necessarily a qualified view. The player emits watch events; ingestion validates session/video/timing and filters obvious duplicate/bot noise. Events are durably logged and partitioned. Stream processors compute near-real-time per-video partial counts, often across buckets, while batch jobs reconcile. The displayed number can be eventually consistent. Creator analytics can be more carefully reconciled from the event source.

Follow-up: Why are likes different from view counts?

Detailed answer: A like is user-specific mutable state and should be idempotent: a user either likes a video or does not. Store the exact reaction keyed by user_id+video_id. Then emit +1/-1 deltas to an eventually consistent aggregate. A view is an event stream with qualification/deduplication semantics and may have many events from one viewer. Keeping the exact per-user state separate from the aggregate prevents counter races.

Follow-up: How would comments scale for a video with 50 million comments?

Detailed answer: Do not store one unbounded partition if the database has partition-size/hotspot limits. Partition by video plus time/hash bucket, maintain indexes for newest/top/thread views, and use cursor pagination. Cache the first/top comment pages because most readers never traverse deeply. Comment count is an async aggregate. Replies carry parent IDs. Moderation/deletion uses tombstones. Playback remains independent if comments are degraded.

Follow-up: How do you notify 100 million subscribers of a creator?

Detailed answer: Never synchronously fan out during the publish transaction. Publish a durable notification event. Audience workers scan subscriber partitions, apply notification preferences/relevance/rate limits, and enqueue delivery in batches. Checkpoint progress and use idempotency keys. Spread delivery to protect push/email providers. In many products, only a subset receives immediate push while the upload appears in a subscription/home feed for everyone else.

Follow-up: Push or pull for the subscription feed?

Detailed answer: Use a hybrid. Fan-out-on-write works well for ordinary channels because subscriber sets are moderate and reads become cheap. For celebrity channels, writing one feed item into tens of millions of inboxes is expensive and creates spikes, so store the upload once and merge it at read time or through an asynchronous shared feed layer. Recommendations already require pull/ranking, making a hybrid natural.

Follow-up: How do you delete a video that is cached globally?

Detailed answer: First change authoritative metadata so new playback authorization fails immediately. Emit high-priority tombstones to search, recommendations, feeds, and moderation caches. If media URLs require short-lived signed authorization, cached bytes cannot be newly accessed without permission. Where necessary, issue CDN purge/invalidation. Async garbage collection later deletes renditions/originals according to retention rules. Logical unavailability must happen before physical deletion finishes.

Follow-up: How do you prevent a private video from leaking through CDN?

Detailed answer: The CDN should not be the authority for visibility. Playback begins with metadata/authorization that verifies the viewer and returns short-lived signed manifest/segment access or a protected CDN token. Cache keys and token validation must prevent unauthorized reuse. A visibility change revokes future authorization quickly. For highly sensitive private media, use stricter token lifetimes and purge strategy.

Follow-up: How do search and recommendations learn about a newly published video?

Detailed answer: The publish transaction writes authoritative video state and emits an outbox/event containing video_id and version. Search indexing consumes it to fetch/index title, description, transcript, tags, and visibility. Recommendation pipelines ingest metadata and early engagement features. These are derived systems and may lag slightly, but a restriction/deletion uses a high-priority suppression path so safety does not wait for normal eventual indexing.

Follow-up: How do you design recommendations without going too deep into ML?

Detailed answer: Describe the serving architecture. Candidate generators independently retrieve videos from subscriptions, similar content, collaborative behavior, trending, and exploration. Union/dedupe perhaps thousands of candidates. A ranking service scores a smaller set using user, video, context, and freshness features from an online feature store. Post-ranking applies safety and diversity. Events update offline/streaming features. If ML is unavailable, fall back to subscriptions/trending.

Follow-up: How do you handle moderation before and after publication?

Detailed answer: Some checks are blocking—for example malformed media, malware, or product-defined high-risk signals—so the video remains private/processing until they complete. Other classifiers can run asynchronously and update moderation state. Store decisions separately with model/policy versions. A restriction event propagates to playback authorization, search, recommendations, comments, and notifications. Human review handles uncertain cases. Idempotent reprocessing supports model upgrades.

Follow-up: What is the role of the event bus in this design?

Detailed answer: It decouples the authoritative upload/metadata path from many downstream consumers: transcoding, thumbnails, captions, moderation, fingerprinting, search, counters, analytics, recommendations, notifications, and creator analytics. Producers commit durable state and publish via an outbox/transactional pattern. Consumers process independently and retry. This prevents one slow subsystem from blocking video publication or playback.

Follow-up: How would multi-region upload and playback work?

Detailed answer: Creators upload to a nearby region/object endpoint for latency. The original is durably replicated according to policy. Transcoding can run near the object or in compute-efficient regions, producing immutable assets. Playback metadata/authorization is active-active or regionally replicated, while CDN serves media globally from edge caches. Cross-region synchronous calls are kept out of the segment path. Deletion/restriction events receive priority global replication.

Follow-up: What should still work if recommendations, comments, and analytics are all down?

Detailed answer: Core playback. The viewer should still be able to open an authorized video and stream it from CDN using metadata/playback services. Home feed can degrade to subscriptions/popular cached lists, comments can show unavailable, and counters can remain stale. Analytics events can buffer in the log. Designing these dependencies as optional around the playback core is a major availability principle.

## 49. Additional Detailed Interview Q&A

1. Why keep the original upload after transcoding?

Detailed answer: It allows future codec/bitrate improvements, new device formats, better thumbnails/captions, and reprocessing without asking the creator to re-upload. Originals live in cheaper durable storage and can follow lifecycle policies.

2. How do you avoid duplicate processing events?

Detailed answer: Every job has video_id, asset_version, job_type, and deterministic job ID. Workers record completion idempotently. Re-delivery sees the existing successful output and acknowledges instead of encoding again.

3. Why are media segments immutable?

Detailed answer: Immutability enables long CDN TTLs, simple cache correctness, safe replication, deterministic rollback, and no reader locking. New processing creates a new asset version rather than mutating bytes in place.

4. How do you support seeking?

Detailed answer: Segments are time-indexed and manifests map playback time to segment sequence. The player jumps to the nearest suitable keyframe/segment and resumes downloading from there.

5. What is origin shielding?

Detailed answer: A regional cache layer between many CDN edges and object origin. Multiple edge misses converge on the shield, which fetches one copy and protects the origin from fan-in.

6. What is request coalescing?

Detailed answer: If many requests miss the same cache key simultaneously, one request performs the upstream fetch while others wait for that result instead of all fetching independently.

7. How do you choose segment duration?

Detailed answer: Short segments improve startup, seek, and ABR reaction but increase HTTP/manifest overhead and reduce encoding efficiency. Longer segments do the opposite. Choose a few-second class duration based on latency/product needs.

8. How would you support 4K without exploding cost?

Detailed answer: Generate it only for sources/devices/content where justified, use efficient codecs, store immutable assets in tiered object storage, and rely on CDN. Encoding can be scheduled at lower priority because 4K is not required for initial publish.

9. How do you update title without retranscoding?

Detailed answer: Video metadata is separate from media assets. Update the authoritative metadata record, increment metadata version, and emit search/recommendation index update events. Renditions remain unchanged.

10. How do you make publish atomic across metadata and event emission?

Detailed answer: Use a transactional outbox: commit the authoritative video state and an outbox row in one transaction. A relay publishes the event and marks it sent. Consumers are idempotent.

11. What if search still shows a deleted video?
