## 59. Deep Dive: Guest-to-Account Merge Architecture

![59. Deep Dive: Guest-to-Account Merge Architecture — source diagram](/diagrams/t-53v5dmwjqy1n-kix-ldwv6g2wb99b.png)

- Merge is a transactional transformation of two user-intent sets, not a database UNION.

- Use normalized line identity so the same offer/options can be combined while distinct seller/size/subscription choices remain separate.

- The account cart is the durable destination. Guest cart becomes a tombstone pointing to the resulting account-cart version.

- Compare-and-swap the account version so a device mutation that races with login is not lost.

- Coupon state, price and availability are recomputed after structural merge.

- If the account cart changed during merge, retry the merge against the newest version using the same merge transaction ID.

## 60. Deep Dive: Shared / Family Carts

- A shared cart is not just a normal cart with more readers; it introduces collaborative write semantics and ACLs.

- Model owner plus member roles such as viewer/editor/checkout-authorized.

- Each mutation records actor ID and cart version for audit.

- Use the same per-cart serialized/versioned write path so two family members cannot overwrite one another.

- Optional activity feed can show who added/removed an item.

- Checkout permission should be explicit because shared viewing does not imply authority to spend.

- Shared carts can be separate objects instead of overloading a user's personal cart, which keeps merge and ownership semantics cleaner.

## 61. Deep Dive: Flash-Sale / Limited Inventory Mode

- Normal carts do not reserve inventory, but flash-sale products may require a short hold to prevent a terrible checkout experience.

- Create a separate reservation service with reservation_id, SKU, quantity, owner, expiry and state.

- Reservation is time-bounded, for example 2-10 minutes, and does not turn the cart database into the inventory authority.

- Cart line can reference the reservation token and countdown.

- Checkout converts reservation to committed inventory consumption idempotently.

- If the timer expires, reservation is released and the cart line remains but returns to ordinary unavailable/non-reserved state.

- Do not silently extend reservations on every cart read; renewal policy must be deliberate to prevent stock hoarding.

## 62. Deep Dive: Coupon and Promotion Consistency

- Coupon attachment to the cart and promotion calculation are separate concepts. Attaching code SAVE20 does not guarantee the code will still be valid at payment time.

- Persist the coupon code and last evaluation result/version for UX.

- Promotion engine evaluates eligibility using user, lines, quantities, seller, current time, and rule version.

- If two coupons are mutually exclusive, the cart can choose best discount or require explicit user selection according to product policy.

- Checkout re-evaluates every promotion from the immutable checkout snapshot.

- Promotion budget exhaustion is analogous to inventory: a displayed promotion may become unavailable before checkout unless a short-lived benefit reservation exists.

- Explain removed/changed discounts explicitly; silent total changes reduce trust.

## 63. Deep Dive: Price Quote Service

- For higher assurance, introduce a short-lived quote object rather than treating cart totals as authoritative.

- Quote fields: quote_id, cart/snapshot version, line prices, taxes, shipping, discounts, currency, expiration, pricing-rule version.

- Quote creation batches authoritative reads from pricing/promotion/tax/fulfillment.

- Checkout can accept only an unexpired quote whose snapshot matches the order request.

- Quote expiration is expected; regenerate instead of extending indefinitely.

- A quote simplifies payment amount correctness because the payment request references one immutable amount breakdown.

## 64. Deep Dive: Persistence Schema Options

| Model | Advantages | Trade-offs |
| --- | --- | --- |
| One document per cart | Single-key read/write, simple versioning | Document size limit, whole-document rewrites |
| Cart header + line rows | Fine-grained updates, large carts | Multi-row read/transaction complexity |
| Event-sourced cart | Perfect history, flexible projections | Operational complexity, replay cost |
| CRDT/mergeable lines | Active-active regions | Complex product semantics for set/remove/coupons |

For an interview-scale consumer cart, a bounded document or header-plus-lines colocated in one partition are both defensible. Choose based on database limits and expected cart size.

## 65. Deep Dive: Event Sourcing as an Alternative

- Instead of storing only current cart state, append events such as ItemAdded, QuantitySet, ItemRemoved and CouponAttached.

- Current cart is a projection of events.

- Benefits: auditability, replay and analytics.

- Costs: event growth, projection recovery, schema evolution and duplicate-event handling.

- Snapshot every N events to bound replay.

- For a typical shopping cart interview, event sourcing is optional; a versioned KV document plus outbox is simpler and usually sufficient.

## 66. Deep Dive: Post-Order Cleanup Race

- Order succeeds from snapshot S containing line A quantity 2 and line B quantity 1.

- While payment was running, another device adds line C and increments A by one.

- A naive 'clear cart' would delete C and the new A increment.

- Cleanup uses snapshot/order ID and compares purchased line identities/quantities.

- For additive quantity semantics, decrement only the quantity consumed by S when the current line still represents the same offer/options.

- Preserve any newer line or excess quantity.

- Cleanup itself is idempotent so payment/order retry cannot repeatedly decrement the cart.

## 67. Deep Dive: Cross-Region Failover

- Cart home region writes version 90 and asynchronously replicates to DR region at version 89.

- Home region fails before v90 arrives. Product must state whether one recent cart edit can be lost (RPO) or whether writes require synchronous cross-region replication.

- Promote secondary under fencing/epoch so the old region cannot later accept independent writes.

- Clients reconnect and read the promoted cart version.

- When the old region returns, replicate from the new authority; do not merge two opaque full-cart histories blindly.

- For stronger RPO, replicate the cart log synchronously or use a consensus-based global store, accepting WAN latency.

## 68. Deep Dive: Abuse and Resource Limits

- Cap number of active lines, saved items, coupon codes and mutation rate.

- Reject extremely large quantities beyond commerce policy.

- Rate-limit automated cart churn that can pressure pricing/inventory dependencies.

- Guest-cart creation needs bot controls to prevent storage exhaustion.

- Expire abandoned guest carts aggressively relative to authenticated carts.

- Per-tenant or marketplace-seller metadata should not allow unbounded custom payloads inside a cart line.

## 69. Deep Dive: Availability During Dependency Failure

| Dependency | Cart behavior | Checkout behavior |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Catalog | Show cached name/image if safe | Must validate purchasable offer |
| Pricing | Show stale/unknown price | Block until authoritative price |
| Inventory | Show stale/unknown availability | Block/reserve authoritatively |
| Promotions | Show previous/pending discount | Re-evaluate before payment |
| Tax | Estimate unavailable | Calculate before final total |
| Recommendations | Ignore failure | No effect |

## 70. More Detailed Interview Follow-Ups

Follow-up: Would you store cart lines separately or as one document?

Detailed answer: For normal consumer carts, one bounded document gives a simple single-key transaction and read. If database document limits or B2B cart sizes are large, colocated line rows are better.

Follow-up: What if the same guest cart is logged into two different accounts?

Detailed answer: Guest merge must claim/tombstone the guest cart atomically. The first successful account merge owns it; the later attempt sees it already merged and follows explicit product policy instead of duplicating items.

Follow-up: How do you support a cart count without reading the cart?

Detailed answer: Persist a small count summary alongside the cart and update it atomically with mutations; cache the summary for header reads.

Follow-up: Can the cart return stale data?

Detailed answer: Derived data can be stale, but the structural cart should provide read-your-writes/per-cart version semantics. Mark price/inventory freshness explicitly.

Follow-up: How would you handle 10,000-line enterprise carts?

Detailed answer: Move from one document to partition-local line records, paginated reads, batch pricing, and perhaps a separate B2B cart service with different limits.

Follow-up: How do you prevent promotion service from becoming a latency bottleneck?

Detailed answer: Compile rules, batch-evaluate lines, cache rule versions, use deadlines, and let cart degrade without final discount while checkout remains authoritative.

Follow-up: Why not store calculated grand total in the cart?

Detailed answer: It becomes stale when quantity, price, tax, shipping, coupon or address changes. Store component observations/version; calculate derived total from current inputs.

Follow-up: What happens if a guest merge succeeds but the response is lost?

Detailed answer: Retry uses the merge transaction ID and guest tombstone to return the already-produced account cart version instead of merging quantities again.

Follow-up: How do you reconcile active cart after an order?

Detailed answer: Consume the successful checkout snapshot/order ID and perform an idempotent line-level decrement/removal, preserving newer concurrent changes.

Follow-up: When would you choose CRDTs?

Detailed answer: Only when true multi-region active-active cart writes are required and product semantics for add/remove/set/merge are explicitly defined. A home-region writer is simpler for most commerce systems.

## 71. Interview Whiteboard Plan

- Draw client -> cart service -> partitioned KV/document store.

- Add catalog, pricing, promotions and inventory as side enrichment services rather than cart ownership.

- Write 'cart_version + operation_id' beside the mutation path.

- Draw guest cart and user cart flowing into an explicit merge box.

- Draw checkout snapshot as the hard boundary into order/payment/inventory reservation.

- Show outbox/change stream to analytics/reminders.

- Finish with home-region ownership and asynchronous DR replica.

## 72. Extended Correctness Invariants

| Invariant | Mechanism |
| --- | --- |
| Retry does not duplicate an additive mutation | operation_id dedupe |
| A stale device cannot overwrite newer cart state | expected version / intent commands |
| Guest merge happens once | merge ID + guest tombstone |
| Cart price is never mistaken for permanent guarantee | freshness metadata + checkout validation |
| Cart item does not imply reserved stock | separate inventory authority |
| Checkout is stable despite later cart edits | immutable snapshot |
| Successful order cleanup preserves newer cart changes | snapshot-aware line cleanup |
| Dependency outage does not erase structural cart | cart persistence independent from enrichment |

notes.title: Design Amazon / Large-Scale E-commerce Platform
notes.description: Goal Design a global Amazon-style marketplace supporting product discovery, search, product detail pages, carts, inventory, checkout, payments, orders, shipment
notes.content:
Design Amazon / Large-Scale E-commerce Platform

Advanced System Design Interview Guide

Problem 24 | Catalog, Search, Cart, Inventory, Checkout, Orders, Payments & Flash Sales

> Goal
> Design a global Amazon-style marketplace supporting product discovery, search, product detail pages, carts, inventory, checkout, payments, orders, shipment tracking, reviews, recommendations, sellers, promotions, and extreme events such as flash sales. The central challenge is combining read-heavy discovery with correctness-sensitive inventory, money, and order workflows.

> Core interview principle
> Do not force one consistency model onto the whole system. Catalog/search/recommendations can be eventually consistent. Inventory reservation, payment state, order transitions, and idempotent checkout need much stronger correctness. The architecture should explicitly separate these worlds.

## 1. Functional Requirements

| Area | Requirements |
| --- | --- |
| Discovery | Browse categories, search, filters, ranking |
| Product | Product detail, variants, images, seller offers |
| Cart | Add/remove/update quantity, persistent cart |
| Inventory | Available stock, reservations, replenishment |
| Checkout | Address, shipping, tax, promotions, final quote |
| Payment | Authorize/capture/refund with external providers |
| Order | Create, track, cancel, return |
| Marketplace | Multiple sellers/offers per product |
| Social | Ratings and reviews |
| Personalization | Recommendations and recently viewed |
| Operations | Flash sales, fraud controls, observability |

## 2. Non-Functional Requirements

- Product browsing/search should be highly available and low latency.

- Checkout must be idempotent: retries cannot create duplicate orders or charges.

- Do not oversell scarce inventory beyond defined business tolerance.

- Money state must be auditable and reconcilable.

- Search/index freshness can lag product source-of-truth by seconds/minutes.

- A cart can tolerate eventual synchronization; an order cannot silently disappear.

- Services should degrade independently: recommendations/reviews can fail without blocking checkout.

- Global reads, regional writes, disaster recovery, and large traffic spikes are required.

## 3. Scope and Clarifying Questions

- Physical goods first; digital goods are an extension.

- Marketplace supports multiple sellers and fulfillment options.

- Inventory is tracked per SKU and fulfillment location.

- Payment provider is external; we design orchestration and state.

- Search and recommendations are included architecturally.

- Warehouse optimization is out of scope, but fulfillment handoff is covered.

- Returns/refunds are included as post-order workflows.

## 4. Capacity Estimation

| Dimension | Illustrative scale | Implication |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Daily active users | 100M+ | Global read scale |
| Catalog | 100M+ products, far more SKUs/offers | Partitioned source + indexes |
| Search requests | Hundreds of thousands QPS peak | Distributed search + cache |
| PDP reads | Very high | CDN/cache/read models |
| Cart writes | Tens of thousands QPS | Partition by user/cart |
| Orders/day | Millions | Durable workflow |
| Inventory updates | High and bursty | Atomic SKU/location operations |
| Flash-sale SKU | Extreme single-key contention | Special admission/reservation path |

## 5. Core APIs

| API | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| GET /search?q=... | Search products |
| GET /products/{id} | Product detail |
| GET /products/{id}/offers | Seller offers |
| GET /carts/{id} | Read cart |
| PUT /carts/{id}/items/{sku} | Idempotent add/update item |
| POST /checkout/quotes | Price/shipping/tax quote |
| POST /orders | Place order with idempotency key |
| GET /orders/{id} | Order status |
| POST /orders/{id}/cancel | Cancel |
| POST /returns | Start return |
| POST /reviews | Create review |

## 6. Core Data Model

| Entity | Important fields |
| --- | --- |
| Product | product_id, title, brand, category, attributes, media |
| SKU | sku_id, product_id, variant attributes |
| Offer | offer_id, sku_id, seller_id, price, fulfillment, condition |
| Inventory | sku_id, location_id, on_hand, reserved, version |
| Cart | cart_id/user_id, item snapshots, version, updated_at |
| Reservation | reservation_id, sku, qty, location, expires_at, state |
| Order | order_id, user_id, totals, state, idempotency_key |
| OrderItem | order_id, sku, offer, qty, price snapshot, fulfillment |
| Payment | payment_id, order_id, provider_ref, amount, state |
| Shipment | shipment_id, order_items, carrier, tracking, state |
| Review | review_id, product_id, user_id, rating, text, state |

## 7. High-Level Architecture

![7. High-Level Architecture — source diagram](/diagrams/t-m2kbxlh3032-kix-awqo7cor7dxi.png)

Amazon-style high-level architecture

## 8. Bounded Contexts / Service Boundaries

| Service | Owns | Should not own |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Catalog | Product/SKU descriptive truth | Stock or payment |
| Offer/Pricing | Seller offer, current price rules | Order history |
| Search | Derived searchable documents | Authoritative product state |
| Cart | User intent before checkout | Inventory guarantee |
| Inventory | Stock and reservations | Payment |
| Checkout | Orchestration/quote | Long-term order truth |
| Order | Order lifecycle | Card credentials |
| Payment | Payment workflow/provider refs | Catalog |
| Fulfillment | Shipment lifecycle | Checkout pricing |
| Review | Ratings/reviews | Order transaction |

## 9. Catalog Modeling: Product, SKU, Offer

> Critical distinction
> Product is the conceptual item, SKU is a purchasable variant, and Offer is a seller's commercial proposal for that SKU. A single phone model can have color/storage SKUs, and each SKU can have several seller offers with different price, condition, shipping promise, and fulfillment method.

- Product attributes are category-specific and evolve over time.

- SKU identity should be stable even if price changes.

- Offer is mutable and can become inactive independently.

- PDP read model denormalizes product, selected variants, buy-box-like offer summary, rating summary, and availability hints.

- Do not make the search engine the catalog source of truth.

## 10. Catalog Write and Read Paths

- Seller/internal system submits catalog mutation.

- Catalog service validates schema/category rules and writes authoritative product/SKU version.

- Outbox emits product-changed event.

- Consumers update PDP read model, search document, recommendation features, cache invalidations, and analytics.

- PDP service serves a denormalized cached representation and calls dynamic offer/inventory services only where freshness matters.

> Why CQRS-like read models help
> A product page joins many domains. Building that page from normalized source tables on every request creates latency and coupling. Maintain denormalized read models for stable descriptive data, then overlay dynamic price/availability using bounded calls or cached summaries.

## 11. Search Architecture

![11. Search Architecture — source diagram](/diagrams/t-m2kbxlh3032-kix-dkmb7bae7dab.png)

Product search and indexing

- Inverted index for title, brand, category, attributes, seller text, synonyms.

- Faceted index supports category, price range, brand, rating, delivery promise, availability.

- Query understanding handles spelling, synonyms, units, category intent.

- Candidate retrieval then ranking; exact availability may be checked late for top results.

- Search documents are versioned derived state and can be rebuilt from catalog/events.

## 12. Search Ranking

- Text relevance and field boosts.

- Category/query intent match.

- Price competitiveness and availability.

- Delivery promise and fulfillment quality.

- Rating/review quality with anti-abuse signals.

- Sales/engagement/popularity and freshness.

- Personalization and geography.

- Business/sponsored constraints applied transparently in product logic.

Ranking features should not require dozens of synchronous calls. Precompute most features into the search document or online feature store; fetch only a small amount of dynamic state for top candidates.

## 13. Product Detail Page Read Path

- Resolve product ID and fetch cached PDP read model.

- Fetch/select current offers for requested SKU.

- Fetch availability/delivery summary for viewer region.

- Fetch rating summary and optionally first review page.

- Fetch recommendations asynchronously or with strict timeout.

- Return core page even if recommendations/reviews fail.

| Data | Freshness expectation |
| --- | --- |
| Title/images/specs | Seconds/minutes acceptable |
| Price/offer | Much fresher |
| Inventory message | Fresh hint, not final reservation |
| Rating summary | Eventual |
| Recommendations | Eventual/optional |
| Checkout price | Authoritative recomputation |

## 14. Cart Semantics

- Cart represents intent, not guaranteed stock or guaranteed price.

- Partition primarily by user_id/cart_id.

- Use item-level idempotent upsert rather than append-only duplicates.

- Store selected SKU/offer and display snapshot, but revalidate at checkout.

- Guest cart can be token/device keyed and merged after login.

- Cross-device updates can use optimistic versioning; last-writer/item-wise merge is acceptable depending on UX.

- Cart expiry is much longer than inventory reservation expiry.

## 15. Cart Merge and Conflict Handling

| Scenario | Possible behavior |
| --- | --- |
| Same SKU on two devices | Merge quantities up to limits |
| Item removed on one device | Use version/timestamp semantics |
| Guest logs in | Merge guest and account cart |
| Price changed | Show changed-price message at checkout |
| Offer disappeared | Suggest alternate offer |
| SKU out of stock | Keep item but mark unavailable |
| Quantity exceeds stock | Adjust/ask user during checkout |

## 16. Checkout Is a Workflow, Not One DB Transaction

![16. Checkout Is a Workflow, Not One DB Transaction — source diagram](/diagrams/t-m2kbxlh3032-kix-31s4k8stxc74.png)

Checkout / order saga

- No distributed ACID transaction across inventory, order database, and external payment provider.

- Use saga/orchestrated state machine with durable steps and compensations.

- Every external call carries idempotency/reference keys.

- Persist workflow state before/after side effects so recovery knows what happened.

- Timeout is an unknown outcome, not automatically a failure. Query provider/reservation state before retrying.

## 17. Checkout Idempotency

> Invariant
> The same logical checkout retry must return the same order result and must not create a second order or second payment. Require a client-generated or server-issued idempotency key scoped to the shopper/checkout attempt.

- Receive POST /orders with idempotency key.

- Atomically create/read idempotency record.

- If completed, return stored order response.

- If in progress, return/recover same workflow rather than start another.

- All downstream reservation/payment requests use deterministic operation IDs.

- Store final response/status for safe retries.

## 18. Pricing and Quote Versioning

- PDP price is informational; checkout recomputes authoritative price.

- Quote contains line prices, promotions, shipping, tax, currency, and expiry/version.

- Order stores immutable price snapshots for audit.

- Promotion service should return deterministic decisions for a quote context.

- If quote changes materially before order confirmation, product may require user acceptance.

- Never reconstruct historical order total from today's catalog price.

## 19. Inventory Model

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| on_hand | Physical/accounted units at location |
| reserved | Units held for active checkout/orders |
| available | Typically on_hand - reserved - safety buffers |
| version | Optimistic concurrency/fencing |
| reservation | Temporary durable hold with expiry/state |
| allocation | Location selected for fulfillment |

> Core invariant
> For a strict-stock SKU/location, committed reservations must never exceed sellable stock. The exact implementation can use conditional atomic updates, row locks, compare-and-swap, or serialized partition processing.

## 20. Inventory Reservation Algorithm

- Checkout asks inventory service to reserve SKU quantities with reservation_id.

- Inventory service routes each SKU/location to authoritative partition.

- Atomically check available >= requested quantity.

- If yes, increment reserved and persist reservation with expiry in same correctness boundary.

- Return reservation token/version.

- On order success, convert reservation into committed allocation/decrement semantics.

- On failure/expiry, release exactly once.

- Background sweeper repairs expired holds; event reconciliation detects leaks.

## 21. Preventing Overselling

| Approach | Pros | Cons |
| --- | --- | --- |
| DB row lock/transaction | Simple, strong | Hot row bottleneck |
| Optimistic CAS/version | High concurrency when conflicts low | Retries under contention |
| Atomic conditional counter | Efficient | Needs authoritative single-key operation |
| Serialized partition/actor | Natural ordering | Partition hotspot |
| Preallocated stock buckets | Scales flash sales | More complexity/rebalancing |

For normal SKUs, atomic conditional reservation per SKU/location is usually enough. For extreme flash sales, introduce admission control and stock-token/bucket techniques rather than letting millions of requests contend on one row.

## 22. Multi-Item Reservation

A cart can contain items owned by different inventory partitions. Avoid pretending they can be reserved in one global transaction.

- Attempt reservations with one checkout workflow ID.

- If all succeed, continue.

- If any fails, release successful reservations idempotently.

- Order workflow records every reservation outcome.

- For partial-order products, split fulfillment/order groups explicitly; otherwise all-or-nothing at checkout.

> Subtle failure
> If the checkout service times out after asking inventory to reserve, it must query by reservation_id before issuing another reservation. A timeout means the result is unknown.

## 23. Reservation Expiry

- Reservations need TTL so abandoned checkouts do not lock stock forever.

- Expiry is persisted, not just an in-memory timer.

- A delayed queue/timer wheel can trigger releases, plus a periodic sweeper as safety net.

- Commit vs expiry race needs atomic state transition: ACTIVE -> COMMITTED or ACTIVE -> EXPIRED.

- Payment latency must fit reservation TTL or reservation can be extended with fencing.

- Do not use cache TTL alone as inventory truth.

## 24. Flash Sale Architecture

![24. Flash Sale Architecture — source diagram](/diagrams/t-m2kbxlh3032-kix-tw3s33wgs21p.png)

Flash-sale admission and inventory control

- Cache product page aggressively; do not let refresh traffic hit origin.

- Use waiting room/admission tokens before scarce-stock path.

- Rate-limit per account/device/IP signals and detect bots.

- Queue admitted purchase attempts to smooth burst.

- Preallocate a bounded number of stock tokens across allocator partitions when appropriate.

- A token is not a completed order; checkout/payment still uses idempotent workflow.

- Return sold-out quickly when inventory budget is exhausted.

## 25. Payment State Machine

| State | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| CREATED | Payment intent exists |
| AUTHORIZING | Provider request in progress |
| AUTHORIZED | Funds reserved/approved |
| CAPTURING | Capture requested |
| CAPTURED | Money captured |
| FAILED | Known failure |
| VOIDED | Authorization released |
| REFUNDING | Refund in progress |
| REFUNDED | Refund completed |
| UNKNOWN | Outcome must be reconciled |

> Payment rule
> Never infer payment failure merely from an HTTP timeout. The provider may have charged successfully. Use a merchant operation/idempotency key and query/reconcile provider state.

## 26. Payment Integration

- Create internal payment intent linked to order and amount snapshot.

- Persist operation ID before provider call.

- Call provider with idempotency key.

- Persist returned provider reference/state.

- Receive webhooks asynchronously; dedupe by provider event ID.

- State machine accepts only legal transitions.

- Reconciliation job queries provider for stale/UNKNOWN payments.

- Capture timing depends on business flow; refunds are separate durable workflows.

## 27. Order State Machine

| State | Typical transition |
| --- | --- |
| PENDING | Workflow created |
| RESERVED | Inventory held |
| PAYMENT_AUTHORIZED | Payment approved |
| CONFIRMED | Customer order accepted |
| ALLOCATED | Fulfillment location assigned |
| SHIPPED | Carrier has shipment |
| DELIVERED | Delivered |
| CANCEL_REQUESTED | Cancellation workflow |
| CANCELLED | Cancelled/compensated |
| RETURNED | Return completed |

Keep order state authoritative and append an audit/event history. Avoid arbitrary service writes to order rows; transitions should be validated by the order domain.

## 28. Order Creation and Outbox

- Order DB transaction writes order/order-items and outbox event together.

- Outbox relay publishes OrderConfirmed, OrderCancelled, etc.

- Fulfillment, notifications, analytics, loyalty, and recommendation consumers are idempotent.

- This avoids the dual-write problem where DB commit succeeds but event publish fails.

- Event includes order_id, version, event_id, timestamp, and minimal immutable facts.

## 29. Fulfillment and Shipment

- Order may split into fulfillment groups by seller/location/shipping speed.

- Allocation chooses location based on stock, promise, cost, capacity, and constraints.

- Fulfillment service sends pick/pack/ship tasks to warehouse/seller systems.

- Carrier tracking updates are normalized into shipment state.

- Order page aggregates shipment states into customer-friendly status.

- Shipment failures do not mutate historical checkout price/payment facts.

## 30. Cancellation

- Validate whether item/order is still cancellable.

- Atomically mark cancellation requested with version.

- Stop fulfillment if possible.

- Release inventory if allocation has not consumed it.

- Void authorization or start refund depending on payment state.

- Transition order only when compensations reach defined outcome.

- Use idempotent cancellation ID so retries are safe.

## 31. Returns and Refunds

- Return eligibility is based on immutable order facts plus policy.

- Create return merchandise authorization (RMA) with item quantities/reason.

- Track reverse shipment and inspection where needed.

- Refund service references original payment and uses idempotent refund operation.

- Inventory disposition can be sellable, damaged, quarantine, or discard.

- Order, return, refund, and inventory states are related but separately auditable.

## 32. Seller Marketplace and Offers

- Seller service owns seller identity/status and listing permissions.

- Offer service owns seller-specific SKU price, condition, fulfillment mode, and availability eligibility.

- Product catalog merges equivalent listings into shared product/SKU identity where appropriate.

- PDP ranks/selects offers using price, shipping promise, seller quality, fulfillment, and business rules.

- Order item stores exact offer/seller snapshot used at purchase.

- Seller suspension must quickly suppress offers without deleting historical orders.

## 33. Reviews and Ratings

- Review write verifies product/order eligibility if 'verified purchase' is supported.

- Store exact reviews separately; rating summary is an async aggregate.

- Moderation/abuse detection is asynchronous with fast suppression capability.

- PDP caches rating summary and first/top review pages.

- Deleting/hiding a review emits aggregate correction.

- Search may index review-derived features but not treat them as authoritative.

## 34. Recommendations

- Candidate sources: co-view/co-buy, similar products, category affinity, recently viewed, replenishment, trending.

- Rank using user/context/product/price/availability features.

- Filter unavailable/restricted products late using fresh eligibility signals.

- Recommendation failure must not block product page or checkout.

- Events such as views, cart adds, purchases, returns feed feature pipelines.

- Use cached fallback lists for cold start/service failure.

## 35. Promotions and Coupons

| Concern | Design |
| --- | --- |
| Eligibility | Promotion service evaluates deterministic rules |
| Usage limit | Atomic per-user/global redemption counter where required |
| Stacking | Explicit rule graph/priority |
| Quote | Persist applied promotion IDs and amounts |
| Retry | Same checkout context must not redeem twice |
| Cancellation | Policy decides whether usage is restored |
| Flash coupon | Admission/partitioning for hot global counters |

## 36. Tax and Shipping Quotes

- Tax depends on jurisdiction, item classification, seller, address, and time.

- Shipping depends on fulfillment location, service level, dimensions, capacity, and carrier promises.

- Checkout quote should version external calculation inputs/results.

- Use timeouts/fallbacks carefully; do not invent a price silently if authoritative tax is required.

- Order stores the final accepted tax/shipping amounts for audit.

## 37. Caching Strategy

| Layer | Good cache candidates | Avoid as sole truth |
| --- | --- | --- |
| CDN | Images, static product assets | Inventory |
| Edge/API | Popular PDP read models | Final checkout price |
| Search cache | Popular queries/facets | Authoritative product mutation |
| Service cache | Catalog, seller profile, rating summary | Payment state |
| Client | Cart display, product assets | Reservation truth |

Use versioned keys and event-driven invalidation where freshness matters. For dynamic inventory, cache only hints and revalidate at reservation.

## 38. Partitioning Strategy

| Domain | Partition key | Hotspot note |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Catalog | product_id/category-aware | Popular products mostly read-cacheable |
| Cart | user_id/cart_id | Naturally distributed |
| Inventory | sku_id + location | Flash SKU can be hot |
| Order | order_id or user shard | Need user-order index |
| Payment | payment/order ID | Write volume manageable but correctness critical |
| Comments/Reviews | product_id + bucket | Popular products hot |
| Subscriptions/events | entity/time/hash | Stream partition balance |
| Search | document shard | Distributed fan-out/merge |

## 39. Consistency Matrix

| Data | Model | Reason |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Catalog description | Eventual read models | Availability over instant propagation |
| Search index | Eventual | Derived |
| Cart | Session/read-your-write desirable | User intent |
| Price quote | Versioned snapshot | Audit/revalidation |
| Inventory reservation | Strong atomic transition | Prevent oversell |
| Order transition | Strong within order aggregate | Lifecycle correctness |
| Payment operation | Idempotent durable state + reconciliation | Money |
| Rating count | Eventual | Aggregate |
| Recommendations | Eventual | Derived |

## 40. Failure Scenarios

| Failure | Correct behavior |
| --- | --- |
| Search down | Browse/category/recent fallback; checkout unaffected |
| Recommendation down | Hide module/fallback cached |
| Inventory timeout | Query reservation ID; do not blindly retry new hold |
| Payment timeout | Mark UNKNOWN and reconcile provider |
| Order event bus delayed | Outbox retains events; order remains durable |
| Notification down | Queue/retry; order unaffected |
| Review service down | PDP/checkout still work |
| One region down | Route reads; recover workflows from durable state |
| Flash-sale overload | Admission control/waiting room |
| Cache stale price | Checkout revalidates authoritative quote |

## 41. Multi-Region Design

- Catalog/search/PDP reads can be active-active with regional replicas and CDN.

- Cart can be home-region or conflict-tolerant replicated depending on product needs.

- Inventory for a SKU/location needs a clear authoritative writer/partition to avoid double-selling.

- Order workflow should have a home region with failover fencing to avoid two active orchestrators.

- Payment provider operations use globally unique idempotency keys.

- Events replicate to analytics/search/recommendation systems asynchronously.

- Disaster recovery must preserve workflow state, reservations, order history, and payment references.

> Multi-region correctness
> Active-active reads are easy compared with active-active inventory decrements and payment orchestration. Prefer explicit ownership/fencing for correctness-sensitive aggregates rather than casual multi-master writes.

## 42. Exactly-Once Is Usually an Effect, Not Delivery

- Message brokers may redeliver.

- Consumers store event IDs or use natural idempotency keys.

- Order/payment/inventory transitions reject duplicates and stale versions.

- Outbox avoids lost events from dual writes.

- Inbox/dedupe tables can protect high-value consumers.

- At-least-once delivery + idempotent effects is often the practical design.

## 43. Observability and Business Invariants

| Metric / invariant | Why |
| --- | --- |
| Search/PDP p95/p99 | Discovery UX |
| Checkout success rate | Revenue path |
| Inventory reservation conflict rate | Contention |
| Reserved > sellable invariant | Oversell alarm |
| Payment UNKNOWN age | Money reconciliation |
| Duplicate idempotency-key conflicts | Client/workflow bugs |
| Order stuck by state/age | Saga health |
| Outbox lag | Event propagation |
| Flash-sale queue depth | Admission health |
| Price mismatch rate | Quote/catalog drift |
| Cancellation/refund aging | Post-order health |

## 44. Security and Fraud Boundaries

- Never store raw card credentials unless operating within appropriate payment-security scope; tokenize through provider.

- Authenticate seller/catalog mutations strongly.

- Protect coupon/redemption endpoints from automation and replay.

- Use server-side price calculation; never trust client totals.

- Rate-limit checkout and flash-sale attempts.

- Audit sensitive order/payment state transitions.

- Fraud/risk service can influence payment/fulfillment but should have explicit timeout/fallback policy.

## 45. End-to-End Normal Purchase Example

- User searches 'wireless headphones'; search returns ranked product IDs.

- PDP serves catalog read model, offer summary, rating, and approximate availability.

- User adds SKU/offer to persistent cart.

- Checkout recomputes current offer, promotions, shipping, and tax.

- Client accepts quote and POSTs order with idempotency key.

- Workflow reserves inventory using deterministic reservation IDs.

- Order aggregate is created and payment authorization starts.

- Provider authorizes; webhook/reply is deduplicated.

- Order becomes CONFIRMED; outbox emits event.

- Fulfillment allocates inventory and creates shipment.

- Customer sees order status while analytics/notifications run asynchronously.

## 46. End-to-End Flash Sale Example

- Millions open cached product page; CDN protects origin.

- Buy action first passes bot/rate/admission checks.

- Only bounded requests receive purchase tokens or enter controlled queue.

- Inventory allocator consumes a finite stock-token budget or serialized reservation partition.

- Losers receive sold-out quickly instead of hammering databases.

- Winners enter normal idempotent checkout/payment workflow.

- Expired/failed winners release stock token/reservation.

- Reconciliation ensures allocated + available + reserved matches stock accounting.

## 47. Final Production Architecture

- Catalog is authoritative for products/SKUs; offers/pricing are separate commercial state.

- Search and PDP read models are derived, denormalized, cached, and rebuildable.

- Cart stores user intent and does not guarantee price or stock.

- Checkout is a durable saga with an idempotency key.

- Inventory uses atomic reservations with expiry and explicit commit/release transitions.

- Payment uses provider idempotency, state machine, webhooks, UNKNOWN-state reconciliation, and auditable references.

- Order owns lifecycle truth and publishes events through transactional outbox.

- Fulfillment, notifications, reviews, analytics, and recommendations consume events independently.

- Flash sales add edge caching, admission control, waiting room/queue, bot protection, and bounded stock allocation.

- Global reads can be active-active, while inventory/order/payment use clear ownership and fencing.

> One-sentence architecture
> Make discovery highly cached and eventually consistent, but funnel the purchase path through a durable idempotent workflow that atomically reserves scarce inventory, records immutable order/price facts, coordinates payment through recoverable state machines, and publishes side effects asynchronously.

## 48. Key Trade-offs and Common Mistakes

| Mistake / decision | Better reasoning |
| --- | --- |
| Cart reserves inventory for days | Cart is intent; reserve briefly at checkout |
| Single distributed transaction | Saga + idempotency + compensation |
| Search is source of truth | Search is derived index |
| Client sends final price | Server recomputes authoritative quote |
| Timeout = payment failure | Timeout = unknown; reconcile |
| One inventory row under flash sale | Admission + partition/token strategy |
| Exactly-once broker assumption | At-least-once + idempotent effects |
| Everything active-active | Ownership/fencing for critical writes |
| PDP blocks on recommendations | Optional module with timeout/fallback |

## 49. Interviewer Follow-Ups — Detailed Answers

Follow-up: Why should adding an item to cart not reserve inventory?

Detailed answer: A cart can live for days or weeks, while inventory is scarce shared state. Reserving at add-to-cart would let abandoned carts lock stock and would require huge reservation cleanup. The cart should represent purchase intent and display an availability hint. The real guarantee starts during checkout with a short-lived reservation. If the product requires a special hold model, make that an explicit business feature with a short TTL rather than default cart semantics.

Follow-up: How do you prevent two users from buying the last item?

Detailed answer: Route the SKU/location reservation to one authoritative correctness boundary. Execute an atomic conditional transition such as 'if available >= quantity then increment reserved and create reservation'. This can be a transaction with row lock, compare-and-swap version, atomic conditional update, or serialized partition. Only one request can observe and consume the final sellable unit. Cache values are never used to decide the final reservation.

Follow-up: What if inventory reservation succeeds but checkout times out before receiving the response?

Detailed answer: The reservation request carries a deterministic reservation_id derived from the checkout workflow. On timeout, the orchestrator queries inventory by that ID. If ACTIVE, continue with the same hold; if FAILED, stop; if absent, retry the same idempotent operation. Creating a new random reservation after a timeout can double-reserve stock, so unknown outcomes must be resolved before retrying.

Follow-up: How do you handle multiple items whose inventory lives on different shards?

Detailed answer: Use a saga, not a cross-shard global lock. Attempt each reservation under the same checkout workflow, record every result durably, and if any required item fails, issue idempotent release commands for successful holds. The order can proceed only after all required reservations are confirmed. If the product allows partial fulfillment, model that explicitly as separate fulfillment/order groups rather than accidentally creating a partial order.

Follow-up: How do you avoid duplicate orders when the user taps Pay twice?

Detailed answer: Require an idempotency key for the logical checkout attempt. Atomically map that key to one workflow/order. A second request reads the same in-progress or completed record and returns the same result. The inventory reservation ID and payment provider idempotency key are derived from that same workflow so duplicate HTTP requests cannot create duplicate holds or charges.

Follow-up: Why is a payment timeout dangerous?

Detailed answer: The network may have failed after the provider successfully authorized or captured money. If we mark it failed and issue a fresh payment, the customer can be charged twice. Persist the provider operation ID before calling, use the provider's idempotency key, move the internal payment to UNKNOWN when outcome is unclear, and query the provider or wait for a signed webhook. A reconciliation worker resolves stale unknown states.

Follow-up: Where should price be validated?

Detailed answer: At checkout, server-side. Search/PDP prices are read-optimized and can be stale. The checkout service fetches authoritative offer/pricing rules, promotions, shipping, and tax to create a versioned quote. The accepted order stores immutable line-price and discount snapshots. Never trust a total supplied by the client and never reconstruct an old order from current prices.

Follow-up: How would you design a flash sale for 10,000 units and 10 million buyers?

Detailed answer: Do not allow all 10 million requests to contend on the inventory row. Serve the product page from CDN, then put purchase attempts through rate limits, bot checks, a waiting room/admission token, and a bounded queue. Only a controlled number reach the inventory allocator. The allocator can use serialized processing or preallocated stock-token buckets totaling no more than sellable stock. Winners then enter normal idempotent checkout; expired/failed winners release their token or reservation.

Follow-up: How do stock tokens avoid overselling?

Detailed answer: The token issuer creates at most N valid tokens for N units, possibly split across partitions with fixed budgets. A purchase attempt must atomically consume one token before entering the scarce-stock path. Tokens have IDs and states so retries cannot consume twice. Rebalancing unused budget across partitions must itself be controlled. The token is an admission/reservation primitive, not proof of payment or completed order.

Follow-up: How do you expire inventory reservations safely?

Detailed answer: Persist expires_at and reservation state. Use a delayed queue or timer system to trigger expiry, plus a sweeper for missed timers. The key race is commit versus expiry: both attempt an atomic state transition from ACTIVE. Only one wins. If COMMITTED wins, expiry does nothing; if EXPIRED wins, checkout cannot later commit that reservation without acquiring a new valid hold.

Follow-up: Why use an outbox for orders?

Detailed answer: Creating an order and publishing OrderConfirmed are two different systems. If the DB commit succeeds but broker publish fails, fulfillment may never start. If publish happens first and DB rolls back, consumers see a nonexistent order. Write the order state and outbox event in the same local transaction. A relay publishes the outbox until acknowledged. Consumers are idempotent, so retries are safe.

Follow-up: How should search handle an out-of-stock product?

Detailed answer: Search can carry a near-real-time availability feature for ranking/filtering, but it should not be the final stock authority. For top results, a fresh availability service can suppress clearly unavailable offers. Even then, stock can change between search and checkout. The only purchase guarantee is the inventory reservation. This lets search remain fast and available without pretending it has transactional stock truth.

Follow-up: How would you model Amazon marketplace sellers?

Detailed answer: Separate product/SKU identity from seller offers. Multiple sellers can list the same SKU with price, condition, fulfillment mode, and seller quality. PDP chooses/ranks offers using commercial rules and delivery promise. The order item stores the exact seller/offer snapshot. Seller suspension suppresses future offers quickly but does not rewrite historical orders.

Follow-up: What happens if the recommendation service is down during checkout?

Detailed answer: Nothing critical. Recommendations are an optional read-side feature. PDP can omit the module or serve cached popular items. Cart, quote, inventory, order, and payment must not depend on recommendation availability. This failure-domain separation is a strong design signal in an e-commerce interview.

Follow-up: How do you handle cancellation after payment authorization but before shipment?

Detailed answer: Order enters a cancellation workflow. Stop fulfillment if possible, release inventory/allocation according to its state, and void the payment authorization if funds were only authorized. If already captured, initiate an idempotent refund. The order does not jump directly to CANCELLED until required compensations reach a known state. Every step is retryable and auditable.

Follow-up: How do you handle cancellation after shipment?

Detailed answer: Usually it becomes a return/refusal workflow rather than a simple cancellation because inventory is physically in transit. The system tracks shipment outcome, creates an RMA if required, receives/inspects the item, determines inventory disposition, and issues refund according to policy. The important design point is that post-shipment reversal is a separate durable workflow.

Follow-up: How do you support active-active regions without double-selling inventory?

Detailed answer: Do not casually accept independent writes to the same scarce stock in two regions. Assign a SKU/location authoritative region/partition, or use a globally linearizable datastore if justified. Failover requires fencing/epoch so the old writer cannot continue after ownership moves. Reads can be global; correctness-sensitive reservation writes have explicit ownership.

Follow-up: What data can be eventually consistent?

Detailed answer: Search documents, recommendations, rating aggregates, analytics, many catalog read models, and displayed counters can lag. Inventory reservation transitions, order state changes, payment operation identity, coupon redemption limits where financially important, and authoritative visibility/ownership require stronger guarantees. The design should state this per domain rather than claiming the whole platform is strongly consistent.

Follow-up: How would you reconcile inventory if bugs or message loss occur?

Detailed answer: Maintain auditable movements/reservations and periodically verify accounting invariants: on-hand, reserved, allocated, shipped, returned, adjustments. Compare reservation records with order states and detect leaked ACTIVE reservations, double releases, or negative availability. Repair through explicit compensating adjustments, not silent overwrites. High-value inventory systems need reconciliation just like payment systems.

Follow-up: Give the one-minute end-to-end purchase flow.

Detailed answer: Search returns derived product candidates; PDP combines cached catalog with dynamic offer/availability hints. Cart stores intent. Checkout creates a versioned authoritative quote. POST /orders uses an idempotency key and starts a durable saga. Inventory atomically creates short-lived reservations. Order state is persisted, payment is authorized using a provider idempotency key, and unknown outcomes are reconciled. On success, order becomes confirmed and an outbox publishes to fulfillment/notifications/analytics. On failure, reservations are released and payment is voided/refunded as needed. Flash sales add admission control before this same correctness path.

## 50. Additional Detailed Interview Q&A

1. Product vs SKU vs offer?

Detailed answer: Product is the conceptual item, SKU is a purchasable variant, and offer is a seller-specific commercial listing for that SKU.

2. Why can the PDP show stale stock?

Detailed answer: The PDP is read-optimized and stock changes continuously. It may show a fresh hint, but checkout reservation is authoritative.

3. Why store price snapshots on order items?

Detailed answer: Historical orders must remain auditable even when catalog prices/promotions change later.

4. What is the buy-box-like read problem?

Detailed answer: Many seller offers must be ranked into a default offer using price, delivery, fulfillment, seller quality, and eligibility without making PDP slow.

5. Why use cursor pagination for orders/reviews?

Detailed answer: Offset pagination becomes expensive and unstable at large depth; cursors use stable sort keys.

6. How do you merge guest and logged-in carts?

Detailed answer: Read both carts, merge item-wise under product rules, cap quantities, surface unavailable/changed offers, then idempotently retire the guest cart.

7. What if a coupon has only 1,000 redemptions?

Detailed answer: Use an authoritative atomic redemption counter/reservation, not an eventually consistent analytics count.

8. What if promotion service times out?

Detailed answer: Follow explicit policy: fail quote, retry boundedly, or omit only optional promotion. Never silently invent a discount.

9. How should order IDs be generated?

Detailed answer: Globally unique, non-colliding IDs such as time/random or allocated IDs; avoid a single central sequence bottleneck.

10. How do you find a user's orders if order DB is sharded by order_id?

Detailed answer: Maintain a user_id -> ordered list/index of order IDs or choose a shard strategy that supports user history while preserving distribution.

11. Why separate payment from order?

Detailed answer: Payment has provider-specific state, webhooks, reconciliation, refunds, and security boundaries; order should reference it rather than embed provider logic.

12. What is a payment webhook race?

Detailed answer: Webhook can arrive before synchronous API response. Both paths must update the same payment state machine idempotently by provider operation/event IDs.

13. How do you avoid stale service instances committing after failover?

Detailed answer: Use fencing tokens/epochs attached to ownership-sensitive writes; storage rejects operations from older epochs.

14. How do you rebuild search?

Detailed answer: Replay catalog/offer snapshots or change streams into a new versioned index, validate it, then atomically switch query traffic.

15. How do you cache popular product pages?

Detailed answer: Cache stable product read models at CDN/API layers with versioned keys; overlay dynamic price/stock data with shorter TTL or bounded calls.

16. What if one seller changes price every second?

Detailed answer: Offer/pricing service handles mutable offer state and emits versioned changes; search may lag, while checkout always revalidates the chosen offer.

17. How do you prevent negative inventory?

Detailed answer: Atomic conditional reservation/commit transitions plus invariants and reconciliation; never decrement from stale cached values.

18. How do you support preorders/backorders?

Detailed answer: Model a different inventory promise with future supply/allocation rules rather than pretending physical on-hand exists.

19. Why should fulfillment consume order events asynchronously?

Detailed answer: Warehouse/carrier systems are slow/external and should not extend checkout latency or transaction boundaries.

20. What is the final architecture summary?

Detailed answer: Use cached derived systems for discovery; cart for intent; checkout as an idempotent saga; inventory reservations for stock correctness; payment state/reconciliation for money; order as lifecycle truth; outbox/events for fulfillment and all secondary systems.

## 51. Scenario-Based Deep Dives

Payment provider returns timeout, then webhook says authorized.

Keep payment in UNKNOWN after timeout. When the signed webhook arrives, dedupe by provider event ID and transition to AUTHORIZED if legal. The checkout saga resumes from durable state. It must not issue a second authorization merely because the original HTTP call timed out.

The last unit is reserved, but payment fails.

Payment failure triggers compensation. Inventory release uses the original reservation_id and an atomic ACTIVE -> RELEASED transition. The unit becomes available again. If release event is delayed, TTL/sweeper and reconciliation eventually repair it, but normal compensation should be immediate.

A flash-sale service crashes after issuing 100 stock tokens.

Token state must be durable. On recovery, reconcile ISSUED/CONSUMED/EXPIRED tokens against reservations/orders. Unconsumed expired tokens can return to the available budget. Never recreate 100 replacement tokens blindly, or total issued stock can exceed physical stock.

Search says ₹999 but checkout says ₹1,099.

Search index/PDP data can lag. Checkout fetches authoritative offer/pricing and creates the current quote. The UI should explicitly show the price change before final confirmation if required. The order stores ₹1,099 only after user acceptance; the stale search value is never trusted for charging.

Primary order region fails mid-checkout.

Workflow state, idempotency record, reservations, payment operation IDs, and order records must be durably replicated. Failover acquires a higher fencing epoch before resuming. Recovery inspects each step by deterministic IDs rather than replaying side effects blindly. Unknown payment/reservation outcomes are queried/reconciled.

## 52. 45-Minute Interview Flow

| Time | Coverage |
| --- | --- |
| 0-5 min | Scope, requirements, scale, consistency split |
| 5-10 min | HLD, service boundaries, data model |
| 10-15 min | Catalog/PDP/search/cart |
| 15-25 min | Checkout saga + idempotency + inventory reservation |
| 25-31 min | Payment + order state/outbox |
| 31-35 min | Flash sale and hot-key handling |
| 35-39 min | Fulfillment/cancel/returns |
| 39-42 min | Caching, partitioning, multi-region |
| 42-45 min | Failures, invariants, trade-offs, summary |

## 53. 30-Second Final Interview Answer

> 30-second answer
> I would separate the read-heavy discovery path from the correctness-sensitive purchase path. Catalog and seller offers feed denormalized PDP models and a distributed search index; cart stores intent only. Checkout creates an authoritative quote and starts an idempotent saga. Inventory atomically creates short-lived reservations so scarce stock cannot be oversold. Order owns the lifecycle, payment uses provider idempotency plus UNKNOWN-state reconciliation, and order events are published through an outbox to fulfillment, notifications, analytics, and recommendations. Flash sales add CDN caching, waiting-room/admission control, queues, bot protection, and bounded stock tokens before the same checkout path. Global reads can be active-active, while inventory/order/payment use explicit ownership and fencing.

## 54. Final Interview Checklist

- Product/SKU/offer distinction explained.

- Catalog source-of-truth vs search/PDP read models covered.

- Search, ranking, facets, PDP dynamic overlays covered.

- Cart semantics and merge conflicts covered.

- Checkout saga and idempotency covered in detail.

- Inventory reservation, multi-item compensation, TTL, oversell prevention covered.

- Flash-sale admission, queueing, stock-token strategy covered.

- Payment state machine, timeout/UNKNOWN, webhooks, reconciliation covered.

- Order state machine and transactional outbox covered.

- Fulfillment, cancellation, returns/refunds covered.

- Marketplace sellers, reviews, recommendations, promotions covered.

- Caching, partitioning, consistency matrix, multi-region, fencing covered.

- Failures, observability, security, invariants covered.

- 20 detailed follow-ups, 20 detailed Q&As, 5 scenario deep dives, and interview flow included.

## 55. Advanced Drill: Invariants You Should State Explicitly

| Invariant | Why it matters |
| --- | --- |
| One idempotency key -> one logical order | Prevents duplicate checkout |
| Reservation commit/release happens once | Inventory correctness |
| Reserved stock never exceeds sellable budget | No oversell |
| Order total equals immutable accepted quote facts | Financial audit |
| One provider operation ID maps to one payment intent | No double charge |
| Order state transitions are monotonic/legal | Workflow correctness |
| Outbox event version never exceeds committed aggregate version | Event consistency |
| Old region epoch cannot mutate current owner state | Failover safety |

Interviewers often reward explicit invariants because they reveal where strong consistency is truly required. State the invariant first, then choose the mechanism that enforces it.

## 56. Advanced Drill: Backpressure and Overload

- Protect checkout with concurrency limits before databases saturate.

- Prioritize in-flight paid/checking-out users over optional recommendations.

- Use queue depth and oldest-message age as scaling signals.

- Shed expensive nonessential PDP modules first.

- Use bounded retries with jitter; unbounded retries amplify outages.

- Circuit-break failing tax/payment dependencies only with product-safe fallback behavior.

- Flash-sale waiting rooms convert uncontrolled concurrency into bounded admission.

- Preserve durable intent/state before returning retryable errors.

## 57. Advanced Drill: Reconciliation Jobs

| Reconciler | Checks |
| --- | --- |
| Payment | Internal state vs provider captures/refunds |
| Inventory | Reservations/allocations vs orders and stock ledger |
| Order | Stuck states vs downstream acknowledgments |
| Outbox | Unpublished/old events |
| Promotion | Redemption count vs accepted orders |
| Shipment | Carrier status vs internal shipment state |
| Refund | Requested vs provider-completed amounts |

> Why reconciliation matters
> Distributed systems do not stay correct only because the happy-path code is correct. Timeouts, duplicate messages, operator mistakes, and external providers create ambiguous states. Reconciliation is a first-class correctness mechanism, especially for money and inventory.

## 58. Review Quiz with Answers

1. Does cart guarantee inventory?

Answer: No. It stores intent; checkout reservation provides the temporary guarantee.

2. What prevents duplicate checkout?

Answer: A durable idempotency key mapped to one workflow/order.

3. Why not use a global distributed transaction?

Answer: External payment and partitioned services make it impractical; use a saga with idempotent steps.

4. What is the final stock authority?

Answer: The inventory service's atomic reservation state, not cache/search.

5. What does payment timeout mean?

Answer: Unknown outcome until provider state is reconciled.

6. Why use outbox?

Answer: Atomically couple committed domain state with eventual event publication.

7. What changes for flash sale?

Answer: Admission/waiting room, bot controls, queueing, and bounded scarce-stock allocation.

8. What can be eventual?

Answer: Search, recommendations, rating aggregates, many read models.

9. What needs fencing?

Answer: Ownership-sensitive failover such as order/inventory writers.

10. Most important architecture split?

Answer: Eventually consistent discovery vs correctness-sensitive purchase workflow.

notes.content:
Design Uber / Ride-Hailing System

Real-Time Location, Matching, Trips & Dispatch

> Goal
> Design a ride-hailing platform. This problem combines high-frequency location updates, geospatial indexing, nearby-driver search, dispatch/matching, trip state machines, concurrency, real-time communication, ETA/routing, surge, payments, failures, and multi-region/city partitioning.

## 1. Problem Statement

Design a ride-hailing system where riders request trips, nearby available drivers are discovered and matched, both sides receive real-time updates, the trip progresses through pickup and completion, and the rider is charged.

> Core interview challenge
> Location data is extremely write-heavy and ephemeral, while trip assignment must prevent one driver from accepting conflicting rides. Separate the location/dispatch plane from the durable trip/payment plane.

## 2. What the Interviewer Is Testing

- Real-time driver location ingestion at very high write rates.

- Geospatial partitioning and nearby-driver lookup.

- Matching/dispatch under contention.

- Driver availability and single-assignment correctness.

- Trip lifecycle/state-machine design.

- WebSockets/push notifications and reconnect handling.

- ETA/routing integration.

- Hotspots such as airports, stadiums, and city centers.

- Eventual consistency for location versus stronger consistency for trip assignment.

- Failure recovery, idempotency, observability, and regional/city isolation.

## 3. Clarifying Questions

- Rider requests one pickup and destination; assume standard point-to-point rides.

- Drivers continuously publish GPS while online.

- Need nearest eligible driver, not globally optimal fleet assignment initially.

- Can multiple drivers be offered one ride? Yes, but only one can win.

- Do we need scheduled rides? Treat as follow-up.

- Do we own maps/routing? Assume an internal or external Maps/ETA service.

- Do we need payments? Include integration, but focus on location and dispatch.

- Geographic scope? Multi-city and multi-region.

- Ride types? Economy first; vehicle class becomes an eligibility filter.

### 3.1 Interview Scope from the Video — Start Small

Start with three user journeys: (1) rider receives a fare estimate, (2) rider requests a trip and gets a nearby match or a clear failure, (3) driver accepts/declines and navigates to pickup, then destination. Explain these before adding scaling infrastructure.

Out of initial scope: pooled/scheduled rides, ratings and sophisticated fleet optimization. They remain optional follow-ups in later sections; do not lead with them.

Clarify latency targets: aim for approximately 1–3 seconds for a successful dispatch attempt where supply exists; bound the full search/retry experience (e.g., respond with a match or NO_DRIVER within 60 seconds). Both are illustrative product targets, not guaranteed system measurements.

Peak-demand requirement: a concert or stadium release can overload a single city zone even when average global QPS is low. Design and measure peak per-zone throughput, not only global averages.

## 4. Functional Requirements

| Area | Requirement |
| --- | --- |
| Driver | Go online/offline; send location and availability |
| Rider | Request quote/ride; cancel; view driver approach |
| Dispatch | Find eligible nearby drivers and match one |
| Trip | Track requested → assigned → pickup → in-progress → completed/cancelled |
| Realtime | Push assignment, driver movement, trip state |
| Maps | ETA, route, distance |
| Pricing | Fare estimate and optional surge |
| Payment | Charge after completion; handle failure asynchronously |
| Safety/Ops | Audit state changes and support incident tooling |

## 5. Non-Functional Requirements

| Property | Expectation | Implication |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Location freshness | Seconds | In-memory/geo store; TTL |
| Dispatch latency | ~1–3 seconds target | Nearby search + parallel offers |
| Trip correctness | One active trip assignment per driver | Atomic conditional assignment |
| Availability | High within each city | City isolation and failover |
| Scale | Millions of online drivers/riders | Partitioned ingestion and geo indexes |
| Realtime | Low-latency updates | WebSocket gateway/pub-sub |
| Durability | Trip/payment history retained | Transactional durable DB |

## 6. Capacity Estimation

| Dimension | Assumption | Approx. |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Online drivers | 2M | 2 million |
| Location interval | Every 4 sec | 500K location updates/sec |
| Location event size | ~150 B logical | ~75 MB/s before replication/overhead |
| Ride requests/day | 20M | ~230 avg/s; thousands/s peak |
| Nearby search | Several per request/dispatch retry | High geo-query QPS |
| Realtime sessions | Millions | Horizontally scaled gateway fleet |
| Trip history | 20M/day | Billions/year |

> Key implication
> Location ingestion can dwarf trip creation by orders of magnitude. Do not write every GPS update synchronously into the same relational database that stores trips.

## 7. Core APIs and Streams

| Interface | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| POST /drivers/status | Online/offline/vehicle availability |
| location stream | driver_id, lat, lon, heading, speed, timestamp, sequence |
| POST /rides/estimate | Fare/ETA quote |
| POST /rides/request | Create ride request |
| POST /rides/{id}/cancel | Cancellation |
| POST /offers/{id}/accept | Driver acceptance |
| POST /trips/{id}/arrive / start / complete | Trip transitions |
| WebSocket / realtime channel | Assignments, driver position, trip state |
| GET /trips/{id} | Authoritative trip snapshot |

### 7.1 What the API Gateway Actually Does

Authentication/authorization: Verify rider/driver identity and authorize trip and offer commands.

Routing: Route quote, ride, dispatch and payment commands to the responsible services.

Rate limiting: Limit abusive booking, cancellation and location-polling requests.

Load balancing: Spread HTTP traffic across stateless application instances; do not store authoritative ride state in gateway memory.

## 8. Core Data Model

| Entity | Important fields |
| --- | --- |
| Driver | driver_id, vehicle_type, city_id, account state |
| DriverPresence | driver_id, online, availability, last_seen |
| DriverLocation | driver_id, cell_id, lat/lon, heading, timestamp, seq |
| RideRequest | ride_id, rider_id, pickup, destination, class, status |
| DispatchOffer | offer_id, ride_id, driver_id, expires_at, status |
| Trip | trip_id, ride_id, driver_id, rider_id, state, version, timestamps |
| PricingQuote | quote_id, route/distance, surge multiplier, expires_at |
| PaymentRef | trip_id, payment_id, amount, state |

### 8.1 Detailed Database Models

Use relational/transactional storage for riders, drivers, quotes, offers, rides, trips, payments and ratings. The live location and geo-index rows below describe an ephemeral store, not permanent OLTP tables. Types are illustrative (UUID, TIMESTAMPTZ, DECIMAL) and should match your DB choice.

Rider (durable)

| Column | Data type | Purpose / constraints |
| --- | --- | --- |
| rider_id | UUID | PK; stable authenticated rider identity |
| name | VARCHAR(120) | Display name |
| phone_e164 | VARCHAR(20) | Verified contact; encrypted/masked where appropriate |
| account_status | VARCHAR(24) | ACTIVE / BLOCKED / DELETED |
| created_at | TIMESTAMPTZ | Account creation time |

Driver (durable)

| Column | Data type | Purpose / constraints |
| --- | --- | --- |
| driver_id | UUID | PK; authenticated driver |
| city_id | BIGINT | Home/operational city; indexed |
| name | VARCHAR(120) | Display name |
| phone_e164 | VARCHAR(20) | Protected contact |
| vehicle_id | UUID | FK → Vehicle.vehicle_id |
| account_status | VARCHAR(24) | ACTIVE / SUSPENDED / OFFBOARDED |
| created_at | TIMESTAMPTZ | Created timestamp |

DriverPresence (short-lived operational state)

| Column | Data type | Purpose / constraints |
| --- | --- | --- |
| driver_id | UUID | PK/key; one latest record |
| city_id | BIGINT | Routing ownership |
| online | BOOLEAN | Driver has enabled availability |
| availability | VARCHAR(24) | AVAILABLE / RESERVED / ON_TRIP; advisory only |
| last_seen_at | TIMESTAMPTZ | Heartbeat time |
| session_epoch | BIGINT | Reject stale sessions after reconnect |
| ttl_seconds | INT | Expire stale presence |

DriverLocation / GeoIndex (ephemeral)

| Column | Data type | Purpose / constraints |
| --- | --- | --- |
| driver_id | UUID | Key / unique latest coordinate |
| city_id | BIGINT | Location routing partition |
| cell_id | VARCHAR(64) | Geohash/H3/S2 cell; geo lookup |
| latitude | DECIMAL(9,6) | Latest GPS latitude |
| longitude | DECIMAL(9,6) | Latest GPS longitude |
| heading_deg | SMALLINT | Optional heading, 0–359 |
| speed_mps | DECIMAL(7,2) | Optional speed |
| gps_at | TIMESTAMPTZ | Device timestamp, bounded/trusted validation |
| sequence_no | BIGINT | Reject older updates |
| expires_at | TIMESTAMPTZ | TTL / freshness bound |

RideRequest (durable)

| Column | Data type | Purpose / constraints |
| --- | --- | --- |
| ride_id | UUID | PK |
| rider_id | UUID | FK → Rider.rider_id |
| quote_id | UUID | FK → PricingQuote.quote_id |
| pickup | JSONB | Pickup coordinates / address |
| destination | JSONB | Destination coordinates / address |
| vehicle_class | VARCHAR(32) | Eligibility constraint |
| city_id | BIGINT | Owning city/region |
| status | VARCHAR(24) | REQUESTED / ASSIGNED / CANCELLED / NO_DRIVER |
| idempotency_key | VARCHAR(128) | Unique per rider & booking action |
| created_at | TIMESTAMPTZ | Creation time |
| version | BIGINT | Optimistic concurrency |

DriverAssignment (strongly consistent)

| Column | Data type | Purpose / constraints |
| --- | --- | --- |
| driver_id | UUID | PK or unique active driver owner |
| ride_id | UUID | Unique active ride assignment |
| assignment_epoch | BIGINT | Monotonic owner epoch / fencing |
| state | VARCHAR(24) | AVAILABLE / RESERVED / ON_TRIP |
| version | BIGINT | Conditional update / CAS |
| updated_at | TIMESTAMPTZ | Transition timestamp |

Trip (durable)

| Column | Data type | Purpose / constraints |
| --- | --- | --- |
| trip_id | UUID | PK |
| ride_id | UUID | UNIQUE FK → RideRequest.ride_id |
| rider_id | UUID | FK → Rider.rider_id |
| driver_id | UUID | FK → Driver.driver_id |
| state | VARCHAR(24) | ASSIGNED / ARRIVING / ARRIVED / IN_TRIP / COMPLETED / CANCELLED |
| started_at | TIMESTAMPTZ | Nullable trip start |
| completed_at | TIMESTAMPTZ | Nullable completion |
| cancelled_at | TIMESTAMPTZ | Nullable cancellation |
| final_distance_m | INT | Optional measured distance |
| final_fare | DECIMAL(12,2) | Frozen settlement amount |
| version | BIGINT | Guard state transitions |

Payment (durable / transactional)

| Column | Data type | Purpose / constraints |
