## 7. High-Level Architecture

![7. High-Level Architecture — source diagram](/diagrams/t-1zyk8264g8mn-kix-rh1agen9z0a9.png)

## 8. Edit Lifecycle

- User types; client immediately applies edit to its local model.

- Client creates unique op_id with base revision/state.

- Operation travels over persistent session to collaboration service.

- Permission and session validity are checked.

- Document owner/leader orders or merges the operation.

- Operation is transformed/CRDT-applied against concurrent edits.

- Authoritative operation is durably appended.

- Server ACKs sender with committed revision/state.

- Remote collaborators receive the resulting operation.

- Clients apply it relative to pending local operations and converge.

## 9. Why Local-First Rendering Matters

- Waiting for a network round trip per keystroke feels unusable.

- The client optimistically applies its own operation immediately.

- Pending unacknowledged operations are tracked separately from acknowledged base state.

- Remote operations must be transformed/merged against local pending operations before rendering.

- If server rejects permission or detects unrecoverable state, client resynchronizes and surfaces the conflict.

## 10. The Concurrency Problem

![10. The Concurrency Problem — source diagram](/diagrams/t-1zyk8264g8mn-kix-9ozjy3glfrri.png)

> The failure mode
> If Alice and Bob both edit revision 10 and every client simply applies remote positions literally, character offsets shift and replicas can diverge. The system needs Operational Transformation, CRDTs, or another formally defined convergence mechanism.

## 11. Operational Transformation (OT)

- Operations are expressed relative to a base document revision.

- A central server establishes an authoritative order.

- When operation B was created against an older revision, transform B against operations committed since its base.

- Transformation changes positions/ranges while preserving intended effect.

- Server broadcasts transformed canonical operations.

- Clients also transform incoming remote operations against their own pending local operations.

> Example
> Base text ABC. Alice inserts X at position 1; Bob concurrently inserts Y at position 2. If Alice's insert commits first, Bob's insert position may transform from 2 to 3 so it still targets the original logical location.

## 12. OT Client/Server Flow

![12. OT Client/Server Flow — source diagram](/diagrams/t-1zyk8264g8mn-kix-wrecd28xks8y.png)

## 13. OT Transformation Cases

| Concurrent operations | Typical concern |
| --- | --- |
| Insert vs insert | Tie-breaking and shifted position |
| Insert vs delete | Delete range shifts/expands depending location |
| Delete vs delete | Overlapping ranges must not double-delete |
| Format vs insert | Inserted content inherits/doesn't inherit style by rule |
| Format vs delete | Formatting range shrinks around deleted content |
| Structural blocks | Paragraph/list/table semantics need richer ops |

- Transformation functions must satisfy convergence properties; ad-hoc index adjustment is unsafe.

- Tie-break concurrent inserts deterministically using server order or stable client/op identity.

- Rich-text editors usually operate on structured document models rather than one flat string.

## 14. CRDT Alternative

- A CRDT assigns stable logical identities/positions so replicas can merge operations without a single total-order transform step.

- Operations are designed to be commutative/idempotent under defined conditions.

- Sequence CRDTs represent text positions using element identifiers rather than fragile numeric offsets.

- CRDTs can simplify offline peer-like merging but add metadata/tombstone complexity.

- Production systems may use hybrid/custom algorithms; in interviews, explain the trade-off rather than claiming one is universally superior.

## 15. OT vs CRDT

| Dimension | OT | CRDT |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Coordination | Usually central revision/order | Can merge concurrent replica ops |
| Operation form | Position/range + transform | Stable identifiers/causal metadata |
| Offline editing | Possible but reconciliation is complex | Natural fit conceptually |
| Metadata growth | Operation history/snapshots | Identifiers/tombstones can grow |
| Implementation | Transform functions are subtle | CRDT design/compaction is subtle |
| Interview choice | Great for centralized editor | Great for offline/multi-replica model |

> Recommended interview framing
> Choose one primary model and go deep. For a Google-Docs-like centralized service, OT with one logical document leader is easy to explain. Mention CRDT as an alternative and compare its offline/convergence trade-offs.

## 16. Document Ownership and Sequencing

- Hash doc_id to a collaboration shard or directory-selected leader.

- One active logical leader owns canonical revision ordering for a document under the OT model.

- All edit operations for the active document route to that leader.

- Leader keeps hot document state/history window in memory.

- Ownership can migrate when load changes, but fencing prevents two authoritative leaders.

- Different documents scale independently across many collaboration shards.

## 17. Durable Operation Log

- Every committed edit has stable op_id and revision/causal metadata.

- Append operations to durable partitioned storage keyed by doc_id.

- Do not rewrite the entire document for each keystroke.

- Operation log enables history, replay and recovery.

- Idempotency on op_id prevents duplicate append after retry.

- Periodic snapshots cap replay length.

## 18. Snapshots and Compaction

- Document accumulates operations after snapshot revision S.

- Background worker materializes document through revision K.

- Serialize compact document tree/content as snapshot K.

- Atomically publish snapshot pointer/version.

- Keep operations after K for live clients/history window.

- Older operations may move to archival history according to retention.

- Recovery loads snapshot K and replays K+1..latest.

> Important
> Compaction must never make an active client's base revision impossible to reconcile. Keep enough transform/history state or force that client through a full resync.

## 19. Reconnect and Resynchronization

![19. Reconnect and Resynchronization — source diagram](/diagrams/t-1zyk8264g8mn-kix-iemocaprrym6.png)

- If client revision is recent, send missing canonical operations.

- If required transform history was compacted, send a fresh snapshot and rebase/merge pending edits.

- Duplicate offline op_ids remain idempotent.

- Client should persist its pending operation queue locally before claiming offline edits are safe.

## 20. Offline Editing

- Client keeps a local durable document replica and operation queue.

- User edits optimistically while disconnected.

- Each offline operation carries stable identity and causal/base state.

- On reconnect, first obtain server changes since known state.

- Transform/rebase OT operations or merge CRDT operations.

- Upload local operations idempotently.

- If semantic conflict cannot be resolved automatically, preserve content and surface a user-visible conflict rather than dropping edits.

## 21. Presence and Collaborator Cursors

- Presence is ephemeral: online state, cursor, selection, viewport, typing/activity.

- Send through low-latency pub-sub scoped to active document.

- Coalesce cursor movements; do not send every mouse pixel.

- Use TTL/heartbeat so crashed clients disappear automatically.

- Presence positions must transform as edits shift the document.

- Do not persist every cursor update in the document history.

## 22. Permissions and Sharing

| Role | Capabilities |
| --- | --- |
| Owner | Manage document and sharing |
| Editor | Edit/comment according to policy |
| Commenter | Comment/suggest but not direct edit |
| Viewer | Read only |

- ACL check occurs on open/join and sensitive mutations.

- Long-lived sessions must react to permission revocation.

- ACL has its own version; collaboration servers receive invalidation events.

- A user downgraded from editor should stop producing accepted edits promptly.

- Share links use scoped tokens and explicit policy, not guessable document IDs.

## 23. Permission Revocation During Editing

> Follow-up
> Alice is editing while the owner revokes her access. The ACL update becomes authoritative, invalidates active collaboration sessions, and the document leader rejects subsequent operations from Alice. Already committed operations remain in history; uncommitted local edits should be preserved client-side for copy/recovery rather than silently discarded.

## 24. Comments, Suggestions and Anchors

- Comments reference stable document ranges/anchors rather than raw screen coordinates.

- Anchors transform as nearby edits occur.

- Suggestion mode represents proposed insert/delete/format changes with author/state metadata.

- Accept/reject suggestion becomes a canonical document operation.

- Deleting the referenced content can collapse or orphan a comment according to product rules.

- Mentions trigger asynchronous notifications outside the edit critical path.

## 25. Rich Text Document Model

- Use a structured tree: document -> blocks -> paragraphs/lists/tables -> inline spans/text.

- Operations target stable nodes/ranges where possible.

- Formatting attributes are explicit marks/styles, not raw HTML diffs.

- Schema validation prevents malformed collaborative states.

- Tables, lists and embeds need operation semantics beyond character insertion/deletion.

- Version the schema and migration logic for old documents.

## 26. Embedded Images and Files

- Client requests asset upload session and uploads directly to object storage.

- Document operation inserts an asset reference/node, not binary bytes.

- Asset service validates metadata, generates previews and controls access.

- CDN serves authorized immutable/derived objects.

- Deleting an embed creates a document operation; physical asset garbage collection is delayed until no references/history require it.

## 27. Autosave Semantics

- Realtime committed operations are already the autosave mechanism.

- UI 'Saved' means all local pending operations have been acknowledged/durably committed.

- Do not run a periodic full-document PUT every few seconds.

- Metadata such as title may use separate debounced writes.

- Offline UI distinguishes 'saved locally' from 'saved to cloud'.

## 28. Version History

- Revision history is derived from immutable operations plus snapshots.

- Group fine-grained operations into human-friendly named/time revisions for UI.

- Restoring an old version should create a new canonical revision representing restored content, not erase later history.

- Store author and timestamp metadata for audit/history.

- Historical snapshots can be generated lazily and cached.

## 29. Search and Indexing

- Search is asynchronous and outside realtime edit path.

- Indexing workers consume committed document revisions/operation checkpoints.

- Search may lag the latest keystroke slightly.

- Index permissions/ACL filters carefully to avoid data leakage.

- For encrypted-client-only content, server-side full-text search requires a different security model.

## 30. Partitioning Strategy

| Data | Partition key |
| --- | --- |
| Collaboration ownership | doc_id |
| Operation log | doc_id |
| Snapshots | doc_id/object key |
| Metadata | doc_id with owner/user secondary indexes |
| Presence | doc_id |
| ACL | doc_id |
| Assets | asset_id |
| Search | search-engine-specific shard |

## 31. Hot Document Problem

- A viral document with thousands of simultaneous editors can overload one logical leader.

- Keep one canonical ordering authority but scale socket fan-out and presence independently.

- Batch/coalesce operations where semantics allow.

- Use hierarchical regional fan-out for remote operations.

- Rate-limit presence and cursor traffic aggressively.

- Large viewer populations can consume snapshot/read replicas while only editors join collaboration path.

- At extreme editor counts, product may cap active editors or use specialized hierarchical collaboration.

## 32. Multi-Region Architecture

- Clients connect to nearby realtime gateways.

- A document has one home collaboration leader/region under centralized OT.

- Remote gateways forward edits to the home leader; canonical operations fan back out regionally.

- Snapshots/logs replicate to secondary regions.

- Failover requires fencing old leader before new leader accepts revisions.

- Read-only viewers may use regional snapshot replicas/CDN while editors use authoritative collaboration route.

## 33. Leader Failover

- Leader owns document partition under epoch E.

- Committed operations are in replicated durable log.

- Leader fails or loses lease.

- Control plane grants epoch E+1 to replacement and fences E.

- Replacement loads recent snapshot/hot state and replays committed operations.

- Gateways refresh routing and reconnect sessions.

- Clients resend unacknowledged op_ids; idempotency returns existing commit or safely applies missing operation.

## 34. Backpressure

- Bound per-session outbound buffers.

- Drop/coalesce ephemeral presence before durable edit operations.

- Slow clients fall behind and resync rather than blocking the document leader.

- Batch network frames without changing operation order.

- Protect hot documents with per-doc quotas and isolated shards.

- Snapshot/export/search work runs on separate pools.

## 35. Failure Scenarios

| Failure | Recovery |
| --- | --- |
| Gateway dies | Client reconnects and syncs from revision |
| Client retries op | op_id deduplication |
| Leader dies after commit before ACK | Retry returns/replays committed op |
| Leader dies before commit | Pending client op resubmits |
| Presence service dies | Cursors disappear temporarily; document unaffected |
| Snapshot worker fails | Operation log remains source of truth |
| Asset processing delayed | Embed shows pending state |
| ACL revoked | Invalidate session; reject future edits |
| Region outage | Fenced failover + replay |
| Slow client | Disconnect/resync from snapshot+ops |

## 36. Exactly-Once Editing?

- Network delivery is not exactly once.

- Every operation has stable op_id; retries are at least once.

- Authoritative log applies one logical operation once.

- Clients deduplicate remote canonical operation IDs/revisions.

- User-visible exactly-once effects emerge from idempotency + deterministic merge, not magical transport.

## 38. Security

- Authenticate user/device and authorize every document session.

- Use unguessable document identifiers but never rely on secrecy of IDs alone.

- Encrypt data in transit and at rest.

- Protect share-link tokens with scope/expiry/revocation.

- Audit sharing and sensitive administrative actions.

- Sanitize rich content/export paths against script/injection risks.

- Rate-limit abusive collaboration and comment/mention traffic.

## 39. End-to-End Concurrent Edit Example

- Revision 100 contains 'HELLO'.

- Alice and Bob both start from revision 100.

- Alice inserts '!' at end; Bob deletes first 'H'.

- Alice's op reaches leader first and commits as revision 101.

- Bob's base=100 is stale, so leader transforms Bob's delete against Alice's insert.

- Bob's transformed delete still targets original H and commits as revision 102.

- Leader broadcasts canonical operations.

- Alice transforms Bob's remote op against any pending local state; Bob receives Alice's earlier canonical op/ACK state.

- Both converge to 'ELLO!' at revision 102.

## 40. End-to-End Offline Example

- Phone goes offline at revision 500 and persists local snapshot.

- User performs ten edits; client stores stable offline op IDs.

- Meanwhile desktop advances server document to revision 520.

- Phone reconnects and asks for changes after 500.

- Server supplies 501..520 or a newer snapshot if history window was compacted.

- Phone rebases/transforms its pending edits against server changes.

- Rebased operations upload idempotently and receive canonical revisions.

- Any irreconcilable semantic conflict preserves user text in a recoverable copy rather than dropping it.

## 41. Common Interview Mistakes

- Saying 'use WebSockets' without solving concurrent edits.

- Using last-write-wins for the entire document.

- Writing full document to DB on every keystroke.

- Using client timestamps to order edits.

- No idempotency for retried operations.

- No reconnect or stale-revision strategy.

- Treating cursor/presence as durable history.

- No snapshot/compaction plan.

- Ignoring permission revocation during an active session.

- Claiming OT/CRDT without explaining one concrete concurrent-edit example.

- Running two active OT leaders for the same document without coordination.

- Letting slow clients backpressure the collaboration leader.

## 42. Final Production Architecture

- Nearby realtime gateways maintain persistent client sessions.

- doc_id routes edit traffic to one logical collaboration owner under centralized OT.

- Clients apply edits locally and send stable op_ids with base revision.

- Leader transforms stale operations against canonical history, assigns revision, durably appends, then ACKs/broadcasts.

- Clients transform remote operations against local pending operations and converge.

- Snapshots periodically compact operation history and bound recovery time.

- Reconnect sync uses missing operations or snapshot + rebase.

- Presence/cursors use separate ephemeral pub-sub.

- ACL, assets, search, exports and notifications remain separate from the keystroke hot path.

- Multi-region failover uses replicated logs plus fencing to avoid dual authoritative leaders.

> One-sentence architecture
> Use local-first clients, a fenced per-document collaboration leader, deterministic OT (or a clearly chosen CRDT alternative), an idempotent durable operation log plus snapshots, revision-based reconnect, and separate ephemeral presence/fan-out so concurrent and offline edits converge without putting storage or slow clients on the keystroke path.

## 43. Interviewer Follow-Ups — Detailed Answers

Follow-up: Why not just lock the document while someone edits?

Detailed answer: It destroys collaboration and availability. The goal is concurrent intent-preserving edits, so use OT/CRDT rather than coarse locks.

Follow-up: Why not last-write-wins?

Detailed answer: Two users changing different parts would overwrite one another. LWW is suitable for some metadata fields, not a collaborative text body.

Follow-up: How does OT handle stale operations?

Detailed answer: The server transforms the stale operation against every canonical operation committed after its base revision, producing an equivalent operation on the current state.

Follow-up: What guarantees convergence?

Detailed answer: All replicas process canonical operations under the same transformation rules/order and reconcile local pending operations consistently. Transformation functions must satisfy required convergence properties.

Follow-up: OT or CRDT?

Detailed answer: For a centralized Docs-like service, OT with one document leader is easy to reason about. CRDTs are attractive for offline/decentralized merging but trade this for identifier/tombstone metadata and compaction complexity.

Follow-up: What if two users insert at the same position?

Detailed answer: Use deterministic tie-breaking: canonical server order or stable operation/client identity. Every replica applies the same rule.

Follow-up: What if a client disconnects with pending edits?

Detailed answer: Persist pending ops locally. On reconnect, fetch server changes, rebase/transform pending operations, then resend using the same op_ids.

Follow-up: When can the UI say Saved?

Detailed answer: When all local pending edits are durably acknowledged by the authoritative collaboration service. Offline state should say saved locally, not saved to cloud.

Follow-up: How do you recover a crashed leader?

Detailed answer: Fence the old epoch, load the latest snapshot, replay committed operations to the durable frontier, then accept resubmitted unacknowledged op_ids idempotently.

Follow-up: Why snapshots?

Detailed answer: Without them, opening/recovering a long-lived document could require replaying millions of operations. Snapshots bound replay cost.

Follow-up: Can you delete old operations after snapshot?

Detailed answer: Only after considering history retention and active stale clients. Keep enough transformation/recovery history or force old clients through a snapshot resync.

Follow-up: How do collaborator cursors stay correct?

Detailed answer: Cursor/selection anchors are transformed along with document edits. Cursor events themselves are ephemeral and coalesced.

Follow-up: How do you handle 10,000 viewers?

Detailed answer: Serve snapshots/read state from scalable read infrastructure and fan out canonical updates hierarchically; viewers do not all need heavyweight editor state.

Follow-up: How do you handle 1,000 editors?

Detailed answer: One canonical ordering authority may remain, but isolate the document, scale gateways/fan-out, coalesce presence, batch I/O, and potentially enforce product limits at extreme concurrency.

Follow-up: What happens if permissions are revoked mid-session?

Detailed answer: ACL version invalidation terminates/downgrades the active session. The leader rejects future edits; already committed edits remain valid history.

Follow-up: How do comments survive edits?

Detailed answer: Anchor comments to stable logical ranges/nodes and transform those anchors as edits occur. Define behavior when referenced content is fully deleted.

Follow-up: How are images handled?

Detailed answer: Upload directly to object storage, then insert a small asset-reference node as a canonical document operation.

Follow-up: How do you restore an old version?

Detailed answer: Materialize the historical state and commit a new operation/revision that restores that content. Do not erase intervening history.

Follow-up: What if the server receives the same op twice?

Detailed answer: op_id idempotency maps retries to the existing committed result, preventing duplicate text.

Follow-up: Give the one-minute design.

Detailed answer: Clients render edits locally and send idempotent operations with base revision over WebSockets. A doc_id routes to one fenced collaboration leader. Under OT, stale operations are transformed against canonical operations since their base, then durably appended with a new revision before ACK/broadcast. Clients reconcile remote ops with local pending edits. Snapshots compact history; reconnect uses missing operations or snapshot plus rebase. Presence is ephemeral pub-sub, assets use object storage, ACL changes invalidate sessions, and replicated logs plus fencing provide regional failover.

## 44. Additional Detailed Q&A

1. What is base revision?

Detailed answer: The canonical document revision against which the client created an operation.

2. What is canonical revision?

Detailed answer: The authoritative ordered position assigned after merge/transform.

3. Why stable op_id?

Detailed answer: Retry deduplication and client/server reconciliation.

4. Why not send HTML diffs?

Detailed answer: HTML is presentation-oriented and unstable; structured operations are deterministic and schema-valid.

5. What is a tombstone in CRDTs?

Detailed answer: Metadata marking logically deleted elements so concurrent references can still merge; compaction is needed.

6. Can revisions have gaps?

Detailed answer: Yes if allocation permits; monotonic authoritative ordering matters more than gaplessness.

7. What is a hot document?

Detailed answer: One doc whose editors/fan-out/operation rate dominates a collaboration shard.

8. What is a collaboration shard?

Detailed answer: A server/process group owning active document sessions and canonical edit processing.

9. Why separate presence?

Detailed answer: It is high-rate, ephemeral and safe to lose.

10. How are mentions delivered?

Detailed answer: Commit comment/content first, then asynchronously emit notification events.

11. What happens to a slow editor?

Detailed answer: Bound buffers; disconnect and revision-resync instead of blocking everyone.

12. How is title editing handled?

Detailed answer: Separate metadata version/LWW or simple optimistic concurrency; it need not use character OT.

13. Can document search be synchronous?

Detailed answer: No need; asynchronously index committed revisions.

14. How do exports work?

Detailed answer: Read a stable snapshot/revision and render outside collaboration path.

15. Why checksum document state?

Detailed answer: Detect rare replica/replay divergence and trigger resync.

16. How do you move a doc leader?

Detailed answer: Quiesce/fence old owner, transfer/replay state, increment epoch, update routing.

17. How are schema changes handled?

Detailed answer: Version document model/operations and migrate snapshots deterministically.

18. Can two regions both edit the same document?

Detailed answer: Yes through nearby gateways, but under centralized OT their edits converge at one authoritative document leader.

19. What survives presence outage?

Detailed answer: All document edits/history; only cursors/online indicators temporarily degrade.

20. Most important invariant?

Detailed answer: Every accepted operation has one durable identity and all valid replicas converge to the same document state.

## 45. Scenario-Based Deep Dives

Two users concurrently delete overlapping ranges.

The chosen algorithm must ensure overlapping content is deleted once and both replicas converge. In OT, transform the second delete against the first so its range shrinks/remaps; never apply stale raw indexes.

Leader commits an edit but crashes before ACK.

The client retries the same op_id after reconnect. Recovery replays the committed log; idempotency returns the existing canonical revision rather than inserting the text twice.

A user edits offline for three days.

On reconnect, the old transform window may be compacted. Send a recent snapshot/current state, rebase or merge the locally persisted pending operations, then upload them idempotently. Preserve a conflict copy if semantic merge cannot safely retain intent.

A viral document gets 50,000 viewers and 200 editors.

Editors use the canonical collaboration leader; viewers use scalable snapshot/read replicas. Canonical operation fan-out is hierarchical/regional, presence is heavily coalesced, and the document gets isolated capacity.

Owner revokes an editor while that editor has local pending changes.

ACL invalidation prevents new server commits after revocation. Already committed changes remain. Pending local text is preserved on the client for recovery/copy but is not silently forced into the now-protected document.

## 46. Advanced Drill: Client State Machine

| State | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Base | Last fully acknowledged canonical document |
| Pending | Locally applied operation sent but not ACKed |
| Buffer | New local edits created while pending exists |
| Remote arrival | Transform remote against pending/buffer and vice versa |
| ACK | Advance base; send/merge buffered work |
| Resync | Replace/reconcile base from snapshot/history |

- A simple OT client often allows one outstanding pending operation plus a local buffer to simplify transformations.

- On ACK, buffered edits can become the next pending operation.

- Remote canonical ops are transformed against pending local intent before display.

- The exact algorithm varies, but the interview answer must show that optimistic local edits are not blindly overwritten by remote changes.

## 47. Advanced Drill: Correctness Invariants

| Invariant | Mechanism |
| --- | --- |
| All replicas converge | OT/CRDT rules + canonical ordering/causality |
| Retry does not duplicate edit | op_id idempotency |
| Accepted edit recoverable | durable operation log before ACK |
| One OT authority per doc | leader ownership + fencing |
| Old client can recover | revision sync or snapshot + rebase |
| Presence loss cannot lose text | separate ephemeral path |
| Slow client cannot stall doc | bounded buffers + resync |
| Permission revoke takes effect | ACL version invalidation |

## 48. Advanced Drill: OT Walkthrough

- Base revision 10: ABCD.

- Alice deletes B at position 1; Bob concurrently inserts X at position 2.

- Alice's delete commits first as revision 11, producing ACD.

- Bob's operation was intended between original B and C.

- Transform Bob's insertion against Alice's delete: position 2 becomes position 1.

- Apply transformed Bob op to ACD -> AXCD.

- Commit as revision 12.

- Broadcast canonical operations; every replica reaches AXCD.

> What interviewer wants
> You do not need to derive a complete OT algebra on the whiteboard. You do need to demonstrate that stale numeric positions cannot be applied directly and show one correct transformed example.

## 49. Advanced Drill: Snapshot Strategy

- Snapshot every N operations or when replay bytes/time exceed threshold.

- Hot documents snapshot more frequently than cold documents.

- Snapshot asynchronously from an exact revision boundary.

- Store checksum/schema version and latest operation revision.

- Keep at least a rolling transform window after snapshot.

- Archive older history separately if version-history retention requires it.

- Validate snapshot by replaying a sample/checksum before promoting pointer.

## 50. Advanced Drill: Multi-Region Trade-Offs

| Choice | Benefit | Cost |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Single home leader | Simple deterministic OT | WAN RTT for remote editors |
| Regional active leaders | Lower local RTT | Hard cross-region concurrent merge/consensus |
| CRDT multi-replica | Natural concurrent merge | Metadata/compaction and product semantics complexity |
| Edge viewers only | Cheap global reads | Editors still route to home |

For an interview, optimize first for correctness. A home collaboration leader plus nearby socket gateways is defensible; only introduce multi-leader CRDT complexity when requirements demand low-latency offline/active-active editing.

- Rich-text structured model and assets.

- Hot documents and fan-out.

- Multi-region leader/fencing trade-offs.

- Backpressure, failures and observability.

- 20 detailed follow-ups, 20 additional Q&As, 5 scenarios, advanced OT/client/snapshot drills, and colorful diagrams.

## 55. Deep Dive: Comments, Suggestions, and Stable Anchoring

- A comment should not be anchored only by numeric character offsets because concurrent inserts and deletes shift those offsets. Anchor it to logical document positions or node/range identifiers that participate in the same transformation/merge model as edits.

- When a range is partially deleted, shrink the comment anchor to the surviving content. When the entire range disappears, retain an orphaned/collapsed anchor according to product policy so the discussion is not silently lost.

- Suggestion mode is not merely colored text. A suggested insertion/deletion has author, creation revision, state, and a target range. Accepting or rejecting it generates canonical document operations so every collaborator observes the same result.

- Comments can have their own versioned thread state—open, resolved, reopened—without forcing every comment message into the character-edit operation stream.

- Mention notifications are asynchronous. First commit the comment/suggestion, then emit a notification event; a notification outage must not roll back the document.

## 56. Deep Dive: Document Schema and Structural Editing

- Real editors contain paragraphs, headings, lists, tables, code blocks, links, footnotes, images and formatting spans. Model the document as a validated tree rather than one giant string.

- Structural operations include split paragraph, join blocks, wrap list, insert table row, delete node, move node and apply mark. Each operation defines valid preconditions and deterministic behavior under concurrency.

- Node identifiers reduce ambiguity when a remote operation refers to content whose surrounding character positions changed.

- Schema validation runs before commit so malformed client operations cannot corrupt the shared document tree.

- Schema migrations are versioned. A recovered historical operation must be interpreted under compatible rules, or snapshots must be migrated before replay.

- Large pasted content should be chunked/batched into bounded operations so one client cannot monopolize the collaboration event loop.

## 57. Deep Dive: Testing the Collaboration Algorithm

- Property test convergence: generate concurrent operation sets, deliver them in allowed different orders, and verify all replicas end with the same document.

- Property test preservation: characters inserted by a user should not disappear unless a causally valid delete removes them.

- Run randomized insert/delete/format workloads against a simple reference implementation.

- Crash the leader at every point around append, ACK and broadcast; retries must never duplicate a logical operation.

- Simulate offline clients that reconnect after thousands of revisions and after compaction boundaries.

- Inject duplicate, delayed and reordered network frames; op_id/revision handling must remain correct.

- Compare document checksums at canonical revision boundaries and alert on divergence.

- Load-test viral documents separately from the normal many-small-documents workload.

## 58. More Interview Follow-Ups

Follow-up: Can the collaboration server keep the whole document only in memory?

Detailed answer: It can cache the hot document in memory, but durable operation history and snapshots remain authoritative. A process crash must be recoverable without relying on its RAM.

Follow-up: What happens if a remote operation arrives before an earlier revision?

Detailed answer: Do not apply it blindly. Buffer until the missing revision arrives or trigger gap recovery. Canonical revision continuity is part of the client protocol.

Follow-up: How do you move a comment when text before it is inserted?

Detailed answer: Transform its anchor positions using the same positional semantics as document operations, or use stable logical anchors whose relative positions survive the insert.

Follow-up: How do you prevent one paste from blocking everyone?

Detailed answer: Set operation-size limits, chunk large structural changes, bound per-event work, and yield/batch fan-out while preserving canonical ordering.

Follow-up: What if the same user edits from two devices offline?

Detailed answer: Treat devices as independent replicas with stable operation identities. On reconnect, both sets merge against server state using the chosen OT/CRDT semantics; user identity alone must not imply one linear local history.

Follow-up: Can the server broadcast before durable append?

Detailed answer: It can reduce latency speculatively, but then clients may observe edits that disappear after failure. A simpler interview contract is durable commit before canonical ACK/broadcast.

Follow-up: How do you know a snapshot is safe to use?

Detailed answer: It carries doc_id, exact canonical revision, schema version and checksum. Recovery replays only operations after that revision and can verify resulting checksum/invariants.

Follow-up: What if the operation log is temporarily unavailable?

Detailed answer: Stop acknowledging new canonical edits or enter an explicitly defined degraded mode. Do not claim edits are saved if the durability contract cannot be met.

Follow-up: How do you support read-only public documents cheaply?

Detailed answer: Serve a recent immutable/materialized snapshot from CDN/read replicas and optionally stream public deltas; do not allocate full editor session state to every viewer.

Follow-up: What is the hardest correctness bug?

Detailed answer: Replica divergence: two users believe they are at the same revision but render different state. Detect it with revision/checksum telemetry and recover via authoritative snapshot resync.

## 59. Interview Whiteboard Plan

- Start with two editor clients connected to regional realtime gateways.

- Draw doc_id routing into one collaboration leader and write 'canonical revision' beside it.

- Below the leader draw durable operation log plus periodic snapshot store.

- Show one concurrent Alice/Bob edit and explicitly transform/merge it.

- Add presence pub-sub as a separate dashed/ephemeral path.

- Add ACL service and object storage for images outside the keystroke path.

- Finish with standby/replay plus fencing for leader failure and snapshot+ops for reconnect.

S3

S3 is not a filesystem/database

Very common question: “How would you upload/download files securely?”



RDS

MySQL/PostgreSQL

Multi-AZ

Difference between Read Replica vs Multi-AZ

RDS vs running MySQL yourself on EC2



VPC — very importantYou don’t need networking depth, but you absolutely should understand:

VPC

Public subnet

Basic architecture:



Internet → ALB → EC2/ECS in private subnet → RDSBe able to explain why database servers should not normally be publicly accessible.

Policy

CloudWatch

Triggering Auto Scaling/alarm notifications



Lambda + API GatewayLearn only basics:

Event-driven

Pay-per-use

Good for short/event-based workloads

SQS and SNSThis is especially useful because system-design interviews often mix these with AWS.SQS

Queue

Know:SNS = fan-outSQS = queue/buffering



DynamoDB Only learn basics unless the JD explicitly mentions it:

Very scalable

For you, the most important architecture to memorize conceptually is:

notes.content:
AWS EC2 : 







EC2 (Elastic Compute Cloud)



• Amazon EC2 is a web service that provides resizable compute capacity in the cloud.  

You can scale the compute capacity up and down as per the computing requirement changes.  

Amazon EC2 changes the economics of computing by allowing you to pay only for the resources that you actually use.  

• EC2 is an example of IAAS  

• We can scale the compute capacity up and down as per the computing requirement changes.



Features of EC2

• Provides scalable computing capacity  

• Launch as many or as few virtual servers as you need  

• Configure security and networking  

• Manage storage  



Amazon Machine Image (AMI)

• Its gives the basic information about the instance created also shown running states of instance.



Instance Type

• It store the information about instance such as ram, cpu etc.



Key Pairs

a) Used secure system to store the private key  

b) Public key is store by AWS  

c) Private key is store in secure place instead of password we can used a key pair to access the ec2  

d) Private key never be recovered  



Amazon EBS (Elastic Block Store) Volumes

• EC2 is a virtual server in a cloud while EBS is a virtual disc in a cloud.  

• Amazon EBS allows you to create storage volume and attach them in to the EC2 instances.



Security Group

• Used for handle the incoming and outgoing traffic.  

• We can modify the security groups according to our requirement.



Elastic IP Address

• This feature provides static public IPv4 addresses for dynamic cloud computing.  

• This ip's can be attached to EC2 instances.  

• Elastic IP can be quickly re-map to new instances, if your current EC2 instance fails



Tags

• It's a meta data that you can define for your amazon EC2 resources.  

• Tags helps you to classify our AWS resources in different ways If you have number of resources then tag help us to find the specific resource



Virtual Private Cloud

• It helps you to define in which amazon VPC you want to launch the instance.



Amazon EC2 Pricing

Amazon EC2 instances are priced per second according to five different options:



• On-demand (you can pay as per your demand like if you want service for 1hr then you can only able to pay for 1hr and then you can stop)  

• Spot instances (Spot Instances are useful for those applications that have flexible start and end time, discounted short-term capacity if available)  

• Savings Plans (commitment to a certain amount of usage)  

• Reserved Instances (discounted reserved long-term capacity, if your application is ready and you have long term plane then you can used this pricing)  

• Dedicated Hosts (A dedicated host is a physical server with EC2 instance capacity which is fully dedicated to your use., on-demand hourly or by reserved instances)

notes.content:
EC2 Interview Questions



🔹 Basic EC2 Concepts



1. What is Amazon EC2 and how does it work?

   Amazon EC2 (Elastic Compute Cloud) is a web service that provides resizable compute capacity in the cloud. It allows users to run virtual machines (instances) with different configurations. Users can scale up/down based on demand.



2. What are the different instance types in EC2? How do you choose the right one?

   Instance types include General Purpose (t2, t3), Compute Optimized (c5), Memory Optimized (r5), Storage Optimized (i3), etc. The choice depends on workload requirements such as CPU, memory, and IOPS.



3. What is an AMI and what does it contain?

   Amazon Machine Image (AMI) is a template that contains the software configuration (OS, application server, applications) required to launch an instance.



4. How do you launch an EC2 instance using the AWS Management Console and CLI?

   - Console: Go to EC2 Dashboard > Launch Instance > Select AMI > Choose Instance Type > Configure > Launch.  

   - CLI: Use `aws ec2 run-instances` with required parameters.



5. What is the difference between EC2 and EBS?

   EC2 is a virtual server; EBS (Elastic Block Store) is virtual disk storage attached to EC2 instances.





🔹 Security and Access



6. What are security groups in EC2? How do they differ from NACLs?

   Security groups act as virtual firewalls for instances to control inbound/outbound traffic. NACLs are stateless and operate at the subnet level.



7. What is a key pair in EC2, and why is it important?

   Key pairs (public/private) are used to securely SSH into EC2 instances. AWS stores the public key, and the user downloads the private key.



8. How would you SSH into an EC2 instance?

   Use the command `ssh -i <key.pem> ec2-user@<public-ip>` with the private key file and the instance’s public IP.



9. What is an Elastic IP? Why and when would you use it?

   An Elastic IP is a static public IPv4 address that can be associated with EC2 instances. It is used to maintain a fixed IP address despite instance stops/restarts.



10. How do you securely connect to your EC2 instance without exposing the private key?

    Use EC2 Instance Connect (browser-based), bastion host, or Systems Manager Session Manager.





🔹 Storage and Volumes



11. What is the difference between EBS and Instance Store?

    EBS is persistent and survives instance stop/start. Instance Store is temporary and data is lost if the instance is stopped/terminated.



12. Can you resize or modify an EBS volume attached to an EC2 instance? How?

    Yes, use the AWS Console or CLI to modify the volume, then use OS-level tools (like `resize2fs` for Linux) to resize the filesystem.



13. What are the steps to back up an EC2 instance?

    - Create an AMI  

    - Take EBS snapshots  

    - Use AWS Backup service



14. How can you automate the creation of AMIs from EC2?

    Use AWS CLI/SDK with automation tools like Lambda or scheduled tasks using AWS EventBridge.







🔹 Networking



15. What is a VPC and how does EC2 fit into it?

    A Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) is a virtual network. EC2 instances are launched inside subnets of a VPC, allowing control over networking.



16. How do you configure EC2 instances in public and private subnets?

    - Public subnet: Attach Internet Gateway and public IP  

    - Private subnet: Use NAT Gateway for internet access without exposing public IP



17. How does EC2 handle inbound and outbound traffic?

    Traffic is controlled using security groups (instance level) and NACLs (subnet level).







🔹 Scaling and Availability



18. What is an Auto Scaling Group (ASG) in EC2?

    ASG automatically scales EC2 instances in or out based on defined metrics (CPU, traffic, etc.) to maintain availability and performance.



19. How do you implement High Availability (HA) with EC2?

    Deploy EC2 instances across multiple Availability Zones (AZs), use Elastic Load Balancers (ELB), and Auto Scaling.



20. What is the role of Load Balancer in EC2 setup?

    Distributes incoming application traffic across multiple EC2 instances in different AZs for fault tolerance.



21. How does EC2 work with Route 53 for DNS routing?

    Route 53 routes user requests to EC2 instances using domain names, enabling geo-based routing, failover, and weighted load balancing.





🔹 Pricing and Cost Optimization



22. What are the different pricing models for EC2?

    - On-demand  

    - Spot Instances  

    - Reserved Instances  

    - Savings Plans  

    - Dedicated Hosts



23. When should you use Spot Instances over On-Demand?

    For fault-tolerant and flexible applications that can handle interruptions, such as big data and CI/CD jobs.



24. What are Reserved Instances and when would you use them?

    They offer significant discounts for long-term (1-3 years) workloads with predictable usage.



25. How do you monitor and optimize EC2 costs in DevOps projects?

    Use Cost Explorer, Budgets, CloudWatch metrics, Rightsizing recommendations, and automation for start/stop unused resources.



🔹 Automation & DevOps Integration



26. How do you provision EC2 instances using Terraform/CloudFormation?

    Define infrastructure as code using `.tf` or YAML/JSON templates, specifying instance type, AMI, and key pairs.



27. How do you install software or run scripts automatically on EC2?

    Use user data scripts during instance launch to install packages and configure the environment.



28. How do you integrate EC2 into a CI/CD pipeline (e.g., CodeDeploy)?

    Use AWS CodeDeploy with deployment groups tied to EC2 instances to automatically push application updates.



29. What are user data scripts and how are they used in EC2?

    User data scripts run at the first boot of an EC2 instance, often used for bootstrapping software.



30. How can Jenkins deploy code to EC2 instances?

    Use SSH or CodeDeploy plugins, configure credentials, and trigger deployment jobs from Jenkins pipelines.

notes.content:
AWS EC2 - Interview Study Notes

Beginner to Intermediate | Full-Stack / Backend Interview Focus



Goal of these notesUnderstand EC2 well enough to explain how a production application is launched, secured, stored, scaled, monitored, and cost-optimized in AWS.

1. What is Amazon EC2?

Amazon EC2 (Elastic Compute Cloud) provides resizable virtual compute capacity in AWS. An EC2 instance behaves like a virtual server where you choose the operating system, CPU/RAM class, networking, storage, security rules, and software you want to run.

Typical workloads: Spring Boot/Node.js APIs, web servers, background workers, batch jobs, CI/CD runners, and custom software.

You control the operating system and application. AWS manages the underlying physical infrastructure.

EC2 is an Infrastructure-as-a-Service (IaaS) compute service.



Typical highly available EC2 web architecture across multiple Availability Zones.

2. Core EC2 Launch Building Blocks

When launching an EC2 instance, think in terms of these building blocks:



The main choices involved when launching an EC2 instance.

Concept
	What to Remember

AMI
	The operating system / machine image used to boot the instance.

Instance Type
	Defines CPU, memory, networking capability, and other hardware characteristics.

VPC + Subnet
	Defines where the instance is placed in the AWS network.

Security Group
	Stateful virtual firewall attached to the instance/network interface.

Key Pair / Session Manager
	Ways to securely access the instance.

IAM Role
	Temporary AWS permissions for applications running on the instance.

User Data
	Bootstrap script or cloud-init configuration used at launch.

EBS
	Persistent block storage commonly used for the root disk and data volumes.

3. AMI (Amazon Machine Image)

An AMI is the image used to boot an EC2 instance. It contains the software configuration needed to start the machine.

Examples: Amazon Linux, Ubuntu, Windows Server, or a custom company image.

A custom AMI can contain your preinstalled runtime, agents, configuration, and application dependencies.

AMIs are Region-specific, but they can be copied to another Region.

A single AMI can be used to launch many identical instances.

Interview answerAMI is the template/image; EC2 instance is the running virtual machine created from that image.

4. EC2 Instance Types

An instance type determines the hardware resources available to your instance. You choose a family based on workload characteristics.

Category
	Designed For
	Examples of Workloads

General Purpose
	Balanced CPU, memory, networking
	Web/API servers, dev/test, small-medium apps

Compute Optimized
	Higher compute performance
	CPU-heavy services, encoding, batch compute

Memory Optimized
	Large memory footprint
	In-memory databases, caches, analytics

Storage Optimized
	High local storage throughput / IOPS
	Search, data processing, storage-heavy workloads

Accelerated Computing
	GPU / specialized accelerators
	ML training/inference, graphics, HPC

How to read an instance name

Example: m7g.large. The family letter indicates the workload family, the generation number indicates the generation, the suffix can indicate processor/platform characteristics, and the size (.large, .xlarge, etc.) indicates relative capacity.

Interview tipYou do not need to memorize every EC2 family. Know the major categories and explain how you would choose based on CPU, memory, network, and cost requirements.

5. EC2 Storage: EBS vs Instance Store

EC2 can use persistent EBS storage and, for some instance types, temporary local instance-store storage.

Feature
	EBS
	Instance Store

Persistence
	Persists independently of normal instance stop/start
	Data is tied to the physical host and is ephemeral

Common use
	Root volume, application data, databases
	Temporary caches, scratch data, buffers

Snapshot support
	Yes
	Not like EBS snapshots

Attach model
	Network-attached block storage in an AZ
	Local storage physically attached to host

After stop/start
	EBS data persists
	Instance-store data is lost

Common EBS volume types to know:

gp3 - general-purpose SSD; a common default choice.

io2 - provisioned IOPS SSD for demanding, latency-sensitive workloads.

st1 - throughput-optimized HDD for large sequential workloads.

sc1 - cold HDD for infrequently accessed, throughput-oriented data.

6. EC2 Networking Basics

Every EC2 instance is launched into a VPC and a subnet.

Private IPv4 address: used for communication inside the VPC.

Public IPv4 address: can provide internet reachability when routing and security are configured.

Elastic IP: a static public IPv4 address that can be associated with supported AWS resources.

ENI (Elastic Network Interface): a virtual network interface containing IP addresses, MAC address, and security groups.

Public subnet: route table typically has a route to an Internet Gateway.

Private subnet: no direct route to an Internet Gateway for inbound internet access; outbound internet access commonly uses NAT.

7. Security Groups

A security group acts as a stateful virtual firewall for EC2. Inbound rules control allowed incoming traffic, and outbound rules control allowed outgoing traffic.

Stateful: response traffic for an allowed connection is automatically permitted.

Rules are allow rules; security groups do not use explicit deny rules.

An instance can have multiple security groups.

Prefer security-group references between application tiers instead of broad CIDR ranges where practical.

Purpose
	Protocol
	Port
	Recommended Source

SSH to Linux
	TCP
	22
	Your office/VPN IP or controlled access path

RDP to Windows
	TCP
	3389
	Your office/VPN IP or controlled access path

HTTP
	TCP
	80
	ALB security group or required clients

HTTPS
	TCP
	443
	ALB security group or required clients

App Port
	TCP
	e.g. 8080
	Load balancer / upstream 

service security group

Custom tcp : any port number : for custom app ports

8. Connecting to EC2



Common secure access patterns for EC2.

Linux: SSH commonly uses a key pair. AWS stores the public key on the instance; you protect the private key.

Windows: the key pair can be used to decrypt the Administrator password, then connect by RDP.

Systems Manager Session Manager can provide interactive shell access without opening inbound SSH/RDP, if the instance is configured correctly.

Security best practiceAvoid opening SSH (22) or RDP (3389) to 0.0.0.0/0 in production. Restrict the source, use a VPN/bastion where needed, or prefer Systems Manager Session Manager.

9. IAM Role / Instance Profile

Applications on EC2 often need to access services such as S3, CloudWatch, SQS, DynamoDB, or Secrets Manager. Use an IAM role associated with the EC2 instance through an instance profile.

The application receives temporary AWS credentials automatically.

Do not hardcode long-lived AWS access keys inside the server or source code.

Apply least privilege: give the role only the permissions the application actually requires.

Common interview questionHow should an EC2 application access S3? Attach an IAM role/instance profile with the required S3 permissions instead of storing access keys on the server.

10. EC2 User Data

User data lets you provide launch-time instructions to an EC2 instance. On Linux, this is commonly a shell script or cloud-init configuration.

Install packages at startup.

Configure the application.

Download artifacts or configuration.

Start application services.

Useful with launch templates and Auto Scaling so replacement instances configure themselves consistently.

Simple example:

#!/bin/bashdnf install -y java-21-amazon-correttosystemctl enable myappsystemctl start myapp

ImportantDo not place passwords or long-lived secrets in user data. Instance metadata and user data can be visible to software or users that already have access to the instance.

11. Instance Metadata / IMDS

EC2 Instance Metadata Service (IMDS) provides information about the running instance from inside the instance, such as instance identity and temporary credentials associated with an IAM role.

IMDSv2 uses session-oriented requests and is the recommended secure configuration.

Applications and agents can use metadata without hardcoding instance-specific values.

Treat metadata access as security-sensitive; restrict unnecessary access from applications/containers.

12. EC2 Instance Lifecycle



The core EC2 instance states and common transitions.

Action
	Compute Billing
	EBS Data
	What Changes

Reboot
	Continues
	Persists
	Same instance; equivalent to OS reboot

Stop
	Instance compute not billed while stopped
	Persists
	Can start again; public IPv4 may change unless using Elastic IP

Hibernate
	Compute stops after hibernation completes
	Persists, including saved RAM to EBS
	Processes resume from saved memory when supported

Terminate
	Stops
	Root EBS is deleted by default unless configured otherwise
	Instance is permanently deleted



Very common interview distinctionStop is temporary and you can start the same instance again. Terminate permanently deletes the instance.

13. EC2 Pricing / Purchasing Options



Major EC2 purchasing options and when they fit.

Option
	Core Idea
	Best Fit

On-Demand
	No long-term commitment; pay for usage
	Short-term, unpredictable, dev/test, burst workloads

Savings Plans
	Commit to a consistent $/hour usage level for 1 or 3 years
	Steady baseline compute usage

Spot
	Uses spare EC2 capacity at large discount; can be interrupted
	Fault-tolerant batch, CI/CD, analytics, stateless workloads

Reserved Instances
	Commitment-based EC2 pricing tied more closely to instance configuration
	Existing workloads and some specific reservation needs

Dedicated Hosts / Instances
	Single-tenant hardware options
	Compliance, isolation, or software licensing requirements

Capacity Reservations
	Reserve EC2 capacity in a specific Availability Zone
	Workloads that must have capacity available when needed



2026 AWS guidance to rememberSavings Plans are generally the preferred flexible commitment-based discount model for many new EC2 workloads. Reserved Instances still exist and remain an interview topic, but do not confuse a pricing discount with a Capacity Reservation.

14. Spot Instances

Spot is cheap because AWS can reclaim the capacity when needed.

Use only for interruption-tolerant workloads.

Applications should checkpoint work, retry, and tolerate instance replacement.

Good examples: batch processing, CI runners, analytics, rendering, and stateless workers.

Do not place irreplaceable state only on the local instance.

15. EC2 Auto Scaling + Load Balancer



EC2 Auto Scaling adjusts instance count while a load balancer distributes traffic.

Launch Template defines how new EC2 instances should be launched.

Auto Scaling Group (ASG) manages desired, minimum, and maximum capacity.

Scale out: add instances when demand increases.

Scale in: remove instances when demand decreases.

ALB/ELB health checks and EC2 health checks help determine which instances should receive traffic or be replaced.

Distribute instances across multiple Availability Zones for higher availability.

16. Launch Templates

A Launch Template stores reusable EC2 launch configuration such as AMI, instance type, security groups, key pair, storage, IAM role, and user data.

Commonly used by Auto Scaling Groups.

Versioned, so configuration can evolve safely.

Helps create consistent replacement instances.

17. Monitoring EC2

Use CloudWatch and EC2 status checks to understand instance health and performance.

Common metrics: CPUUtilization, NetworkIn/Out, disk/EBS metrics, status-check metrics.

By default EC2 sends CloudWatch metrics at 5-minute intervals; detailed monitoring provides 1-minute intervals.

Memory and filesystem utilization usually require the CloudWatch Agent or another monitoring agent.

Use CloudWatch alarms for high CPU, status-check failures, or application thresholds.

EC2 Status Checks

Check
	What It Detects

System status check
	Underlying AWS host, power, or network infrastructure issues.

Instance status check
	Problems inside the individual VM such as OS/network configuration.

Attached EBS status check
	Issues with attached EBS reachability/health.

Application status check
	Optional HTTP/HTTPS application-level health monitoring.

18. EC2 + EBS Snapshots / AMIs

EBS snapshot = point-in-time backup of an EBS volume.

AMI = bootable machine image that can reference EBS snapshots for its volumes.

Use snapshots for backup and restore; use AMIs to launch similarly configured EC2 instances.

For consistent application-level backups, coordinate with the application/database as needed.

19. High Availability Pattern

Avoid designing a production application around one EC2 instance.

Deploy multiple EC2 instances.

Spread them across at least two Availability Zones where appropriate.

Place them behind an Application Load Balancer.

Use an Auto Scaling Group to maintain and scale capacity.

Keep application state external: RDS, ElastiCache, S3, EFS, etc., as appropriate.

Monitor with CloudWatch and alarms.

Key design principleAn EC2 instance should be replaceable. Production architectures become more resilient when servers are treated as disposable compute rather than a unique machine that cannot fail.

20. Common Interview Scenarios

Scenario: I cannot SSH to a Linux EC2 instance.

Check instance state -> correct IP/DNS -> route/Internet Gateway or private access path -> security group port 22 -> NACL -> key/user -> OS firewall/sshd. Consider Session Manager.

Scenario: The website on EC2 is not reachable.

Check ALB/target health if used -> security groups -> correct listener/port -> application process -> OS firewall -> subnet/route -> health-check path.

Scenario: CPU is constantly at 95%.

Use CloudWatch to confirm -> inspect application/process -> optimize -> choose a larger/more suitable instance type or scale horizontally with an Auto Scaling Group.

Scenario: Disk is full.

Identify filesystem usage -> increase EBS volume if needed -> extend partition/filesystem -> remove/rotate logs -> add monitoring and alarms.

Scenario: A Spot instance disappeared.

Spot is interruptible. Use fault-tolerant design, checkpoints, multiple capacity pools, Auto Scaling, and persistent/external storage.

Scenario: Need zero/low downtime during traffic spikes.

Use ALB + Auto Scaling across multiple AZs, health checks, stateless app servers, externalized session/data, and appropriate scaling policies.

Scenario: Application needs S3 access.

Attach an IAM role/instance profile with least-privilege S3 permissions; do not hardcode access keys.

21. EC2 vs Other AWS Compute Services

Service
	Abstraction
	You Manage
	Typical Use

EC2
	Virtual machine
	OS + runtime + app
	Maximum VM-level control

ECS on EC2
	Containers on EC2
	Cluster capacity + containers
	Containerized services

Fargate
	Serverless containers
	Containers/app
	Containers without managing EC2 hosts

Lambda
	Functions
	Function code/config
	Event-driven/serverless workloads

22. Must-Know EC2 Interview Questions

What is EC2?

What is an AMI?

AMI vs EC2 instance?

What is an instance type and how do you choose one?

What is the difference between EBS and instance store?

What happens when you stop an EC2 instance?

Stop vs reboot vs terminate?

What is a security group? Is it stateful?

How do you securely SSH to an EC2 instance?

Why use an IAM role instead of AWS access keys on EC2?

What is EC2 user data?

What is a Launch Template?

How do Auto Scaling and ELB work with EC2?

On-Demand vs Savings Plans vs Spot?

What is a Capacity Reservation?

How do you make an EC2-based app highly available?

How do you monitor EC2?

System status check vs instance status check?

Public IP vs Elastic IP?

What would you check if your EC2 app is unreachable?

23. Final EC2 Interview Cheat Sheet

Keyword
	One-Line Meaning

EC2
	AWS virtual server / resizable compute

AMI
	Boot image/template for EC2

Instance Type
	CPU + RAM + networking/hardware profile

EBS
	Persistent block storage

Instance Store
	Temporary local host storage

Security Group
	Stateful instance-level virtual firewall

Key Pair
	Public/private key credentials commonly used for SSH

IAM Role
	Temporary AWS permissions for the EC2 application

User Data
	Launch-time bootstrap/configuration script

Launch Template
	Reusable EC2 launch configuration

ALB + ASG
	Traffic distribution + automatic EC2 scaling

CloudWatch
	Metrics, alarms, monitoring

On-Demand
	Flexible pay-as-you-go

Savings Plans
	Usage commitment for lower cost

Spot
	Deep discount, interruptible capacity

Capacity Reservation
	Guarantees capacity in an AZ

Stop
	Compute off; EBS persists; instance can restart

Terminate
	Instance permanently deleted



If you are short on time, revise these firstEC2 basics -> AMI -> instance types -> EBS -> security groups -> IAM role -> user data -> lifecycle -> On-Demand/Savings Plans/Spot -> ALB + Auto Scaling -> CloudWatch.

24. AWS Documentation References

Amazon EC2 instance state changes - AWS EC2 User Guide

Amazon EC2 billing and purchasing options - AWS EC2 User Guide

Amazon EC2 security groups for your EC2 instances - AWS EC2 User Guide

Amazon EC2 AMI lifecycle - AWS EC2 User Guide

Amazon EC2 key pairs and Amazon EC2 instances - AWS EC2 User Guide

Run commands when you launch an EC2 instance with user data - AWS EC2 User Guide

Use instance profiles - AWS IAM User Guide

Monitor your instances using CloudWatch - AWS EC2 User Guide

Status checks for Amazon EC2 instances - AWS EC2 User Guide
