31. What IAM permissions does a basic SQS consumer need?

Answer: Typically sqs:ReceiveMessage, sqs:DeleteMessage, and sqs:ChangeMessageVisibility on the target queue. A producer normally needs sqs:SendMessage.

32. What is a receipt handle?

Answer: A temporary identifier returned when a message is received. It is used to delete or change visibility for that received copy and changes if the message is received again.

33. What metrics would you monitor?

Answer: ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible, ApproximateNumberOfMessagesNotVisible, ApproximateAgeOfOldestMessage, and message sent/received/deleted counts.

34. Why might FIFO processing be slow?

Answer: A hot MessageGroupId can serialize work because only one message from that group is processed at a time. Use multiple meaningful groups when business ordering allows it.

35. When should I choose Standard over FIFO?

Answer: Choose Standard for most high-throughput asynchronous work when strict ordering is not required. Choose FIFO only when ordering/deduplication requirements justify it.

30. Final SQS Interview Cheat Sheet

Keyword
	One-Line Meaning

SQS
	Managed message queue

Producer
	Sends messages

Consumer
	Receives/processes/deletes messages

Standard Queue
	At-least-once, best-effort ordering, very high throughput

FIFO Queue
	Strict order per group + deduplication features

MessageGroupId
	Ordering/parallelism boundary in FIFO

Deduplication ID
	Prevents duplicate sends within FIFO dedup window

Visibility Timeout
	Temporary hide after ReceiveMessage

Receipt Handle
	Token used to delete/change visibility

Long Polling
	Wait for messages; max 20 seconds

Retention
	1 minute-14 days; default 4 days

Max Message
	1 MiB

Delay Queue
	Initial delivery delay; max 15 minutes

DLQ
	Holds repeatedly failing messages

maxReceiveCount
	Receives before DLQ redrive

Idempotency
	Safe if same message is processed more than once

Lambda ESM
	Lambda service polls SQS and invokes function

Partial Batch
	Retry only failed Lambda batch records

SNS + SQS
	Fan-out + durable independent queues

CloudWatch
	Queue depth, in-flight count, age, alarms



If you are short on time, revise these firstWhat SQS is -> producer/consumer -> Standard vs FIFO -> at-least-once + idempotency -> visibility timeout -> Receive/Delete -> long polling -> retention -> DLQ -> Lambda integration -> SNS vs SQS -> interview Q&A.

31. Current AWS Notes Worth Remembering

SQS message size is currently up to 1 MiB; many older notes still say 256 KB.

Standard queues provide at-least-once delivery and best-effort ordering.

FIFO queues preserve order within MessageGroupId and provide deduplication/exactly-once processing features.

Long polling can wait up to 20 seconds.

Visibility timeout can be configured up to 12 hours; default is 30 seconds.

Message retention can be configured up to 14 days; default is 4 days.

Lambda event source mappings support partial batch responses for SQS.

FIFO queues can enable high-throughput mode when needed.

32. AWS Documentation References

Amazon SQS Developer Guide - What is Amazon SQS?

Amazon SQS standard queues

Amazon SQS FIFO queues

Amazon SQS visibility timeout

Amazon SQS short and long polling

Amazon SQS dead-letter queues

Amazon SQS queue configuration parameters and quotas

AWS Lambda - Using Lambda with Amazon SQS

AWS Lambda - Partial batch responses for SQS

notes.content:
AWS API Gateway - Interview Study Notes

Beginner-Friendly to Intermediate | Full-Stack / Backend Interview Focus

Goal of these notesUnderstand API Gateway from first principles: what it does, when to use it, API types, routes/resources, integrations, Lambda proxy flow, authorization, traffic management, CORS, stages, custom domains, monitoring, and common system-design/interview scenarios.

1. What is Amazon API Gateway?

Amazon API Gateway is a managed AWS service for creating, publishing, securing, monitoring, and managing HTTP, REST, and WebSocket APIs.

It acts as a front door between API clients and backend services.

Backends can include AWS Lambda, HTTP services, ECS/EC2 applications behind load balancers, and supported AWS services.

API Gateway handles API-management concerns so your backend can focus on business logic.

It scales as request traffic changes; you do not provision API Gateway servers.



The simplest mental model: client -> API Gateway -> backend service.

2. Why Do We Use API Gateway?

Expose a clean public API without exposing backend implementation details.

Route requests to Lambda, containers, EC2 services, or HTTP backends.

Apply authentication/authorization before traffic reaches the application.

Configure throttling and quotas to protect downstream services.

Support CORS for browser clients.

Publish separate stages such as dev, test, and prod.

Use a custom domain such as api.example.com.

Collect access logs and CloudWatch metrics.

Build RESTful APIs or real-time WebSocket APIs.

Beginner mental modelAPI Gateway is to APIs what a managed front desk/security/routing layer is to a building: it receives requests, checks rules, routes them, and returns responses.

3. API Gateway API Types



The first design decision is choosing HTTP API, REST API, or WebSocket API.

Type
	Communication
	Strength
	Typical Use

HTTP API
	HTTP request/response
	Simpler, lower-cost RESTful API
	Lambda/HTTP microservices, OAuth/JWT APIs

REST API
	HTTP request/response
	Most API-management features
	API keys, usage plans, caching, request validation, WAF, private API endpoints

WebSocket API
	Persistent bidirectional connection
	Backend can push messages to clients
	Chat, notifications, live dashboards, games

4. HTTP API vs REST API

Feature
	HTTP API
	REST API

Core RESTful routing
	Yes
	Yes

Lambda / HTTP integrations
	Yes
	Yes

JWT/OIDC authorizer
	Built in
	Commonly Cognito/Lambda/IAM patterns

Automatic CORS handling
	Yes
	More manual/configured

Automatic deployments
	Supported
	Deployment workflow is more explicit

API keys / usage plans
	No
	Yes

Per-client throttling quotas
	No
	Yes via usage plans

Request validation
	Limited compared with REST API
	Yes

API caching
	No built-in stage cache
	Yes

AWS WAF integration
	Not the same feature set
	Yes

Private API endpoint
	No
	Yes

Cost/complexity
	Lower / simpler
	Higher / more features

Interview answerUse HTTP API when you need a straightforward Lambda/HTTP API and do not need REST API's advanced API-management features. Use REST API when those extra features matter.

5. WebSocket API

WebSocket APIs are different from normal request/response APIs. A connection stays open, so the client and backend can send messages independently.

Useful when the server needs to push data to the client without polling.

Common routes include $connect, $disconnect, and $default plus custom message routes.

Typical use cases: chat apps, live notifications, collaboration, games, live financial/status updates.

HTTP vs WebSocketHTTP API/REST API: client sends request, server returns response. WebSocket: persistent two-way connection allows server push.

6. Core API Gateway Components



A request moves through a route/method, authorization, integration, deployment, and stage.

Concept
	Meaning

Resource
	REST API path object, such as /users.

Method
	REST API HTTP operation on a resource, such as GET /users.

Route
	HTTP/WebSocket API routing key, such as GET /users.

Integration
	Backend API Gateway invokes.

Deployment
	Point-in-time representation/snapshot of API configuration.

Stage
	Named environment/reference such as dev, test, prod, or $default.

7. Routes, Resources, and Methods

Suppose you are building an Orders API:

Request
	Meaning
	Possible Backend

GET /orders
	Fetch orders
	Lambda getOrders

POST /orders
	Create an order
	Lambda createOrder

GET /orders/{id}
	Fetch one order
	Lambda getOrder

DELETE /orders/{id}
	Delete order
	Lambda deleteOrder

Path parameters: /users/{id}

Query parameters: /users?page=2

Headers: Authorization, Content-Type, custom headers

Body: JSON payload for POST/PUT/PATCH

8. Integrations

An integration tells API Gateway where to send the request.

Integration
	Example
	When Used

Lambda
	API Gateway -> Lambda function
	Serverless APIs

HTTP/HTTP Proxy
	API Gateway -> public HTTP service
	Existing APIs/microservices

Private Integration
	API Gateway -> VPC Link -> ALB/NLB/private service
	Private ECS/EC2 services

AWS Service
	API Gateway -> supported AWS service action
	Direct service integrations in selected designs

Mock (REST API)
	API Gateway creates response without backend
	Testing/simple fixed responses

9. Lambda Proxy Integration



Proxy integration is the most common API Gateway + Lambda pattern.

API Gateway passes request information to Lambda as an event.

The event contains method/route information, headers, query parameters, path parameters, body, and request context.

Lambda runs the business logic.

Lambda returns a response that API Gateway converts to HTTP response data.

HTTP APIs support Lambda proxy payload format versions 1.0 and 2.0.

Why proxy integration is popularLess mapping configuration in API Gateway; the Lambda function receives the request context and has more control over the response.

10. Proxy vs Non-Proxy / Custom Integration

Area
	Proxy Integration
	Non-Proxy / Custom

Setup
	Simpler
	More configuration

Request mapping
	Request largely passed through in defined proxy format
	Explicit mapping templates/parameters

Response mapping
	Backend returns expected proxy response
	API Gateway maps integration response

Use case
	Most Lambda/HTTP APIs
	Legacy/special transformations and strict mappings

11. Authentication and Authorization



Protect APIs at the gateway rather than implementing every auth check independently in each backend.

Option
	Best For
	How It Works

AWS IAM
	AWS-to-AWS/service access
	Requests are signed with AWS SigV4 credentials.

JWT Authorizer
	HTTP APIs with OAuth 2.0/OIDC
	API Gateway validates JWT issuer/audience/scopes.

Amazon Cognito
	User authentication in AWS-centric apps
	Cognito issues user tokens used to protect API routes/methods.

Lambda Authorizer
	Custom auth rules
	API Gateway invokes Lambda to make authorization decision.

NONE
	Public endpoint
	No gateway-level auth; use only intentionally.

12. API Keys and Usage Plans

REST APIs support API keys and usage plans.

API keys identify API consumers/clients.

Usage plans associate API keys with deployed stages and can configure throttling and quotas.

Do NOT use an API key as your only authentication/authorization mechanism.

API keys can appear in headers/logs and are not equivalent to a user identity/token.

Interview trapAPI key answers 'which client/consumer is this for usage-plan purposes?' It does not securely answer 'who is the user and what are they authorized to do?'

13. Throttling



Throttling is protection against excessive request rate; REST caching is a separate performance feature.

Throttling limits request rate and burst traffic.

When limits are exceeded, API Gateway can return HTTP 429 Too Many Requests.

There are service/account-level throttling considerations.

REST API usage plans can add per-client throttling/quotas using API keys.

Throttling protects backend capacity but should not be treated as a complete cost-control/security mechanism.

14. Caching

REST APIs can use API Gateway stage/method caching.

A cache hit can return a stored response without invoking the backend.

This can reduce backend load and latency for cacheable GET-style requests.

Caching has additional cost and requires correct cache keys/TTL/invalidation design.

HTTP APIs do not provide the same built-in stage cache feature.

When not to cacheAvoid blindly caching personalized, frequently changing, or authorization-sensitive responses unless cache keys and security behavior are carefully designed.

15. CORS

CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing) is a browser security mechanism. It matters when frontend JavaScript calls an API hosted on a different origin.

Example frontend: https://app.example.com

Example API: https://api.example.com

The browser may send an OPTIONS preflight request before the real request.

HTTP APIs have built-in CORS configuration and can automatically respond to preflight requests.

Configure allowed origins, methods, headers, and credentials carefully.

Common debugging issueA backend can work perfectly in Postman/curl but fail in a browser because CORS is enforced by browsers, not by Postman.

16. Stages and Deployments



Stages let the same API definition be published as dev/test/prod environments.

Deployment = a publishable point-in-time API configuration.

Stage = named environment/reference such as dev, test, prod.

REST API changes normally must be deployed to a stage before clients see them.

HTTP APIs can use automatic deployments, especially with a $default stage.

Stage variables/settings can differ by environment.

17. Custom Domain Names

Default API URL is generated by API Gateway and is not very friendly.

Custom domain example: https://api.example.com

Use an ACM TLS certificate for HTTPS.

Create DNS mapping, commonly with Route 53, to the API Gateway domain.

Map a base path/API mapping to a particular API and stage.

Typical architectureRoute 53 DNS -> API Gateway custom domain -> API stage -> integration.

18. Endpoint Types and Private APIs

For REST APIs, endpoint type controls how clients reach API Gateway.

REST API Endpoint
	Meaning
	Typical Use

Regional
	API endpoint in one AWS Region
	Most modern public API designs

Edge-Optimized
	Traffic enters through CloudFront edge network
	Historically useful for geographically distributed clients

Private
	Accessible privately from VPC through interface VPC endpoint
	Internal/private REST API

Do not confusePrivate API endpoint = clients reach API Gateway privately. Private integration = API Gateway reaches a private backend through a VPC Link. These solve different sides of the connection.

19. Private Integrations and VPC Link



VPC Link lets API Gateway reach private backends such as ALB/NLB or ECS services.

Useful when your backend should stay in private subnets.

HTTP APIs and REST APIs can use modern VPC link private integrations.

A common flow is API Gateway -> VPC Link -> ALB/NLB -> ECS/EC2 service.

HTTP API private integrations can also integrate through AWS Cloud Map in supported architectures.

The backend itself does not need a public internet-facing endpoint.

20. Request / Response Transformation and Validation

REST APIs support request validation for parameters and request bodies.

API Gateway can transform headers, query strings, paths, and payloads depending on API type/integration.

REST non-proxy integrations can use mapping templates for more explicit transformations.

Keep transformations simple where possible; complex business logic belongs in the backend.

Design principleAPI Gateway should enforce API-level concerns. Business rules such as pricing, inventory, and transaction logic belong in application services.

21. Monitoring and Logging

Use CloudWatch metrics to monitor request counts, latency, errors, and throttling.

Enable access logging with useful request context fields.

REST APIs can use execution logging for deeper API Gateway execution details.

Use AWS X-Ray where supported/appropriate for tracing REST API requests.

Monitor 4XX and 5XX error rates with CloudWatch alarms.

Metric / Signal
	What It Suggests

4XX errors
	Client request, auth, validation, route, or throttling problems

5XX errors
	Gateway/integration/backend failures

Latency
	Total time client waits at API layer

Integration latency
	Time spent waiting on backend integration

429 responses
	Throttling limit exceeded

22. Common HTTP Status Codes

Code
	Meaning
	Common API Gateway Context

200
	Success
	Backend returned successful result

400
	Bad Request
	Invalid payload/parameters

401
	Unauthorized
	Authentication/token problem

403
	Forbidden
	Authenticated but not allowed, IAM/policy/authorizer issue

404
	Not Found
	Wrong route/resource or application result

429
	Too Many Requests
	Throttling

500
	Internal Server Error
	Backend/integration failure

502
	Bad Gateway
	Invalid integration response / backend proxy issue

504
	Gateway Timeout
	Integration/backend did not respond in time

23. API Gateway + Lambda Typical Architecture

1.  Frontend calls POST /orders.

2.  API Gateway checks CORS and authorization.

3.  API Gateway routes POST /orders to the Lambda integration.

4.  Lambda validates business data and calls DynamoDB/RDS/other services.

5.  Lambda returns status and response body.

6.  API Gateway sends HTTP response to client.

Good serverless patternAPI Gateway handles API management; Lambda handles business logic; DynamoDB/RDS stores data; IAM controls service permissions; CloudWatch monitors the stack.

24. API Gateway + ECS / EC2 Architecture

1.  Client calls API Gateway.

2.  API Gateway authenticates/throttles/routes the request.

VPC Link sends request to a private ALB/NLB.

4.  Load balancer sends traffic to ECS tasks or EC2 instances.

5.  Application returns response through the same path.

Why add API Gateway if ALB already exists?API Gateway adds API-specific capabilities such as authorizers, API keys/usage plans, request management, stages, custom API publishing, and API-focused observability. ALB focuses primarily on load balancing Layer-7 traffic.

25. API Gateway vs Application Load Balancer (ALB)

Area
	API Gateway
	ALB

Primary purpose
	API management/front door
	Load balancing for applications

Backends
	Lambda, HTTP, AWS services, private integrations
	EC2, ECS, IP, Lambda

Auth
	IAM/JWT/Cognito/Lambda authorizers
	OIDC/Cognito authentication options, SG/network controls

API keys/usage plans
	REST API supports
	No

Stages/deployments
	Yes
	No API lifecycle concept

Caching
	REST API caching
	No built-in API response cache

WebSocket
	API Gateway WebSocket APIs
	ALB supports WebSockets as HTTP upgrade

Best fit
	Managed APIs/serverless/API products
	Web apps, services, load balancing

26. API Gateway vs Lambda Function URL

Area
	API Gateway
	Lambda Function URL

Routing
	Multiple routes/services
	One Lambda function endpoint

Authorization
	Many options
	Simpler NONE or AWS_IAM model

API management
	Rich
	Minimal

Custom domains
	Supported through API Gateway
	Not the same built-in API Gateway domain feature

Use case
	Production API platform
	Simple webhook / small single-function endpoint

Interview shortcutFunction URL is the simpler direct Lambda endpoint. API Gateway is the fuller API-management layer.

27. Common Interview Scenarios

Scenario: Need a cheap simple Lambda RESTful API.

Start with an HTTP API unless you need REST API-only features.

Scenario: Need API keys, usage plans and per-client quotas.

Use a REST API.

Scenario: Need OAuth/JWT authorization for an HTTP API.

Use an HTTP API JWT authorizer.

Scenario: Need custom authorization logic.

Use a Lambda authorizer.

Scenario: Frontend gets a CORS error but Postman works.

Configure CORS/OPTIONS behavior and allowed origin/method/header values.

Scenario: Backend ECS service must remain private.

Use API Gateway private integration through a VPC Link to ALB/NLB/service discovery.

Scenario: One API consumer is overloading your backend.

Use throttling; for REST APIs, usage plans can add per-client limits.

Scenario: Repeated GET endpoint is expensive.

For REST APIs, consider API caching if the response is safely cacheable.

Scenario: Need internal API reachable only from VPC.

Consider a private REST API endpoint.

Scenario: Need chat/live notifications.

Use API Gateway WebSocket API.

28. Troubleshooting Checklist

1.  Confirm the client is calling the correct API endpoint, stage, route/path, and HTTP method.

2.  Check authorization: token, IAM signature, authorizer configuration, and permissions.

3.  Check CORS if failure occurs only in a browser.

4.  Check API Gateway access/execution logs and CloudWatch metrics.

5.  Check integration configuration and backend permissions.

6.  For Lambda, check Lambda logs and returned proxy-response format.

7.  For private integrations, check VPC Link state, load balancer listener, target health, routing, and security groups.

8.  Check throttling if clients receive HTTP 429.

9.  Check timeout/latency if requests end in 504 or slow responses.

29. Interview Questions with Answers

1. What is Amazon API Gateway?

Answer: API Gateway is a managed AWS service used to create, publish, secure, monitor, and manage REST, HTTP, and WebSocket APIs. It acts as a front door between clients and backend services such as Lambda, HTTP applications, ECS/EC2 services, and supported AWS services.

2. Why would you use API Gateway in front of Lambda?

Answer: It gives the Lambda function an HTTP API endpoint and adds routing, authorization, CORS, throttling, stages, custom domains, and monitoring. Lambda focuses on business logic while API Gateway manages the API layer.

3. What are the three major API Gateway API types?

Answer: HTTP API, REST API, and WebSocket API. HTTP and REST APIs use request/response HTTP communication, while WebSocket APIs provide persistent bidirectional communication.

4. HTTP API vs REST API - what is the main difference?

Answer: HTTP APIs are simpler and generally lower cost. REST APIs provide more API-management features such as API keys/usage plans, per-client throttling, request validation, caching, WAF integration, and private API endpoints.

5. What is a route in API Gateway?

Answer: A route maps an incoming request pattern to an integration. For an HTTP API, an example route is GET /users. In REST APIs, the similar model is resource + method.

6. What is an integration?

Answer: The integration is the backend API Gateway invokes after a request matches a route/method. Examples include Lambda, an HTTP endpoint, a VPC Link private backend, or a supported AWS service.

7. What is Lambda proxy integration?

Answer: It is an integration where API Gateway sends request information to Lambda in a defined event structure and Lambda returns a proxy-formatted result containing the HTTP status, headers, and body.

8. What is a stage?

Answer: A stage is a named environment or reference through which a deployed API is invoked, such as dev, test, or prod. A stage can have its own settings and URL mapping.

9. Deployment vs stage?

Answer: A deployment is a point-in-time publishable API configuration. A stage is the named environment/reference that points to a deployment and exposes it to clients.

10. What authorization methods can API Gateway use?

Answer: Depending on API type, common options include AWS IAM authorization, JWT/OIDC authorization, Amazon Cognito, and Lambda authorizers for custom rules.

11. Is an API key an authentication mechanism?

Answer: No. API keys are primarily used to identify API consumers for REST API usage plans and metering/throttling. Use IAM, JWT/Cognito, or a Lambda authorizer for real authentication/authorization.

12. What is a Lambda authorizer?

Answer: A Lambda authorizer is a Lambda function invoked by API Gateway to run custom authorization logic and decide whether a request should be allowed.

13. What is throttling?

Answer: Throttling limits request rate/burst traffic to protect API Gateway and downstream backends. Requests above the allowed rate can receive HTTP 429 Too Many Requests.

14. What are usage plans?

Answer: REST API usage plans associate API keys with API stages and optionally configure client-specific request throttling and quotas.

15. What is API Gateway caching?

Answer: REST API caching stores integration responses at the API Gateway stage/method layer. A cache hit can return a response without invoking the backend, reducing latency and backend load.

16. What is CORS?

Answer: CORS is a browser security mechanism controlling whether frontend JavaScript from one origin can call an API at another origin. API Gateway must return appropriate Access-Control-* headers and sometimes handle OPTIONS preflight requests.

17. Why can an API work in Postman but fail in the browser?

Answer: A common reason is CORS. Browsers enforce CORS rules while tools such as Postman usually do not.

18. What is a VPC Link?

Answer: A VPC Link lets API Gateway integrate with private resources inside a VPC, commonly through an ALB or NLB, so the backend does not need to be publicly accessible.

19. Private API vs private integration?

Answer: A private REST API controls how clients privately reach API Gateway. A private integration controls how API Gateway reaches a private backend through a VPC Link. They solve opposite sides of the request path.

20. What is a custom domain in API Gateway?

Answer: It replaces the generated execute-api URL with a friendly hostname such as api.example.com. You typically use an ACM certificate and DNS mapping, then map the domain/path to an API stage.

21. API Gateway vs ALB?

Answer: API Gateway is an API-management service with routes, authorizers, stages, usage plans, and API publishing features. ALB is primarily a Layer-7 load balancer for distributing HTTP/HTTPS traffic across application targets.

22. API Gateway vs Lambda Function URL?

Answer: A Lambda Function URL is a simpler direct HTTP endpoint for one Lambda function. API Gateway supports richer routing, authorization choices, API lifecycle, custom domains, multiple backends, throttling, and API-management features.

23. When would you use a WebSocket API?

Answer: Use it when you need persistent two-way communication or server push, such as chat, notifications, live dashboards, collaboration, or multiplayer applications.

24. How would you secure a public API?

Answer: Use HTTPS, appropriate authorization (IAM/JWT/Cognito/Lambda authorizer), least-privilege backend IAM permissions, throttling, validation, logging/monitoring, and where applicable AWS WAF. Do not rely on API keys alone for security.

25. What would you check if API Gateway returns 502?

Answer: Check the backend/integration response format, Lambda errors, permissions, integration configuration, and logs. For Lambda proxy integration, malformed Lambda responses are a common cause.

26. What would you check for 504 Gateway Timeout?

Answer: Check backend response time, integration timeout behavior, downstream dependencies, database calls, network paths, and whether the operation should be asynchronous instead of a long synchronous API request.

27. How can API Gateway call a private ECS service?

Answer: Create a private integration using a VPC Link, connect the API route to an ALB/NLB or supported service-discovery target, then route traffic to the private ECS tasks.

28. Can API Gateway directly perform business logic?

Answer: It can perform API-level routing, transformations, validation, authorization, and some direct AWS service integrations, but complex business logic should normally live in Lambda or application services.

29. How do you monitor API Gateway?

Answer: Use CloudWatch metrics and alarms, access logs, REST API execution logs where appropriate, backend logs such as Lambda CloudWatch Logs, and tracing such as X-Ray where supported.

30. Which API type should I choose in a normal serverless interview scenario?

Answer: If the requirements are a simple Lambda/HTTP RESTful API, HTTP API is a strong starting point. Choose REST API when requirements explicitly need its advanced features. Choose WebSocket API for persistent bidirectional communication.

30. Final API Gateway Interview Cheat Sheet

Keyword
	One-Line Meaning

API Gateway
	Managed front door/API-management service

HTTP API
	Simpler/lower-cost RESTful API product

REST API
	Feature-rich API management

WebSocket API
	Persistent bidirectional API

Route
	Incoming method/path mapped to integration

Resource + Method
	REST API routing model

Integration
	Backend invoked by API Gateway

Lambda Proxy
	Pass request context to Lambda and return proxy response

Deployment
	Point-in-time API configuration

Stage
	dev/test/prod published environment

IAM Auth
	AWS-signed request authorization

JWT Authorizer
	Validate OAuth/OIDC JWT tokens

Lambda Authorizer
	Custom authorization logic

API Key
	Client identifier for REST usage plans - not authentication

Usage Plan
	REST API API-key quotas/throttling

Throttling
	Limit request rate/burst; excess can return 429

REST Cache
	Cache responses to reduce backend calls

CORS
	Browser cross-origin access rules

Custom Domain
	Friendly API hostname

VPC Link
	Connect API Gateway to private VPC backend

Private REST API
	API Gateway endpoint privately reachable from VPC

CloudWatch
	Metrics, alarms, and logs

429
	Throttled

502
	Bad integration/backend response

504
	Backend/integration timeout



If you are short on time, revise these firstWhat API Gateway is -> HTTP vs REST vs WebSocket -> route/resource/method -> integrations -> Lambda proxy -> authorization -> API keys are not auth -> throttling -> CORS -> stages/deployments -> VPC Link -> API Gateway vs ALB -> interview Q&A.

31. Current AWS Notes Worth Remembering

HTTP APIs are intentionally simpler and lower-feature than REST APIs.

REST APIs support API keys/usage plans, request validation, caching, AWS WAF integration, and private API endpoints.

HTTP APIs support built-in CORS configuration, JWT/OIDC authorization, and automatic deployments.

Modern VPC Link V2 private integrations can connect HTTP and REST APIs to private ALB/NLB resources; HTTP APIs also support AWS Cloud Map integrations.

API keys should not be used as the sole authentication/authorization mechanism.

32. AWS Documentation References

Amazon API Gateway Developer Guide - What is Amazon API Gateway?

Choose between REST APIs and HTTP APIs

API Gateway HTTP APIs

API Gateway REST APIs

API Gateway WebSocket APIs

Lambda integrations / Lambda proxy integrations

Usage plans and API keys for REST APIs

Throttle requests to REST APIs

CORS for HTTP APIs and REST APIs

Stages and deployments

Custom domain names and API mappings

Private integrations and VPC links

notes.content:
AWS ECS - Interview Study Notes

Beginner to Intermediate | Full-Stack / Backend Interview Focus

Goal of these notesUnderstand how Amazon ECS runs containers, how task definitions/services/clusters fit together, Fargate vs EC2, networking, IAM, scaling, deployments, logging, and common production interview scenarios.

1. What is Amazon ECS?

Amazon Elastic Container Service (ECS) is AWS's managed container orchestration service. You provide container images and configuration; ECS schedules, runs, monitors, replaces, and scales container tasks on supported compute capacity.

ECS is an orchestrator. Docker builds/runs containers; ECS coordinates containers across compute infrastructure.

Common workloads: REST APIs, Spring Boot/Node services, microservices, workers, scheduled jobs, and background consumers.

ECS integrates with ECR, IAM, VPC, ALB/NLB, CloudWatch, Auto Scaling, Secrets Manager, and other AWS services.

Simple interview definitionECS is AWS's managed container orchestration service for deploying and operating Docker/container workloads without managing your own Kubernetes control plane.



A typical ECS flow from container image to running service tasks.

2. ECS Core Building Blocks



Cluster, Task Definition, Task, and Service are the four concepts you must distinguish clearly.

Concept
	What to Remember

Cluster
	Logical grouping/boundary for services, tasks and capacity.

Task Definition
	Versioned blueprint describing one or more containers.

Task
	A running instantiation of a task definition.

Service
	Maintains a desired number of tasks and handles deployments/replacements.

Standalone Task
	Run-to-completion or one-off task not continuously maintained by a service.

Memorize thisTask Definition = blueprint. Task = running copy. Service = keeps N copies running.

3. Container Image and Amazon ECR

Your application is packaged as a container image.

Amazon ECR is AWS's managed container image registry and is commonly used with ECS.

Typical CI/CD flow: build image -> tag image -> push to ECR -> register new task definition revision -> deploy ECS service.

Use immutable image tags or image digests in disciplined production pipelines to make deployments reproducible.

4. ECS Compute Options



ECS can run tasks on multiple compute models. Fargate vs EC2 is the core interview comparison.

Feature
	Fargate
	ECS on EC2
	ECS Managed Instances

Infrastructure
	AWS manages servers
	You manage EC2 fleet
	AWS manages EC2-backed infrastructure

Control
	Less host-level control
	Maximum host control
	EC2 variety with less infrastructure work

Billing model
	Task CPU/memory/runtime
	EC2 instance capacity
	Managed compute + EC2-style capabilities

Good for
	Most standard container services
	Specialized hosts, GPUs, custom tuning, high utilization
	Need specialized EC2 capabilities but less fleet management

Networking
	awsvpc required
	awsvpc/bridge/host/none (OS-dependent)
	awsvpc/host depending on configuration

Interview shortcutFargate = less infrastructure management. ECS on EC2 = more control and potentially more tuning/cost optimization responsibility.

5. Task Definition

A task definition is a versioned JSON blueprint for the containers in an ECS task.



The task definition contains runtime, networking, security, logging, and container configuration.

Family + revision: e.g. orders-api:17.

Container image URI, CPU/memory, command/entry point, environment variables and port mappings.

Task role and task execution role.

Logging configuration such as awslogs to CloudWatch Logs.

Secrets from Secrets Manager or Systems Manager Parameter Store.

Health checks and volumes where needed.

ImportantRegistering a new task definition creates a new revision. Existing running tasks do not magically change until you deploy/run the new revision.

6. ECS Service

An ECS service is used for long-running applications. The ECS service scheduler maintains the desired number of healthy tasks.

Desired count = how many task replicas you want running.

If a task crashes, the service launches a replacement.

A service can integrate with ALB/NLB and service discovery.

Updating the service to a new task definition revision starts a deployment.

ExampleDesired count = 3. One task crashes. ECS service detects the loss and launches another task to return to 3.

7. Fargate Networking and awsvpc



A common production pattern: public ALB, private ECS tasks, security-group-to-security-group access.

Fargate tasks always use awsvpc network mode.

With awsvpc, each task gets its own elastic network interface (ENI), private IP, and security groups.

For private-subnet tasks that need internet access, use NAT or suitable VPC endpoints depending on the dependency.

For ECR image pulls without general internet access, VPC endpoints can be used for relevant AWS services.

Interview architectureInternet -> ALB in public subnets -> ECS tasks in private subnets -> RDS/ElastiCache in private subnets.

8. ECS on EC2 Networking Modes

Mode
	How It Works
	Interview Note

awsvpc
	Task gets its own ENI/IP
	Recommended unless you specifically need another mode.

bridge
	Docker bridge network on EC2 host
	Supports dynamic host port mapping; common older EC2 pattern.

host
	Container uses host network stack
	High performance but port conflicts limit placement.

none
	No external networking
	Rare/specialized use.

9. Load Balancer Integration

Application Load Balancer is common for HTTP/HTTPS microservices.

ECS registers healthy service tasks into an ALB target group.

ALB health checks determine whether a task should receive traffic.

Path/host rules can route different URLs/domains to different ECS services.

Network Load Balancer is useful for Layer-4/TCP/UDP/TLS style workloads.

Example/users/* -> User ECS service target group; /orders/* -> Order ECS service target group.

10. Health Checks

Container health check: command defined in the task definition runs inside the container.

Load balancer health check: ALB/NLB probes the registered target.

ECS uses service/task health signals to replace unhealthy tasks.

Health endpoints should verify the application is ready to serve traffic, not merely that the process exists.

11. ECS IAM Roles



The task role and task execution role solve different permission problems.

Role
	Used By
	Typical Permissions

Task Role
	Application code inside container
	S3, DynamoDB, SQS, SNS, Secrets APIs as required

Task Execution Role
	ECS agent/platform on task's behalf
	Pull private ECR image, write logs, fetch referenced secrets

Container Instance Role
	EC2 hosts when using ECS on EC2
	Register EC2 host with cluster and agent operations

Most asked IAM questionTask execution role = ECS/platform actions. Task role = your application's AWS API permissions.

12. Secrets and Configuration

Non-sensitive configuration can be environment variables.

Sensitive values should come from Secrets Manager or Systems Manager Parameter Store rather than baked into the image.

The task execution role may need permission to retrieve secrets referenced by the task definition.

Application-specific runtime AWS access should use the task role.

13. ECS Service Auto Scaling



Two different scaling problems: number of tasks vs amount of EC2 host capacity.

Service Auto Scaling changes the ECS service desired task count.

It uses Application Auto Scaling and CloudWatch metrics.

Target tracking is usually the simplest option: maintain CPU, memory, or another supported metric around a target value.

Step scaling and scheduled scaling are also available; predictive scaling exists for suitable patterns.

Example: average CPU > target -> add tasks. Demand falls -> remove tasks within configured min/max limits.

14. ECS Cluster Auto Scaling (EC2)

When ECS runs on EC2, adding more tasks does not help if the cluster lacks CPU/memory capacity. Capacity providers can integrate ECS with an EC2 Auto Scaling Group.

Service Auto Scaling: changes task count.

Cluster Auto Scaling: changes EC2 container-instance count.

Capacity provider managed scaling can add/remove EC2 instances based on task demand and capacity reservation.

Classic interview trapTask scaling and host scaling are separate concerns on ECS/EC2. Fargate removes most host-capacity management from you.

15. Capacity Providers

Capacity providers let ECS decide which compute capacity should run tasks and can manage scaling strategies.

Fargate and Fargate Spot can be used through capacity-provider strategies.

For ECS on EC2, a capacity provider can be associated with an EC2 Auto Scaling Group.

Strategies can use base and weight values to distribute tasks among capacity providers.

16. Fargate Spot

Runs eligible Fargate tasks on spare AWS capacity for a lower price.

Tasks can be interrupted, so workloads must tolerate replacement.

Good for stateless workers, batch processing, asynchronous consumers, and fault-tolerant services.

Use normal Fargate for baseline capacity and Fargate Spot for cost-optimized extra capacity when appropriate.

17. ECS Deployment Strategies



Rolling and blue/green are the main interview topics; ECS also supports newer native traffic-shifting strategies.

Strategy
	Behavior
	Use

Rolling
	Gradually replaces old tasks with new tasks
	Default/common balance of safety and resource efficiency

Blue/Green
	Runs old and new revisions separately, then switches traffic
	Validation before production and quick rollback

Canary
	Shifts a small percentage first, then the remainder
	Reduce risk by testing with limited production traffic

Linear
	Moves traffic in equal increments over time
	Gradual controlled rollout

Interview focusBe strongest on rolling vs blue/green. Know canary and linear as current ECS-native options.

18. Rolling Deployment Controls

minimumHealthyPercent controls how many existing healthy tasks must remain during a rolling deployment.

maximumPercent controls how many total tasks may temporarily run above desired count during deployment.

New tasks typically start receiving load balancer traffic after they become healthy.

Deployment circuit breaker/rollback features can help recover from failed deployments.

19. Service Discovery and Service Connect

Not every service-to-service call should go through a public load balancer.

AWS Cloud Map can provide service discovery using DNS.

ECS Service Connect provides managed service-to-service connectivity, discovery and traffic features for ECS services.

For a beginner/intermediate full-stack interview, know the purpose; deep configuration is usually unnecessary.

20. Persistent Storage

Storage
	Use
	Notes

Container / ephemeral storage
	Temporary files, caches, scratch space
	Do not keep irreplaceable state only inside the task.

Amazon EFS
	Shared POSIX filesystem
	Useful when multiple tasks need shared persistent files.

Amazon EBS
	Block volume attached to supported ECS tasks
	Useful for stateful/specialized workloads; requires appropriate ECS infrastructure configuration.

S3
	Object storage outside container
	Best for files/objects rather than mounted POSIX disk semantics.

Design principleTreat ECS tasks as replaceable. Put durable state in services such as RDS, DynamoDB, S3, EFS, or other appropriate storage.

21. Logging and Monitoring

awslogs log driver commonly sends container stdout/stderr to CloudWatch Logs.

CloudWatch metrics can monitor CPU, memory, running/pending task count and service-level health.

Container Insights provides deeper ECS/container observability when enabled.

Use CloudWatch alarms for service availability and scaling signals.

Use CloudTrail to audit ECS API changes and deployments.

22. ECS Exec

ECS Exec lets authorized operators run commands inside a running container for debugging without opening SSH to the task.

It integrates with AWS Systems Manager Session Manager mechanisms and IAM authorization.

It must be enabled/configured correctly on the service/task and requires appropriate permissions.

Use it for controlled debugging, not as a substitute for proper logs, metrics, or immutable deployments.

23. ECS vs EKS vs EC2 vs Lambda

Service
	Model
	Best When
	You Manage

ECS
	AWS-native container orchestration
	You want containers without Kubernetes complexity
	Task/service config; compute depends on Fargate vs EC2

EKS
	Managed Kubernetes
	Kubernetes APIs/ecosystem are required
	Kubernetes workload/config and possibly worker capacity

EC2
	Virtual machines
	Need VM/OS-level control
	OS, runtime, app and scaling architecture

Lambda
	Functions/serverless
	Short event-driven functions with serverless execution
	Function code/config, not servers

24. ECS vs Docker

Docker/container runtime builds and runs containers.

ECS orchestrates containers: placement, desired count, health replacement, deployments, networking integration, IAM integration and scaling.

Simple answerDocker runs a container. ECS operates containerized applications at service/cluster scale.

25. Common Interview Scenarios

Scenario: Task keeps stopping immediately.

Check stopped reason -> application exit code/logs -> task definition CPU/memory -> environment/secrets -> image/command -> IAM/network dependencies.

Scenario: ALB returns 503 for ECS service.

Check service has running tasks -> target group registrations -> health-check path/port -> security groups -> application listens on correct container port.

Scenario: Fargate task in private subnet cannot pull ECR image.

Check route to NAT or required ECR/S3 VPC endpoints, DNS, security/NACL rules and task execution role permissions.

Scenario: App inside task gets AccessDenied to S3.

Check task role, not task execution role, and verify least-privilege S3 permissions/resource ARN.

Scenario: Service CPU is high.

Use ECS Service Auto Scaling to increase desired tasks; also investigate app bottleneck and downstream limits.

Scenario: ECS on EC2 has pending tasks despite service scaling.

Cluster may lack host capacity; inspect task placement/resource requirements and capacity provider/EC2 Auto Scaling.

Scenario: Need zero/very low downtime deployment with easy rollback.

Use blue/green or another controlled traffic-shifting strategy with health validation.

Scenario: Need shell access to debug a Fargate container.

Use ECS Exec with appropriate IAM/SSM configuration instead of SSH.

26. Troubleshooting a Pending or Stopped Task

Check ECS service events and the task stopped reason.

Confirm image exists and task execution role can pull it.

Check CPU/memory values and available capacity (especially ECS on EC2).

Check subnet, route table, security group, DNS and required endpoints/NAT.

Check secrets/configuration permissions.

Check application command, environment and logs.

Check load balancer target health and container port mapping if service is behind ALB/NLB.

27. Must-Know ECS Interview Questions

What is ECS?

ECS vs Docker?

Cluster vs Task Definition vs Task vs Service?

What is a desired count?

Fargate vs ECS on EC2?

What is ECS Managed Instances?

What is a task definition revision?

Task role vs task execution role?

How does ECS integrate with ECR?

Why does Fargate require awsvpc?

How does an ALB route to ECS tasks?

How do health checks work?

Service Auto Scaling vs Cluster Auto Scaling?

What is a capacity provider?

What is Fargate Spot?

Rolling vs blue/green deployment?

What is minimumHealthyPercent / maximumPercent?

How should ECS containers store secrets?

How do ECS tasks get persistent storage?

What is ECS Exec?

ECS vs EKS?

How would you troubleshoot a task that keeps stopping?

28. Final ECS Interview Cheat Sheet

Keyword
	One-Line Meaning

ECS
	AWS managed container orchestration

Cluster
	Logical group/boundary for ECS workloads and capacity

Task Definition
	Versioned container blueprint

Task
	Running copy of a task definition

Service
	Keeps desired task count running

ECR
	AWS container image registry

Fargate
	Serverless compute for ECS containers

ECS on EC2
	ECS tasks running on your EC2 fleet

awsvpc
	Task gets ENI/IP/security groups

Task Role
	AWS permissions used by app code

Execution Role
	Permissions ECS needs to start/run task

Desired Count
	Number of service task replicas

ALB Target Group
	Healthy ECS tasks that receive traffic

Service Auto Scaling
	Changes number of tasks

Cluster Auto Scaling
	Changes EC2 capacity

Capacity Provider
	How ECS selects/manages compute capacity

Fargate Spot
	Interruptible discounted Fargate capacity

Rolling
	Gradually replace tasks

Blue/Green
	Run old/new and switch traffic

EFS
	Shared persistent filesystem

ECS Exec
	Run debug commands in a container without SSH



If you are short on time, revise these firstECS basics -> Cluster/Task Definition/Task/Service -> Fargate vs EC2 -> task definition -> awsvpc/networking -> ALB -> task role vs execution role -> service scaling vs cluster scaling -> rolling vs blue/green -> logging/troubleshooting.

29. Current AWS Notes Worth Recognizing

Fargate tasks require awsvpc networking.

AWS recommends awsvpc for ECS on EC2 unless another network mode is specifically needed.

ECS Managed Instances is a newer managed compute option that keeps access to many EC2 capabilities while AWS manages more of the infrastructure lifecycle.

ECS Service Auto Scaling supports target tracking, step, scheduled, and predictive scaling options.

ECS supports native deployment strategies including rolling, blue/green, linear, and canary; rolling remains the standard default/common interview baseline.

notes.content:
AWS EKS - Interview Study Notes

Beginner to Intermediate | Full-Stack / Backend Interview Focus

Goal of these notesUnderstand Kubernetes fundamentals and how Amazon EKS manages the Kubernetes control plane while integrating worker compute, networking, IAM, load balancing, storage, scaling, and observability with AWS.

1. What is Amazon EKS?

Amazon EKS (Elastic Kubernetes Service) is AWS's managed Kubernetes service. It runs a conformant Kubernetes control plane for you while your applications run as Kubernetes workloads on compute such as EC2 nodes, AWS Fargate, or EKS Auto Mode.

AWS manages the Kubernetes control plane infrastructure, availability, scaling, patching, and replacement of unhealthy control-plane components.

You still use standard Kubernetes APIs and tools such as kubectl, Deployments, Services, ConfigMaps, Secrets, and Ingress.

EKS integrates Kubernetes with AWS services such as VPC, IAM, ELB, EBS, EFS, CloudWatch, and Route 53.

Simple interview definitionEKS is managed Kubernetes on AWS: AWS manages the control plane, while you deploy containers as Kubernetes workloads on AWS compute.



EKS separates the AWS-managed Kubernetes control plane from your worker/data plane.

2. EKS vs Self-Managed Kubernetes

Area
	Self-Managed Kubernetes
	Amazon EKS

Control plane
	You deploy and operate API server, etcd, controllers
	AWS manages it

High availability
	You design and maintain it
	Built into EKS control-plane architecture

Patching/upgrades
	You manage control plane
	EKS manages control-plane infrastructure; you choose supported version upgrades

Worker nodes
	You manage
	You choose Auto Mode, managed/self-managed EC2 nodes, or Fargate

Kubernetes API
	Standard Kubernetes
	Standard conformant Kubernetes

3. Kubernetes Building Blocks You Must Know



These Kubernetes resources appear constantly in EKS interviews.

Resource
	Interview Meaning

Pod
	Smallest Kubernetes execution unit; contains one or more tightly related containers.

Deployment
	Manages stateless Pods, replica count, rolling updates, and rollback.

ReplicaSet
	Ensures the desired number of Pod replicas; normally managed by a Deployment.

Service
	Stable network endpoint/load balancing for a set of Pods.

Ingress
	HTTP/HTTPS routing rules from outside the cluster to Services.

ConfigMap
	Non-sensitive application configuration.

Secret
	Sensitive configuration object; protect access and consider external secret stores/encryption.

Namespace
	Logical partition for resources and policies.

DaemonSet
	Runs a Pod on each matching node; common for agents.

StatefulSet
	Stable identity and storage behavior for stateful applications.

4. Control Plane vs Data Plane

Plane
	Contains
	Who Manages It in EKS

Control Plane
	API server, scheduler, controller manager, etcd
	AWS

Data Plane
	Worker compute running kubelet, container runtime, and Pods
	AWS/user depending on compute option

Interview pointEKS does not mean AWS automatically manages every EC2 worker node. That depends on whether you choose Auto Mode, managed node groups, self-managed nodes, or Fargate.

5. EKS Control Plane High Availability

Each EKS cluster has its own managed control plane.

EKS distributes control-plane components across multiple Availability Zones.

AWS documentation describes at least two API server instances and three etcd instances across three Availability Zones.

EKS monitors and replaces unhealthy control-plane instances and scales the control plane as needed.

The Kubernetes API endpoint can be configured for public access, private access, or both.

What you manageYou choose when to upgrade Kubernetes versions and must ensure workloads/add-ons remain compatible, but you do not SSH into or administer EKS control-plane servers.

6. Compute Options



Current EKS compute choices. Most interviews focus on managed node groups and Fargate; Auto Mode is increasingly relevant.

Option
	Server Management
	Flexibility
	Best Fit

EKS Auto Mode
	AWS handles much of node/infrastructure lifecycle
	High, but opinionated managed model
	Reduce Kubernetes infrastructure operations

Managed Node Groups
	EKS manages EC2 node-group lifecycle
	High
	Most EC2-based EKS workloads

Self-Managed Nodes
	You manage EC2 lifecycle
	Maximum
	Special AMIs/kernel/bootstrap/customization

Fargate
	No EC2 nodes to manage
	More constraints
	Serverless Pod compute

7. Managed Node Groups

Managed node groups provision EC2 worker nodes as part of an EC2 Auto Scaling group.

EKS automates node provisioning, updates, termination, and draining during managed operations.

Node groups can use On-Demand or Spot capacity.

Use labels and taints to influence which workloads are scheduled to which nodes.

Choose self-managed nodes only when you need deeper EC2/AMI/bootstrap control than managed node groups provide.

Interview shortcutManaged node group = Kubernetes worker nodes are still EC2 instances, but EKS manages much of their lifecycle.

8. EKS on Fargate

Fargate runs eligible Kubernetes Pods without you provisioning EC2 worker nodes.

Fargate profiles determine which Pods/namespaces are scheduled onto Fargate.

Each Fargate Pod has its own compute boundary.

Fargate supports ALB/NLB integration using IP targets.

Fargate has important limitations such as no DaemonSets, privileged containers, GPUs, HostNetwork, or HostPort.

EKS Fargate Pods run in private subnets.

When to useUse Fargate when you prefer serverless Pod compute and your workload fits its restrictions. Use EC2 nodes for broader Kubernetes flexibility, specialized hardware, or daemon/privileged workloads.

9. EKS Auto Mode

EKS Auto Mode extends AWS management beyond the Kubernetes control plane to much of the infrastructure required to run workloads.

Automatically provisions and consolidates compute capacity.

Includes managed capabilities for Pod/service networking, DNS, load balancing, block storage, node monitoring, and Pod Identity integration.

Builds its compute autoscaling capabilities on Karpenter concepts.

Useful to know as a modern option, but interviews may still focus heavily on traditional managed node groups + add-ons.

Do not confuseEKS Auto Mode is still Kubernetes/EKS. It reduces infrastructure management; it does not replace Kubernetes objects such as Pods, Deployments, and Services.

10. EKS Networking and Amazon VPC CNI



Traditional EC2-backed EKS clusters commonly use Amazon VPC CNI so Pods receive VPC addresses.

An EKS cluster is associated with a VPC and subnets.

For EC2 worker nodes, Amazon VPC CNI provides Pod networking and can assign VPC IP addresses to Pods.

This gives Pods direct VPC connectivity but makes subnet/IP-address planning important.

Security groups protect nodes and, for supported configurations, can also be applied to Pods.

CoreDNS provides Kubernetes DNS inside the cluster.

Common issueIf Pods cannot be scheduled or created at scale, insufficient subnet IP addresses can be one possible cause in VPC-CNI-based clusters.

11. Service Types

Service Type
	Purpose
	Typical Use

ClusterIP
	Internal virtual IP inside cluster
	Default internal service-to-service communication

NodePort
	Opens a port on every node
	Usually an implementation building block; less common directly in production

LoadBalancer
	Requests an external/cloud load balancer
	Expose TCP/UDP/HTTP services through AWS load balancing

ExternalName
	DNS alias to an external name
	Reference an external service through Kubernetes DNS

12. Ingress and AWS Load Balancer Controller



AWS Load Balancer Controller reconciles Kubernetes resources into AWS ALB/NLB infrastructure.

Ingress provides Layer-7 HTTP/HTTPS host/path routing rules.

AWS recommends the AWS Load Balancer Controller for EKS load-balancer integration.

Ingress commonly provisions an Application Load Balancer (ALB).

Service type LoadBalancer can provision a Network Load Balancer (NLB).

With IP target mode, traffic can be sent directly to Pod IPs instead of node ports.

EKS Auto Mode includes load-balancing capability without installing the traditional controller yourself.

13. Kubernetes Deployment and Rolling Update

A Deployment defines the desired image, Pod template, and number of replicas.

When the image/template changes, Kubernetes can gradually create new Pods and remove old Pods.

Readiness probes prevent a Pod from receiving Service traffic before it is ready.

Liveness probes help detect a stuck/broken application and trigger container restart.

Rollback can return a Deployment to an earlier revision.

Interview distinctionReadiness = should this Pod receive traffic? Liveness = should Kubernetes restart this container?

14. ConfigMap vs Secret

Resource
	Stores
	Interview Guidance

ConfigMap
	Non-sensitive configuration
	Environment variables, config files, feature flags

Secret
	Sensitive values
	Passwords/tokens/certs; restrict RBAC and consider KMS/external secrets

ImportantKubernetes Secret data is not magically safe merely because it is called a Secret. Protect etcd/encryption, RBAC, access paths, and consider AWS Secrets Manager/Parameter Store integrations.

15. IAM Permissions for Pods



Do not give every Pod the worker node's broad IAM permissions.

Applications inside Pods often need S3, DynamoDB, SQS, Secrets Manager, or other AWS APIs.

EKS Pod Identity maps an IAM role to a Kubernetes service account using an EKS association.

IRSA (IAM Roles for Service Accounts) is the older widely used OIDC-based pattern and remains supported.

AWS currently recommends EKS Pod Identity when possible for EKS workloads.

Both approaches support fine-grained IAM permissions per workload/service account.

Interview answerUse a dedicated Kubernetes service account mapped to a least-privilege IAM role. Do not hardcode AWS keys and do not rely on the broad EC2 node IAM role.

16. Human / kubectl Access to the Cluster



IAM authenticates the caller; Kubernetes/EKS policies determine what the caller can do.

kubectl ultimately communicates with the Kubernetes API server.

EKS access entries are the recommended AWS-native mechanism for granting IAM principals cluster access.

An access entry can associate an AWS-managed EKS access policy or map to Kubernetes groups/RBAC.

The legacy aws-auth ConfigMap is deprecated for managing cluster access, though older clusters/interview questions may still mention it.

Two layersAWS IAM identifies/authenticates the principal. Kubernetes authorization (RBAC or EKS access policies) determines allowed Kubernetes actions.

17. Kubernetes RBAC

Object
	Purpose

Role
	Permissions inside one namespace.

ClusterRole
	Cluster-wide permissions or reusable permission set.

RoleBinding
	Assigns a Role/ClusterRole to subjects within a namespace.

ClusterRoleBinding
	Assigns a ClusterRole across the cluster.

Apply least privilege; avoid casually granting cluster-admin.

Do not confuse Kubernetes RBAC permissions with AWS IAM permissions to S3/EC2/etc.

18. Autoscaling: HPA vs Node Scaling



Application replicas and cluster compute capacity are separate scaling layers.

Scaler
	What It Scales
	Trigger / Purpose

Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA)
	Pod replica count
	CPU, memory, or custom/external metrics

Vertical Pod Autoscaler (VPA)
	Pod resource requests/recommendations
	Right-size CPU/memory; use carefully with HPA

Cluster Autoscaler
	Node group size
	Pending Pods that need more node capacity

Karpenter
	EC2 node capacity/type
	Provisions right-sized nodes from workload requirements

EKS Auto Mode
	Cluster compute automatically
	AWS-managed provisioning/consolidation based on workload needs

Most important distinctionHPA adds/removes Pods. Karpenter/Cluster Autoscaler/Auto Mode add or remove worker compute when Pods cannot fit or capacity can be consolidated.

19. Taints, Tolerations, Labels, and Node Selectors

Labels attach metadata to Kubernetes objects such as nodes and Pods.

nodeSelector / node affinity lets Pods prefer or require particular nodes.

Taints repel Pods from nodes.

Tolerations let matching Pods be scheduled onto tainted nodes.

Useful for GPU nodes, Spot nodes, dedicated workloads, or isolation by workload type.

ExampleTaint GPU nodes with workload=gpu:NoSchedule, then give only GPU workloads a matching toleration.

20. Persistent Storage: EBS and EFS

AWS Storage
	Kubernetes Integration
	Typical Use

Amazon EBS
	EBS CSI driver + PersistentVolume/PersistentVolumeClaim
	Block storage for one workload/node-AZ attachment patterns

Amazon EFS
	EFS CSI driver
	Shared POSIX file storage across multiple Pods/nodes/AZs

PersistentVolume (PV) represents storage.

PersistentVolumeClaim (PVC) is a workload's request for storage.

StorageClass can dynamically provision storage.

Stateful interview pointContainers and Pods are replaceable. Persistent data should live outside the container's ephemeral filesystem.

21. Observability

CloudWatch can collect control-plane logs, application logs, metrics, and alarms depending on configuration.

Container Insights provides container/cluster observability.

Prometheus-compatible metrics are common for Kubernetes applications.

kubectl logs, kubectl describe, events, Pod status, and Deployment status are first-line troubleshooting tools.

Distributed tracing can be added through OpenTelemetry/X-Ray-compatible tooling.

Useful commandskubectl get pods -A | kubectl describe pod <name> | kubectl logs <pod> | kubectl get events | kubectl get svc/ingress/deploy

22. Common Pod States / Failures

State / Error
	Typical Meaning

Pending
	No suitable node/capacity, PVC issue, Fargate profile mismatch, scheduling constraints

CrashLoopBackOff
	Container starts and repeatedly crashes

ImagePullBackOff
	Image cannot be pulled: name/tag/auth/network/ECR permission issue

ErrImagePull
	Immediate image pull failure

OOMKilled
	Container exceeded memory limit

Evicted
	Node pressure or scheduling/resource condition caused eviction

Running but NotReady
	Container runs but readiness probe is failing

23. Typical Troubleshooting Flow

kubectl get pods -o wide - determine status, node, restart count.

kubectl describe pod - read Events and scheduling/probe/image errors.

kubectl logs - inspect application/container output.

Check Deployment/ReplicaSet desired vs available replicas.

Check Service selectors and Endpoints/EndpointSlices.

Check Ingress / AWS Load Balancer Controller and target health.

Check security groups, subnets, route tables, DNS, and network policies.

For AWS API failures, verify Pod Identity/IRSA and IAM permissions.

For Pending Pods, inspect requests/limits, taints, affinity, node capacity, and autoscaler events.

24. EKS Security Areas

Use private worker subnets where possible and carefully control the Kubernetes API endpoint.

Restrict security groups and Kubernetes network policies.

Use least-privilege IAM roles for Pods.

Use RBAC/access entries for human/CI access.

Keep cluster version, nodes, add-ons, and images patched.

Use image scanning and trusted registries such as ECR.

Protect Secrets and consider KMS/external secret-management solutions.

Use Pod Security Standards/admission controls appropriate to your organization.

Audit using Kubernetes/EKS control-plane logs, CloudTrail, and runtime/security tooling.

25. EKS vs ECS

Area
	EKS
	ECS

Orchestrator
	Kubernetes
	AWS-native ECS scheduler/orchestrator

Portability/ecosystem
	Large Kubernetes ecosystem; portable APIs
	Deep AWS simplicity/integration

Operational complexity
	Higher; Kubernetes concepts/control
	Usually simpler

Core unit
	Pod
	Task

Desired app state
	Deployment/StatefulSet/etc.
	ECS Service

Networking/load balancing
	Kubernetes + AWS controllers
	ECS native AWS integrations

Best fit
	Teams needing Kubernetes ecosystem/standards
	Teams wanting simpler AWS-native containers

Interview answerChoose EKS when Kubernetes itself is a requirement or ecosystem advantage. Choose ECS when you want AWS-native container orchestration with less Kubernetes operational complexity.

26. EKS vs Fargate - Do Not Confuse the Terms

EKS is the Kubernetes control/orchestration service. Fargate is one possible compute option for running Pods.

EKS + managed node groups = Kubernetes Pods on EC2 worker nodes.

EKS + Fargate = Kubernetes Pods on serverless Fargate compute.

EKS Auto Mode = managed EKS model that automates much of cluster infrastructure.

ShortcutEKS tells you how containers are orchestrated. Fargate tells you who manages the underlying compute.

27. Common Interview Scenarios

Scenario: Pods are Pending after a traffic spike.

Check resource requests, node capacity, taints/affinity, subnet IPs, then verify Karpenter/Cluster Autoscaler/Auto Mode can add appropriate nodes.

Scenario: One Pod needs S3 but other Pods must not have S3 access.

Use a dedicated Kubernetes service account mapped to a least-privilege role with EKS Pod Identity or IRSA.

Scenario: Expose /api and /admin through one ALB.

Use Ingress host/path rules and AWS Load Balancer Controller.

Scenario: Need to run a logging agent on every EC2 worker node.

Use a DaemonSet. Fargate does not support DaemonSets.

Scenario: Application Pods are running but ALB says unhealthy.

Check readiness/health path, Service selector/ports, Ingress annotations, target type, security groups and application listener.

Scenario: Need cheaper fault-tolerant worker compute.

Use Spot managed node groups or appropriate Karpenter/Auto Mode capacity strategy; design Pods to tolerate interruption.

Scenario: Developer can authenticate to AWS but kubectl is forbidden.

Check EKS access entry/RBAC permissions; AWS authentication alone does not imply Kubernetes authorization.

28. Must-Know EKS Interview Questions

What is EKS?

What does AWS manage in EKS?

Control plane vs data plane?

Pod vs Deployment vs Service?

What is Ingress?

ClusterIP vs NodePort vs LoadBalancer?

EKS managed node group vs self-managed nodes?

EKS on Fargate vs EC2 nodes?

What is EKS Auto Mode?

How does Pod networking work with VPC CNI?

What does AWS Load Balancer Controller do?

Readiness vs liveness probe?

ConfigMap vs Secret?

How should a Pod access S3 securely?

EKS Pod Identity vs IRSA?

How do developers get kubectl access?

What are EKS access entries?

What is Kubernetes RBAC?

HPA vs Cluster Autoscaler vs Karpenter?

What are taints and tolerations?

How do EBS/EFS integrate with EKS?

Why is a Pod stuck in Pending?

CrashLoopBackOff vs ImagePullBackOff?

EKS vs ECS?

29. Final EKS Interview Cheat Sheet

Keyword
	One-Line Meaning

EKS
	Managed Kubernetes on AWS

Control Plane
	API server + scheduler/controllers + etcd; AWS-managed

Data Plane
	Worker compute that runs Pods

Pod
	Smallest Kubernetes workload unit

Deployment
	Manages stateless Pod replicas and updates

Service
	Stable networking for a set of Pods

Ingress
	HTTP/HTTPS routing to Services

Managed Node Group
	EKS-managed EC2 worker-node lifecycle

Fargate
	Serverless compute for eligible Pods

EKS Auto Mode
	AWS-managed Kubernetes infrastructure automation

VPC CNI
	AWS Pod networking integration

AWS Load Balancer Controller
	Creates/manages ALB/NLB from Kubernetes resources

EKS Pod Identity
	Maps IAM role to Kubernetes service account

IRSA
	OIDC-based IAM role for service account

Access Entry
	Recommended IAM-principal access mapping to EKS API

RBAC
	Kubernetes authorization

HPA
	Scales Pod replicas

Karpenter
	Provisions right-sized EC2 nodes

Cluster Autoscaler
	Adjusts node-group capacity

Taint/Toleration
	Repel/allow Pods on selected nodes

PV/PVC
	Persistent Kubernetes storage abstraction/request

EBS CSI
	Block storage integration

EFS CSI
	Shared file storage integration



If you are short on time, revise these firstEKS basics -> control plane vs worker nodes -> Pod/Deployment/Service/Ingress -> managed node groups vs Fargate -> VPC CNI -> ALB/NLB integration -> Pod Identity -> access entries/RBAC -> HPA vs node autoscaling -> probes -> EKS vs ECS.

30. Current AWS Notes Worth Remembering

EKS runs the managed control plane across multiple Availability Zones for high availability.

EKS access entries are recommended for IAM-principal access; the legacy aws-auth ConfigMap approach is deprecated.

AWS recommends EKS Pod Identity for Pod-to-AWS IAM permissions when possible; IRSA remains supported.

EKS Auto Mode can manage compute autoscaling, networking, load balancing, storage, DNS, and other infrastructure functions.

AWS Load Balancer Controller is the recommended traditional controller for reconciling Kubernetes Service/Ingress resources with AWS load balancers.

Managed node groups automate EC2 node lifecycle and draining; Fargate removes EC2 node management but has Kubernetes feature limitations.

31. AWS Documentation References

Amazon EKS User Guide - Amazon EKS architecture

Amazon EKS User Guide - Managed node groups

Amazon EKS User Guide - AWS Fargate

Amazon EKS User Guide - EKS Auto Mode

Amazon EKS User Guide - EKS networking / Amazon VPC CNI

Amazon EKS User Guide - AWS Load Balancer Controller

Amazon EKS User Guide - EKS Pod Identity and service accounts

Amazon EKS User Guide - EKS access entries

Amazon EKS User Guide - Autoscaling with Karpenter and Cluster Autoscaler
